records.finding: Woodard & Curran told the MSGSA board and joint committees that MercedWRM was updated for the 2025 GSP and the DWR-funded Merced MAR project: ET aligned with the GAP's OpenET data, DWR land use, and DWR AEM aquifer data. It is now linked to GRATT for GSA-run scenarios; only the three GSAs have log-ins, and none used it yet.
records.quantitative_detail: MercedWRM in use about 15 years (as of 2026-03-12); Merced MAR funded by a 2022 DWR SGM grant; MSGSA FY2026/27 budget: $5,000 hydrology and modeling update for optional MercedWRM runs (none spent in FY2025/26) and $50,000 basin-wide modeling costs (about $7,000 spent in FY2025/26)
records.agenda_item: 11. Merced MAR Presentation
records.evidence_text: The WRM has again has been a tool in the pocket of the sub basin for about 15 years now. And effectively part of this effort and also part of the five year update, what we did is we updated this model to the latest and greatest data and not just for the wrm, but also to make sure that it aligns with a lot of the other tools you're using to achieve sustainability first and foremost. ... We really, really want to that your WRM to make sure that it aligned with the water counting platform. ... the Airborne Electromagnetic Survey, or what's known as the Basin Characterization Program, provided us a lot of a really, really good data
records.notes: Also answers ISW-1.1b (inputs); the land-use switch, tool access (GSAs only, state none) and not-yet-used status come from the 2026-03-09 joint committee and the budget figures from 2026-05-14.

records.finding: Merced MAR, shown to the joint committees, reports how recharge water splits between storage and stream interaction: in a test run about two-thirds of roughly 40,000 AF stayed in storage and a third went to stream interaction and subsurface flow. Recharge beside rivers yields more stream interaction than groundwater-level gain. This is a recharge output, not a pumping-depletion figure.
records.quantitative_detail: Example scenario only: about 40,000 AF of recharge (transcript says '40,000ft'; time basis not stated); about 2/3 retained in storage and groundwater levels, about 1/3 to stream interaction and subsurface flow combined (not split)
records.meeting_body: Merced GSP Joint Coordination Committee and Stakeholder Advisory Committee
records.agenda_item: 7. Merced Managed Aquifer Recharge (MercedMAR) Tool Presentation
records.evidence_text: And then what are the changes in stream flow? Right, because every time we divert water for recharge, you are impacting the stream system. So there's be less, potentially less flow in some of the winter months. But then because of increased groundwater levels, we have less shear depletions. ... And so what you can see here is that for instance, as this example put about 40,000ft in, about 2 thirds of that stays in the basin for storage and ground levels and we lose about a third of it to stream interaction and subsurface flow. ... You put water right next to the river system, you just do a bunch of recharge there. You're going to see a lot more stream interaction, stream impacts than you are going to be changing groundwater levels, right?
records.notes: Transcript labels this speaker as the meeting room, so attribution to Amador rests on his presentation context; the split was given as a point example with no range (ISW-1.8a) and must not be compared with the GSP's 504,400 AFY pumping-depletion figure; also bears on ISW-1.5b.

records.finding: Presenting the WY2025 annual report, Woodard & Curran told the MSGSA board ISW thresholds were met because groundwater-level thresholds were met, while reporting 10 of 29 proxy wells (34%) below minimum thresholds and saying compliance is judged against interim milestones (3 of 29 below). No ISW-specific metric was shown; the joint committees' review three days earlier omitted ISW.
records.quantitative_detail: WY2025: 10 of 29 representative wells below minimum threshold (34%); 26 of 29 below measurable objective; 3 of 29 below the 2025 interim milestone, excluding 2 wells not measured; undesirable result defined as 25% of wells below minimum threshold for two consecutive years; groundwater storage down about 98,000 AF in WY2025
records.agenda_item: 12. Water Year 2025 Annual Report
records.evidence_text: And below minimum thresholds, if we have a certain number of wells, in our case 25% of the wells below that minimum threshold for two consecutive years, that's what constitutes undesirable results. ... So looking first at groundwater levels, 10 of the 29 wells are below the minimum threshold. So that's, that's 34%. But again, we're really looking at that inner milestone when we're looking at sustainability here in, in 2026. ... The last sustainable indicator is the depletions of interconnected surface waters. And again, like storage, we use groundwater levels as a proxy. So since we're meeting our groundwater levels thresholds, we're also meeting the thresholds for depletions of interconnected surface water.
records.notes: WY2024 exceedance status was not stated, so no undesirable-result determination can be drawn; at the 2026-03-09 joint committee the same consultants' indicator table covered levels, storage, quality and subsidence only.

records.finding: The three GSAs' July 2026 contract amendment with Woodard & Curran scopes the WY2026 annual report with no ISW or stream-depletion section, limits the MercedWRM update to extending the historical simulation, and excludes any work arising from DWR's forthcoming depletion guidance. The model is rerun yearly, but no depletion figure is scheduled from it.
records.quantitative_detail: Amendment 11 total $246,674 shared by the three GSAs (MSGSA 58% share = $143,070): Task 41 WY2026 Annual Report $69,144; Task 23 on-call support $131,220; Task 40 meeting support $46,331; approved 4-0 by the MSGSA board on 2026-07-09

This scope does not include any additional technical needs that may arise depending on the nature of the depletions best management practice/guidance anticipated to be published by DWR later in calendar year 2026.

records.section: 1.5 Per-well Attribution and the Cumulative Pumping Problem
records.finding: In November 2025 the MSGSA board (6-0) revised its well-consistency rule so a new well is consistent if the parcel it serves is enrolled in the allocation, replacing per-well historic-use caps. Staff called enrollment the real check. No stream-proximity or depletion test was raised, so per-well review now rests on the allocation alone.
records.quantitative_detail: Rule 1 first adopted April 2022; revision approved 6-0 on 2025-11-13
records.speaker_role: mixed — MSGSA staff and Zanjero consultant (unlabeled)
records.agenda_item: 8. Rule 1: Well Consistency Determinations Modification and Groundwater Allocation Rule Reorganization
records.evidence_text: It has now been updated to address the fact that we have an allocation and essentially we were saying anybody would be consistent so long as they are consistent with the allocation and the rest by this gsa. ... The real check is making sure that the parcel that the well is on and that the well is serving is enrolled in the allocation.
records.notes: Speakers are unlabeled in the transcript, and the stream-proximity absence rests on the full item discussion read, not on a statement that none is needed.

records.section: 1.5 Per-well Attribution and the Cumulative Pumping Problem
records.finding: Zanjero told the MSGSA board the riparian-area rule (adopted May 14, 2026) exists because remote-sensed ET on uncultivated riparian land above eligible rain would otherwise be debited as pumped groundwater, and set the 150-foot width against a roughly 100-foot ET pixel. No speaker asked whether that riparian ET is groundwater- or stream-supported.
records.quantitative_detail: Riparian Areas: at least 7 acres per parcel, each area at least 1 acre; at least 150 ft wide along natural watercourses; remote-sensing pixel about 100 ft; designation permanent; applies only to parties using remote sensing, not meter reporters; 2026 delineation window closed 2026-08-31
records.agenda_item: 9. Riparian Inactive Areas Modification to the Allocation Rule (discussion)
records.evidence_text: If you are concerned that the remote sensing may overestimate its consumption, just heard the eligible inches number and if the eligible consumed number out of the remote sensing meets higher than that and we subtract the eligible inches. There's a chunk of water. We're going to assume you pumped and applied ... they shall have an average width of at least 150ft. ... because the pixel size again is about 100ft. So your measure, the remote sensing is going to be influenced by things on edges that you start getting a smaller width.
records.notes: Findings 14 and 15 sit in the outline's other section; adoption on 2026-05-14 followed a staff report saying remote-sensed consumption on Riparian Areas is not counted against the allocation, and a director's request to also exclude tree-lined man-made canals was not adopted (Data Needs also fits).

records.finding: MSGSA voted 6-0 to stay a pilot GSA for Phase 2 of the DWR-funded Groundwater Accounting Platform. The California Water Data Consortium said the pilot would fold GRATT and MercedWRM modeling into the platform and explore what accounting frameworks and data are needed for recharge and to better understand ISW. No ISW deliverable, budget or schedule was stated.
records.quantitative_detail: Phase 2: new five-year DWR grant to the California Water Data Consortium; MSGSA experts' (Zanjero) participation costs covered by the grant; vote 6-0 on 2026-01-08
records.speaker_role: NGO/advocate — California Water Data Consortium (Hannah Ake)
records.agenda_item: 7. Groundwater Accounting Platform Phase 2 Pilot
records.evidence_text: What we're going to do with this next phase of work is work with you all and work on integrating GRATT and that modeling functionality that you all are going to learn about later on into the groundwater accounting platform so that all is displayed in one place for you all to understand and see a bit more clearly. But then part of this work is also going to be working in these pilot basins to better understand what accounting frameworks and data we need to better account for recharge in those specific areas to better understand interconnected surface water, things like that. So a lot of it will be exploratory and trying to develop those accounting frameworks that we might not have clear answers for right now.
records.notes: ISW is mentioned once and loosely, so this is exploratory intent rather than a commitment; MIUGSA was also invited to continue as a pilot, and Phase 2's stated focus is recharge and extreme-weather accounting.

records.finding: MIUGSA staff proposed a 3%-per-year loss on unused carryover, derived from the Merced GSP groundwater model's estimate of groundwater retained when not pumped, and in answer to a question named losses to stream systems and inter-basin flow as causes. Modeled stream losses thus enter the carryover rule only lumped with other losses, not as an ISW term or quantity.
records.quantitative_detail: Modeled aquifer retention about 97% per year, 20-year average; carryover loss 3% per year (about 9% over the 3-year allocation period); new MIUGSA allocation 3.3 AF/ac over 3 years starting 2026-01-01
records.agenda_item: Groundwater Accounting Update and Upcoming MIUGSA Board Policy Considerations
records.evidence_text: So as we do that in Order to come up with the proposed numbers, what we did is we used the Merced GSP groundwater model. So we're staying consistent with overall GSP to estimate the portion of groundwater retained in the aquifer if groundwater is not extracted. ... on average over over a 20 year period the aquifer retains approximately 97% per year or otherwise stated there's a 3% loss per year on carryover. ... Yeah, so shallow groundwater, you generally see losses to stream systems or you know, other kind of like higher, higher level changes when it's deeper. I mean if it's, if it's not pumped, there's some groundwater movement between basins.
records.notes: Proposed for the January 14, 2026 MIUGSA board and reported adopted on 2026-03-09 without the rate restated; the stream share of the 3% was not quantified, the answer on causes is unlabeled, and staff called it a modeling exercise with built-in assumptions but gave no range (ISW-1.8a).

records.finding: Under the allocation rule's unpaid fallowing path, fields marked inactive stay in OpenET monitoring until staff approve the designation, and staff look back over the months already monitored for applied water before approving; the board moved the deadline from January 31 to May 1 partly to allow that look-back. This adds an ET screen to finding 39's irrigation-absence test, which still checks whether water was applied, not how much was saved.
records.quantitative_detail: Inactive designations approved: fewer than 100 (as of July 9, 2026, all in January 2026); deadline Jan 31 -> May 1 (permanent), one-time reopening to Aug 31, 2026; about 4 months of OpenET record available at a May 1 designation; vote 4-0; GAP contract $48,000/yr x 5 yrs + $50,000 customization (incl. fallowed-land self-reporting) = $290,000, paid from Phase 1 fee parcel-based water budget funds

records.finding: Quarterly OpenET monitoring of the paid Phase 1 LRP kept showing shortfalls after the WY2025 Annual Report: 9 of 14 agreements exceeded their allowed consumptive use at Q3 WY2025 and 5 of 10 at Q3 WY2026, and the board waived the minimum water-use reduction both years so payments could go out by November 1. Staff attribute the shortfalls to trees left in place, low baseline water use in the minimum-use calculations, and carryover soil moisture.

records.finding: The GSA's consultant confirmed on the record that idling land does not reduce its allocation: an inactive field loses only its rain (effective-precipitation) credit, while its sustainable yield and Additional Pumping Allowance stay usable anywhere in the owner's AMA, and permanently inactive riparian areas keep the allocation tied to parcel area. This independently confirms finding 33's reading of the Rules.
records.quantitative_detail: Riparian designation (adopted May 14, 2026): min. 7 acres per parcel, min. 1 acre per area, min. 150-ft average width along natural watercourses; permanent, cannot be redesignated irrigated
records.speaker_role: consultant — Zanjero (item presenter; speaker labels absent)
records.agenda_item: 9. Inactive Parcel Deadline Modification in Groundwater Allocation Rule
records.evidence_text: So the, the parcel, that parcel that you're going to mark as inactive does not get rain credit. It just basically gets blanked out. You still do get sustainable yield and any APA that might associate with that particular eligible acre is still available for you to use within your ama. You just don't get the rain at all.
records.notes: Speaker unlabeled; the item was presented by Greg Young (Zanjero). May 14, 2026 wording on riparian areas: 'Still get the allocation associated with those lands, because that's parcel area.'

records.finding: MIUGSA staff proposed a 3% annual loss on carried-over unused allocation (about 9% over a three-year period), taken from the Merced GSP groundwater model's estimate of water retained in the aquifer, and no cap for now, so growers cannot build up paper water indefinitely. MIUGSA adopted a carryover policy by March 2026.
records.quantitative_detail: Proposed carryover loss 3% per year (~97% retained per year, 20-year average from GSP model), ~9% over a 3-year allocation period; MIUGSA allocation 3.3 AF/acre over 3 years from Jan 1, 2026; no carryover cap proposed
records.agenda_item: Groundwater Accounting Update and Upcoming MIUGSA Board Policy Considerations (carryover)
records.evidence_text: what we did is we used the Merced GSP groundwater model. So we're staying consistent with overall GSP to estimate the portion of groundwater retained in the aquifer if groundwater is not extracted. ... on average over over a 20 year period the aquifer retains approximately 97% per year or otherwise stated there's a 3% loss per year on carryover. ... we don't want to allow folks to just build a paper water for forever.
records.notes: The Mar 9, 2026 joint meeting reported MIUGSA adopted 'a carryover policy for unused allocation' without restating the rate, so adoption of the 3% figure is not confirmed in these meetings. Basin-wide rule; not specific to repurposed land.

records.finding: When the board advanced Project 9 to DOC in November 2025, a director asked for an annual water-savings estimate and no clear figure was given, and the review committees had asked the applicant to recalculate savings; another director questioned groundwater conserved versus money spent. In March 2026 MSGSA's representative told the joint committees the MLRP has no acreage or water-savings target.
records.quantitative_detail: MLRP programme target: none, in acres or AF (Mar 9, 2026); Project 9 annual water savings: not stated at approval
records.speaker_role: mixed — board members and consultant (Valley Eco)
records.agenda_item: 5. Multibenefit Land Repurposing Program (Project 9; Prop 4 letter discussion)
records.evidence_text: Request to recalculate estimated water savings of the project. ... Do you have an estimate of the amount of water savings per year based on the right allocations? ... The benefits have been limited in terms of who's benefiting and the amount of groundwater that's being actually conserved versus the amount of money money that's being spent. ... where the first ones had zero now we've got some
records.notes: Transcript has no speaker labels; the reply to the savings question is garbled ('If we say this thing goes to perpetuity it's 85') and may be a figure, and a director answered that the last two approved projects include water savings where the first had none.

records.finding: EKI reported the WY2025 Phase 1 LRP saving as an OpenET consumptive-use reduction of 4,655 AF on 4,114 enrolled acres, with incentive payments of about $2.08M, or $447 per AF against an original rule-of-thumb goal of about $300 per AF. Staff added that this is cost per AF of reduced consumption, not reduced applied water, and that applied-water savings would be larger but were not quantified, which bears on how finding 32's 4,655 AF figure should be read.
records.quantitative_detail: WY2025 (single water year): 14 active agreements on 4,114 acres (139 new acres in 2 new agreements); 4,655 AF consumptive-use reduction (OpenET); payments ~$2.08M = $506/acre = $447/AF; original rule-of-thumb ~$300/AF; 3 agreements closed out at end of WY2025
records.speaker_role: consultant — EKI (Chris Heppner), with a GSA staff clarification
records.agenda_item: 6. Land Repurposing Program year in review
records.evidence_text: That brought the total for this year to 14 agreements that were active during the year. With 4114 acres total. Based on our calculations at the end of the water year, these lands saved groundwater consumptive use of 4,655 acre feet. ... incentive payments were, you know, about 2.08 million total coming out at, you know, 506 per acre or 447 per acre foot. ... that 447 is your cost per acre foot of reduced consumption, but it is not the cost per acre foot of the reduced applied water because we know there is no applied water on those acres
records.notes: The applied-water clarification is under the generic 'Board Room' label (context suggests GSA staff); no applied-water savings figure was given.

records.finding: Two documents in the same March 2026 board packet give different water benefits for the MLRP-supported Bear Creek Ranch project: the staff memo says fallowing plus enhanced recharge yields a net benefit of about 6,500 AF/year, while the Chair-signed letter to Congressman Gray says the project reduces pumping by up to 2,860 AF/year. Finding 30 cites ~5,400 AFY of decreased pumping for Bear Creek Ranch; none of the three figures comes with a stated method or baseline.
records.quantitative_detail: Staff memo: ~6,500 AF/yr net benefit (fallowing + enhanced recharge) on ~1,171 acres; letter: pumping reduction up to 2,860 AF/yr, >1,000 acres restored; finding 30: ~5,400 AFY decreased pumping; letter approved 5-0 (Mar 12, 2026)
records.speaker_role: GSA staff — MSGSA staff memo; letter signed by the MSGSA Chair
records.agenda_item: 9. Bear Creek Ranch Project Letter of Support
records.evidence_text: Through the fallowing of this farm ground and enhanced recharge, the Merced Subbasin would get a net benefit of approximately 6,500 acre-feet per year. ... It will make a major contribution to achievement of the locally authored Merced Subbasin Groundwater Sustainability Plan by reducing groundwater pumping up to 2,860 acre-feet per year.
records.notes: The 6,500 AF/yr figure combines reduced pumping and recharge while 2,860 AF/yr is pumping only, so the figures may measure different things; the letter supports a federal request by River Partners and Reclamation District 2092.

records.finding: The LRP baseline method was clarified in October 2026: EKI said applicants in all three enrolment rounds were scored using a mix of CalSIMETAW water-use factors and OpenET, while the contractual minimum reductions and all monitoring use OpenET. Staff said several fields were already using very little groundwater when their average use was set, so stopping irrigation produced less saving than expected; in September 2025 EKI likewise described deficit-irrigated orchards with little room to reduce.
records.quantitative_detail: 3 enrolment rounds; scoring basis CalSIMETAW factors + OpenET; contract minimums and monitoring basis OpenET
records.agenda_item: 8. Land Repurposing Program
records.evidence_text: in each of those three rounds was using a combination of the calcimita water use factors as well as open et. ... I'm pretty sure it's Open ET for all of the contractual. ... some of these fields were likely already using a very minimal amount of groundwater when we set kind of what their average use was. And then we expected a decline, but they were already very low.
records.notes: 'Calcimita' is the transcript's rendering of CalSIMETAW; EKI hedged ('I believe', 'pretty sure') and said he would need to check the precise scoring methodology.

records.finding: Repurposed land is not yet represented in the subbasin's new DWR-grant-funded MercedMAR recharge decision-support tool: the modeller said the repurposing and recharge projects described earlier in the meeting, including MLRP-funded ones, are not yet in the model, and a participant hoped to use it after the grant ends to see what impact those projects have. No meeting examined described how MLRP project savings enter the water budget or the allocation ledger.
records.speaker_role: mixed — consultant (MercedMAR modeller; firm name garbled in transcript) and an unidentified participant
records.meeting_body: Merced GSP Coordination Committee and Stakeholder Advisory Committee (joint meeting)
records.agenda_item: 7. Merced Managed Aquifer Recharge (MercedMAR) Tool Presentation
records.evidence_text: So they're not actually in the model yet but with grad they would have the ability or a user would have the ability to incorporate ... So we have this MLRP grant now we have this MLRP plans going forward that hopefully when the grant ends we'll still be able to find funding to continue implementing the plan and then using this to see what sort of impact those types of projects would have.
records.notes: Speaker labels are absent and the passage is garbled; the question that prompted it referred to 'the projects that Brad talked about' (MLRP and non-MLRP recharge/floodplain projects).

records.section: 2.5 Data Source and ET Product Choice
records.finding: Growers dispute OpenET on unirrigated land: in the TAC's cover-crop review a grower reported OpenET values of 12 to 25 inches a year on a field cover-cropped without irrigation for five years, and the Zanjero consultant conceded every method embeds assumptions. The TAC asked growers for field APNs so staff could compare OpenET signatures; this is the residual-ET problem finding 31 documents for LRP parcels.
records.quantitative_detail: One unirrigated cover-cropped field: OpenET 12-25 in/yr over 5 years; 2024 ~25 in ET vs ~15 in rain (grower's figures, rain months not matched per consultant)
records.agenda_item: 3. Groundwater Allocation Rule and Cover Crops
records.evidence_text: I pulled a field that we have that's been planted to the same cover crop for the last five years. And I've got years where open et says 12 inches and I've got years where open et say 25 inches. ... whether we're using a meter, whether using remote sensing we're coming at, there's assumptions embedded in all of those.
records.notes: The grower introduced himself as an east-side grower speaking online, TAC membership not stated; on Sept 11, 2025 he made a similar public comment on trees left standing, and on May 14, 2026 a speaker (apparently a director) said he wanted to switch from OpenET to meters but had missed the deadline.

records.section: 2.5 Data Source and ET Product Choice
records.finding: MIUGSA staff said ET-based extraction estimates are hard to match farm by farm and that flow meters are likely the long-term basis. The Merced area had no CIMIS station feeding OpenET for two years; Merced College tentatively agreed to host one, and the GSA may install its own ET sensors to check OpenET.
records.quantitative_detail: No CIMIS station in the Merced area for ~2 years (as of Jan 2026); MID meter grant ~300 meters requested (~100+ ordered, ~180 awaiting access agreements); account statements to ~1,264 accounts covering ~119,000 acres (>10 acres); meter deadlines Mar 1, 2026 (groundwater-only) and Mar 1, 2027 (surface-water users)
records.agenda_item: Groundwater Accounting Update
records.evidence_text: as of the last two years, the Merced area has not had a SIMIS station and that CMS data is incorporated directly into openet to get the evapotranspiration values. ... one of the things that we, the gsa, may do or may want to do is install local environmental sensors. ... realistically, at the end of the day, flow meters are probably going to be the place for us to go to
records.notes: 'SIMIS'/'CMS' are transcription errors for CIMIS; on Mar 12, 2026 an MSGSA director reported MIUGSA had identified a CIMIS site. No speaker linked the CIMIS gap to MSGSA's LRP results. Basin-wide rule; not specific to repurposed land.

records.section: 2.5 Data Source and ET Product Choice
records.finding: MSGSA's Phase 2 fee report says OpenET is used because it is free and supplies the annual consumptive use behind the allocation rule. It budgets up to $120,000 a year for an alternative provider, collected only if the board finds OpenET inappropriate or OpenET starts charging; otherwise the GSA will keep evaluating ET data and may adjust policies for data limitations or grower concerns.
records.quantitative_detail: OpenET cost to GSA: $0; alternative remote sensing: max $120,000/yr, scaled from ETSGSA Land IQ contract (~$79,000 through Feb 2026; ETSGSA ~100,000 irrigated of ~139,000 acres vs MSGSA ~181,000 irrigated of ~338,000 acres)
records.speaker_role: consultant — Zanjero (Phase 2 Funding Mechanism Engineer's Report, adopted by the board Apr 9, 2026)
records.agenda_item: 7. Phase 2 Fee Engineer's Report
records.evidence_text: At present, OpenET data is available at no cost to the GSA and is used to determine annual consumptive use, which is a foundational input for administering the Groundwater Allocation Rule and calculating water use relative to allocated groundwater volumes. ... this element will only be collected if the Board determines that continued reliance on OpenET data is not appropriate for administration of the Groundwater Allocation Rule or if OpenET switches to a subscription service
records.notes: The engineer's report was drafted by Zanjero with the board's Phase 2 Fee Ad Hoc Committee (Mar 12, 2026 memo); the report does not discuss the LRP's use of OpenET. Basin-wide rule; not specific to repurposed land.

records.finding: The program manager framed the Merced MLRP's goals as groundwater sustainability, direct disadvantaged-community benefits and habitat connectivity. Later updates listed co-benefits including grassland and floodplain restoration, recharge with habitat, a community park, species-focused and agrivoltaic design, a native-seed supply, and SEEDS youth and community workshops; none of these benefits was quantified at the meetings.
records.quantitative_detail: SEEDS summer programmes >200 students at 2 schools (June 2026); community workshop ~20-25 families (English and Hmong); project sizes: Bear Creek Ranch ~1,090 acres (transitional seeding), Nevada Ranch 150 acres, Le Grand park 20 acres, Amsterdam recharge 15 acres
records.meeting_body: Merced GSP Coordination Committee and Stakeholder Advisory Committee (joint meeting)
records.agenda_item: 6. Multibenefit Land Repurposing Program Update
records.evidence_text: The program goals are to increase the primary goals or to increase groundwater sustainability, provide direct disadvantaged community benefits and increase habitat connectivity.
records.notes: Co-benefit list compiled from several program updates; the regional goals statement is the only programme-level framing heard.

records.finding: Valley Eco described how MLRP applications are scored: after an eligibility screen each project gets four scores from a technical committee and three from a board subcommittee, the highest-scoring go to Stakeholder Advisory Committee review, and committee and SAC modification requests become contract conditions. Board packets name both scoring bodies, but no formula, weights or award threshold was stated, consistent with finding 45.
records.quantitative_detail: 7 scores per project (4 technical committee + 3 board subcommittee); development round: 12 applications, 2 ineligible, 1 duplicate, $1,471,000 requested vs $750,000 available, 6 projects funded ($749,650)
records.agenda_item: 7. Multibenefit Land Repurposing Program
records.evidence_text: The scoring criteria are actually built by the regional partners based on Department of Conservation guidelines. They're also built by the stakeholder advisory. ... It goes through a first round of committee scoring. They get four scores. Then it goes to a subcommittee of this board. It gives three scores too new. ... After you get those seven scores, they go to stakeholder review. We move forward with the highest scoring projects objectively to that stakeholder review.
records.notes: The two scoring bodies are named in the Nov 13, 2025 and Mar 12, 2026 staff reports; 'too new' is a transcription artifact.

records.finding: Staff reported in March 2026 that only a handful of Managed Wetland parcels had opted in to receive an allocation and that the GSA and Zanjero were still delineating the wetland areas under the Allocation Rule. This shows the opt-in-only Managed Wetland allocation in findings 57 and 40 in use but with few takers in the rule's first year.
records.quantitative_detail: Managed Wetland opt-ins: 'a handful' (no number given), March 2026
records.speaker_role: GSA staff — MSGSA (Lacey McBride, staff report)
records.agenda_item: 14. Staff Report
records.evidence_text: We're working with Zanjero on the managed wetland delineation. We only have a handful of these. They were opted in during the opt in process, but the GSA is working with them to actually delineate out where those managed wetland areas are according to the groundwater allocation rule.
records.notes: No count was given, and it was not stated whether these parcels took Method 1 or the Managed Wetland Water Allocation.

records.finding: MLRP implementation contracts set a monitoring regime: DOC requires monitoring objectives, pre-project photo plots and performance measures before groundbreaking; MSGSA may use site visits, photo plots and remote sensing during implementation and make annual site checks for 10 years after; and the proponent files a final outcome report against the Merced MLRP Monitoring Plan. This conflicts with finding 44's absence of re-checking, though the Plan's metrics were never stated.
records.quantitative_detail: Annual site access for 10 years after implementation; Nevada Ranch final outcome report due Feb 28, 2027; Task 6 Monitoring budget $136,040 (Valley Eco share $33,660, Sept 2025); up to $85,000 of monitoring funds expected in the extension period (Apr 2026)
records.speaker_role: GSA staff — MSGSA project implementation contract (Nevada Ranch) in board packet
records.agenda_item: 6. Multibenefit Land Repurposing Program (Nevada Ranch implementation contract)
records.evidence_text: The California Department of Conservation (DoC) requires that monitoring objectives are identified, pre-project photo plots established, and initial photos taken before project implementation actions take place ... Site monitoring may include activities such as quarterly site visits, photo plots, and remote sensing. ... site access will be provided for MSGSA and its agents once annually for the ten (10) years following project implementation to confirm ongoing project management and operations.
records.notes: The Monitoring Plan itself was not in any packet examined; the same passage answers MLRP-2.7b (methods). Development project contracts (Apr 2026) allow site visits only during the development phase.

records.finding: When OpenET showed LRP participants short of their contracted reductions, the GSA judged compliance by the absence of applied groundwater rather than by the amount saved: waivers required a written attestation, a staff site visit showing no applied water, and an ET-trend comparison with similar irrigated fields. A director later described the test the same way (no water applied, so requirements met), which corroborates finding 39's point that verification tests irrigation rather than savings and shows it also governs the paid LRP.
records.quantitative_detail: 3 waiver criteria; waivers approved Sept 11, 2025 (WY2025) and Oct 8, 2026 (WY2026), and in Oct 2026 staff said the board had done the same in each of the past two years; payments due Nov 1
records.agenda_item: 9. Land Repurposing Program
records.evidence_text: With Board direction, minimum water use reduction values will be waived for Phase 1 LRP participants who 1) have provided written attestations of no applied groundwater to their repurposed fields, 2) where site visits by MSGSA staff confirm no indication of applied water use, and 3) where comparisons of evapotranspiration trends of the repurposed fields and similar irrigated fields show distinct differences supporting the notion that groundwater was not applied during the reporting period.
records.notes: The Jan 8, 2026 remark ('they're not applying water... So they met the requirements... We're trust but verified') is unlabeled and appears to be a director answering a public question.

records.finding: LRP monitoring yielded stated lessons but no mid-programme change: in September 2025 a director said tree removal should have been required, yet in October 2026 staff confirmed growers were never asked to remove trees, and the board again waived the minimums after a director said the program had design deficiencies. The LRP ends after WY2027 and is not being continued.
records.quantitative_detail: Lesson first stated Sept 11, 2025; no tree-removal requirement by Oct 8, 2026 (LRP year 4); LRP ends after WY2027
records.speaker_role: mixed — GSA staff and board members
records.agenda_item: 8. Land Repurposing Program
records.evidence_text: We have not asked the growers to remove the trees. It was not a requirement of the LRP program. ... They are out of compliance because the monitoring that we're using and the values that we set early on perhaps were too low. ... So I think we have to accept the fact that we had some deficiencies in how the program was designed and we're just going to have to get through the final, finalize this out.
records.notes: The 'deficiencies' remark is unlabeled and appears to be a director just before the motion; Nevada Ranch orchard removal is recorded side by side, not as a response to LRP results.

records.finding: The GSA's stated route for sustaining the MLRP after the grant is more state money, not local revenue: the board voted to join a grantee letter asking DOC to prioritise Prop 4 MLRP funding to stabilize work underway, over one director's objection, and staff doubled the FY2026/27 grant-writing budget to $50,000 anticipating Prop 4 SGMA and MLRP solicitations.
records.quantitative_detail: Prop 4 MLRP: $200M allocated, ~$32M expected in FY2026 (Nov 2025 statement); grant-writing budget $25,000 -> $50,000 (FY2026/27); letter vote recorded in transcript as 'four one with one abstention'
records.speaker_role: mixed — consultant (Valley Eco) and board member
records.agenda_item: 5. Multibenefit Land Repurposing Program (Prop 4 funding letter)
records.evidence_text: It is our position in the position of sort of partners in the region that the Department of Conservation should prioritize funding to stabilize work underway. ... I'm basically not a big fan of continuing to ask for more money.
records.notes: Director unlabeled in transcript; Dec 11, 2025 a public commenter urged the board to keep pursuing state and federal money; the Feb 11, 2026 update gave different, garbled Prop 4 figures.

records.finding: The Phase 2 Prop 218 fee replacing the Phase 1 fee funds administration (including the GAP), monitoring, data and studies, and domestic well mitigation; none of the listed activities is monitoring or stewardship of repurposed land, and the report says MSGSA will not continue the LRP. With MLRP contracts calling for 10 years of post-implementation site checks, this corroborates finding 51 that no post-grant funding source is identified.
records.quantitative_detail: Phase 2 fee max $15.11/acre/yr on ~186,315 eligible acres; max budget $2,815,000/yr (Category 1 $1,250,000; Category 2 $840,000; Category 3 $725,000); adopted June 2026; MLRP grant ends Mar 2028; post-implementation site access 10 years
records.speaker_role: consultant — Zanjero (Phase 2 Funding Mechanism Engineer's Report, adopted by the board Apr 9, 2026)
records.agenda_item: 7. Phase 2 Fee Engineer's Report
records.evidence_text: As detailed further in this Report, these include activities such as: funding needed to employ an executive director and technical staff with dedicated office space; providing funds for legal challenges and regulatory compliance; grant writing; website maintenance, updates, and ADA compliance; Groundwater Accounting Platform (GAP) subscription, customization, and support, and alternative remote sensing services for the GAP; technical support and studies; addressing data gaps including drilling and equipping new monitoring wells and providing on-going required monitoring and analysis; and domestic well mitigation program implementation.
records.notes: Absence judged from a word search of the engineer's report (repurposing/MLRP appear only in background, consultant history and a grant-writing table); the list says 'such as', so it is not exhaustive.

records.finding: Dust now appears as a claimed benefit of an MLRP project in a board-approved document: the March 2026 letter supporting the Bear Creek Ranch project, signed by the MSGSA Chair, says the project will improve public health by reducing herbicide and fertilizer use and blowing dust. No dust baseline, metric or monitoring was mentioned, consistent with finding 48's point that dust is named but never measured.
records.quantitative_detail: Bear Creek Ranch: ~1,171 acres of irrigated farm ground per staff memo (>1,000 acres per letter); letter approved 5-0
records.speaker_role: board member — letter signed by MSGSA Chair Lloyd Pareira, Jr. (board approved)
records.agenda_item: 9. Bear Creek Ranch Project Letter of Support
records.evidence_text: It will also improve public health in the vicinity by reducing herbicide and fertilizer use and blowing dust.
records.notes: The letter supports a federal appropriations request by River Partners and Reclamation District 2092; the vote is from the transcript.

records.finding: Dust from fallowed land came up in the TAC's cover-crop review: the consultant relayed growers' concern that ground cover kept on fallow land to stop dust raises OpenET-measured use, and a grower warned that bare fields bring air problems. The June 2026 draft gives no extra credit for cover crops on fields without applied water, and no dust-control condition or measurement was proposed.
records.quantitative_detail: Draft cover-crop credit (irrigated fields only): up to +2 in when rainfall >=9 and <12 in, up to +3 in when >=12 in; 0 for fields without applied water
records.agenda_item: 3. Groundwater Allocation Rule and Cover Crops
records.evidence_text: It's on there to make sure it doesn't create dust or something, but it may actually transpire more water. So am I going to get dinged for that? Because if so, I'm not going to put anything on the ground. ... is a farmer going to say, oh, I'm not going to do anything, I'm going to leave that as dirt? Then we have air issues and all the other stuff.
records.notes: Dec 11, 2025 a director flagged abandoned orchards as a growing problem for neighbours; the TAC draft (June 11, 2026 packet, Sec. 2.5.3.6) was referred to a board committee and not adopted by Aug 2026.

records.finding: Speaking for MSGSA at DWR's Fall 2025 GSA Forum, county staff said the GSA deliberately used voluntary land repurposing in Phase 1 to get early consumption cuts and buy time while the allocation rule was built, and that its incentive programmes (MLRP and recharge incentives in the allocation rule) had been under-subscribed before the allocation took effect. Staff said the aim is land-use change with multiple benefits rather than plain fallowing and that MLRP outreach has been a huge challenge.
records.quantitative_detail: No figures used (a required consumption reduction of 'about 150' was stated with units lost in the transcript)
records.speaker_role: GSA staff — Lacey McBride, Merced County (staff to MSGSA)
records.agenda_item: Projects and management actions conversation (moderated by DWR)
records.evidence_text: They intentionally had started like a two phased approach where they for GSP implementation where they started with some voluntary land repurposing to get some of those early reductions in groundwater consumption and basically buy some time while they develop the allocation. ... And so those incentive programs have been under subscribed which I think has been really interesting to see.
records.notes: Secondary (statewide DWR) meeting; the passage concerns only MSGSA.

records.finding: Grassland Water District presented SB 1108 to create a Grassland Ecological Area Conservancy, a voluntary state agency able to hold conservation easements, whose boundary follows MSGSA's adopted MLRP wildlife-corridor boundary in an area expected to see pumping cuts and some land retirement. The presenter said in passing that the corridor aligns with RCIS priorities; no accounting role for the conservancy was described.
records.quantitative_detail: Proposed 9-member board weighted to locals; start-up cost under $0.5M/yr per presenter; other conservancies received $10-15M in bond funds at start; Senate Natural Resources Committee hearing Mar 24, 2026
records.speaker_role: NGO/advocate — Grassland Water District representative (bill sponsor)
records.agenda_item: 6. Grassland Ecological Area Conservancy
records.evidence_text: This is the, your, your adopted MLRP wildlife corridor boundary that had a lot of input into that development. And so this is, this aligns well with the essential habitat corridors that have been prioritized by the state cdfw, caltrans, the MLRP process, the RCIS process. ... the conservancy would have the ability to hold easements, voluntary easements, working with landowners to essentially, you know, add conservation easements.
records.notes: Grassland Water District is a water district, not a GSA or NGO; the RCIS reference is a passing remark and no RCIS document was named; informational item, no board action.

records.finding: The locally funded Phase 1 LRP, one of the two tracks in finding 28, is ending: the Phase 2 fee report adopted in April 2026 says MSGSA has elected not to continue it, the Phase 1 fee that paid for it has sunset, and the remaining incentive payments come from Phase 1 fund balance. Staff said in October 2026 that the LRP does not continue after WY2027 and its parcels could become a pipeline for future MLRP projects.
records.quantitative_detail: Phase 1 fee max $24.94/acre irrigated (adopted 2022, sunset FY2025/26); LRP expenditure $2,080,458 (FY2024/25 estimated actual); $1,437,480 payable Nov 2026 (year 4); 14 agreements in WY2025, 10 in WY2026 (3 closed after WY2025); final year WY2027; EKI LRP monitoring and close-out task $15,000 (Oct 8, 2026 amendment)
records.speaker_role: consultant — Zanjero (Phase 2 Funding Mechanism Engineer's Report, adopted by the board Apr 9, 2026)
records.agenda_item: 7. Phase 2 Fee Engineer's Report
records.evidence_text: Phase 2 is set to start in 2026 and requires that the MSGSA implement the Allocation Approach in combination with potential expansion of the Phase 1 tools of continued land repurposing/fallowing and importing surface water into the GSA. ... In addition, the MSGSA has elected not to continue the Land Repurposing Program
records.notes: No reason for not continuing was given in the meetings; agreement counts are as stated (14 minus 3 closed does not equal 10 and was not explained).

records.finding: A local water manager told the board that Woodard & Curran calls him before each GSP annual report and he supplies the benefits of grant-funded projects he manages, including a dairy recharge reservoir that took about 900 AF in one year and the Bear Creek floodplain conversion retiring over 1,000 acres. Some project benefits thus enter the annual report as proponent-supplied figures, consistent with finding 30.
records.quantitative_detail: Reservoir ~300 AF capacity cycled 3 times = ~900 AF in one water year (described as above-normal year on Mar 9, 2026); >1,000 acres to be retired to floodplain
records.speaker_role: public commenter — local water manager whose clients include Sandy Mush Mutual Water Company
records.agenda_item: 3. Public Comment Period
records.evidence_text: So this is a dairy in our subsidence area that added 900 acre feet in one year. So another project we're following thousands of acres or over a thousand acres will not be farmed again. ... before the Woodward and Current does their sub base at the report, they call me and I go through the list of projects I work on, Sandy Mush all my other clients and I give them the benefits of all these projects into the GSP annual report.
records.notes: Commenter unnamed in the transcript; the same projects were presented on Mar 9, 2026 by 'Brad', manager of several small water districts (probably Brad Samuelson, TAC member); his figures are self-reported.

records.finding: MIUGSA's Stakeholder Guidance Committee works as a pre-board review step in practice: staff brought four January 2026 policies (domestic well mitigation, allocation, allocation period, carryover) to it and said its recommendations would go to the board with the staff proposals; the original three-year allocation period also came from committee input. Finding 61 notes the Rules give it no role.

records.finding: Adopted terms of the basin-wide domestic well program (MSGSA vote 6-0, January 2026; the other GSAs by February): wells failing from groundwater-level decline after January 28, 2020, domestic-only and at most 2 AFY; reimbursement up to $30,000 per well, including wells already replaced; emergency bottled or hauled water reimbursed outside the cap; 180 days to finish; written appeal within 30 days.
records.quantitative_detail: Cap $30,000 per well; eligibility from Jan 28, 2020; de minimis 2 AFY; 180-day completion limit; appeal within 30 days; MSGSA vote 6-0 on Jan 8, 2026
records.agenda_item: 10. Domestic Well Mitigation Program
records.evidence_text: The cause of the well failure is declining groundwater levels resulting from overdraft pumping that occurred after January 28, 2020. This is one of the first changes that was made that I want to highlight here ... The domestic well mitigation program will support and reimburse applicants in obtaining their own emergency supply and hauled water and if necessary will supply that emergency supply themselves. And this will not come from the $30,000 cap. ... the program is setting a limit of 180 days after the mitigation award is approved for the applicant to complete the mitigation measures.
records.notes: The eligibility start moved from wells existing before Sept 1, 2025 (Aug 2025 draft) to failures after July 19, 2022 (Nov 2025) to January 28, 2020; the November 3 transcript's '$3,000' retroactive cap conflicts with the board's $30,000.

records.finding: Finding 85 says the domestic well program has no fee linkage and runs apart from agricultural accounting. Outside the Rules, MSGSA's Phase 2 fee, adopted in June 2026 and charged per acre on parcels receiving an allocation, has a dedicated domestic-well category of up to $725,000 a year; $450,000 of Phase 1 money is budgeted for it in FY2026/27.
records.quantitative_detail: Category 3 max $725,000/yr ($75,000 emergency water, $50,000 administration, $600,000 long-term = 20 wells x $30,000); Phase 2 max $2,815,000/yr over ~186,315 acres = $15.11/acre; FY2026/27 Phase 2 rate $5.02/acre; Phase 1 DWMP fund $800,000 collected, $450,000 budgeted FY2026/27

records.finding: DWR's February 2025 GSP approval, as summarized in EKI's proposal to the GSAs, includes a corrective action on ISW. It asks the GSAs to tie depletion MTs and the undesirable-result definition to beneficial uses of surface water, set quantifiable MTs and MOs under DWR's ISW guidance, define connectivity segments and timing, and work with agencies and stakeholders on affected users.
records.quantitative_detail: DWR approval February 2025; Periodic Evaluation with updated GSP due 2027-01-28.
records.speaker_role: consultant — EKI proposal summarizing DWR's February 2025 recommended corrective actions
records.agenda_item: Item 2 – GSP Implementation Services: master services agreement with EKI (not to exceed $976,300)
records.evidence_text: RCA 5: Interconnected Surface Waters (ISWs) (a) Relate ISW depletion MTs and UR criteria to beneficial uses of surface water. (b) Use ISW guidance to establish quantifiable MTs, measurable objectives (MOs), and management actions. (c) Continue filling data gaps, collecting data, and implementing the strategy to manage ISW depletion and define connectivity segments and timing. (d) Coordinate with regulatory agencies and stakeholders to better understand all potentially impacted beneficial uses and users. ... (5) Explain how RMWs for ISW depletion protect beneficial uses.
records.notes: The wording is EKI's summary of DWR's letter, not DWR's own text; the letter is listed under documents EDF may not have.

records.finding: To answer DWR's corrective action, EKI is adding riparian GDEs, almost all along the river corridors, to the chronic-lowering undesirable result (30-ft depth screen plus NDVI/NDMI trends) rather than to the ISW criterion. Its reasoning is that ISW depletion is defined as pumping-caused streamflow loss, while GDEs are users of groundwater, so environmental users along the rivers are judged through groundwater levels.
records.quantitative_detail: GDE screen: depth to water 30 ft or less (TNC/DWR guidance); ICONS ISW classes cited on 2026-04-14: under 20 ft connected, 20–50 ft uncertain; about 1,200 GDE polygons.
records.speaker_role: mixed — TAC member question, consultant (EKI) answer
records.agenda_item: Item 6 – SGMA related updates: GDE recommended corrective action
records.evidence_text: So what's your rationale for including them as part of the chronic groundwater level decline undesirable result as opposed to the interconnected surface water undesirable result? ... But the rationale that they are, they fall under groundwater level is that under sigma regulation, the depletion of interconnected surface water has a contingency on it that's due to pumping. So it's a depletion that's caused by pumping in the basin. Groundwater dependent ecosystems are beneficial users of groundwater, so it's more aligned with how we assess the well. ... And we identified all three streams are as completely connected.
records.notes: The questioner (ETSGSA side) is addressed as 'Mike'. This bears on Finding 118 because environmental beneficial users are being addressed outside the ISW criterion.

records.finding: For the Periodic Evaluation EKI proposed keeping 2015 groundwater-level MTs as the ISW proxy and publishing model depletion estimates each year without basing policy on them. Depletion rate-and-volume SMCs, possibly referenced to pumping-caused depletion in 2015, would follow by the next five-year update: 2030 as stated, corrected to 2032 in August.
records.quantitative_detail: Depletion-based SMC target: 2030 (stated 2026-06-09), corrected to 2032 (2026-08-11); Periodic Evaluation due to DWR 2027-01-28; candidate MT reference = modelled pumping-caused depletion in 2015.
records.agenda_item: Item 6 – SGMA related updates: approach to address ISW recommended corrective action
records.evidence_text: So we can basically do this depletion analysis with the model and then understand how much depletion was caused by pumping in 2015. That would be our basic reference point. ... So we have a firm plan to propose to EWR that we will move to ISW sustainable management criteria based on depletion and rate by 2030. But we will not do it right now because we don't have enough data and information. ... every year we will provide you with depletion analysis based on our current model. So we will put the results out. It's just we will not make policy based on it until we have a little bit more time and A little bit more data.
records.notes: This is a proposal brought for TAC feedback, not a vote. The 2032 correction came in reply to a TAC question on 2026-08-11.

records.finding: In August 2026 EKI presented the subbasin's first pumping-attributable depletion analysis: a no-pumping run subtracted from business-as-usual in C2VSim-TM, WY1991–2025, shown as monthly, seasonal and along-river plots. No depletion volumes were stated aloud. Depletion peaks in irrigation months, with September highest on the Merced, and approaches zero toward the San Joaquin.
records.quantitative_detail: Simulation period WY1991–2025; highlighted years 2014, 2015 and 2025; no numeric depletion values read into the record (plots were in the meeting packet, which is not in the WaterOne corpus).
records.agenda_item: Item 7 – SGMA related updates: P/MA and ISW corrective actions
records.evidence_text: We basically did the no pumping scenario, which is how we do the depletion. So we subtract a hypothetical scenario that there is no pumping in the basin from business as usual. And the difference would be the depletion due to pumping. What's in that graph is basically showing all the years since 1991 to 2025 in very thin lines. ... But when you go up in the monthly, you can see September is actually our highest month, although it's not considered summer, as we have in the bottom plot. ... And then you get towards the San Joaquin River. You almost have no depletion due to pumping.
records.notes: In June 2026 EKI said this framework was set up for the WY2025 Annual Report but not run there, to avoid publishing preliminary results before the model update.

records.finding: EKI reported that modelled pumping depletion on what is apparently the Tuolumne is generally lower after 2016. It attributed this to both the model enhancement and post-2016 basin changes, 'probably mostly' the latter, and said depletion does not track water-year type (2023 exceeded 2022). The GSP's historical estimates will not be rerun with the updated model.
records.quantitative_detail: Comparison of pre- and post-2016 within WY1991–2025 runs; 2023 depletion greater than 2022; the GSP historical water budget used a pre-1.0 beta IWFM code with bugs, versus current version 1.5 (2025-12-09).
records.agenda_item: Item 7 – SGMA related updates: ISW corrective action
records.evidence_text: And you can see that generally it's a little bit less after 2016. And it's a combination. It's a combination of enhancement but also combination of things changed after 2016. ... It's a combination and probably mostly due to impacts that happen in the basin. But one other thing that's interesting in this is that it doesn't depletion due to pumping doesn't necessarily go with the water year type. ... you have like the pumping that happened in 2023 actually had more depletion caused than 2022.
records.notes: The river is transcribed as 'tolly mirror', read here as the Tuolumne. No figures were stated, so the size of the decline is unknown; on 2025-12-09 EKI confirmed the updated model will not be used to revise GSP historical estimates.

records.finding: EKI's depletion scenario removes all Turlock Subbasin pumping at once while holding neighbouring basins' pumping and boundary conditions fixed. The model thus isolates in-subbasin pumping, which the level proxy cannot, but only collectively; no split by GSA or well was presented. Whether the Merced, Modesto and Delta-Mendota GSAs use matching methods or criteria on the shared rivers is not yet coordinated.
records.speaker_role: consultant — EKI (Amir Mani), answering a TAC question
records.agenda_item: Item 7 – SGMA related updates: ISW corrective action
records.evidence_text: So the first part is when we do the due to pumping part. So we remove the pumping in the Turlock sub basin. So whatever we show based on subtraction or scenarios should only be due to the pumping that we put in Turlock sub basin. Now that's not in a vacuum, as you know. ... Now, in terms of how Merced deals with this or how Modesta deals with it or Delta Mendela deals with this, are they doing the same thing? Are they proposing the same criteria? That's something that we also need to coordinate, and I agree with you.
records.notes: This also answers ISW-1.5c (cumulative pumping). A TAC member reported on 2026-01-26 that DWR staff asked how the GSAs will coordinate ISW with neighbouring subbasins.

records.finding: Meetings report that DWR TSS clusters 1, 2 and 4 were finished by October 2025 and a fourth, ETTSS-03 on a river-well site, was drilled November–December 2025 for spring-2026 measurement. records.quantitative_detail: 4 TSS clusters: 3 completed in FY2024-25 per the June 2025 monitoring scope; the 4th started about 2025-11-03 and was complete December 2025; DWR to use at least 3 for monthly water-quality sampling (January 2026).

records.finding: EKI re-tested river connectivity under DWR's ISW white paper using stream gauges, the TSS nested wells and the shallow levels available. It found all three rivers flow perennially and are connected almost everywhere. The upper Tuolumne and Merced reaches rest on interpolated contours because shallow wells are lacking, so the GSAs assume connection as a conservative default until new shallow wells are in.
records.agenda_item: Item 7 – SGMA related updates: ISW corrective action
records.evidence_text: But what we intend to do is go through what we have as data, extreme gauges, the TSS fills the shallow water levels that we have and see how it's connected to the river. ... And what we found basically is that all rivers in the, in the basin are always flowing and they're almost in every part connected. ... Also, we have a lot of data gaps, so we don't have a great coverage of shallow water levels along the river. ... we are taking the conservative assumption that it is connected.
records.notes: No finding covers how connectivity was determined; Finding 90 (node classification) is the closest. The September 2025 proposal lists the intended lines of evidence (NHD, gauges, streambed elevations, LiDAR, shallow wells, ICONS, isotopes).

records.section: 1.5 Per-well Attribution and the Cumulative Pumping Problem
records.finding: EKI's September 2025 proposal offered depletion-sensitivity heatmaps (stream-capture maps). These would show where pumping location, rate and timing most deplete each river and where cutting extraction would ease undesirable results: a location-specific attribution tool. The Task Order 9 scope approved in January 2026, at the same $128,900 ceiling, does not include it.
records.quantitative_detail: Optional Subtask 9.1 (ISW depletion sensitivity heatmaps) priced at $34,253 within Optional Task 9 ($128,900) in the September 2025 proposal; approved Task Order 9 (January 2026) is split $17,100/$64,600/$38,000/$9,200 with no heatmap task.
records.agenda_item: Item 2 – GSP Implementation Services: master services agreement with EKI
records.evidence_text: the improved Model with enhanced ISW representation, will be utilized to provide vital insights with respect to: (1) where there is adynamic interconnection between groundwater and surface water and stream seepage is sensitive to groundwater pumping, (2) data to generate spatial risk maps (i.e., stream capture maps; Leake and Haney, 2010 ) that can convey area s most sensitive to groundwater extraction that can inform monitoring well placement, and (3) define areas where groundwater extraction can be reduced to mitigate URs.
records.notes: That the heatmaps are absent from Task Order 9 comes from reading its scope in the 2026-01-13 packet. No meeting discussed dropping them, so no reason can be given.

records.section: 1.5 Per-well Attribution and the Cumulative Pumping Problem
records.finding: EKI said modelled pumping depletion differs by river, by reach and by month. On the Merced it is largest mid-basin near the pumping centre and near zero toward the San Joaquin. Any depletion-based criterion should therefore be set by river segment, and possibly by season, rather than as one basin number. No segments or averaging period have been chosen.
records.agenda_item: Item 7 – SGMA related updates: ISW corrective action
records.evidence_text: I want to segmentize the river. When we want to put a polish in, right. We don't want to treat the western part of the river that's pretty different than the eastern part. ... So it can't be just one number or one depletion for the basin. It should be specific to segments of different rivers. ... Do we want to do different seasons? Do we want to do sub annual? Do you want to do annual? So those are the things that we are just exploring right now.
records.notes: This is exploratory and no option has been chosen. DWR's RCA 5(c) also asks for connectivity segments and timing.

records.finding: New DWR TSS nested wells show shallow-screen levels well above medium and deep levels in the Eastern Principal Aquifer, yet most Eastern ISW RMWs are screened at the deeper interval. EKI said the shallow interval governs depletion, that TSS data are in neither the GSP nor the model calibration, and that one year of record is too short to rely on.
records.quantitative_detail: TSS screens about 60–80 ft (shallow) versus about 200 ft (deeper) below ground, per the 2026-03-10 discussion and February 2026 slides (e.g., ETTSS-02: Upper 60–80 ft, Middle 140–160 ft, Lower 260–280 ft); about one year of record as of March 2026.
records.agenda_item: Item 6 – SGMA related updates: approach to address ISW recommended corrective action
records.evidence_text: So if you look at those different colors, red and green, these are different basically shallow screen, medium screen and deeper screen. And you can see actual difference between the levels. So the levels in the shallow screen is actually a lot higher than the screen, the medium screen or deeper screen than we have. And in the eastern side of the basin, for example, Most of our RMWs that we have, even in the ISW monitoring network have depths and screens more closer to that green line. So what we're reading as groundwater levels in those bells corresponds to this green screen depth.
records.notes: On 2026-03-10 EKI said 'the shallow one is the one that we should care for depletion and the GDEs' and that TSS data were not in the model calibration or the GSP.

records.finding: EKI said C2VSim-TM's single thick top layer cannot reproduce the separate shallow and deeper levels the TSS wells show, so calibration near the rivers is limited even where shallow data exist. The proposed fix is to split layer 1 and add shallow wells. A TAC participant summed up the gap as a matter of model architecture, not calibration.
records.quantitative_detail: The top (unconfined) model layer is layer 1; Task Order 9 excluded any grid or layer refinement.
records.agenda_item: Item 7 – SGMA related updates: ISW corrective action
records.evidence_text: The reason that it's not a perfect calibration is because the model is a bit coarse in terms of the layer. So it would be the better way to go with it, as you know, is basically that top layer in the model, we divide it into a shallower and kind of a deeper parts of the layer and then they can actually produce different, different levels based on a semi architect between them if it needs to be. So that's not in the C2B SIM or Kerloc model right now. So in some parts it can't be 100% calibrated even if you have the data. ... But the model has limitations related to simulating isw.
records.notes: The questioner is addressed as 'Mike' (likely ETSGSA General Manager Mike Tietze); transcript speaker labels are unreliable.

records.finding: February 2026 slides show that TSS-4, the cluster intended as the Merced River ISW RMW, was built much further west than the GSP location, with its shallowest screen at 115–135 ft and provisional SMCs from nearby wells. EKI said some ISW network wells are too far and too deep for ISW, and the network will be revised in the Periodic Evaluation.
records.quantitative_detail: TSS-4 (ETTSS-04) screens: Upper 115–135 ft, Middle 290–310 ft, Lower 550–590 ft below ground; provisional MT 86 / MO 100 (elevation, as given on the slide).
records.agenda_item: Item 6 – SGMA related updates: WY2025 Annual Report (ISWs)
records.evidence_text: TSS-4 was intended as RMW of ISW (Merced River) ... MT: 86 / MO: 100 based on nearby wells ... Actual location is much further west ... EKI will look into ISW RMS as part of the Periodic Evaluation and in conjunction with the addition of new TSS wells.

Staff noted that access agreements give permission but cannot be enforced, and warned that DWR may require the well to be replaced. This is an acknowledged reliability limit on a compliance well that also serves the ISW network.

And we were not able to contact him again this season after several attempts. ... Can we find a way to access this location more reliably? Because if, if we can't, DWR is going to ask us to, to replace that well with a different well.

The adopted FY2026-27 budget reserves $300,000, with timing and cost share still to be set with EKI and WTSGSA. In April 2026 staff could not say whether the wells would go ahead that year.

That should be plenty for that task and when that task gets implemented and how much of costs will be determined in consultation with EKI and WTS gsa. records.finding: WTSGSA installed its dedicated monitoring-well project, 8 wells at 7 sites for $517,420, by June 2026. The sites were picked from a 33-site plan that included river/ISW sites, after staff weighed river wells against interior wells within budget. Staff then said river wells are probably still needed, but where and how to place them is not yet known.
records.quantitative_detail: 8 wells at 7 sites, contract $517,420 (awarded November 2025); 33 specified sites; over $580,000 set aside; well depths 85–235 ft; one dual shallow/deep site (Delhi).
records.speaker_role: GSA staff — WTSGSA/TID staff (transcript labels unreliable)
records.agenda_item: Item 6 – SGMA related updates: WTSGSA monitoring well project

We don't, we probably need to put some river wells in, but we, we probably don't know where and how to put those in until we have a little bit more information.
records.notes: The trade-off between river and interior wells comes from 2025-10-14; the meetings do not say whether any of the 8 wells is an ISW well.

records.finding: EKI said that even after the funded update, model uncertainty is too high to set depletion criteria. A further structural refinement, splitting layer 1, plus shallow wells is needed, which EKI hopes to fund through Prop 4 grants. A TAC member warned of compliance risk because the commitment to DWR rests on unbudgeted work, and EKI offered 'subject to funding' wording with a simpler fallback.
records.quantitative_detail: Prop 4 SGM grant: draft guidelines out by August 2026, applications expected spring–summer 2027, awards late 2027 or early 2028 (per 2026-08-11 joint TAC).
records.agenda_item: Item 6 – SGMA related updates: approach to address ISW recommended corrective action

Again, we are set up to do this analysis, but the accurate level of accuracy and the uncertainty in the model right now, even after our enhancement, would be high. ... What RSW needs is a structural refinement. ... And we are hoping we can do that through Prop 4 and through Grant work. ... There's, I guess there's a certain amount of risk with this approach because it does rely on a future effort which we haven't budgeted for yet. ... we'll present an alternative simplified approach or something like that to basically.
records.notes: The risk remark is labelled 'Michael I. Cooke' (WTSGSA TAC chair) in a transcript with unreliable labels; the fallback wording was suggested by Anona Dutton (EKI).

records.finding: EKI relayed, from other basins' experience, that DWR will not accept staying on the level proxy for want of a model or data and wants visible progress with the best tools available. DWR has set no timeline because its long-awaited ISW guidance is still unreleased. DWR staff had separately asked in January how the GSAs would coordinate ISW with neighbouring subbasins.
records.quantitative_detail: DWR ISW guidance awaited 'for the past two years or so' (as of August 2026).
records.agenda_item: Item 7 – SGMA related updates: ISW corrective action
records.evidence_text: But what we know based on other basins talking to the BR is that they don't want to hear that we don't have a model or we don't have data. So we're just going to stick to the groundwater level of proxy and don't do anything. ... So they want to see movement. They want us to use of your best available tools and data and then updating and adapting it on their sigma process. But they are not also forceful. ... They haven't given us timelines to be honest with you, because their guideline has been. Everyone was waiting on their guideline for the past two years or so.
records.notes: This is a secondhand account of DWR's position; the January item was reported by a TAC member, not by DWR.

records.finding: The priority action area the ETSGSA board rescinded in October 2025 was at ETSGSA-08, a cone-of-depression well the meetings do not describe as an ISW RMW. The false IM exceedance arose because resurveyed elevations at the well fell 16 ft while SMCs borrowed from a neighbouring well moved only 3 ft, and because the 2027 IM had been extrapolated from a handful of data points.
records.quantitative_detail: Reference-point shift: 16 ft at ETSGSA-08 versus 3 ft at proxy well EWD01 (April 2023 survey); 2027 IM revised from +8 ft (GSP) and +5 ft (post-resurvey) to −7 or −11 ft msl; PAA rescinded by board vote 2025-10-23.
records.speaker_role: mixed — consultant (Provost & Pritchard) and ETSGSA staff
records.agenda_item: Item 6 – ETSGSA-08 Priority Action Area
records.evidence_text: The well is part of our monitoring network in the cone of Depression area. ... Because the SMC for ETSGSA08 was based on EWD. the SMC were only decreased by 3 feet in elevation, which was the. difference in elevation at EWD01. However, the groundwater levels decreased by 16 feet because ETSGSA. 08 had a much larger, a 16-foot. discrepancy in the reference point elevation. ... the IM should never have been set at 8 feet in the first place.
records.notes: Included because Finding 110 sets this rescission beside ISW RMWs under review. The corpus's minutes and agenda for this meeting are 2022 documents, so only the transcript was used.

records.finding: Uncertainty in the ISW modelling reaches the TACs only as spoken caveats. EKI said the depletion simulation contains inaccuracy and is not '100% correct', the January WY2025 flux figures were flagged as likely to change, and a TAC participant asked that limitations be stated prominently to DWR. No ranges, error bands or calibration statistics were cited in the meetings.
records.quantitative_detail: No ranges or statistics cited; WY2025 net stream–aquifer flux figures were presented 2026-01-13 with the caveat that they would change after model refinement.
records.agenda_item: Item 7 – SGMA related updates: ISW corrective action
records.evidence_text: Now again there is inaccuracy in this simulation. I'm not saying it is 100% correct, but this is something that we've seen in other analysis too. ... what I think is important in this analysis as we present it to the DWR is to make sure that we can talk about what the uncertainties are and how we're moving forward to resolve them. ... So, you know, that needs to be, I think prominently stated.
records.notes: The 2026-08-11 slides are not in the corpus, so presentation material may carry ranges that were not reviewed here.

records.finding: EKI's GSP dashboard is shared with member agencies, not the public, and already shows ISW RMW status against SMCs. A TAC member asked for per-river depletion plots; EKI offered quick per-river plots now and a model-results tab later. In June the WTSGSA TAC chair floated opening the viewer more widely, but nothing was decided.
records.agenda_item: Item 7 – SGMA related updates: P/MA dashboard
records.evidence_text: I was wondering how hard would it be or would it be beneficial to add it to the dashboard, where you go click on, you know, on that on the river and you know, you get that to pop up right where it shows when it depletes, when it. ... I think we previously discussed probably adding some functionality to this dashboard to cover some of the modeling results. I think that's the more long term vision for this. ... So that's something we can quickly probably add as kind of energy measurements till we implement a more kind of broad tab if the joint type desires on the model results.
records.notes: The requester's name is garbled in the transcript; access being limited to member agencies is from the 2026-06-09 and 2026-08-14 discussions.

records.finding: ETSGSA staff reported in August 2025 that DWR's review letter on the WY2024 Annual Report raised concern about levels below MTs and an undesirable result for surface water–groundwater interaction, and asked for specific items in future annual reports. Staff described this as being put 'on notice' and said the IMs had been set below the MTs on purpose.

Our, um, groundwater levels were below minimum thresholds, and that we were in a state of undesirable results relative to surface groundwater interaction, and very likely, or very possibly, headed in that direction. ... Um, so they registered their concern, and they said that there are certain things that they want to see. ... They're basically putting us on notice that they're watching very closely, because we are in. ... Our internal milestones, or we low minimum thresholds for a reason, because we knew we were going to get there.

records.finding: ETSGSA-02, whose ISW and chronic-level IM exceedances set off an Appendix K priority action area, was reached in December 2025 after several unmeasured seasons. The monitoring consultant reported no 2027 IM exceedance and levels above the MT. Staff noted DWR's WY2024 letter had demanded the well be monitored or replaced, and said the area looked like a problem only before resurvey data were processed.
records.quantitative_detail: Access regained December 2025; missed depth-to-water values back-calculated from transducer data; no 2027 IM exceedance; level above MT and rising over the last three years (per 2026-01-13 TAC).
records.speaker_role: mixed — consultant (Provost & Pritchard) and ETSGSA staff/board

But there's been no exceedances of the 2027 IM and currently the the water level is sitting above the MT. ... DWR in their letter regarding our last annual report specifically said that, you know, we haven't been monitoring able to monitor as well for a while. You need to either start monitoring it or replace it.
records.notes: The ISW role of ETSGSA-02 comes from Finding 104; the meetings do not say whether the ETSGSA-02 priority action area has formally ended.

records.finding: EKI told the joint TACs the WY2025 Annual Report would present the Merced and Tuolumne ISW exceedances as an undesirable result only 'in theory', since levels are above IMs and the basin is on its glide path. EKI said it does not expect the condition to change while Eastern Principal Aquifer MTs stand. Both boards heard the same framing in February 2026.
records.quantitative_detail: Undesirable-result test: >50% of a river's RMWs below MT in Fall; met on Merced and Tuolumne in WY2024 and WY2025; ETSGSA board was told the aim is to be above MT 'by 2032 or earlier'.
records.agenda_item: Item 6 – SGMA related updates: WY2025 Annual Report
records.evidence_text: So not to basically cause too much stir of surprise in terms of your causing undesirable result, but showing that yes, in theory the comparison would mean an undesirable result if it happened after the implementation period. ... Water year 2024 was would be undesirable result on both rivers. It's the same condition this year again on both rivers. Merced and Ptolemy, because of the minimum thresholds that are set in the eastern principal aquifer, we don't expect that to change, but we are on path.
records.notes: 'Ptolemy' is the transcript's rendering of Tuolumne. The packet slide for this meeting likewise says the undesirable result 'Would have occurred' on both rivers.

records.finding: ETSGSA holds and administers the DOC block grant but delivers it through contracted firms: Formation Environmental, the General Manager's employer, coordinates project development (Task 2) and programme management and reporting (Task 7), while EKI, ESA, Self-Help Enterprises and two RCDs hold task contracts. Formation contracts are approved separately with the GM out of the room.

Stakeholder Advisory Committee); ESA $150,000 (Task 2 permitting/CEQA); Formation $300,000 (Tasks 2 and 7); Gregg Drilling $10,000 and Geophysical Imaging Partners $50,000 (recharge characterization, 4 pilot sites); $818,500 within MLRP grant budget, reimbursed by DOC. Later: Self-Help Enterprises +$75,000 (2025-08-28); East Stanislaus RCD $114,500 and East Merced RCD $118,202.50 released through 2027-03-31 (2025-09-25); EKI +$195,000 implementation support (2026-09-24).
