records.finding: DOC told ETSGSA it intends to give existing block grantees continuity funding under a Prop 4 'phase three' from April 2027, so ETSGSA deferred earthwork-heavy basin projects to the 2027 dry season and advanced vegetative-cover projects to spend Round 2 funds on time. The Round 2 term was later extended to June 2028.
records.quantitative_detail: Deferred basin/earthwork components (3 pilot + 5 full-scale projects) ≈ $2.5M of reserved incentives; ≈ $20,000 per project kept for design/permitting; ≈ $2.343M redirected to vegetative-cover projects; cap ≈ $1M per applicant; pre-extension final invoicing deadline March 2027; ETSGSA requested extension to March 2028 (2026-03-10); legislature approved and Governor signed Round 2 extension to June 2028 (reported 2026-09-08 and 2026-09-24).
records.speaker_role: mixed — GSA staff (General Manager, inferred) and consultant (EKI)
records.agenda_item: 6. Multi-Benefit Land Repurposing Program (MLRP)

records.notes: The GM's remarks sit under a generic room-microphone label in the transcript; Round 3 guidelines and a new grant agreement were not yet in hand.

records.finding: By September 2026 the programme had moved past architecture: four pilot agreements were recorded (July 2026) with construction due after the 2026 harvest, and seven full-scale projects were authorized or on the docket, for 11 projects worth about $4.7M. The January–March 2026 solicitation drew about $15M of requests against roughly $4.1M remaining after pilots.
records.quantitative_detail: 11 projects (4 pilot + 7 full-scale), grand total ≈ $4.7M (2026-09-24); components: 7 extended multibenefit fallowing, 6 orchard swale rewilding, 4 constructed basin, 2 stormwater pond; 2026 solicitation: 20 applications, ≈ $15M requested vs ≈ $4.1M available after pilots, 9 projects advanced 2026-03-26; pilot agreements all recorded by 2026-07-23; MLRP acreage described by the GM as 'under a thousand acres' (2026-09-24).
records.speaker_role: consultant — EKI Environment & Water (Chris Heppner, MLRP lead)
records.agenda_item: 8. Multi-Benefit Land Repurposing Program

And then the seven full scale projects including one approved in August or authorized by the GSA in August. And then the six that are on the, on the docket for today. ... grand total we are roughly 4.7 million, you know, accounted for under these 11 projects.

records.finding: For the IFP, ETSGSA dropped its proposed groundwater-only eligibility rule and made surface water a ranking question: a partly surface-irrigated field is credited only with its consumed groundwater unless the grower shows the freed surface water displaces pumping on another field. The MLRP application instead excludes surface-water-irrigated land outright.
records.quantitative_detail: Worked example (GM): field with 200 AF ET and 100 AF surface water ranks at 200 AF only if the 100 AF is moved to a groundwater-irrigated field, otherwise at 100 AF; one applicant account (607 ac) was under surface-water review in January 2026 and later had acreage cut.
records.speaker_role: GSA staff — General Manager Mike Tietze (Formation Environmental, contracted); attribution inferred from context
records.agenda_item: Incentivized Land Fallowing Program policy (adopted at this meeting)
records.evidence_text: So, what we had wanted to do was, initially, we had proposed that only… fields that are exclusively irrigated with groundwater would be eligible. ... This is an accounting question, it's not an eligibility question. Okay? You are eligible if you're using groundwater, at least partially on a field, you're eligible for this program. ... If surface water is used, then you have to transfer that surface water use to another field, to replace groundwater use. Otherwise, we're… we're not interested, or not as interested in that investment.
records.notes: Board members contested the rule at length; the IFP policy was adopted the same day subject to legal clean-up; attribution to the GM inferred from context.

records.finding: In the first verification cycle about one-third of self-reported fallow fields passed the automated ET screens and two-thirds needed imagery review. The platform also flagged just over 5,000 acres of unreported fields with fallow ET signatures; these stayed charged to the owner's account unless a modification was filed.
records.quantitative_detail: Reporting period 2025 (preliminary): ~5,600 ac self-reported fallow (5,586 ac final, 2026-02-26); ~2,097 ac approved on ET thresholds (adjustment just over 1,000 AF); ~3,500 [ac] under imagery review; zeroing all reported fallow ≈ 6,000 AF less consumptive groundwater use; unreported fallow-signature fields just over 5,000 ac; screens: ET minus effective precipitation < 0.5 AF/ac per year or July ET < 0.1 AF/ac; 11.14 ac (2 usage locations) failed the crop-removal test (2026-02-26).
records.speaker_role: GSA staff — General Manager Mike Tietze (Formation Environmental, contracted); attribution inferred from context
records.agenda_item: 5. Update regarding groundwater use fee implementation
records.evidence_text: We are as far as our data based thresholds go, that is if a parcel is, excuse me, if a field is less than a half an acre foot per acre or if a field is less than 0.1 foot in, in in July it is considered verified fallowed and that's about one third of the reports fall into that category and have been accepted. And then the remaining 2/3 are require follow up using imagery. ... Unreported fallowing. Now these are fallowed fields that were not reported, excuse me, fields that were not reported as fallowed but that have an ET signature that indicates that they are. And that would be either less than a half a foot of ET minus EP or less than a tenth of a foot in July. And that's just over 5,000 acres.
records.notes: Preliminary figures; the transcript says '3,500 acre feet' under review where acres appear meant; that unreported fallow stayed in consumptive use unless the owner filed a modification is from the 2026-03-26 board discussion.

records.finding: First-year appeals exposed a gap: electrical-meter appeals let about 305 acres of unirrigated but standing orchard count as fallow although standing trees showed roughly 1.5–1.6 ft of ET. Rules version 4 (August 2026) now accept meter-based fallow claims only where trees or vines have been pushed over, and exclude permanent or newly planted fields from 'fallow'.
records.quantitative_detail: Appeal no. 5 ≈ 305 ac approved on meter data (2026-06-25); standing-tree ET ≈ 1.5–1.6 ft per year vs fallow screens of 0.5 AF/ac per year or 0.1 AF/ac in July; crops must be pushed over by the July 1 deadline.
records.speaker_role: GSA staff — General Manager Mike Tietze (Formation Environmental, contracted); attribution inferred from context
records.agenda_item: 9. Rules, Regulations and Implementation Guidelines
records.evidence_text: and then the last one is specifying that meter appeals. So those are cases where somebody saying they're going to use mechanical EM or electrical meters to report their groundwater usage that apply to fallowed fields are only applicable if those fallowed fields meet the definition of fallow fields. In other words, specifically what we're getting at is we want those trees or vines to be pushed over.
records.notes: Revisions adopted by Resolution 2026-06 at this meeting (roll call recorded); the 305-acre appeal and ET figures are from the 2026-06-25 board.

records.finding: The GM described two guardrails on fallowed and IFP land: ET screening that no groundwater is applied, and removal of those polygons' ET from the consumed-groundwater totals reported to DWR as the performance metric. Asked about pumping, he said verification covers 'the subtraction side' of the accounting but not the supply side.
records.speaker_role: mixed — GSA staff (General Manager, inferred) answering a board member
records.agenda_item: 10. Incentivized Land Fallowing Program
records.evidence_text: So there's two guardrails there. The first guardrail is that we're verifying that they're not using groundwater so that ET is not consumed. ... For that polygon where we know groundwater is not a applied, we're subtracting that from, from groundwater accounting values so that when we report it to the DWR as our performance metric, it's not counted as groundwater. ... How are we verifying there was no groundwater electrical charge? Are we doing that? So right now we're not doing that. ... we're verifying on the, on the subtraction side of the accounting, but, but not on the, on the supply side.
records.notes: On 2026-02-26 the GM added that ET checks and site visits under the IFP agreement's access right can confirm no irrigation; speaker labels are generic, so attribution is inferred.

records.finding: Incentive agreements are recorded against the enrolled parcels so later buyers are bound: IFP enrollees forfeit allocation on enrolled acreage for the three-year term, and MLRP agreements run ten years from project acceptance. Whole-parcel IFP enrollees may also reclassify to the non-irrigated assessment, repaying the difference if they later revert.
records.quantitative_detail: IFP term 3 reporting periods; MLRP term 10 years from GSA project acceptance (2026-01-22); non-irrigated assessment $1.54/ac (2025-10-14) vs irrigated $17.75/ac (2025-10-23); pilot MLRP agreements all recorded by 2026-07-23; IFP agreements still being re-signed and not yet recorded on 2026-09-08.
records.speaker_role: consultant — legal counsel (Baker Manock & Jensen), attribution inferred
records.agenda_item: 7. Incentivized Land Fallowing Program (b. draft IFP Agreement template)
records.evidence_text: And the notation that the participants will forfeit their allocation for the enrolled acreage for the duration of the program participation, which is three years here. ... And we do recommend that these agreements be reported for enforceability and to make sure that if the property is sold during the three year term, that any subsequent buyers know that those portions of those parcels are and will send program.
records.notes: 'reported' and 'are and will send program' are transcription errors for recorded/enrolled (EKI said the same day agreements are 'recorded with the county'); the same summary says no dryland or cover cropping is permitted on IFP acreage, which conflicts with the GM's 2025-10-23 description.

records.finding: IFP rotation is allowed only within the parcel(s) named in the recorded agreement, with the paid acreage matched every year; staff cautioned that rotating onto fields with different historical use (sweet potatoes versus almonds) changes the savings the ranking assumed. This is a geographic limit on where enrolled demand reduction may move.
records.quantitative_detail: Example discussed: 40 of 160 ac fallowed each year on a 3-year rotation, paid for 40 ac only.
records.speaker_role: mixed — GSA staff (General Manager), legal counsel and ESA consultant (attributions inferred)
records.agenda_item: Incentivized Land Fallowing Program policy (adopted at this meeting)
records.evidence_text: It would have to be whatever we are paying you for, the acreage, that acreage would have to be matched each year. ... I do think, um, part of the ranking process is that we calculate the estimated consumed groundwater savings on each field. So, if you are changing that field, it might have different consumed groundwater savings, and so we need to be careful that It's… if they're going to allow that, that it's similar enough savings. ... we would need to keep any… I'll call it rotational for this discussion, any rotational following of X amount of acreage to the same parcel. Okay. Because we would have to report an agreement against that specific parcel
records.notes: Speakers are not labelled in this transcript; the board left rotation details to individual agreements rather than the policy text.

records.finding: MLRP agreements carry a DOC-required recharge certification that project recharge stays in the subbasin and is not released for pumping during the term, yet landowners still receive a share of recharge credit from MLRP-funded basins under ETSGSA's credit split, which DOC accepts. Grant money is treated as GSA funds in that split.
records.quantitative_detail: Credit split for GSA-incentivized projects: grower 40% during a 3-year recovery period then 80% (GSA water) or 50% then 95% (grower water) (policy adopted 2026-01-22); benefit estimates use a time-weighted 10-year average split (2026-03-26).
records.speaker_role: mixed — consultant (EKI) and Board Chair, confirmed by EKI
records.agenda_item: 8. Multi-Benefit Land Repurposing Program (c. pilot project agreements)
records.evidence_text: Attachment E is the recharge certification. Again this is a doc requirement. So for projects that are claiming recharge as a benefit, the gsa, you know, as part of, as part of the action that you may take today to approve execution of these agreements, you know, you would also be approving that recharge certification which is basically just acknowledging that, you know, recharge that is accruing due to these projects accruing to the sub basin will you know, sort of be held in the basins trust and not released for pumping during the term of the agreement. ... Those basins that are funded by mlrp, there is a credit split with how much benefit that landowner will get based on their MLRP participation. So they will not be getting 100% of the credit for that activity.
records.notes: On 2026-01-22 legal counsel said MLRP law requires recharge to stay in the subbasin and not be available for extraction 'But what we've been told by DOC is that they are still holding to credit split scenario'; how the grower's credited share squares with the certification was not explained.

records.finding: Asked whether fallowing produced real savings, the GM said gross component reductions (about 32,000 AF) exceeded the net GSA-wide reduction partly because some fallowers 'took their allocation and they used it somewhere else'. Leakage from allocation-retaining self-directed fallowing is acknowledged but appears only as the gap between gross and net, not as a tracked quantity.
records.quantitative_detail: Gross component reductions ≈ 32,000 AF vs net 24,256 AF ET below the 171,000 AF baseline (reporting period 2025, single year); self-reported fallow ≈ 5,600 ac (~11,700 AF ET).
records.speaker_role: mixed — board member question; GSA staff (General Manager, inferred) answer
records.agenda_item: 7. FY 2026/2027 SGMA Operational Budget and PMA Budget (demand reduction results)
records.evidence_text: Is that actual groundwater savings or are they just following and then moving that groundwater to still using it somewhere else? Well, if they were using it someone else or somewhere else, it would be showing up in our consumptive use. So some of it is being moved somewhere else. Our overall consumptive use savings were less than, than this total 32,000. And some of that is because of the, the ET and those non reported fields is still being counted as consumptive groundwater use. And some of it is that they took their allocation and they used it somewhere else.
records.notes: The data to quantify reallocation exist at account level in the accounting platform (hence the tool tag; Data Needs also fits); speaker labels are generic.

records.finding: Benefits used to select full-scale MLRP projects are 10-year design estimates of the GSA's share only: recharge from basin footprint, soil hydraulic properties, wetting duration and TID water reliability (about 57% of years), scaled by a time-weighted credit split, plus roughly 2.5 AF/ac/yr of demand reduction for irrigated land removed.
records.quantitative_detail: Reliability ≈ 57% of years; demand reduction ≈ 2.5 AF/ac/yr (spoken as 'two and a half acres per, per acre per year'); 10-year GSA-share benefit / GSA incentive cost examples: 5-ac recharge basin ≈ 17,400 AF / ≈ $620,000 (figure doubtful); ~20-ac creekside basins ≈ 10,000 AF / ≈ $700,000; 18-ac floodwater ponds ≈ 2,500 AF / ≈ $247,000; 30-ac extended fallowing + 1.5-ac basin ≈ 1,300 AF / ≈ $280,000; 40-ac fallowing ≈ 900 [AF] / ≈ $360,000; 110-ac fallowing ≈ 2,500 AF / just under $1M.
records.speaker_role: consultant — EKI Environment & Water (Chris Heppner, MLRP lead)
records.agenda_item: 6. Multi-Benefit Land Repurposing Program
records.evidence_text: And you know, the way that the benefit is estimated, it uses the, you know, the footprint of the basin, in this case 5 acres. It uses the hydraulic properties of the soil underneath. ... It uses the reliability of that water, you know, an estimate, you know, coming from the GSA's agreement with TID on the, you know, sort of availability of replenishment water. It's obviously not every single year. It's closer to, I think 57% of the years. ... So the split percentage that was used in estimating these benefits is the weighted average of like the sort of initial payback period and the post payback period over 10 years.
records.notes: Per-acre factor (≈2.5 AF/ac/yr) differs from Appendix K's 2.9 and CalETa's 2.7 AF/ac (findings 127, 132); a board member queried the 17,400 AF figure for a 5-acre basin; on 2026-05-12 EKI said automated tools generate packet budgets and benefit calculations.

records.finding: ETSGSA reported reporting-period 2025 consumptive groundwater use 24,256 AF below the 171,000 AF GSP baseline against a roughly 17,000 AF ET target. Unreported fallowing detected in Land IQ data was credited only above a 10-year Land IQ/DWR average fallowing rate, an additionality adjustment not covered by the existing finding.
records.quantitative_detail: Single reporting period 2025: baseline ≈ 95,000 irrigated ac, 171,000 AF ET (≈ 211,000 AF extraction); target ≈ 17,000 AF ET (≈ 21,000 AF extraction) reduction; achieved 24,256 AF ET (≈ 30,000 AF extraction) below baseline; allocation ≈ 166,000 AF ET on ~10,000 ac more irrigated land than baseline; unreported fallow ≈ 4,876 ac above the long-term average (10-yr average ≈ 2,200 vs ≈ 7,100 in 2025, spoken as acre-feet); cover crop ≈ 26,000 ac.
records.speaker_role: GSA staff — General Manager Mike Tietze (Formation Environmental, contracted); attribution inferred from context
records.agenda_item: 7. FY 2026/2027 SGMA Operational Budget and PMA Budget (demand reduction results)
records.evidence_text: And so relative to the 171,000 baseline, we achieved a 24,000 acre foot reduction relative to our baseline condition in the GSP or a 29, almost 30,000 acre foot reduction in groundwater extraction. ... We had additional following that was identified from the land IQ data. Now this was almost 5,000 acres above the long term baseline following rate. And what we found when we looked at historical data, land use data reported by Land IQ and DWR over about a 10 year period.
records.notes: 24,256 AF is ET (consumptive use) and ~30,000 AF is extraction, different quantities; finding 133's ~146,000 AF actual matches 171,000 − 24,256; the long-term average figures are spoken as acre-feet but compared with acres.

records.finding: The joint TACs funded a model refinement (Task Order 9) replacing land use frozen at 2015 with post-2023 land use and ET drawn from Land IQ and the GSAs' accounting data, explicitly so that East Turlock's land-use-focused demand management shows up in model projections. Historical GSP water budgets are not to be revised.
records.quantitative_detail: Optional Task Order 9 not-to-exceed $128,900 (approved by the Joint TACs 2026-01-26); land use and ET refined from 2023 onward.
records.speaker_role: consultant — EKI Environment & Water (Amir Mani, joint GSP consultant)
records.meeting_body: Turlock Subbasin Joint Technical Advisory Committees (ETSGSA/WTSGSA)
records.agenda_item: SGMA related updates — groundwater model enhancement work plan
records.evidence_text: But now we are basically 10 years ahead of that Land use a lot has changed in the basin. A projects that specifically the Eastern Telugu GSA is doing focuses on land use, focused on ET and keeping this in 2015 will not be representative of conditions currently. ... Because right now, if you want to for example, show there are some demand management actions being taken place in the basin and how they will work out in 15 years. If we start from 2015 conditions, we are not really showing exactly how it's going to turn out.
records.notes: Index lists this joint meeting under WTSGSA; 'Eastern Telugu GSA' is a transcription of East Turlock GSA; the update targets current water budgets and project effects, per the consultant's 'Yes' to a TAC question.

records.finding: Under the credit split policy (adopted 22 January 2026), the share of surface-water and recharge credit that the GSA keeps from GSA-incentivized projects, MLRP basins included, is not redistributed to accounts but counted as GSA-wide groundwater demand reduction. The recovery rate is pegged to the $316/AF Category 3 fee.
records.quantitative_detail: Recovery period 3 water-receiving years at $316/AF; costed projects ≈ $200–$400/AF, average ≈ $200–250/AF; grower share 40%→80% (GSA incentive + GSA water), 50%→95% (GSA incentive, grower water), 80% (GSA water only), 100% (no GSA role).
records.speaker_role: mixed — TAC member question; GSA staff (General Manager, inferred) answer
records.agenda_item: 6. Policies, Rules and Regulations — draft Consumed Surface Water and Recharge Credit Calculation Policy
records.evidence_text: What happens with the GSA credits? Are those going to be distributed over all the accounts? No, those are taken as groundwater demand reduction. So basically because they're not given to the grower to subtract from their consumptive groundwater use, they're retained as a groundwater sustainability benefit to the gsa.
records.notes: Speaker labels in this transcript are generic; the policy itself was adopted at the 2026-01-22 board meeting.

records.finding: MLRP and IFP project polygons are being digitized in the accounting platform as excluded areas: their ET is not counted and no allocation is issued. Rules and Regulations version 4 (August 2026) wrote project areas and reported fallowed fields into the excluded-area definition; no step comparing excluded polygons' ET with expected savings was described.
records.quantitative_detail: Rules and Regulations version 4 adopted 2026-08-27 (Resolution 2026-06); excluded areas receive no allocation and their ET is not counted.
records.speaker_role: GSA staff — General Manager Mike Tietze (Formation Environmental, contracted); attribution inferred from context
records.agenda_item: 9. Rules, Regulations and Implementation Guidelines (a. proposed updates)
records.evidence_text: Excluded areas, we are starting to digitize project polygons. So MLRP and IFP polygons in the gap and those are going to be excluded areas from groundwater accounting, which means that a, in this case that ET will not be accounted. However, neither will there be an allocation for project areas.
records.notes: ESA said on 2026-03-26 a 'projects module' would also set up each recharge project's credit split per its agreement; the ET data for excluded polygons still exist, so a comparison is computationally possible.

records.section: 2.5 Data Source and ET Product Choice
records.finding: The joint GSP consultant listed published OpenET data, alongside Land IQ ET, Turlock Irrigation District's own ET estimates and East Turlock's accounting platform, as newer ET sources for refining the subbasin model. This is a mention of candidate model inputs, not adoption of OpenET for ETSGSA accounting.
records.speaker_role: consultant — EKI Environment & Water (Amir Mani, joint GSP consultant)
records.meeting_body: Turlock Subbasin Joint Technical Advisory Committees (ETSGSA/WTSGSA)
records.agenda_item: SGMA related updates — groundwater model enhancement work plan
records.evidence_text: So what we intend to do is that now that we have access to land iq, ET data, open ET data is published. TEL aggregation district have their own water budget and the ET estimations. The Easterlock GSA has the groundwater accounting platform and the ET estimations.
records.notes: Finding 164 states OpenET appears in no Turlock document; this is a single passing mention ('TEL aggregation district' = Turlock Irrigation District), so labelled adds rather than contradicts.

records.section: 2.5 Data Source and ET Product Choice
records.finding: TAC members declined to pursue a meter grant because it would undercut Land IQ as the GSA's 'standard' measuring mechanism; meters remain an appeal or backup route. Elsewhere the GM cited Land IQ's own ±5% accuracy claim, and appeals substituting electrical-meter data for Land IQ ET have been decided.
records.quantitative_detail: Land IQ claimed accuracy ±5% (per GM at Stanislaus WAC, 2025-07-30); Land IQ ET/precipitation contract ≈ $125,000 FY 2026-27 vs $131,000 prior year (2026-05-28); electrical-meter appeals need a pump efficiency test every 3 years (rules v4, 2026-08-27); one appeal contesting Land IQ ET with an alternative method reported 2026-04-23.
records.agenda_item: 9. Other GSP implementation matters — grant opportunities
records.evidence_text: I would agree. I think that will confuse our landowners with, you know, we're promoting land IQ as our measuring mechanism. It would I think send the mixed message of but we'll also pay you to go have a meter and go in a completely different measurement method. You know, I mean they can obviously use them for backups but I think our standard is land IQ as the GSA and that's what we should stick with.
records.notes: The speakers are unlabelled TAC members responding to staff's question about a WaterSMART meter grant; no local field validation of Land IQ ET was described.

records.finding: The GM told the board DOC's grant requires direct benefits to disadvantaged communities, which ETSGSA's farmland-based projects do not directly provide; their DAC benefits are acknowledged but, in his words, only qualitative. He proposed setting aside about 10% of the implementation budget for a Delhi community park with Merced County and Leadership Counsel.
records.quantitative_detail: Set-aside ≈ 10% of the project implementation budget (proposal, 2025-09-25); later offer of up to $200,000 from the planning/permitting task for site selection and concept design (2026-03-10, 2026-04-23).
records.speaker_role: GSA staff — General Manager Mike Tietze (Formation Environmental, contracted); attribution inferred from context
records.agenda_item: 8. Update on MLRP Program
records.evidence_text: So, um, one of the requirements of the, um, MORP grant program and funding legislation. is that there has to be some direct benefit to disadvantaged communities. And most of our projects, you know, where they do the most good in terms of sustainability, is… in the heart of our farmland, and so the benefits to DICs are real and acknowledged, um, both in terms of, you know, economics and flood attenuation and… groundwater, uh, benefits that, you know, in the area and downstream. ... Our take is that, um, for us to… meet the DAC direct benefit goals that we need to have some amount of set-aside. ... I can't point to anything except, like, a qualitative benefit
records.notes: Transcript labels the speaker as the Chair; content (his talks with the county and DOC) identifies the GM; 'MORP' and 'DICs' are transcriptions of MLRP and DACs.

records.finding: The GM framed MLRP creekside basins on Sand and Mustang Creeks, fed by the planned Erie pipeline, as multi-benefit projects for recharge, flood attenuation, habitat and runoff water quality, and proposed MLRP-funded mobile gauging stations because creek flow data are sparse. No co-benefit metric was named.
records.speaker_role: GSA staff — General Manager Mike Tietze (Formation Environmental, contracted); attribution inferred from context
records.agenda_item: 7. Project updates
records.evidence_text: And by putting it into sand, by putting water into Sand Creek and Mustang Creek and putting creekside basins along those locations, we can have multi benefit projects that provide recharge, attenuate flood flow, improve habitat and improve water quality in runoff overall. And so in order to do that, we would like to start gathering information regarding the hydrologic behavior of Sand Creek and Mustang Creek as those data are currently pretty sparse.
records.notes: Gauging stations were still at proposal stage on 2026-09-24; transcript labels are generic.

records.finding: DOC would not allow MLRP funds for the county's preferred Delhi park site because it has not been farmed since about 2000, so the park MOU is on hold and ETSGSA is meeting DOC on other ways to meet the direct-DAC-benefit requirement, including grower-hosted education days. A year after it was raised, the requirement remained unmet.
records.quantitative_detail: Site not farmed since ≈ 2000; ETSGSA had offered up to $200,000 of MLRP planning funds for site selection and concept design (2026-04-23); requirement first raised 2025-08-28.
records.speaker_role: GSA staff — General Manager Mike Tietze (Formation Environmental, contracted); attribution inferred from context
records.agenda_item: 8. Multi-Benefit Land Repurposing Program
records.evidence_text: Merced county is interested in a particular site that seems to be a good fit. However, it has not been used for agricultural purposes since about the year 2000. And in consulting with the DOC, they indicated that unfortunately, because of the length of time since it's been used for agricultural purposes that they would not approve spending MLRP funds on that project. ... So the MoU is currently on hold ... A meeting with Chris and I to talk about what our options are going to be for meeting the grant requirement for direct disadvantaged community benefits.
records.notes: A board member suggested the eligibility cutoff is land farmed since 2015/SGMA; the GM did not confirm a cutoff year.

records.finding: ETSGSA publicly presented its MLRP scoring rubric: four DOC benefit categories, groundwater weighted highest, plus a 10% 'other', with sub-criteria including cost per acre-foot, share of area in habitat, and proximity to priority action areas, disadvantaged communities and at-risk domestic wells. Finding 139 says there is no DAC scoring input; Finding 153 says the criteria are published in no reviewed document.
records.quantitative_detail: Ratings low/medium/high (some binary or 4-level) × sub-criterion weights → total score 0–1 (TAC, 2025-11-18) or 0–100 (board, 2025-11-20); 'other' category 10%; CDFW habitat-connectivity layer used; February 2026 revision merged community and economic benefits and added surface-water-use, multibenefit pond/floodplain and general-feasibility criteria (TAC-approved); example totals 56, 55 and 45 points (2026-03-26).
records.speaker_role: consultant — EKI Environment & Water (Chris Heppner, MLRP lead)
records.agenda_item: 7. Multi-Benefit Land Repurposing Program (application and scoring process)
records.evidence_text: These four categories are, you know, coming from the DOC guidelines and requirements. So habitat, sorry, groundwater sustainability, benefits to habitat, benefits to disadvantaged communities and benefits to the local economy. ... the groundwater sustainability category is the sort of primary category. So that one does get the sort of greatest weight in the scoring process. ... For example cost effectiveness in terms of dollars per acre, feet of groundwater, demand reduction. ... Some of these are spatial factors that depend on the project location. For example, it's location relative to priority action areas or location relative to disadvantaged Communities or quote unquote, at risk wells, domestic wells, or you know, habitat connectivity.
records.notes: Numeric weights were on slides and are not in the transcript; finding 141 (no DAC mapping layer) is also in tension, since DAC proximity is a spatial sub-criterion, but the layer used is not named; the board approved the application package 2025-11-20.

records.finding: The scoring workflow changed: the TAC asked to be removed, leaving the Stakeholder Advisory Committee as the only review between staff scoring and the board. The GM said the SAC exists to meet DOC's community-involvement requirement and is mostly Delhi residents with a few farmers; board members asked for more landowners on it.
records.speaker_role: mixed — consultant (EKI) and GSA staff (General Manager Mike Tietze)
records.agenda_item: 8. Multi-Benefit Land Repurposing Program (b. scoring process)
records.evidence_text: And at the last TAC meeting there was a, you know, discussion about, you know, roles within the workflow. And the TAC basically suggested that, you know, they could be, they could be removed from the workflow and, and to really just kind of keep the, the SAC as the main sort of post, post staff stakeholder group to, to weigh in on things before it comes to the, to the board. ... The SAC is something that is being instituted to meet a requirement from the Department of Conservation for community involvement. ... So we have a few community members, the majority of them are from Delhi and we also have a few farmers that have been participating
records.notes: Finding 153 describes ranking reviewed by both a TAC and a SAC; at the 2026-03-24 SAC meeting members rated each top project 1–5 with written comments.

records.finding: When the rubric was applied, constructed basins scored highest on cost-effectiveness and groundwater benefit, so staff split the remaining ~$4.1M into separate basin and non-basin budgets to keep a mix of project types. The scores therefore rank projects within buckets rather than across the whole portfolio.
records.quantitative_detail: 20 applications split into 28 component projects; top 9 selected (5 basin ≈ $2–2.5M; 4 non-basin ≈ $1.5M); 2 alternates per bucket; total ≈ $4.1M; ≈ $1M cap per applicant; SAC ratings on a 1–5 scale.
records.speaker_role: consultant — EKI Environment & Water (Chris Heppner, MLRP lead)
records.agenda_item: 6. Multi-Benefit Land Repurposing Program
records.evidence_text: we found that constructed basin projects generally scored the highest, you know, according to the rubric, they get a lot of points for being cost effective and providing, you know, high groundwater sustainability benefits. ... And so we wanted to, you know, find a way to maintain diversity of project types. So we decided that it would be best to sort of divide the total available funds into, you know, a couple of sort of buckets, one for basin projects and one for non basin projects.
records.notes: Board gave direction (no formal vote) to proceed with the nine projects; projects were presented anonymously at the board's request.

records.finding: ETSGSA also prices the multibenefit obligation outside the per-acre rate ladder: MLRP construction incentives reimburse up to 75% of bids versus 50% for non-MLRP projects because of the ten-year term and multibenefit requirement, and the credit split assumes a 50% MLRP cost share for the same reason. Adding DAC education days earns extra scoring points.
records.quantitative_detail: Type 2 maximum reimbursement 75% (MLRP) vs 50% (non-MLRP) of contractor bids or landowner estimates; example cap: 10 AF basin capacity × $5,400/AF = $54,000; credit-split cost-share assumption 50% for MLRP (2026-01-13); board member challenge: 8.2 ac orchard swale rewilding = $106,600 of Type 1 over 10 years (≈ $1,300/ac/yr) vs IFP $730/ac/yr (2026-02-26).
records.speaker_role: consultant — EKI Environment & Water (Chris Heppner, MLRP lead)
records.agenda_item: 8. Update on MLRP Program (a. draft Incentive Payment Procedures)
records.evidence_text: we've actually made the MLRP project, um, percentage, um. Higher than it was previously, so it's set at 75% here. And the reason is, is that, you know, MLRP projects, um. You know, they do have… a greater commitment, a 10-year commitment, and they also have a requirement to achieve multiple benefits
records.notes: Incentive Payment Procedures adopted by the board at this meeting; the 50% credit-split assumption and the DAC education points come from later meetings (GM statements).

records.finding: Each MLRP agreement attaches a project-specific benefit summary of quantified benefits that the participant must maintain for ten years from GSA acceptance, backed by a GSA right of access and inspection. No procedure was described for checking delivered benefits against that summary.
records.quantitative_detail: Agreement term 10 years from GSA project acceptance.
records.speaker_role: mixed — legal counsel (Baker Manock & Jensen, inferred) and consultant (EKI)
records.agenda_item: 7. Multi-Benefit Land Repurposing Program (b. template MLRP Landowner Agreement)
records.evidence_text: We've developed, you know, as part of those agreements, a sort of quick benefits summary that will allow, you know, all parties to be clear on, you know, sort of what are the, what are the quantified benefits that are being, you know, proposed and included in each of the projects. ... So first the term of the agreement will be 10 years and that'll be 10 years from a project acceptance by the GSA. ... and then the 10 year, 10 year period the benefits that were described in that benefit summary and then the project packet they must be maintained by the project participant. The second key provision that GFC really emphasized is the ability to access and the right to inspect.
records.notes: 'GFC' appears to be a transcription of DOC; the board approved the template with a fixed 10-year term.

records.finding: Staff proposed project-specific operating plans as a condition of final MLRP project acceptance, scaled to the GSA dollars involved; the GM floated RCD checks of vegetative cover every three years. TAC members resisted added paperwork, and EKI said neither DOC nor other block grantees have issued operating guidance for recharge-type MLRP projects.
records.speaker_role: mixed — consultant (EKI) and GSA staff (General Manager, inferred)
records.agenda_item: 6. Multi-Benefit Land Repurposing Program (MLRP)
records.evidence_text: having that plan in place would be a condition for final project acceptance. So it's not something that we would put off indefinitely into the future and accept the project without the plan being in place. ... So I, I think developing a simple form to do that and if, if your project is rewilding an orchard swale, then that might involve, you know, every three years having the RCD go out to see if the covered crop is still behaving as it should
records.notes: A proposal, not adopted; the RCD check would add a third-party look to the landowner self-monitoring described in finding 327; TAC direction was to keep it light and check peer grantees' practice.

records.finding: For recharge credits from MLRP and non-MLRP basins, staff set a phased method: year one, SSURGO conductivity × area × inundation time; from year two, metered inflow minus outflow with a 5% loss deduction, or on-site percolation tests with staff gauge and camera or transducer; from year three, one measured method is required.
records.quantitative_detail: Evaporation/loss correction 5%; phase-in over years 1–3; annual basin-scale percolation test required from the third year of operation (2026-07-23); 7–8 recharge facility registrants in 2026; at one site measured infiltration was 'several times higher' than SSURGO indicated.
records.speaker_role: consultant — EKI Environment & Water (Chris Heppner, MLRP lead)
records.agenda_item: 6. Multi-Benefit Land Repurposing Program (MLRP) — recharge monitoring and quantification
records.evidence_text: pertains to both MLRP projects that are, that involve some sort of recharge as well as non MLRP projects. ... method one, you're looking at the recharge based on published saturated hydraulic conductivity values from sergo. ... And then method 2b is that rate and duration based approach similar to method one. But in this case we have on site percolation tests. ... And then moving beyond that, year three and beyond, we would require at that point implementation of either method 2a or 2b at all recharge facilities, registered recharge facilities, in order to qualify for recharge credits.
records.notes: Guidelines adopted as staff implementation guidelines (presented to TAC and board); a TAC member questioned stage-only estimates where outflow is unmeasured.

records.finding: ETSGSA is extending its accounting platform, using development funded through the California Water Data Consortium's recharge accounting project, so MLRP monitoring photos and measurements can be submitted online on custom forms assigned to each registered project. IFP polygons were uploaded; MLRP reporting was targeted for late 2026; recharge calculations stay in offline spreadsheets.
records.quantitative_detail: IFP project polygons uploaded by 2026-08-11; project reporting forms targeted before end of 2026; 7 recharge facility operators awaiting registration.
records.speaker_role: mixed — GSA staff (General Manager, inferred) and consultant (ESA, Savannah Tjaden)
records.agenda_item: 9. Other GSP implementation matters — current and anticipated updates to the Groundwater Accounting Platform
records.evidence_text: there are several improvements that are currently being made that allow registration of projects within the groundwater accounting platform, and that will very soon be available for us not to just upload the project polygons, but also monitoring information and various other different documents that are associated with those projects. So that when we implement a project that requires monitoring, like our mlrp, projects may require photos to be taken or measurements to be submitted that those will be able to be submitted online ... So it would be GSA managers can create custom monitoring and reporting forms based on the requirements per project type or program and then assign them to a registered project.
records.notes: In development, not yet live; ESA described the consortium project as DWR-funded; still a document repository, with no stated link to the consumptive-use ledger.

records.finding: The GM cited hydrographs that rebound quickly where surface water arrived but keep falling in the cone of depression when recommending $2.5M of IFP rather than $1M as 'insurance', and the board approved it. The GM had earlier said pilot MLRP projects were sited in or beside areas below interim milestones.
records.quantitative_detail: IFP funding approved up to $2.5M per year for one 3-year cycle (2026-01-22); scenarios evaluated $260,000, $1M and $2M; ≈ $2.3M then in PMA accounts.
records.speaker_role: GSA staff — General Manager Mike Tietze (Formation Environmental, contracted); attribution inferred from context
records.agenda_item: 10. Incentivized Land Fallowing Program
records.evidence_text: The indicators that we have from looking at hydrographs is that in areas where we have surface water available, such as the area near the Highline Canal, that we're seeing a pretty rapid response from providing that surface water and getting people on surface water when it's available. And what we're seeing in the con of depression is that there's more downward momentum in that area, which indicates to us that it's likely that it's going to require more effort. That effort comes through a following. So a million dollars may be enough, but $2.5 million buys us more insurance moving forward.
records.notes: The hydrograph reading is qualitative and no causal attribution to fallowing was claimed (on 2026-05-28 the GM said decline had slowed near fallowing 'but it hasn't turned around').

records.finding: Annual percolation-test results will feed back directly: a declining rate lowers the recharge credit on self-funded basins, while on MLRP basins with required recharge benefits the GSA will instruct the grower to restore performance. In April the TAC discussed borrowing MLRP's pre-defined reporting requirements for all recharge registrations.
records.speaker_role: GSA staff — General Manager Mike Tietze (Formation Environmental, contracted); attribution inferred from context
records.agenda_item: 9. Rules, Regulations and Implementation Guidelines
records.evidence_text: But once it's a requirement going to be performed annually, we'll let the growers know the results. That daily rate will be used to calculate their recharge credit. So if their basin silts up, they'll get a lower credit and we'll advise them of, you know, that it seems to have decreased and then they have the choice of going in and disking or mucking it out to increase that recharge rate. If it is an MLRP project and there are certain benefits that are, that were required to be provided in terms of recharge rates, then we will instruct the grower to maintain their pod.
records.notes: A stated mechanism, not yet applied (annual tests become mandatory from a facility's third year); 'pod' = pond.

records.finding: The GM said what follows the DOC-required ten years is undecided: ETSGSA might allow shorter add-on terms or 'simply consider accounts settled', and it intends incentives, and the fees that fund them, to stop once the basin is sustainable, a 'transitional thing over the next 10 to 20 years'. No post-term monitoring was mentioned.
records.quantitative_detail: MLRP commitment 10 years (DOC requirement); incentives envisaged as transitional over 10–20 years; IFP terms 3 years.
records.speaker_role: GSA staff — General Manager Mike Tietze (Formation Environmental, contracted); attribution inferred from context
records.agenda_item: 8. Update on MLRP Program
records.evidence_text: Uh, okay, so MLRP, uh, the program from the DOC requires a 10-year commitment? And what we do with that, after we start to fund it from our own dollars may be different. But we haven't determined that yet. ... what we may decide is that for land that's repurposed under MLRP, let's say orchard soil rewilding, that after 10 years, we simply consider accounts settled, and you can do with it what you want ... What we want to do is, once we get to that sustainable condition, we want to stop paying incentive payments And then we want to stop collecting the money that enables those incentive payments from you. So we kind of, you know, so this is just intended to be a transitional thing over the next 10 to 20 years.
records.notes: A board member noted ten years of MLRP fallowing payments approaches land purchase cost; on 2025-10-23 the GM said GSA-funded MLRP 'will be phased in after our grant funding... is all used up'.

records.finding: Presenting East Turlock's programme to the county committee, the GM said the GSA already fee-funds the IFP and non-MLRP projects, plans to pivot to paying for MLRP itself, and expects escalating groundwater fees to keep land repurposed after the ten-year term. None of this identifies funding for post-grant monitoring.
records.quantitative_detail: IFP $730/ac/yr (3-year term); MLRP multibenefit fallowing $890/ac/yr (10-year term); ≈ $3–4M unallocated in the GSA's MLRP/PMA reserve (2026-01-13); deferred projects to be funded from 'whatever funding is available... including our groundwater use fees' if Round 3 fails (2026-07-14); Category 3 fee rising from ≈ $138 to ≈ $316/AF (2026-03-26).
records.speaker_role: GSA staff — ETSGSA General Manager Mike Tietze presenting to the county committee (inferred from introduction)
records.meeting_body: Stanislaus County Water Advisory Committee (ETSGSA GM presentation)
records.agenda_item: ETSGSA overview presentation — MLRP in the East Turlock Subbasin
records.evidence_text: And the idea with the MLRP is we pay a little bit more but the expectation is that we subsidize it, we incentivize it for 10 years and after that hopefully it becomes permanent. Because for it not to become permanent is actually going to cost the growers some more money. Right. Because our fees escalate over time ... records.finding: The IFP, ETSGSA's fee-funded non-MLRP fallowing programme, was adopted in October 2025 and funded at up to $2.5M in January 2026, but withdrawals and surface-water corrections cut approved acreage from 3,448 to 2,854 acres and the commitment to $2,083,289. records.finding: IFP savings are counted as each field's average 2023–2024 consumed groundwater use, surface-water corrected, times its acres, and fields are ranked by cost per acre-foot at $730/ac/yr. The board funded fields above 1.5 AF/ac: 3,448 acres at about $370/AF and roughly 7,500 AF a year of pumping reduction, before later reconciliation.
records.quantitative_detail: Applications: 14 applicants, 128 fields, 4,525 ac, average 2023–24 use 0–2.6 AF/ac (≈ 7,741 AF total); scenarios (per year, 3-year commitment): $260K → 7 fields/395 ac/932 AF; $1M → 32/1,372 ac/2,993 AF; $2M → 60/2,768 ac/5,521 AF; cost $310–379/AF, net $288–351/AF after $50/AF avoided TID transitional-water payment; selected ≥ 1.5 AF/ac: 79 fields, 3,448 ac, consumptive savings transcribed 'just under 68800' AF (≈ 6,750–6,800 AF implied by 7,500 AF × 0.9), $370/AF, ≈ 7,500 AF pumping at 90% irrigation efficiency (2026-02-26).
records.speaker_role: GSA staff — General Manager Mike Tietze (Formation Environmental, contracted); attribution inferred from context
records.agenda_item: 10. Incentivized Land Fallowing Program
records.evidence_text: So for each of those, we calculate the consumptive groundwater use for the submitted fields, including a surface water correction. And the consumptive groundwater use gets, gets calculated this year for the average between the 2023 and the 2024. So that historical average gets counted for each field and then multiplied by the area of the field to see how much water per acre wood fallowing of that field yield. And then we rank those fields from lowest to highest in terms of cost per acre foot of consumptive groundwater use reduction. ... So for every acre foot that we save from our following program, that's $50 less that we have to pay for for transitional water to tid.
records.notes: Savings are ex-ante (historical use × acres), not measured after enrolment; the consumptive-savings figure is garbled in the transcript and inferred; the 2025-10-14 TAC was told the budget is a judgement checked against the 17,100 AF target net of other actions and GSA-wide hydrographs.

records.finding: The new MLRP Stakeholder Advisory Committee sits in project selection as an advisory step only: staff scored applications, the SAC rated the nine top-ranked projects 1-5 with written comments, staff summarised the ratings for the board, and the board gave direction. records.finding: ETSGSA's GM separates indirect DAC benefits of farmland MLRP projects (economics, flood attenuation, groundwater) from the direct benefit DOC requires, and proposed meeting it with a Delhi community park carrying a recharge element, funded by about 10% of the project implementation budget. records.section: 3.1.4 Domestic Well Protection as an Equity Outcome
records.finding: Answering DWR's corrective action, the consultant redid the well impact analysis using top of perforations for domestic wells (stricter than the midpoint test the GSAs disputed in comment responses) and reported results by well use type. It found few added impacts at MTs or 2027 IMs and no SMC change; no result was split by DAC status.
records.quantitative_detail: ~6,400 wells (4,300 domestic); ~250 wells (~4%) impacted at 2015 conditions; added impacts at 2027 IMs ~1% of wells, mostly domestic, central/eastern subbasin; preliminary (Mar 2026): 42 domestic wells fully dewatered at MTs vs 62 at IMs
records.agenda_item: 9. SGMA update: well impact analysis (RCA 1)
records.evidence_text: So for domestic wells we used a conservative threshold as the top of perforations. And for non domestic wells we used the midpoint of the screened interval. ... So in summary, the revised well impact analysis demonstrates that few additional impacts at The MT or 2027 interim milestones are likely to occur relative to 2015 conditions. ... there is no need or explanation for this analysis coupled with the groundwater level smc. So there would be no change to the groundwater level smc.
records.notes: Best Management Practices also applies (stricter domestic-well threshold); the consultant said in Feb 2026 it did not expect the redo to change any SMC before running it.
