records.finding: To meet DWR corrective actions the GSAs adopted a representative water-quality network built mainly on public water suppliers' compliance wells (including Delhi and Keyes districts) plus TID drainage and GSA wells, sampling eight constituents with MTs at the MCL unless pre-2015 levels exceed it. No domestic wells were named in the network.
records.quantitative_detail: COCs: arsenic, nitrate, PCE, 1,2,3-TCP, TDS, uranium, manganese, DBCP; nitrate annually, others every 3 years; ~$17,000 per 3 years (WTSGSA) and ~$12,000 per 3 years (ETSGSA); UR: >1 representative sample in a principal aquifer over MT for 3 consecutive years and attributable to GSA action or inaction
records.speaker_role: GSA staff — TID Water Resources Analyst for WTSGSA
records.agenda_item: G2. Groundwater Quality Monitoring Network and Approach
records.evidence_text: we will be using existing water quality monitoring efforts by the public water suppliers who already have to do monitoring for water quality to make sure they're following state drinking water requirements. So EKI reached out and coordinated with the cities of Modesto, Ceres and Turlock, the Hilmar and Delhi community county water districts, and the Keys Community Service District. ... So the constituents of concern that we will be monitoring include arsenic, nitrate, PCE, 123 TCP, total dissolved solids, uranium and then manganese and DBCP were also added to for DWR's comment.
records.notes: Whether finding 211's 160 domestic wells remain in the wider GAMA-based assessment was not stated; the WTSGSA board approved the approach and the joint TAC reviewed it on 2026-08-11.

records.finding: Under an MOU, the Valley Water Collaborative offers residents free domestic-well testing and replacement water and will publicise the GSAs' well mitigation plan and refer dry wells, while the GSAs share nitrate-exceedance data and use water-quality data to site replacement wells. WTSGSA minutes say the GSAs are not expected to fund VWC under current agreements.
records.quantitative_detail: Nitrate drinking-water standard 10 mg/L; VWC Early Action Plan running since ~8 May 2021; SAFER-funded testing for other contaminants since ~1 Jan 2022
records.agenda_item: 9. Draft MOU between ETSGSA and Valley Water Collaborative
records.evidence_text: VWC agrees that as part of its Early Action Plan outreach efforts, VWC will provide residents throughout the Turlock Subbasin with information regarding the two GSAs Well Mitigation Implementation Plan as long as such information is provided to the VWC for dissemination. ... The two GSAs agree that in the implementation of the Well Mitigation Implementation Plan , the GSAs will consult available information regarding water quality and if a replacement well is installed the GSAs will endeavor to install a replacement well that is constructed to draw water from a level where groundwater meets primary drinking water standards.
records.notes: Also answers COM-3.3.2c (water-quality data used in replacement-well siting); WTSGSA adopted the MOU as Resolution 2025-03 on 19 June 2025 per minutes in the 2025-09-11 packet.

records.finding: Water-quality data reach SGMA compliance only through an attribution test: in WY 2025 four first-time MT exceedances (two 1,2,3-TCP, one nitrate, one arsenic) were investigated, judged unrelated to groundwater levels or GSA actions, and so not counted toward undesirable results. The attribution method was not described.
records.quantitative_detail: 4 first-time exceedances, WY 2025 (2 x 1,2,3-TCP, 1 nitrate, 1 arsenic)
records.agenda_item: WY 2025 Annual Report: groundwater quality
records.evidence_text: If there is a first time exceedance, then that's the one that we need to investigate. If it seems like it's caused by GSAs or by groundwater management, then that's exceeding undesirable result triggers. If not, then it's not. ... So we had four of these exceedances the first time exceedances. Two of them were for 1, 2, 3 TCP. We had one nitrate and we had one arsenic. We investigated all four of these. We didn't find any correlation meaningful to groundwater levels. We did not find any correlation with GSA actions.
records.notes: DWR's corrective action later led the GSAs to redefine the water-quality UR to cover degradation from GSA 'action or inaction' (2026-08-14).

records.section: 3.3.3 Domestic Wells and Community Water System Consolidation
records.finding: Domestic-well data in the GSA record come from the state well completion report database, not a GSA inventory: about 4,300 domestic wells, some located only to a township-range centroid, and the consultant said the analysis cannot exclude wells no longer in use, the same gap the GSAs cited when declining a distributional analysis.
records.quantitative_detail: ~6,400 supply wells built since 1970 (4,300 domestic); ~6,000 with screen data, ~360 with total depth only
records.agenda_item: 9. SGMA update: well impact analysis (RCA 1)
records.evidence_text: We have about 6,400 wells across the three types. 4,300 of those are domestic. Of those, approximately 6,400 we have, we have screen information for the vast majority, approximately 6,000. And then there are about 360 wells that we only have total depth for. The location data we have for these is sometimes just the center of the township and range. ... this analysis does not factor in wells that may no longer be in use but are in still in the OSCAR data set.
records.notes: On 2026-07-23 ETSGSA staff confirmed domestic wells pumping under about 2 AF/yr are exempt from its well registration (transcript garbled as '280ft per year'), so no GSA registry of domestic wells exists.

records.finding: Community data now enter MLRP decision support: the scoring rubric includes proximity to disadvantaged communities and to historically dry or at-risk domestic wells, and the top-ranked basin project was credited for being close to such wells. Staff also reported a DAC-benefit layer added to Sustainable Conservation's recharge tool.
records.quantitative_detail: Top-ranked Project 15: 5-acre recharge basin, ~17,400 AF benefit over 10 years, ~$620,000 incentive, score 56
records.agenda_item: MLRP update: full-scale project recommendations
records.evidence_text: Key scoring factors include, you know, high cost effectiveness. This is in the subsidence priority area. It does leverage surface water supplies that are available. It's close to some historically dry or at risk wells.
records.notes: The DAC-layer remark (2026-04-23) is garbled ('added the grant viewer and disadvantaged community benefit layer to the grant'), so which tool holds the layer is uncertain.

records.finding: Of the named tools only DWR's SGMA Data Viewer is used (data uploads, InSAR subsidence, telemetry from DWR monitoring wells). The well impact analysis used DWR well completion reports and a Community Water Center dewatering graphic; the Dry Well Reporting System, SAFER dashboard, Drinking Water Tool and CalEnviroScreen were never named as used.
records.agenda_item: SGMA implementation update (EKI)
records.evidence_text: So GSA has conducted their fall 2025 groundwater sampling and measurement data was QA QC'd and uploaded to the SGMA Data Viewer by EKI and Provostin Pritchard before the deadline.
records.notes: No finding in the file addresses named tools (COM-3.3.4b); CalEnviroScreen appears only in TID's non-SGMA 2026 hazard mitigation plan and was excluded.

records.finding: The GSAs funded a data management system and a Power BI GSP Implementation Dashboard (groundwater conditions, project tracking, data download). Pitched in 2025 as letting people check progress online, it was described on delivery as for member agencies, with no domestic-well, dry-well or DAC data described, so finding 201's community-facing gap remains.
records.quantitative_detail: Optional Task 8 ~$50,000 ($50,398 proposed, approved Apr 2026); dashboard completed by Aug 2026
records.agenda_item: SGMA implementation update (EKI)
records.evidence_text: We also completed the GSP implementation Dashboard for the TELLOC South Basin. I have some screenshots on the right side. This basically provides access to the member NGC's to have to basically review at their convenience the current status and historical status of compliance with the gsp. ... And a third one is it has a tab now for the member users to actually download the data that we use on their own and do their own analysis.
records.notes: Audience is inconsistent: the DMS was designed with 'private and public' sides (2026-04-14) and a download portal 'for anyone' was promised (2026-06-09), but public access was never confirmed.

records.finding: Delhi residents now address the ETSGSA board in person: a Delhi MAC member said residents surveyed the community and that Delhi has no gathering place, backing a park request. The board backed an MOU for park design, but DOC's eligibility ruling later stalled it.
records.speaker_role: public commenter — Delhi Municipal Advisory Council member
records.agenda_item: 2. Public comment
records.evidence_text: We did an application with Paviana, my mom and Blanca and we did a survey with some of the Delhi community and they we send it and it got approved for that how we got the one point million dollars ... So I have all the our history and how we started our plan, our park and community because Delhi doesn't have like that kind of like place to go because we have to go either Turlock or Merced or other cities.
records.notes: Transcript garbles the commenter's town ('Doha') and names; the request is for a community facility, not data, and finding 171 concerns the GSP comment record, so this adds a later in-person channel rather than contradicting it.

records.finding: The findings cite a provisional SVIHM; on 2025-11-13 the Board received a multi-agency update of the USGS final SVIHM (released April 2025) and made the model files public. The consultant said river-aquifer interaction was significantly improved, including removal of modeled drain tile in upper 180/400 and Forebay that took too much river recharge.
records.quantitative_detail: USGS final SVIHM released April 2025; updated SVIHM and seawater intrusion model both simulate through 2022; Board receipt 2025-11-13
records.agenda_item: 6.2 Salinas Valley Integrated Hydrologic Model 2025 Update
records.evidence_text: The USGS released the final their SVIHM in April of this year. It gave us a chance to review. It gave us a chance to recommend improvements to it. Based on those recommended improvements, a group of organizations, a group of agencies and their consultants all worked on updating the svihm. ... Another larger, large improvement was the Salinas River. The interaction between the Salinas river and the aquifers, We've improved that significantly right now. ... Yes, that has been removed. That was the result of us improving the interaction between the river and the aquifers. It allowed us to remove that drain tile. That drain tile was taking away too much river recharge.
records.notes: Whether the revised river-aquifer interaction changes the Amendment 1 Table 5-7 depletion figures was not presented at any meeting reviewed.

records.finding: Pumping inputs to the valley-wide model that simulates river leakage remain approximate: the consultant said pumping location and depth were being refined from reported extraction data, the model cannot represent individual fields, and well information is still lacking for many wells. The findings describe the model type but not these input gaps.
records.agenda_item: 4.1 SVIHM/SWIM Overview
records.evidence_text: And there were some issues about municipal and agricultural pumping, location and depth. Working on those also trying to get as accurate as possible both location of pumping and depth of pumping. Like I said earlier, this model, it won't tell you exactly what's happening on your piece of land, but we do want to say in an area that we know how much pumping is coming from a general area and at what depth. ... We still don't have a lot of information on a lot of those wells. That's part of our what we're working on this year.
records.notes: The second quoted sentence was said of the seawater intrusion model, which shares the valley-wide model's pumping inputs; committees also flagged double counting between riparian surface-water and groundwater extraction reports (2026-01-22, 2026-06-12).

records.finding: April 2026 demand-management model runs reported that pumping cuts raise groundwater levels and reduce Salinas River stream recharge, i.e. less pumping-induced depletion, but gave no volume and judged results only against groundwater-level criteria, with reservoir releases held at baseline. The model produces ISW-relevant output that is not reported against the ISW criteria.
records.quantitative_detail: Illustrative cuts from 2030 to avoid groundwater-level undesirable results by 2040-41: 180-Foot Aquifer 18-27%, 400-Foot Aquifer 27-36%, Eastside 17-25%; Forebay 9% run raised levels 1-5 ft with minor decrease in stream recharge; no stream-recharge volumes stated
records.agenda_item: 6.2 Groundwater Impacts of Demand Management
records.evidence_text: Interestingly, when you raise groundwater levels, if you have a stream and especially where there are some holes in it, you get less stream recharge as well. ... When you had higher groundwater levels due to reduced pumping, you generally got less. It decreased the stream recharge. Right. Ground levels are coming up, especially along the Salinas river. ... And then as I mentioned in the beginning we held reservoir operations the same as in the baseline.
records.notes: Stream recharge here is modeled river leakage, the counterpart of depletion; the presenter called the runs illustrative, not predictive.

records.finding: For the 2027 amendment the mapped ISW extent was re-derived from the updated model using a 10%-of-months connection cutoff (previously 50%), excluding areas over the Salinas Valley Aquitard but keeping southern 180/400 reaches underlain only by shallow clays. Staff said the mapped extent is largely the same as before.
records.quantitative_detail: Connection cutoff: groundwater at or above channel bottom in more than 10% of simulated months (previously 50%); simulated period 1968-2022
records.speaker_role: consultant — Staffan Schorr, Montgomery & Associates (with GSA presenter)
records.meeting_body: SVBGSA 180/400-Ft Aquifer Subbasin Committee (joint meeting with Eastside Committee)
records.agenda_item: 4.3 Periodic Evaluation - New Information Collected/Data Gaps Filled
records.evidence_text: we're looking at the interconnected surface water analysis that we've done for the gsp and we've updated that for the amendment. And the map here, it shows the locations of the ISW shown in blue. And it's a few revisions from the previous mapped extents of these, but it's largely the same. ... We did take a more of a cautious approach. So you'll see in the southern part of the 18400 where it's. There are shallow clays, but not the Salinas Valley aquitard. There may or may not be connectivity, but it's mapped just in case there might be. ... And then we lowered the threshold that we use for identifying the ISW locations from 50% to 10% of the time it's connected. What that means is if the groundwater levels are at or above the channel bottom for more than 10% of the months of this, the simulated model period from 1968 to 2022. ... And then we clipped out where the sva, the aqua tartar exists because we don't, there's not going to be any connection there.
records.notes: Also answers ISW-1.5b and ISW-1.6b; at the 2026-06-12 Forebay/Upper Valley meeting staff said 10%, 50% and 90% cutoffs gave nearly the same extent.

records.finding: The SVOM baseline assumes reservoir releases strictly follow permit and fishery minimum-flow rules. A Coalition representative said MCWRA cut minimum flows below permit levels in 2014-16, and the consultant agreed the model would release more than was actually released then. This tests finding 249's reliance on reservoir operations to judge pumping depletion not unreasonable.
records.quantitative_detail: Drought years cited: 2013-2016; no flow volumes stated
records.speaker_role: mixed — public commenter Nancy Isakson (Salinas Valley Water Coalition) and consultant Derek Williams (M&A)
records.agenda_item: 2.2 Salinas Valley Operations Model (SVOM) Update
records.evidence_text: the model includes the operational scenarios as to how the reservoirs are operated pursuant to their water right permits pursuant to certain fishery targets and minimum flow requirements during 14, 15, 16. That was the time when the Water Resource Agency Board chose to reduce the minimum flows from that required in the permit. ... You are also correct that it does not make a decision of I am going to change the rules, I am going to reduce flows or anything like that. It sticks very strictly to the rules that are set for it. So that would be another reason why it releases more water than might have been released during the 2013, 14, 15 period.
records.notes: The claim that minimum flows were cut is the public commenter's; the consultant confirmed only that the model follows the operating rules.

records.finding: DWR's corrective action to bring the conservation-release period under the ISW criteria is the one corrective action the 2027 draft amendments do not address. The consultant told the Board the change waits for DWR's unreleased ISW policy guidance and advised not getting ahead of DWR, so the carve-out in finding 231 continues.
records.quantitative_detail: Draft amendments released October 2026; written comments by 2026-11-18; public hearing 2027-01-14; submission January 2027
records.agenda_item: 6.3 Draft Groundwater Sustainability Plan (GSP) Amendments
records.evidence_text: And the third one is to change the interconnected surface water sustainable management criteria to include the conservation release period and adjust it according to the guidance they're providing on interconnected surface water. We have adhered to the guidance they've released so far, but they haven't released the big one, the policy document. And we are not making that change in this plan because there isn't policy guidance yet. ... And I would strongly advise you don't get ahead of them on that. ... But that is the one thing we're not. We're not meeting here.
records.notes: On 2026-01-23 staff said this corrective action was issued on the Eastside (2022) GSP but should be treated as applying to 180/400 as well, consistent with finding 234.

records.finding: The consultant told the Advisory Committee that MCWRA river series measure total channel loss in either direction, while depletion due to pumping comes from with/without-pumping model runs that will be redone with the updated model, confirming finding 219's distinction. No updated pumping-attributable depletion figure was presented at any meeting reviewed.
records.quantitative_detail: Meetings reviewed 2025-09-11 to 2026-10-08; no updated depletion volume presented
records.agenda_item: 4.2 Groundwater Conditions and Sustainable Management Criteria
records.evidence_text: So there are different ways to measure depletion. Water Resource Agency has the river series, which looks at essentially loss of water along the river, regardless of what direction it goes. For sigma purposes, we are interested in depletion due to pumping. So there's a couple ways we get at that. One is per sigma, we must monitor the rate of depletion and for the timing of that. And we use the groundwater model for that purpose because you can have no pumping or have pumping and look at the difference between them and we'll be updating that with the updated model soon. For your metrics, we rely on shallow groundwater levels.
records.notes: The absence of an updated figure rests on searches of all scope transcripts and agendas, not on the unpublished amendment text; on 2026-06-12 staff said the rate had been updated but gave no number.

records.section: 1.5 Per-well Attribution and the Cumulative Pumping Problem
records.finding: 2026 discussions of well permitting, including county ordinance updates, CEQA review of new well applications and a Board-requested analysis of a Deep Aquifers well moratorium, were framed entirely around the Deep Aquifers and seawater intrusion. No stream-proximity or ISW criterion was raised, consistent with finding 232.
records.quantitative_detail: None
records.agenda_item: 6.3 Deep Aquifers Management Memorandum
records.evidence_text: Some of the other interim actions that are outside of the GSA's authority, but key for our partners would be supporting the county as they proceed with updating their well permitting policies and ordinances to strengthen them to be more aligned with sgma. And then also a recommendation to strengthen the Water Resources Agency well destruction program. And the issue there is really the concern of the potential for vertical leakage from the, from the seawater intruded aquifers down into the deep.
records.notes: Well permitting is a County of Monterey function; the absence rests on searches for moratorium, well permit, setback and new wells across scope transcripts.

records.section: 1.5 Per-well Attribution and the Cumulative Pumping Problem
records.finding: The Demand Management Framework lists location-varying demand-management fees, including higher fees for lands adjacent to streams or GDEs, as an option. It is the only stream-proximity lever seen in the SVBGSA record, offered as an example that needs strong legal justification; no adopted fee or allocation used it.
records.quantitative_detail: No fee rate stated
records.speaker_role: consultant — ERA Economics (Demand Management Framework document)
records.agenda_item: Demand Management Framework (agenda packet)
records.evidence_text: Acreage DM fees that vary by location. DM fees can be designed to provide incentives according to spatial characteristics. For example, lands in or near a seawater intruded area , or lands adjacent to streams or GDEs may warrant a more persuasive incentive (higher fee). Spatial differences in fees would require strong justification.
records.notes: An option, not a policy, so it does not contradict Absence finding 232; the FY 2027 fees adopted 2026-07-09 were set by subbasin tier with no stream-adjacency differentiation found.

records.section: 1.5 Per-well Attribution and the Cumulative Pumping Problem
records.finding: M&A ran pumping-off superposition scenarios (1980-2022) for two stakeholder groups. Their consultants reported that removing Forebay pumping adds about 40,000 AF/yr of flow into 180/400 and that removing upstream pumping adds at least 15,000 AF/yr of river recharge to 180/400 storage, a cross-subbasin attribution absent from Table 5-7. Staff said the results will not be incorporated into plans.
records.quantitative_detail: Averages 1980-2022 as presented: Forebay pumping off, flow Forebay to 180/400 +~40,000 AF/yr; Upper Valley pumping off, Salinas River flow +~40,000 AF/yr and Forebay to 180/400 +~30,000 AF/yr; combined Upper Valley-off and Forebay-off, at least 15,000 AF/yr added 180/400 storage from river recharge and up to +5 ft groundwater over ~60% of 180/400 (presenter's estimate); stated model accuracy a few percent of a water budget of hundreds of thousands of AF
records.speaker_role: mixed — Derek Williams (M&A, SVBGSA consultant) and Bob Abrams (consultant to Salinas Basin Water Alliance)
records.agenda_item: 2.1 Interbasin Flow Modeling Results
records.evidence_text: The output, as I said, the alliance and the coalition have consultants that will interpret the output for you there. We're not interpreting it ourselves and we aren't incorporating it directly into our plans right now. ... Turn off pumping in the four bay flow increases by about 25,000 acre feet. And flow between the four bay and the 18400 increases by about 40,000 acre feet. ... So a reasonable estimate of the increased groundwater storage in the 18400 is a minimum of 15,000 acre feet per year for the combined upper valley off and four bay off scenarios. And that's all due to recharge, additional recharge from the Salinas River.
records.notes: Runs were funded by the Salinas Valley Water Coalition and Salinas Basin Water Alliance and the figures are their consultants' rounded readings of slides; also answers ISW-1.3a and ISW-1.8b, and stakeholders later cited the study in fee and cost-allocation debates.

records.finding: Screening Salinas River diversion options for the 180/400 area, staff excluded shallow well fields because pumping them would deplete reservoir water released to flow downstream. This is an explicit staff statement that shallow pumping depletes river flow, a point finding 239 handles only through the aquitard definition.
records.quantitative_detail: No volumes stated
records.agenda_item: 4.1 Castroville and Eastside Canals and Alternatives Feasibility Study
records.evidence_text: So the project can't interfere with any existing operations. So that includes stored water that's already committed to existing projects. And project concepts like shallow well fields, where, you know, if you pump a shallow well field, that'll deplete the, the stored water that's released to get downstream.
records.notes: Presenter introduces herself as Emily Gardner earlier in the transcript; an October 2025 water-rights evaluation in the 2025-10-10 packet also warned that shallow well fields may pump river underflow requiring an SWRCB right.

records.finding: New conceptual-model work for the amendment maps potential thin spots or gaps in the Salinas Valley Aquitard and shallow clays, many along the river, and the consultant tied the largest Somavia-reach river losses to one mapped gap. This qualifies finding 239's clean split between pumped aquifers below the aquitard and stream interconnection above it.
records.quantitative_detail: No volumes stated; highest losses located between the Chualar gauge and the first bend of the Somavia Road reach
records.meeting_body: SVBGSA 180/400-Ft Aquifer Subbasin Committee (joint meeting with Eastside Committee)
records.agenda_item: 4.3 Periodic Evaluation - New Information Collected/Data Gaps Filled
records.evidence_text: We identified some potential thin spots or gaps in these clay layers in the aquitard. And in the map they're shown as gray polygons, gray areas. A lot of it's on the, on the river. And so there's potential connections through those, through those small areas. ... So just in general that the highest river flow losses they were identified to occur before the first bend in that Sommavilla road. It's between the Chular river gauge and the bend one there shown on the map. And that's coincides where the potential gap that we've mapped so it makes some sense and that indicates there is some, some sort of a connection with the off aquifer in that area.
records.notes: The amended ISW map still clips out areas over the aquitard (see the ISW-1.1c row), so these gaps are not reflected in mapped ISW; 'off aquifer' is a transcription garble.

records.finding: Staff described DWR's December 2025 information request on the 180/400 Periodic Evaluation and Amendment 1 as four topics centred on seawater intrusion. Keyword searches of the Board's March, August and September 2026 discussions of the responses found no ISW content; the Response 2 document itself was not reviewed.
records.quantitative_detail: DWR letter 2025-12-01 and meeting 2025-12-23; first response April 2026; extension requested to 2026-09-15; four request topics
records.agenda_item: 6.4 180/400 Subbasin GSP 2025 Periodic Evaluation and Amendment 1 Additional Information Response 2
records.evidence_text: So we did that, and last December, we received an additional information request from them on these four specific topics. And all of the discussion that we just had was really driven by, not solely driven, but partially driven by the state's request for additional information about the 180-400 GSP and specifically how we're going to address seawater intrusion.
records.notes: The absence rests on keyword searches (interconnected, ISW, depletion, surface water) of the 2026-03-12, 2026-08-13 and 2026-09-10 transcripts; the Response 2 document itself was not read.

records.finding: With grants ending, the GM proposed turning grant-funded GDE methodology and fieldwork into an ongoing GDE monitoring program and funding ISW corrective-action work from valley-wide Tier 1 fees, though ISW does not apply equally to all subbasins. ISW and GDE work thus shifts from grants (finding 227) to recurring fees; no ISW-specific amount was stated.
records.quantitative_detail: No ISW-specific dollar amount stated; applies to the FY 2027 work plan and budget
records.speaker_role: GSA staff — General Manager (inferred from context)
records.agenda_item: 4.1 Work Plan Draft and Budget Assumptions
records.evidence_text: This is all grant related work we got done developing methodology for gds and conduct field work in all subpatients. And what we think we want to do going forward instead of develop a program program for actually conducting the GDE monitoring. And that would be tier one fee because it is required in all sub basins as one of the SGMA compliance work tasks. ... So we do need to make sure that we have some funding set aside and some time set aside to look at that and consider how we address the recommended corrective actions in including the integrated service order. ... So that for example the ISW it does not applicable to all six sub basins equally because it is about surface water. ... But we're proposing to kind of have this work all done by tier one funding because it is under the five year evaluation.
records.notes: Speaker is unlabeled and inferred to be the GM; 'integrated service order' is a transcription garble of interconnected surface water, and on 2026-08-13 staff said a major change in DWR guidance could not be absorbed much in FY 2027.

records.finding: The consultant says DWR's existing ISW guidance covers measurement and monitoring; what is missing is policy on what depletion is significant and unreasonable and how to balance users, including for conservation releases partly meant to recharge the valley. The GM separately said the river's very different use here may not fit DWR's guidance.
records.speaker_role: consultant — Montgomery & Associates presenter (inferred); GM quoted in additional meeting
records.meeting_body: SVBGSA 180/400-Ft Aquifer Subbasin Committee (joint special meeting with Eastside Committee)
records.agenda_item: 4.4 Annual Report WY 2025 and GSP 2027 Evaluation and Amendment Process
records.evidence_text: They've released some guidance on how you measure it and monitor it. But what we're really trying to get at is that management piece of it. ... The tricky part is when it comes to management, what. How is the state viewing significant and unreasonable? How do you balance uses and users? So we're waiting for that guidance before we really address that and also think about how to approach their recommended corrective action with regards to including conservation releases.
records.notes: The 2026-01-23 speaker is unlabeled and inferred from context to be the consultant presenting the evaluation process; the GM's managed-river concern is from the 2026-02-05 Budget and Finance Committee.

records.finding: The consultant disclosed that the updated SVIHM simulates more Salinas River flow than observed because too much runoff reaches the river, an error found by a stakeholder's consultant; groundwater calibration is described as sound but river modeling may not be ready. The GM said the 2022 model-use policy has no process for reporting or fixing such errors.
records.quantitative_detail: Model-use policy adopted 2022; no magnitude of the river-flow error stated at the Board
records.speaker_role: mixed — consultant (Abby Ostovar, M&A) and GSA staff (General Manager)
records.agenda_item: 6.3 Draft GSP Amendments; 7.3 Groundwater Models Use and Maintenance Policy
records.evidence_text: And as an example, somebody raised, you know, a discrepancy they found between, in the groundwater model, between the simulated and observed groundwater, sorry, surface water flow in the river. Right. We investigated that, looked into it, brought it to the TAC and some of the committees. Essentially there is more runoff that's getting to the river that's resulting in more simulated flow than observed. ... So it does affect river flow in the model. But the groundwater basin is well calibrated to groundwater levels at hand extraction. ... If you want to do river modeling, then you might want to think about whether it's at the right stage ... We do have a policy. The policy was approved by you in 2022, so it's been in place for five, almost four or five years. But it's a policy only. What we're missing is actually process.
records.notes: The effect on modeled ISW depletion was not quantified; Arroyo Seco GSA's manager said in public comment that the model overestimates high flows, and the 2026-08-27 SMC TAC discussion cited on 2026-09-10 is outside this scope.

records.finding: The Demand Management Framework accepted in November 2025, the GSA's route to pumping limits, sets its stages and triggers on the groundwater-level criteria and treats ISW as related to groundwater levels through proxy measurements. No separate ISW trigger is described, consistent with finding 233's identical-threshold design.
records.quantitative_detail: Framework accepted by the Board 2025-11-13; staged triggers (Stage 0-4)
records.speaker_role: consultant — ERA Economics (Demand Management Framework document)
records.agenda_item: Demand Management Framework (agenda packet)
records.evidence_text: This DM Framework focuses specifically on the SMC for groundwater levels. Groundwater modeling indicates that DM alone is unlikely to sufficiently mitigate seawater intrusion. Groundwater in storage and interconnected surface water relate to groundwater levels, either through proxy measurements or calculated relationships.
records.notes: Evidence is the framework text in the Board packet; the acceptance date comes from the 2025-11-13 agenda and later recaps, and the April 2026 demand-management runs likewise evaluated groundwater-level results only.

records.finding: Staff name Central Coast Wetlands Group as lead of the current MLRP grant, with SVBGSA collaborating on the MLRP plan. SVBGSA intends to lead future (Prop 4) applications to widen the scope beyond CCWG's surface-water-quality priorities. Finding 254 names the IRWM Group as grantee; meetings add the day-to-day lead and a planned shift to GSA leadership.
records.quantitative_detail: Current grant runs to 2027-12-31 (Budget & Finance Committee, 2026-02-05).
records.speaker_role: GSA staff (presenter of the FY 2027 work plan; a commenter names her Emily)
records.agenda_item: 4.4 Annual Report WY 2025 Implementation Progress and Work Plan FY 2027
records.evidence_text: And mlrp we are, you know, working with Central Coast Wetlands Group right now. Who's the, who's the lead for the MLRP grant. And the GSA is collaborating on the malrp, which is the plan and also trying to broaden the scope of the MLRP plan for future grant applications. The GSA is going to be the lead and still continuing to work with our project partners. But having the GSA be the lead will potentially expand the kinds of projects that we'll be looking at. Right now it's really focused on the Central Coast Wetlands Group priorities of surface water quality improvement.
records.notes: 'Lead' may differ from 254's 'grantee' (DMF 2025-10-09 says SVBGSA 'in partnership with' the IRWM Group was awarded the grant; 2025-10-02 staff: 'we are not the main agency'); the statement is made at the Langley committee but concerns the lower-valley grant.

records.finding: Staff state the MLRP grant funds land-repurposing concepts in the Langley, 180/400 and Eastside subbasins; on 2026-02-25 staff told the Monterey committee the grant does not apply there. The Response to DWR (269) frames MLRP for lands across all subbasins, so the current grant's footprint is narrower than that stated intent.
records.meeting_body: SVBGSA Langley Area Subbasin Committee (special meeting)
records.agenda_item: 4.3 Draft GSP Amendments - Project and Management Action Updates
records.evidence_text: But we do have grant funding to develop some concepts around how the land could be repurposed here in Sinas Valley, specifically Langley, as well as the 18400 and east side. So that's been broadened to include MLRP.
records.notes: Transcript garbles names ('Sinas', '18400'); Forebay and Upper Valley coverage not stated; the DMF (2025-10-09) describes the grant area as flood-prone lands in the lower Salinas Valley.

records.finding: The DMF prices land repurposing as the difference between irrigated and repurposed land value and tabulates Salinas Valley land sales, noting Castroville (the coastal 180/400) sells at a discount owing to Zone 2B fees, CSIP costs and seawater-intrusion risk. This gives a cost basis for the acquisition instrument (finding 255) that the findings lack.
records.quantitative_detail: Average agricultural land sales 2014-2025, inflation-adjusted (2024 $/acre): cropland Castroville $38,000, Gonzales $54,000, Greenfield $43,000, Salinas $64,000, Soledad $36,000; vineyard $35,000-$55,000. Rental rates $500-$4,000 per acre (ASFMRA) and $3,200 per acre (UC cost studies), time basis not stated. MCWRA Zone 2B charge $355.44/acre, 2024-25.
records.speaker_role: consultant — ERA Economics (Demand Management Framework prepared for SVBGSA)
records.agenda_item: 6.2 Demand Management Framework (draft; Board accepted the Framework 2025-11-13, item 6.4)
records.evidence_text: The cost of repurposing agricultural land is the difference between the value of the land in irrigated agriculture, and the value of the land in its repurposed use ... Land sales in the Castroville area have occurred at a significant discount, influenced by higher fees including MCWRA’s Zone 2B assessment
records.notes: Land values are in DMF Table 18 (fallow bank section); no per-acre-foot conversion is given there.

records.finding: SVBGSA's finance reports carry an $800,000 MLRP grant line running to end-2027, with about $118,000 incurred by December 2025; staff expect a further Prop 4 MLRP round. This is spending reporting the Annual Report lacks (finding 334), though financial only, with no acreage acquired.
records.quantitative_detail: $800,000 SVBGSA MLRP grant line (total); about $118,000 incurred and $425,000 not yet encumbered or incurred, as of 2025-12-31 (finance staff); GM estimate same day: $300,000-$400,000 remaining; '681' remaining figure garbled; end date 2027-12-31; next Prop 4 MLRP cycle about $200 million statewide (GM, 'I believe'); future rounds 'probably along the order of $10 million' (staff estimate, 2026-08-06).
records.speaker_role: GSA staff (finance staff; General Manager Piret Harmon)
records.agenda_item: 3.2 Financial Reports for December 2025; 4.1 Work Plan and Budget Assumptions
records.evidence_text: The old one that's still got quite a bit of time on it is the MLRP grant. We have to. This actually goes through December 2027. So we have quite a bit of time on this one still because there's still about 681 in the total grant. There's 425,000. That hasn't been encumbered or incurred as an expense. We've only incurred about 118 out of the full 800,000. ... There is more money for multi benefit land repurposing in Prop 4 and I believe the number is 200 million in the next cycle.
records.notes: Not stated whether the $800,000 is SVBGSA's subaward of the $10M grant; speakers' remaining-balance figures disagree; the GM said DWR (not DOC) would open the next solicitation.

records.finding: SVBGSA's economist told the Board that $/AF costs of fallowing-based demand management cannot be directly compared with $/AF costs of injection projects such as the BGRP, because fallowing cannot meet the seawater-intrusion minimum threshold. Finding 262 calls the Periodic Evaluation's $/AF/yr fallowing and retirement costs directly comparable with other supply options. Both are recorded; not resolved here.
records.quantitative_detail: 2026-06-11 (same consultant): for the USBR Title XVI no-action alternative, fallowing cost exceeds BGRP cost at about a 30% pumping cut; sensitivity at about a 50% cut.
records.agenda_item: 6.3 Economic Analysis of Demand Management
records.evidence_text: Following demand management does not achieve the objectives of meeting the minimum threshold line. So we can't take a dollar per acre foot cost of demand management and directly compare that to a dollar per acre foot cost of injecting water into the ground for, let's say the BGRP or some other project. Those are two, those are apples and oranges.
records.notes: 'Following' is the transcription of 'fallowing'; on 2026-06-11 ERA did set fallowing cost against BGRP cost, but only to define the federal no-action baseline.

records.finding: A LandWatch letter in the Advisory Committee packet cites ERA's March 2026 Demand Management Economic Impact Analysis: permanent fallowing (land idled and bought outright) costs $645-1,010/AF in 180/400, below temporary fallowing at $1,750-2,100/AF. Finding 262's Periodic Evaluation ranges rank retirement above fallowing; the metrics may differ, so this is not a like-for-like conflict.
records.quantitative_detail: Permanent fallowing direct cost $645-$1,010 per AF, 180/400 (ERA Table 18 as cited); temporary fallowing for a 10% pumping cut $1,750-$2,100 per AF, 180/400 (ERA Table 16 as cited); 10% of 180/400 pumping = 11,796 AF of 117,960 AFY (Periodic Evaluation Table 2-3 as cited). Finding 262: $675-$2,095/AF/yr fallowed, $1,295-$3,210/AF/yr retired. Time basis of the ERA per-AF figures not stated in the letter.
records.speaker_role: NGO/advocate — LandWatch Monterey County (letter citing ERA Economics)
records.agenda_item: 3.2 Integrated Implementation Strategy PMA Final Portfolios (letter dated 2026-07-11 in packet)
records.evidence_text: ERA determined that direct cost of permanent land fallowing for the 180/400 is only $645 to 1,010 per AF. ... permanent fallowing assuming land is idled (no applied irrigation water) and is purchased outright. ... Even the higher direct costs of temporary fa llowing – $1,750 to $2,100 per AF – represent a potentially less expensive alternative for a landowner.
records.notes: Secondary citation of the ERA report by an advocate; on 2026-04-09 a public commenter cited 'permanent fallowing cost' of $450-$1,100/AF from the same report's Table 18 (valley-wide or differently scoped), so figures should be checked against the ERA report itself.

records.finding: SVBGSA's Demand Management Framework says GEMS well-head pumping data may not measure groundwater savings from fallowing at field or parcel level, and the consultant's GEMS/OpenET/crop-map analysis was aggregated only to subbasin level. No meeting described parcel-level consumptive-use tracking for repurposed or fallowed land.
records.speaker_role: consultant — ERA Economics (Demand Management Framework prepared for SVBGSA)
records.agenda_item: 6.2 Demand Management Framework (draft; Board accepted the Framework 2025-11-13, item 6.4)
records.evidence_text: Effective measurement. A fallow bank requires a cost-effective and reasonably accurate way to measure or estimate the water savings created by the program. GEMS or the new GMP may not be suitable because it only tracks pumping at the well head and this limits the ability to measure groundwater savings at the field or parcel level.
records.notes: At the 180/400 Committee (2025-09-24) ERA said ET and applied water were analysed only 'at a sub-basin level' and it was more comfortable showing data at region than farm level.

records.finding: SVBGSA is now developing a Deep Aquifers Demand Management Allocation Program, with work-plan tasks to set a baseline, a sustainable pumping target, an allocation methodology and a monitoring, accounting and enforcement programme. Finding 263's 'no allocation' premise is changing for the deep aquifers; how repurposed land would be treated is not discussed.
records.quantitative_detail: Tasks scheduled over the next three years (staff); no allocations adopted as of 2026-10-08.
records.agenda_item: 4.2 DWR Response 2 - 180/400 GSP Amendment 1 & 2025 Evaluation Information Request
records.evidence_text: For the deep aquifers allocations we've gotten an initial proposal from Montgomery and Associates and ERA for the work that would need to be done to do this right. ... We need to characterize the baseline for an allocation program. This is at a higher level than where we're at now. We need to develop a sustainable pumping target, a framework and methodology for how allocations would be done. We need to have a monitoring, accounting and enforcement program.
records.notes: The programme's footprint (intruded area only vs whole Deep Aquifers extent) was still open per a commenter on 2026-10-08; the DMF (2025-10-09) says any allocation must define whether fallow-bank savings join sustainable yield or count as new water.

records.finding: The DMF sets out transfer and anti-leakage options for any future allocation: farm-unit pooling, limits on moving water into areas of concern, transfer ratios, pumping-density rules, and capped carryover and borrowing. None is adopted, and voluntary fallowing or trading of pumping rights was not among the FY 2027 priorities, as a LandWatch commenter noted on 2026-02-12.
records.speaker_role: consultant — ERA Economics (Demand Management Framework prepared for SVBGSA)
records.agenda_item: 6.2 Demand Management Framework (draft; Board accepted the Framework 2025-11-13, item 6.4)
records.evidence_text: Unused allocation could be allowed to carry over from year to year, perhaps with a limit on the number of years. ... Other spatial concepts include transfer ratios (limiting amounts in and out of a specific area if an allocation is pooled for use somewhere else), allocation density rules (limiting density of pumping to prevent local groundwater issues), and similar rules that may vary spatially.
records.notes: The 2026-02-12 point is a public commenter's (LandWatch), not a staff statement. Basin-wide rule; not specific to repurposed land.

records.finding: SVBGSA's modelling consultant confirmed the seawater-intrusion model holds crops fixed and omits the shift of production and pumping to unconstrained areas that ERA's economic analysis predicts when northern pumping is cut. The DMF warns repurposing may shift rather than cut production, which qualifies finding 264; no anti-leakage rule exists.
records.quantitative_detail: ERA illustrative cut scenarios (2026-04-09): irrigated acreage down about 11% (low) to 17% (high) of about 330,000 acres; gross farm revenue down about 10% to 13.5%, valley-wide.
records.speaker_role: consultant — Montgomery & Associates (Derrik Williams, presenter of item 2.2; inferred)
records.agenda_item: 2.2 SWIM Baseline and No Action Alternative Simulation
records.evidence_text: The crops are set. All we do is we say we might have to fallow land. But that. That redistribution is not included in the modeling. It was only included in the economic analysis later.
records.notes: Speaker unlabelled; ERA said unconstrained areas 'grow a little bit more acreage' and a commenter read its slide as Upper Valley gaining acreage; a 180/400 committee member (2026-08-06) noted ranches straddling the 180/400-Forebay line could cut north and pump more south.

records.finding: Asked whether models account for fallowed land later turning into housing and using water again, staff said the portfolios' 10-20% demand reduction is modelled as 'just less water use', agnostic to land use. A director repeated the concern on 2026-08-13. No accounting for the permanence or later use of fallowed land exists.
records.quantitative_detail: Modelled agricultural demand reduction: 10% in Portfolios 1, 3A and 3B; 20% in Portfolio 4 (2026-07-09).
records.speaker_role: mixed — director question; staff or consultant answer (speaker unlabelled)
records.agenda_item: 6.2 Integrated Implementation Strategy (IIS) PMA Portfolio Evaluation
records.evidence_text: that 100 acres is not likely just to sit there, it's probably going to go off and become houses then, and then you're going to increase the water use back up, but now it's domestic. Do you use your model taking some consideration of that? ... It's not determined yet. It's not determined yet. When we talk about 10% or 20% demand reduction, what we're really talking about is just less water use. We aren't talking about saying we know what the land use is, we're just saying less water use, probably as much.
records.notes: The answering speaker is not labelled in the transcript; ERA added that farming-less effects are handled in the economic analysis, not the groundwater model.

records.finding: The baseline for the modelled 10% agricultural demand reduction in the four northern subbasins, including 180/400, is undecided. Members asked whether it would use GEMS data or land use and which start year; staff said the model used 2022 land use and average hydrology, but the implementation baseline 'still gets to be determined'.
records.quantitative_detail: 10% agricultural demand reduction, possibly 5-7% if projects deliver more (staff); model uses 2022 land use and average hydrology of about 1980-2022.
records.speaker_role: mixed — committee member question; GSA staff and consultant answers
records.meeting_body: SVBGSA Langley Area Subbasin Committee (special meeting)
records.agenda_item: 4.2/4.3 Draft GSP Amendments (discussion)
records.evidence_text: what's our starting point for, for that 10%? Is that, you know, 2019, is that today? ... They're all questions to be answered. Okay, so that's still undetermined ... We just had to pick some, pick some time frames to incorporate in the model, see how groundwater was impacted going forward to think about what a 10% reduction sort of could really look like. I think that still gets to be determined.
records.notes: Link to repurposing: the member asked whether the 10% would be met by best management practices or would require fallowing, so the undecided baseline governs how fallowing savings would be counted; Langley meeting, but the 10% applies to 180/400, Eastside, Monterey and Langley; speakers unlabelled and answers partly contradictory on 2022 GEMS data.

records.finding: The DMF, accepted by the Board in November 2025, envisages a groundwater ledger tracking balances, debits and credits by parcel, well or user to quantify pumping cuts from demand measures, but defers its design to future programmes. For fallow banks it leaves open whether saved water joins sustainable yield or is booked as new water.
records.speaker_role: consultant — ERA Economics (Demand Management Framework prepared for SVBGSA)
records.agenda_item: 6.2 Demand Management Framework (draft; Board accepted the Framework 2025-11-13, item 6.4)
records.evidence_text: Quantify reductions in pumping achieved through DM measures. ... The components of the water budget, tracking system and methods, and approach would be defined as part of future DM measure policies and programs, as specified in future SVBGSA workplans. ... If there is a groundwater allocation it is necessary to define how the water saved by the program is accounted for (e.g., part of the sustainable yield available to all or accounted for separately as new water).
records.notes: Finding 269 already notes accounting as a DMF global element; this row adds the ledger design and the unresolved treatment of conserved water.

records.section: 2.5 Data Source and ET Product Choice
records.finding: OpenET is used in SVBGSA's demand-management work (ERA's crop ET by subbasin) and the consultant proposed it to cross-check self-reported GEMS pumping, but the DMF names local obstacles to remote sensing (small fields, rotating crops, plastic mulch, coastal fog) and favours meters consistent with GEMS. Finding 285's absence holds for the MLRP material only.
records.quantitative_detail: OpenET and DWR crop mapping, 2023 (DMF Figure 12).
records.speaker_role: consultant — ERA Economics (Demand Management Framework prepared for SVBGSA)
records.agenda_item: 6.2 Demand Management Framework (draft; Board accepted the Framework 2025-11-13, item 6.4)
records.evidence_text: In the Salinas Valley, relatively small farm sizes with mixed and rotating crops also presents a challenge for remotely sensed data collection. In addition, the use of plastic mulches and the coastal fog is another challenge for remote sensing. ... An analysis of OpenET evapotranspiration data was developed to establish a range of current water use for major crops.
records.notes: The GEMS cross-check suggestion was made orally by ERA at the 180/400 Committee on 2025-09-24; no local validation of OpenET was described.

records.section: 2.5 Data Source and ET Product Choice
records.finding: Staff reported the UC Davis recharge suitability mapping tool (finding 333) is due by end-2026 and interim versions are already used for site-specific questions. No criteria, weights or outputs were presented in the meetings reviewed.
records.quantitative_detail: Completion expected by 2026-12-31.
records.agenda_item: 3.2 Financial Reports for December 2025 (questions on encumbrances)
records.evidence_text: The UC Davis recharge suitability mapping will be done by the end of this calendar year. But the interim results, you know, some of, you know, they are. We are looking at sort of site specific questions using the tool that they've developed so far
records.notes: Fits 2.5 because finding 333 is filed there; it is a siting tool, not an ET product.

records.finding: Staff say projects identified under the current MLRP grant centre on surface-water-quality treatment, reflecting CCWG priorities; a January 2026 tour for the Assembly Speaker visited a constructed-wetlands site. Groundwater benefits are to be widened in future applications. Water quality is the operative co-benefit, sharpening findings 265, 279 and 280.
records.speaker_role: GSA staff — Emily Gardner (inferred, presenter of item 6.1)
records.agenda_item: 6.1 Castroville & Eastside Canals and Alternatives Preliminary Feasibility Study Update (Q&A)
records.evidence_text: But mlrp, I think it's been mentioned before, so that's, you know, in general repurposing irrigated land to another purpose that requires less groundwater use. And so there are specific projects currently identified in our grant around like water quality, surface water quality treatment. I think that we're broadening the scope of that for future MLRP grant applications.
records.notes: The 2026-01-08 GM report named a ranch and a 'Merritt Lake site constructed wetlands' on the tour (site names garbled in transcript).

records.finding: The DMF proposes that a repurposing programme set incentive payments by pumping reduction plus other benefits, with extra payments for land near streams or benefiting other SGMA indicators, updated annually. This is a pay-for-co-benefit mechanism absent from the GSP documents (finding 283), though no rates or scoring exist yet.
records.speaker_role: consultant — ERA Economics (Demand Management Framework prepared for SVBGSA)
records.agenda_item: 6.2 Demand Management Framework (draft; Board accepted the Framework 2025-11-13, item 6.4)
records.evidence_text: For example, a program may offer additional incentive payments for repurposing that provides benefits for lands near streams or other sustainability indicators under SGMA. ... Land repurposing programs typically offer an incentive that is based on the pumping reduction and other benefits that the parcel would provide. ... The incentive structure for a land repurposing program should be updated annually in response to changes in agricultural market conditions that affect the payment amounts of program participants.
records.notes: Framework-level design only; the current MLRP grant's own selection or payment criteria were not described in any meeting reviewed.

records.finding: The DMF names verification methods for a future land-repurposing or fallow-bank programme (remote sensing, site inspections, satellite imagery and grower reporting), to be fixed in programme rules. No monitoring protocol for the current MLRP grant was described in any meeting, so finding 266's absence stands for the grant itself.
records.speaker_role: consultant — ERA Economics (Demand Management Framework prepared for SVBGSA)
records.agenda_item: 6.2 Demand Management Framework (draft; Board accepted the Framework 2025-11-13, item 6.4)
records.evidence_text: Monitoring and verification. Remote sensing, site inspections, and grower reporting are used to verify compliance. Measurement of water efficiency is important to ensure that program funds are providing a reasonable return on investment. ... Define the process for monitoring to ensure that the parcels are repurposed according to the terms. This typically includes site visits for visual inspection, or satellite imagery can be used.
records.notes: Also answers MLRP-2.7a (requirement to define monitoring in rules); Data Needs would also fit for the grant-level gap.

records.finding: ERA told the Board demand measures, including repurposing, would be corrected through measurement and accounting plus annual and five-year check-ins under the stages-and-triggers framework; the DMF says a repurposing programme should be updated annually for crop markets and groundwater modelling. This is a stated feedback mechanism; no instance yet.
records.quantitative_detail: Annual and 5-year review cycle.
records.agenda_item: Demand Management Framework (discussion)
records.evidence_text: One is a measurement and accounting issue, just to make sure that whatever you're doing, you can actually ensure that you're getting some benefit from that. ... so that you have a check-in on an annual and a 5-year and every. on a periodic basis to update. Um, you know, and change the program.
records.notes: Speaker unlabelled but answering for the Framework's authors; generic to all demand measures, not MLRP-specific.

records.finding: The General Manager placed MLRP among three voluntary, valley-wide demand programmes prioritised for FY 2027 development and said staff would most likely propose funding them through the valley-wide Tier 1 fee, alongside grants. This names a local fee route for programme development, which finding 282 (grant dependence) lacks.
records.speaker_role: GSA staff — General Manager Piret Harmon
records.agenda_item: 6.3 Demand Management Measures Prioritization
records.evidence_text: The other three are voluntary, they are incentive based. Those are low hanging fruit. Mlrp. We have grant Money, of course we're going to continue. Why shouldn't it? We heard earlier it should be under the demand management framework and is on the demand management framework. ... So for those reasons we offering those three programs valley wide and most likely we'll see it as a Tier 1 proposal from staff
records.notes: Funding of post-grant monitoring of repurposed land specifically was not discussed.

records.finding: ERA told the Board that MLRP and similar grants are modest seed money that cannot fund a large demand-management programme in perpetuity, with local fees or assessments covering administration and any incentives. At the 180/400 committee (2026-08-06) a speaker, apparently staff, called a future round 'not problem solving money'. This independently confirms finding 282's risk.
records.agenda_item: 6.2 Integrated Implementation Strategy (IIS) PMA Portfolio Evaluation
records.evidence_text: So when you're talking about a 10% cut in demand management, it's modest amounts of money that's available for grant funding to fund a large demand management program in perpetuity. However, those can be valuable seed funding to set up programs that you can then roll out and implement more widely.
records.notes: The DMF (2025-10-09) likewise says a repurposing programme needs a stable source, from local fees if grants are unavailable.

records.finding: SVBGSA's Demand Management Framework does raise dust: it names managing weeds, pests and dust on fallowed land as a fallow-bank cost and a reason to prefer repurposing to unmanaged fallowing. It sets no dust measure, standard or air-district link, and no board or committee transcript reviewed raised dust. Finding 276 found no mention in the GSP documents.
records.speaker_role: consultant — ERA Economics (Demand Management Framework prepared for SVBGSA)
records.agenda_item: 6.2 Demand Management Framework (draft; Board accepted the Framework 2025-11-13, item 6.4)
records.evidence_text: Fallow agricultural land still requires management to prevent weeds, pests, dust, and other issues. Land repurposing avoids widespread unmanaged fallowing. ... These costs are typically paid as part of a fallow bank program.
records.notes: Passing mention, so labelled adds rather than contradicts; word-boundary searches of all transcripts found no dust or air-quality discussion tied to fallowing.

records.finding: Beyond MA2's fallowing, fallow bank and retirement, the DMF defines 'market-driven' repurposing that pairs incentives with conversion of farmland to housing or commercial use, alongside compensated 'targeted' conversion. 180/400 committee members urged a housing 'carrot' with groundwater limits in 2026; staff noted SVBGSA has no land-use authority.
records.speaker_role: consultant — ERA Economics (Demand Management Framework prepared for SVBGSA)
records.agenda_item: 6.2 Demand Management Framework (draft; Board accepted the Framework 2025-11-13, item 6.4)
records.evidence_text: Market-driven land repurposing. In some areas conversion of farmland to housing, commercial, or industrial uses can generate higher financial returns for landowners through sales, leases, or development partnerships. ... SVBGSA does not have land use authority and would need to coordinate with other agencies for consideration of land use, or similar restrictions, as a DM measure.
records.notes: How the water use of new housing would be netted against savings is not specified; a commenter (2026-08-06) argued such land-use trades conflict with state planning law.

records.finding: The 2026 draft GSP amendments, including 180/400 Amendment 2, carry the Demand Management Framework and call out rotational fallowing and MLRP as their own management actions. This acts on the Periodic Evaluation's note (findings 268/289) that MLRP should be added at the next amendment; drafts only, not adopted.
records.quantitative_detail: Five of six draft amendments published by 2026-10-08 (Monterey due 2026-10-20); comments by 2026-11-18; submission January 2027.
records.agenda_item: 6.3 Draft Groundwater Sustainability Plan (GSP) Amendments
records.evidence_text: The demand management framework is in all of the GSPs saying hey there's this framework. Demand management is a tool. There are stages, it's not necessarily needed but if it's needed it is a tool that's there. And then specific management actions like rotational fallowing or mlrp, the multi benefit land repurposing are called out as their own management actions.
records.notes: That the 180/400 draft specifically lists MLRP is inferred from 'all of the GSPs' (180/400 Amendment 2 confirmed in preparation 2026-06-04); question fit is loose (finding is about plan status, filed under 2.11 in EDF's set).

records.finding: Staff reported FlowWest's HEC-RAS modelling of flow in RCD-maintained secondary channels was finishing in February 2026, with Montgomery & Associates to add groundwater estimates afterwards. The surface-groundwater coupling that finding 288 records as intent is under way; no groundwater-benefit figure appeared in later meetings reviewed.
records.agenda_item: 3.2 Financial Reports for December 2025 (questions on encumbrances)
records.evidence_text: Flowest is finishing up their reports this week. So we should have information around the, you know, looking at the stream channel maintenance work and the basically the volume of water that could be flowing in the secondary floodplain that's maintained by the RCD through the SMP ... And then M&A's piece is to then put some estimates on the groundwater piece. So the flow S piece will be done shortly. The, the groundwater piece that we're sort of adding to the top of that is still underway.
records.notes: Same meeting: the GM said SVBGSA 'should not be the lead agency in river related efforts' and proposed Tier 2 funding for a stream-channel strategy; covers 180/400, Monterey, Forebay and Upper Valley reaches.

records.finding: In August 2025 the board replaced the Subbasin Implementation Committees program with a written Subbasin Committees program that defines the committees as conduits to the broader community and sources of feedback to staff, an advisory role only. In June 2026 the board filled the 180/400 committee's 11 seats from 16 applicants by slates built from directors' votes.
records.quantitative_detail: 180/400 committee June 11, 2026: 16 applicants, 11 seats; slate members needed at least 6 of 11 director votes
records.speaker_role: GSA staff — General Manager Piret Harmon
records.meeting_body: SVBGSA 180/400-Ft Aquifer Subbasin Committee (special meeting, joint session with Eastside Subbasin Committee)
records.agenda_item: Additions to the agenda (oral update on Subbasin Committees Program)
records.evidence_text: So this program was expanded, the word implementation was dropped from the title, so we have a sub-basin Committees program. ... conduit to reach the stakeholders, the broader community. ... the committee members play a vital role in, um, receiving updates and technical information from the agency and disseminating that information back to the communities.
records.notes: Programme applies to all six subbasin committees (MULTI); finding 294 describes the 180/400 committee as 17 members at convening, later capped at 12.

records.finding: The Advisory Committee chair told the board the committee is 'not a policy body' and lacks policy direction to resolve affordability. On the project portfolio it made no recommendation beyond dropping Portfolio 1; the board then selected Portfolio 3A, one of the two it had kept in play.
records.quantitative_detail: Board selected Portfolio 3A on Aug 13, 2026 by 10-1 (per WaterOne recap; roll call partly garbled in transcript)
records.speaker_role: advisory committee member — Advisory Committee chair Curtis Weeks (also Arroyo Seco GSA general manager)
records.agenda_item: 5.2 Advisory Committee Meeting Report April 16 and April 29, 2026
records.evidence_text: But we, as the committee, we don't have that luxury. We're not a policy body. But I'm telling you, the committee members are interested in that. They're interested in affordability.
records.notes: Valley-wide committee (MULTI); on Aug 13 the consultant said 'They did not make a recommendation. They did recommend that we not go forward with portfolio one.'

records.finding: For its Advisory Committee seat the 180/400 Subbasin Committee chose a former SVBGSA director from the agriculture sector over the Castroville CSD general manager, who said he represented a disadvantaged community. In the roll call only committee member Stefani named the CSD manager.
records.quantitative_detail: Castroville CSD: about 7,800 customers (applicant's spoken figure; ~7,500 residents in his written application); roll call: 1 vote for Derbin, every other recorded vote for Secondo (transcript garbled, exact tally unclear)

records.finding: Staff said feedback from committees and from prospective end users in separate meetings on the December 2024 draft made them pause the direct-delivery scenarios for the Brackish Groundwater Restoration Project and study other configurations; staff then recommended an injection-only preferred scenario. records.finding: Staff are rewriting the water-quality SMC so that degradation linked to pumping counts even without GSA action, citing DWR's corrective actions. A commenter said DACs and domestic-well users had commented 'early and often' that the GSA must weigh the effect of its inaction. The change appears in the October 2026 draft amendments.

Problem due to inaction. They commented early and often that the GSA needed to consider not just the effect of their actions, but also the effect of their inaction.

records.finding: When staff describe benefits for domestic users they mean protecting domestic wells and helping households use water efficiently: the rural-residential efficiency program was kept in Portfolio 3A because protecting domestic users is 'a known priority for DWR'. records.finding: Distributive dimension: the valley-wide Demand Management Framework (accepted Nov 2025) records that demand-management costs would fall on economically disadvantaged, largely Latino and farmworker communities, and for domestic pricing measures lists an equity element of protections for low-income households and DACs. No protection is designed yet.
records.quantitative_detail: About 294,000 people in census tracts overlapping the Salinas Valley in 2023 (about 68% of county); average tract median income $94,500 vs state $96,300; domestic fee $5.32 per connection (Tier 1, 2025)
records.speaker_role: consultant — ERA Economics (framework text in agenda packet)
records.agenda_item: 6.2 Demand Management Framework (draft received for input)
records.evidence_text: The baseline conditions for Salinas Valley and broader Monterey County demographics illustrate that many of the communities that depend on the Valley's ground and surface water supplies are economically disadvantaged relative to the state average. ... Equity. Incorporate protections for low-income households and disadvantaged communities, such as health needs, income-based exemptions, or targeted rebates.
records.notes: Valley-wide framework (MULTI) accepted by the board on Nov 13, 2025; unlike the Response to DWR in finding 323 it does contain equity and DAC content.

records.finding: Distributive dimension: a UC Small Farms Network adviser warned that a uniform 10% cut per grower would fall hardest on small-scale underserved farmers who already conserve, and asked to discuss it under demand management. A director from Cal Water argued urban cuts must be proportional to protect Salinas residents. Neither concern was resolved.
records.quantitative_detail: Portfolio modelling assumes a 10% agricultural pumping reduction; director cited 180/400 pumping ~115,700 AFY with urban ~12,300 AFY (about 10%) and Eastside 54,800 AFY with urban about 15% (annual figures, director's numbers)
records.speaker_role: mixed — NGO/advocate (UC Small Farms Network) and board member (Director Granillo, Cal Water)
records.agenda_item: Integrated Implementation Strategy portfolio presentation (public comment)
records.evidence_text: A lot of the small scale underserved farmers that we work with across Salinas Valley are already implementing water conservation practices through irrigation methods like drip tape, diversified crops, cover cropping, so forth. So in theory, if all farmers needed to meet, let's say, a 10% reduction in their groundwater extraction, the farmers that are already implementing water conservation practices would be disproportionately impacted, resulting in an equity issue.
records.notes: Existing 3.1.3 findings (293, 303) concern representation and commenters, so this row adds the distributive dimension; the director spoke as a commenter while travelling and her name is transcribed 'Brenda Cornillo'.

records.finding: Distributive dimension: directors repeatedly asked what seawater-intrusion projects would cost residential and domestic users, and one asked that human-right-to-water and DAC impacts be built into demand management. Staff answered that cost allocation is years away and domestic users are not a single beneficiary class; no DAC-specific cost analysis has been presented.
records.quantitative_detail: Oct 9, 2025: a director estimated residential and business water costs could rise 25-50% and irrigation costs roughly double (director's rough estimate); FY2026 domestic fee $5.32 per connection, Tier 1, all six subbasins (Demand Management Framework table)
records.speaker_role: mixed — board member (Director Velazquez) and GSA staff (General Manager)
records.agenda_item: 6.3 Preferred Integrated Implementation (IIS) Project and Management Actions (PMA) Portfolio

So domestic user is not as a single beneficiary or somebody we need to be considering in a cost allocation. ... It's too early, it's way too early.
records.notes: Nov 13, 2025 a director raised human-right-to-water and DAC impacts and Feb 19, 2026 an Advisory Committee member said DAC impacts are 'always forgotten'; neither got a specific answer.

records.finding: Representative dimension: a director said on the record that community members lack representation on the board and some committees, and asked staff to keep informing the Water Leadership Institute cohort. This independently supports the Community Water Center's 2019 representation concern in finding 293, which rests on a public comment.

But there was a group, a cohort that was, I think the intent was to really make sure that we had more engagement in the community and that there was more outreach to the community.
records.notes: No board response was recorded; on June 4, 2026 a public commenter said over 200,000 residents' drinking water is at stake and 'They're stakeholders too'.

records.section: 3.1.4 Domestic Well Protection as an Equity Outcome
records.finding: Responding to DWR's corrective action that threshold impacts were assessed on too few domestic wells, the consultant is re-evaluating minimum thresholds against domestic well screen depths using the new well-registration data. No split by DAC versus non-DAC areas was mentioned, and no speaker asked for one in the meetings reviewed.

records.finding: The Rural Residents Water Efficiency Pilot reached few people: a board member called 144 survey responses over about four months a poor turnout, and home-assessment uptake was still in single digits in January 2026. Staff now propose it as a permanent rural-residential efficiency program, and it is in Portfolio 3A and the draft 2026 GSP amendments.

records.agenda_item: Communications and outreach update (Water Efficiency Pilot survey)

These measure reach, not effect, but they conflict with finding 313's statement that no outreach metric is published.

The industry average for this type of an agency is 35%. And the website also is a key tool for average and public engagement. It has about 12,000 monthly visitors over the past six months. Right now, the six months prior to this, it had about 9,400 visitors.

records.finding: Presenting DWR's information request, staff listed as a major challenge reaching small water systems, domestic well owners and people who do not attend meetings but will be affected by project decisions. records.notes: On Sept 11, 2025 board alternate Rosa Carrillo said none of the residents on her 65-connection system knew of the WEP survey and many elderly residents cannot fill in online forms.

In January 2026 the GM reported an $80,000 EDF contract paid from Round 2 grants; agricultural commenters asked to review the curriculum.

To meet in the next few months to really be focusing on the curriculum and the specific. ... Right now, we're planning for 4 Saturdays over a 3-month period. ... Um, to give, um, about a 4-hour session for each. ... I would like for us to see 100 people there or more.

records.finding: SVBGSA publishes non-technical, partly bilingual explanations of technical content: a StoryMap with a seawater-intrusion animation (Spanish version live by March 2026, printed version for the Water Leadership Institute), a demand-management stages-and-triggers graphic, and bilingual subbasin one-pagers. None translates SMC status or minimum thresholds, the subject of finding 318.

Our team has created communication materials about demand management. This is one item we worked on the Stages and triggers graphic that explains when different actions might be taken. ... we've worked again with M and A to develop a Spanish version of the Story Map, which is now live on the website as a multimedia tool for the product to access.

records.finding: For the county's domestic well registration, SVBGSA's team used bilingual postcards, flyers and radio PSAs, recorded Zoom sessions, and in-person workshops with one-on-one help filling in forms. Staff also said grant funds offset the initial registration fee and one workshop offered a taco truck. No stipends, childcare or transport support was mentioned.
