So the direct communication with likely well owners has included creating two bilingual postcards. ... We provided a mix of formats, locations and times to ensure access for folks. We also recorded the Zoom presentation so that that's available for anyone who wasn't able to attend an in person workshop. And during these workshops we provided with the support of Water Resource Agency one on one in person support to register wells or ask and answer other questions.
records.notes: The registration program belongs to MCWRA's Groundwater Monitoring Program and is valley-wide (MULTI); the fee offset and taco truck come from staff at the Feb 17, 2026 Langley committee.

records.finding: The draft 2026 GSP amendments, published for comment in October 2026, add a potential well mitigation program as a study-first 'backstop' alongside the rural-residential efficiency program. The consultant listed typical tools (deepening wells, lowering pumps, drilling wells, funding) and possible water-quality use; nothing is designed, funded or adopted.
records.quantitative_detail: Comments due Nov 18, 2026; public hearing planned Jan 14, 2027
records.agenda_item: 6.3 Draft Groundwater Sustainability Plan (GSP) Amendments
records.evidence_text: And then added to this is rural residential efficiency. This is essentially the water efficiency pilot program. ... And then there's a potential well mitigation program added. Say that is a potential tool. The first step would be to study and understand is that something the GSA wants to approve and do but that that is something that many GSAs across the state have as a backstop. ... So GSA is giving money or drilling wells. Drilling wells or providing money to assess wells deepen wells lower the pump could also be used for water quality too.
records.notes: The overview covered the five drafts published (180/400, Eastside, Forebay, Upper Valley, Langley; Monterey due Oct 20) without saying which plans list the program, so its presence in the 180/400 draft is likely but unconfirmed.

records.finding: The 2020 GSP promised to add state and local small water systems (2-4 connections) to the water-quality monitoring network; Amendment 1 dropped them, citing enough coverage from Division of Drinking Water and irrigated-lands wells, county sampling limited to nitrate and arsenic, and county staff burden. DWR asked about this and SVBGSA is defending the removal.
records.quantitative_detail: Small systems = 2-4 connections; Division of Drinking Water systems = 15 or more connections
records.agenda_item: 6.3 180/400-Ft Aquifer Subbasin GSP 2025 Evaluation: DWR Additional Information Request
records.evidence_text: For degraded water quality in the 2020 GSP, we said that in the future we'll include the state and local small water systems. Those are the systems with two to four, we said we include them in the water quality monitoring network. And when we then met with Environmental Health Bureau and looked into this further, and then in GSP Amendment 1, we removed that mainly because we had plenty of, we had sufficient coverage with the wells that don't include those. ... their sampling really just focuses on nitrate and arsenic and we have plenty of that data. It'd be a significant staff burden for them to have the annual processing for us to get that data and integrate it.
records.notes: No Salinas COM finding addresses 3.3.2; the result is that water quality in the smallest domestic-scale systems sits outside the GSA's monitoring network.

records.finding: For DWR's corrective action the consultant tested whether pumping or falling groundwater levels degrade quality for nitrate, arsenic, gross alpha and hexavalent chromium in the 180/400, using Division of Drinking Water data for drinking-water wells and Regional Board data for on-farm domestic and irrigated-lands wells. No statistically significant relationship was found.
records.quantitative_detail: Groundwater-level trend period 1995-2024; SMC metric = number of wells above the regulatory standard compared with a historical baseline, per constituent
records.meeting_body: SVBGSA 180/400-Ft Aquifer Subbasin Committee (joint session with Eastside Subbasin Committee)
records.agenda_item: 4.2 Recommended Corrective Action - Water Quality
records.evidence_text: So for the 18400 that was nitrate, arsenic, gross alpha radioactivity and hexavalent chromium. ... for groundwater quality, that for the drinking water wells, that comes from the Division of Drinking Water from the State Water Resource Control Board, same as in our annual reports. And then for on farm domestic wells and for irrigated lands regulatory program wells, that comes from the regional. ... Both for the 18400 and the east side, none of the others were statistically significant.
records.notes: No Salinas COM finding addresses 3.3.2; a committee member said the WY2025 annual report shows 62% (2024) vs 54% (2025) of domestic wells above the 10 mg/L nitrate limit, his own unverified calculation.

records.finding: Staff said nitrate exceedances will keep being reported but will not drive GSA action because they are 'not related to groundwater management'; staff coordinate instead with the Regional Board and Preservation Inc. The October 2026 draft amendments narrow the SMC to constituents of concern and screen out one-year spikes and exceedances confined to a few wells.
records.quantitative_detail: Draft amendments published Oct 2026
records.meeting_body: SVBGSA 180/400-Ft Aquifer Subbasin Committee (joint session with Eastside Subbasin Committee)
records.agenda_item: 4.2 Recommended Corrective Action - Water Quality
records.evidence_text: There's going to be exceedances that we do continue to report for nitrates, but it's not related to groundwater management. And so we say, here's the, here's the conditions of our basin, but we're not necessarily going to be doing any actions around it because it's not related to groundwater management.
records.notes: No Salinas COM finding addresses 3.3.2; speaker carries a generic room label but answers as staff, and the Oct 8, 2026 description of the new criteria comes from the consultant.

records.finding: SVBGSA's second DWR response commits to a Seawater Intrusion Response Plan that would track intrusion impacts on beneficial users more finely and set response strategies as wells become intruded, an interim measure while large projects are built.
records.agenda_item: 4.2 DWR Response 2 - 180/400 GSP Amendment 1 & 2025 Evaluation Information Request
records.evidence_text: And so this is going to be a program for really tracking seawater intrusion impacts on a more refined level than we currently do now and having response strategies as well as become intruded for those incremental effects. And that's the interim sort of response plan that we identified for the state that is I think key for them to see that we are addressing the problem now.
records.notes: No Salinas COM finding addresses 3.3.2c; the plan came from the June 2026 Deep Aquifers Management Memorandum and it was not said whether drinking-water wells such as Castroville CSD's get specific responses.

records.section: 3.3.3 Domestic Wells and Community Water System Consolidation
records.finding: MCWRA's well registration and Groundwater Monitoring Program, promoted by SVBGSA, collects location, depth and screen data so groundwater levels can be tracked for domestic wells and small systems outside Zone 2C, including the northern 180/400. Staff noted County Environmental Health samples only water quality at the point of entry, not levels.
records.agenda_item: 6.2 SGM R2 Monterey Grant Update (Oral) / committee questions
records.evidence_text: The groundwater monitoring program and the well registration program is really to expand the monitoring ability into the area that hasn't been part of the historic Zone 2C monitoring conducted by the Water Resources Agency. So again, those rural residential areas of Corral and then of Langley and the northern 18400 that are outside of zone 2C don't have quite as much data. ... So there is monitoring that is done by environmental health that's not even at the wellhead. It's at the point of entry into a home that's water quality for their drinking water monitoring programs, but they do not monitor groundwater levels.
records.notes: No Salinas COM finding addresses 3.3.3; statement made at the Monterey committee but explicitly covers the northern 180/400 (MULTI), and June 12, 2026 first-six-month registration counts were lower than state OSCAR records.

records.finding: The Demand Management Framework baseline cites CalEnviroScreen 4.0, with the county Community Health Assessment, as the source for health and social conditions such as access to safe drinking water. It is used descriptively in a consultant report; no meeting showed it used to target or prioritise actions.
records.speaker_role: consultant — ERA Economics (framework text in agenda packet)
records.agenda_item: 6.2 Demand Management Framework (draft received for input)
records.evidence_text: Health & Social Conditions Access to health care, safe drinking water, and affordable childcare are persistent issues ... California Office of Environmental Health Hazard Assessment, CalEnviroScreen 4.0, and Monterey County Health Department, Community Health Assessment (2022).
records.notes: No other listed tool (SAFER dashboard, DWR dry well dataset or system, SGMA Data Viewer, Drinking Water Tool) was used in 2025-26 meetings; the only dry-well reference is a staff mention of the 'dry well reporting program' (Feb 25, 2026, Monterey committee).

records.finding: SVBGSA shares plan content and data through its website: subbasin pages with a written-comment mechanism for the draft 2026 GSP amendments, a planned reader's guide comparing the 2022 plans with the drafts, and a GSA web map to which monitoring data and well reports are uploaded annually.
records.speaker_role: GSA staff (Deputy General Manager Sarah Hargrave)
records.agenda_item: 6.3 Draft Groundwater Sustainability Plan (GSP) Amendments
records.evidence_text: So we are asking for public comments to be submitted to in writing to have mechanisms to do that on each subbasin GS web page. ... So we do intend to have that reader's guide comparison of the 2022 plans with the amended drafts in the next several weeks.
records.notes: The annual web-map upload was described by the consultant at the Feb 25, 2026 Monterey committee; none of these platforms was described as carrying domestic-well or DAC layers.

records.finding: A UC Small Farms Network adviser said well-registration information rarely reaches tenant growers, who often end up paying the fees, and offered to work with staff on outreach to small-scale growers in the 180/400 and Eastside. No staff response was recorded.
records.speaker_role: NGO/advocate — UC Small Farms Network (Carly Deitch)
records.agenda_item: 4.3 Annual Report WY 2025 Implementation Progress and Recommended Work Plan (public comment)
records.evidence_text: Many of the growers I work with do not know about this initiative or are unsure if this ultimately is their responsibility as renters. So what we've seen is that the information often doesn't trickle down past landowners to tenant growers in terms of registration or reporting. And then they're the ones who typically get stuck with paying the fees.
records.notes: Covers 180/400 and Eastside (MULTI); UC Small Farms Network is a university extension program rather than an NGO, described by the speaker as providing SGMA education and technical assistance to small growers.

records.section: 1.5 Per-well Attribution and the Cumulative Pumping Problem
records.finding: YSGA's well-verification step runs at scale: 109 of 130 relevant applications verified since April 2022, 17 queued, 3 failed Tier 1 and need a Tier 2 hydrogeologist report. Board reports in these meetings do not say which Tier 1 criterion failed, so whether stream impacts ever triggered review cannot be told; staff's illustrative example was a nearby contamination site.

These now require a Tier 2 review.

records.section: 1.5 Per-well Attribution and the Cumulative Pumping Problem
records.finding: A public commenter said Dunnigan Hills springs now exist only in limited form because existing vineyard and olive pumping lowered the water table, and urged no new wells. Neither staff nor the board responded on surface-water effects. It was the only time cumulative pumping effects on a surface-water feature came up in the eight meetings.

records.finding: YSGA used AI (ESA) to extract over 100,000 lithologic intervals from about 10,000 well completion reports and is correcting DWR depth errors, to map aquifer and aquitard thickness and refine model layers. This bears on the missing screen-depth and layering data behind findings 378-379, but no speaker tied it to ISW.
records.quantitative_detail: >12,000 digitized WCRs; 82% (>10,000) processed after 17% with unidentifiable form types were set aside; ~95% of processed reports yielded usable data; >100,000 intervals (~12 per report); >91% scored high-confidence (>90%), ~4.5% below 80%. Cost about $50,000 all-in (board Q&A). Yolo County has ~17,000 WCRs (Nov 2025); final QC'd database targeted April 2027 (RFQ).
records.agenda_item: Item 8: Report of the Chair and Executive Officer (ESA presentation on well completion report database)
records.evidence_text: And it's because this can provide a new foundation for analyses in the basins. The ability to characterize the aquifer, creating maps of the distribution and thickness of the aquifer and aquatar may materials across the subbasin using the lithologic data with depths for these thousands of drilled wells. This can feed into the groundwater model. Increasing the resolution of the parameters in the groundwater model with now the observed stratigraphy and improved representations of where the subsurface is changing
records.notes: On Jan 12, 2026 INTERA described DWR-digitized WCRs listing drilled rather than constructed depth (e.g., 300 ft vs 50 ft); the RFQ lists 'model layer delineation based on updated HCM'; Tool Development Opportunity also fits.

records.finding: The board voted to submit the 2027 Periodic Evaluation without a GSP amendment, so ISW gets only a roadmap of data collection and network expansion, with major changes left to 2032. records.finding: Staff said DWR sent every GSA the same ISW corrective action because its ISW guidance is unfinished and now further delayed. A director asked whether the GSA's monitoring capacity will be enough. Staff hope DWR will offer scaled options for small, low-budget GSAs.
records.quantitative_detail: Guidance timing per staff (2026-01-12): promised Q4 2025, then Q1 2026; staff guess Q2 2027. Director (2026-09-21): delayed about 2.5-3 years.

And the reason they did that is because they are still working on finalizing the guidance documents for interconnected surface water, which we recently found out that it's going to be delayed. ... it's been delayed by I think two and a half, three years at this point is there since it will roll over into the next periodic update, is there a concern that we're going to be on the hook for more monitoring in the interim or that our monitoring capacities, this GSA, other GSAs, may not be sufficient to next update? records.finding: As a condition of dropping its CEQA suit over DWR buying Fair Ranch settlement-contract water for instream flow, YSGA approved an MOU barring groundwater-substitution transfers until YSGA finds that North Yolo MA pumping would not cause undesirable results, plus a subsidence GPS station. No stream-depletion test or ISW monitoring is specified.

RD 108 installs one continuous GPS -based subsidence station (cGNSS or equivalent) one year prior to groundwater substitution transfers occurring

records.finding: Repurposing-scale money in Yolo's 2025-26 meetings comes from DWR, not an MLRP grant: DWR would pay Fair Ranch's owner $180 million for rights to 5,000-16,000 AFY of Settlement Contract water for instream flows, and RD 108 has agreed to acquire the roughly 7,500-acre ranch. No meeting or packet mentions MLRP, the Department of Conservation or a block grant.
records.quantitative_detail: $180 million DWR payment to RRG (one-time, as proposed); 5,000-16,000 AF per year of surface water for instream flow (annual); Settlement Contract 29,800 AF per year; Fair Ranch ~7,500 acres (7,521 in MOU)
records.agenda_item: 8. Consideration: RD 108 Management of Fair Ranch

records.finding: The SGMA fee adopted in May 2026 is YSGA's first parcel-level charge tied to land use. In February the consultant said LandIQ cropped acres include rotationally idle fields, even idle three or four years, if once irrigated, so fallowed land would keep paying the Tier 2 agricultural rate; grazing land pays Tier 1 only. The adopted definition leaves idle land's status unclear.
records.quantitative_detail: Tier 1: $1.50 per parcel + $0.76 per acre; Tier 2 agricultural: $2.78 per acre (districted) or $7.94 per acre (undistricted) of cropped or managed-wetland acres; fee level $1.6 million per year from FY2026/27
records.agenda_item: 5. Consideration: Fee Structure
records.evidence_text: It can be idle too, because fields do go into rotation where they're idle. They might even be idle for three or four years. But if that land has been irrigated in the past, that would be included as cropped acre ... It also means that those areas within a parcel, or perhaps it could be the entire parcel that's grazing land. It could be vernal pools. It can be passive uses of land. They do not pay tier two fee.
records.notes: Speaker inferred from the consultant's presentation (generic transcript label), and the May definition (land that produces food, feed or fiber) plus the dry-farm corrections process may change how idle acres are treated, which no later meeting states.

records.finding: YSGA treated the Fair Ranch flow sale as a leakage risk (sold surface water replaced by pumping) and negotiated MOU terms barring groundwater-substitution transfers until YSGA finds North Yolo safe from undesirable results on 10 years of record, a cGNSS subsidence station has run for a year, CEQA is complete, and YSGA approves each transfer.
records.quantitative_detail: Look-back: most recent 10 years of record; cGNSS station at least 1 year before any substitution transfer (MOU names monitoring well F-93MW); flows at stake 5,000-16,000 AF per year
records.agenda_item: 8. Consideration: RD 108 Management of Fair Ranch
records.evidence_text: YSGA has concerns about long -term groundwater pumping impacts in -lieu of using available surface water to irrigate the property. ... The assurances provided by RD 108 related to YSGA’s concerns are as follows – RD 108 will not consider water transfers involving groundwater substitution at Fair Ranch until: 1. YSGA agrees that the North Yolo Management Area is not in a condition where groundwater pumping related to a water transfer would cause undesirable results (determined by analysis of the most recent 10 years of record), 2. RD 108 installs one continuous GPS -based subsidence station (cGNSS or equivalent) one year prior to groundwater substitution transfers occurring , ... 4. YSGA reviews and approves the respective groundwater substitution transfer application.
records.notes: Finding 391's no-leakage-path statement concerns allocation entitlements, whereas this is a transfer-driven pathway, so the row is labelled adds; the MOU also sets a monitoring requirement (MLRP-2.7a) and is one condition for YSGA dismissing its CEQA suit against DWR.

records.finding: The July 2026 Hungry Hollow white paper puts a programme-level number on a land-conversion/management action, unlike Appendix J's N/A or TBD entries: 3,100 AFY on about 3,300 acres, framed as reduced applied water and improved infiltration. It is a planning-level estimate only; the ranking table says performance metrics to quantify the benefit are still to be defined.
records.quantitative_detail: 3,100 AFY on ~3,300 acres (planning-level, annual); six-project portfolio ~11,000 AFY (range 5,400-21,800 AFY); conjunctive use 3,300 AFY on ~2,500 acres; on-farm recharge 4,000 AFY; selection-stage claim for the same project >6,000 AFY on 6,000 acres
records.agenda_item: 4f. Hungry Hollow Working Group consent items (PMA ranking attachment); 9. SGMA Implementation Grant Project Updates (Hungry Hollow White Paper)
records.evidence_text: Voluntary Land Conversion and Water Management Practices : Cover cropping, soil health improvements, and related practices on ~3,300 acres (planning-level benefit estimated as 3,100 AFY reduced applied water/improved infiltration). ... Will need to define performance metrics to quantify recharge b enefits and outcomes.
records.notes: Only the white paper's front matter and executive summary are in the packet, so the estimation method (its Tables 9 and 14) could not be reviewed.

records.finding: YSGA is piloting the California Water Data Consortium's Groundwater Accounting Platform with landowners to track recharge and pumping, and in mid-2026 sought consultants for an initial recharge-accounting and pumping-allocation framework: incentives for wet-period recharge, allocations and extraction fees in dry periods. Nothing is adopted, but the no-allocation baseline in finding 391 is now under active design.
records.quantitative_detail: Groundwater Accounting foundational action $49,000 per year (Feb 2026 draft) and $50,590 per year (FY2027 workplan); RFQ issued 1 June 2026; 15 statements of qualifications from 20 firms (Sept 2026)
records.agenda_item: 6a. YSGA Workplan and Request for Qualifications
records.evidence_text: B. Groundwater Accounting YSGA is currently piloting the Groundwater Accounting Platform developed by the California Water Data Consortium. YSGA anticipates that during this pilot, we will partner with landowners to support the tracking of groundwater recharge and pumping on lands throughout the Subbasin. The YSGA is seeking a highly experienced consulting team of data scientists, licensed geologists, hydrogeologists, or civil engineers with qualifying experience that can work in tandem with YSGA staff to develop an initial groundwa ter recharge accounting and groundwater pumping allocation framework . The framework would provide incentives for landowners to optimize groundwater recharge during wet periods and impose a groundwater pumping allocation and associated groundwater extraction fees during dry periods to prevent the occurrence of undesirable results.
records.notes: Kept in MLRP because finding 391 says a parcel that stops pumping frees nothing for lack of any allocation system; the framework under design would create that entitlement baseline, though no speaker linked it to fallowing. Also answers MLRP-2.3a and 2.2a.

records.section: 2.5 Data Source and ET Product Choice
records.finding: Billing the fee from LandIQ cropped acres exposed misclassification: by July 2026 about 50 landowners had asked to reclassify about 5,100 acres of grazing and dry-farmed land mapped as cropped. This independently confirms land-use data as Yolo's weakest accounting input and shows landowner correction requests have become the validation mechanism.
records.quantitative_detail: ~50 correction requests covering ~5,100 acres (pre-billing, as of 20 July 2026); July minutes record ~5,000 acres corrected
records.agenda_item: 7. Presentation: Fee Study Update
records.evidence_text: we opened up a pre billing corrections process for tier 2 to help clean up the data. There's some land use, the way the satellites pick up the data, they have some grazing land, dry lands, inaccurately classified as cropped acres. And so we've received about 50 unique entries for a request to reclassify 5,100 acres. We're still vetting all the data and going through it, but for the most part it seems to be pretty straightforward that it was inaccuracies with land IQ in accidentally grabbing or classifying grazing land as crushed land.
records.notes: It matters for MLRP because the same layer would be used to see fallowed or retired land; in May the consultant said it cannot tell irrigated from dry-farmed crops, and the July minutes (in the September packet) say corrected where the transcript says requested and still being vetted.

records.finding: Beyond water, the Fair Ranch MOU and staff report name habitat restoration, floodplain and open-space protection, public access and the RCD's 2023 Carbon Farm Plan as outcomes of the repurposing deal. All are good-faith commitments: none carries a metric, a monitoring duty or a reporting line to YSGA.

records.agenda_item: 8. Consideration: RD 108 Management of Fair Ranch

RD 108 acknowledges the Carbon Farm Plan for Fair Ranch prepared in December 2023 by the Yolo County Resource Conservation District (RCD) and agrees to consider its implementation in good faith as part of its stewardship of Fair Ranch. ... Nothing in this provision requires RD 108 to implement any specific practice identified in the Carbon Farm Plan. ... Facilitat ed by entering into the MOU, RD 108’s acquisition of the Property will allow the Property to continue agricultural uses, prevent encroachment of development into floodplains and preserve open space, and may allow for restoration of some of the lands to nat ural conditions.

records.finding: CDFW's Yolo Bypass Wildlife Area manager told the board that paying even the Tier 1 fee (just under $13,000 a year) would mean pumping less in fall, cutting habitat and public recreation acres. The board adopted the fee without exempting CDFW.
records.quantitative_detail: CDFW Tier 1 just under $13,000 per year (staff estimate); Wildlife Area 16,771 acres total, ~7,000 acres flooded wetland habitat in a typical year, 2,051 acres farmable rice (~100 acres kept as habitat), ~1,700 acres irrigated pasture (manager, Feb 2026)
records.speaker_role: state agency — CDFW (Yolo Bypass Wildlife Area manager)
records.agenda_item: 5. Public Hearing: Yolo Subbasin Fee Study Adoption

records.finding: Hungry Hollow projects were ranked on a nine-criterion, 36-point rubric that scores co-benefits (drought, flood, habitat), economic benefits and benefits to domestic wells and small water systems alongside groundwater impact, and the white paper prices avoided flood damage at $16.80-$173+ per acre per year. This goes beyond Appendix J's hydrology-only schema, but applies only at selection.
records.quantitative_detail: Rubric maximum 36 points (9 criteria, up to 4 each); avoided flood damage $16.80-$173+ per acre per year (historical estimate, inflation adjusted)
records.agenda_item: 4f. Hungry Hollow Working Group consent items (ranking attachments B1/B2); 9. SGMA Implementation Grant Project Updates (Hungry Hollow White Paper)
records.evidence_text: 4 Co -benefits - Mitigation of drought impacts. - Stormwater capture (i.e. flood management). Anticipated to limit flooding potential of Goodnow Slough and reduced flood damag e to culverts, roads, and crops. - Water supply reliability. - Support habitat. 4 5 Economic Benefits PMA maintains land value, ability for landowners to obtain loans, and grower operations. 2 6 Benefits to small water systems/domestic wells - Benefits nearby shallow domestic wells - Addresses Human Right to Water ... Collectively, the portfolio offers approximately 11,000 AFY in recharge benefits (range: 5,400–21,800 AFY), sufficient to offset modeled groundwater storage deficits in the area while providing substantial co-benefits including reduced flood damage (historically estimated at $16.80–$173+/acre annually; inflation adjusted), improved soil health, habitat enhancement, and agricultural resilience.
records.notes: Scores are assigned by YSGA staff when ranking projects, and no post-implementation co-benefit monitoring is described.

records.finding: YSGA adopted a permanent Prop 26 fee (May 2026; $1.6 million a year from FY2026/27) that funds groundwater accounting and monitoring, ending reliance on grants for core work. Staff were explicit that area projects, including Hungry Hollow land management and district recharge, must be paid by beneficiaries with no grant guarantee.
records.quantitative_detail: Fee level $1.6 million per year (FY2026/27); Groundwater Accounting $49,000-$50,590 per year; SCNY voluntary recharge contributions $335,000 for Jul-Dec 2025 and >$650,000 from 66 entities by July 2026
records.agenda_item: 7. Hungry Hollow project prioritization; 8. Fee study process and funding mechanism
records.evidence_text: Also, the YSGA's JPA is very clear about how the current funding structure is tied to sub basin wide initiatives. So any special areas that have projects going on are meant to be funded by beneficiaries only. ... So we were very clear from the beginning that you know, whatever you choose, just know that there will have to be you, the landowner contributing to making this happen and that we can't guarantee on grant funding to support these.
records.notes: That no fee line covers repurposed-land monitoring is the analyst's reading of the six adopted foundational actions.

records.finding: On 12 January 2026 the board approved five Hungry Hollow priority projects chosen by a landowner working group, including a voluntary land conversion and water management practices project (cover cropping, soil-health and land-management changes). The GSP's aspirational cover-crop incentive (P 77) is now an approved project, but it has no secured funding and is still at planning stage.
records.quantitative_detail: At selection: sign up 6,000 acres, ~6,000 AF in-lieu/direct recharge goal (annual); July 2026 white paper: ~3,300 acres, 3,100 AFY planning-level benefit; area deficit target ~6,000-6,600 AFY
records.agenda_item: 7. Consideration: Hungry Hollow Groundwater Working Group Project Prioritization
records.evidence_text: The fourth one is voluntary land conservation and water management practices. And the goal there is to sign up 6,000 acres to improve soil absorption and filtration. Recognizing that There are acres out there that could potentially implement overcropping in certain areas or increase that, or also look at ways they're managing the land to try and improve the conditions. And that there would be an in lieu slash direct recharge goal, about 6,000 acre feet.
records.notes: The transcript says land conservation while the packet title is Voluntary Land Conversion and Water Management Practices (PMA #8), and landowners were told grant funding is not assured.

records.finding: Dunnigan Water District reported recharge on land out of production: a landowner has idled Dunnigan's last rice fields for years so the district and The Nature Conservancy could test recharge (over 1,000 AF applied), and the district digs recharge ponds on private land under agreements of up to 20 years. No accounting of recharge credited to these lands was described.
records.quantitative_detail: >1,000 AF applied over two TNC projects (cumulative); ponds cost $30,000-$50,000 each; landowner agreements up to 20 years; DWD recharge ~3,000 AF in 2025
records.speaker_role: board member — Dunnigan Water District manager
records.agenda_item: 9. SGMA Implementation Grant Project Updates (Dunnigan Area Recharge Program)
records.evidence_text: These are the last remaining rice fields in Dunnigan. And the landowner here is a huge supporter of groundwater recharge and has idled his fields for a number of years to allow us to experiment with recharge. We've partnered with the Nature Conservancy for two different projects where we applied well over a thousand acre feet of water to these fields. ... And the we sign an agreement with the landowner for a period up to 20 years where the district has the ability to apply water to these recharge basins.
records.notes: Speaker identified by the chair's introduction (Jordan Navarrot, DWD manager and YSGA director), and the idled-field system upgrade was still awaiting agreement terms with the landowner.

records.finding: The board-approved Fair Ranch MOU (May 2026) is the most concrete repurposing arrangement in the meetings: the 7,521-acre ranch stays farmed except for fallowing to supply Healthy Rivers and Landscapes flows (about 1,400 AF in some years), fallowing under DWR's forbearance agreement (possibly permanent), and habitat on 10-20% of the ranch under a DWR easement. Acquisition is still pending.
records.quantitative_detail: 7,521 acres; HRLP fallowing ~1,400 AF in certain years (annual, when called); habitat on 10-20% of the ranch; MOU approved 18 May 2026
records.agenda_item: 8. Consideration: RD 108 Management of Fair Ranch (draft MOU attached)
records.evidence_text: 5. Excepting fallowing that occurs customarily for farm management/stewardship reasons, t he Fair Ranch p roperty will continue to be farmed with three potential exceptions , the implementation of which is subject to the prior completion of any necessary environmental review : a. Fallowing as needed to make water available for th e Sacramento River Settlement Contractors conveyance to the proposed Healthy Rivers and Landscapes Program (“HRLP”) (about 1,400 acre -feet from the Fair Ranch in certain years ) or to satisfy the proportionate obligations of the Fair Ranch under the Drought Protection P rogram Agreement with Reclamation . b. To meet the terms of the “Instream Flow and Forbearance Agreement ” with DWR , which run s with the land . If this w ould result in permanent fallowing , RD 108 would first review with the County in connection with implications under the Williamson Act . ... c. To create habitat as expected under the “Easement ” with DWR, which run s with the land (anticipated by RD 108 to be 10 -20 percent of the Ranch) .

records.finding: RD 108's representative told the board the Healthy Rivers and Landscapes agreement will fallow about 36,000 acres of Feather and Sacramento rice in three of every five years, with compensation, to supply flows; staff warned that less surface water means more groundwater reliance in Yolo. No method for tracking the groundwater effect of that fallowing was discussed.
records.quantitative_detail: ~36,000 acres (~7% of industry rice) fallowed 3 of every 5 years; ~1,000,000 AF programme contribution (as stated, programme-wide); Fair Ranch share ~1,400 AF in certain years (May 2026 MOU)
records.speaker_role: mixed — board member (RD 108) and GSA staff

So we're Talking about almost 36,000 acres between the two river systems will be followed on three out of about every five years. They'll be fallowed to make this water available that we are. We're putting up almost a million acre feet of water to, to make this healthy rivers and landscape program work. So there are some, there is compensation for that water that's going to be put on the table as part of the entire program. ... So the nexus with the YSJ is that as we constantly talk about, Right. Yola sub basin has historically been in a good situation because of ample surface water supplies. But if surface water supplies are not available in the future, that's going to be an impact to groundwater.
records.notes: The acreage spans several Sacramento Valley subbasins and the Yolo share was not stated; figures are a member's report, not a YSGA staff analysis.

records.finding: A director pointed staff to NRCS, Point Blue and California Rice Commission flooding programmes that pay for water; staff answered that the first problem is how to measure, track and account for recharge on enrolled fields for board reporting, before layering in outside funding. External programmes remain unreconciled with YSGA accounting, consistent with the linked finding.
records.speaker_role: mixed — board member (environmental representative) and GSA staff
records.agenda_item: 10. SGMA Implementation Grant Project Updates

Yeah, I think we're going to be pulling in more and more pieces as we try to build a framework of just getting the pieces together. Because I think the biggest thing for us is once we get people signed up, how are we going to measure and track and keep all that accounting for the, the board's reporting requirements and then from that, okay, how do we scale and bring in these other sources of funding?
records.notes: Speakers are unlabeled in the transcript, and the minutes in the January 2026 packet attribute the suggestion to Director Wrysinski.

records.finding: YSGA's managed-wetland mapping (finding 407) now has an operational use: the adopted fee charges managed-wetland acres the same Tier 2 rate as cropped acres, as water-using land, using a YSGA layer built from state data and Ducks Unlimited mapping. The state-owned Yolo Bypass Wildlife Area is exempt from Tier 2 but billed Tier 1.
records.quantitative_detail: Tier 2 $2.78 (districted) / $7.94 (undistricted) per agricultural acre; Yolo Bypass Wildlife Area ~9,500 cropped or managed-wetland acres (staff estimate, Feb 2026); CDFW Tier 1 just under $13,000 per year
records.agenda_item: 5. Consideration: Fee Structure
records.evidence_text: What this does, it only charges for the land that is actively using water to either grow crops or to keep the land as wetland for environmental or for recreational purposes. ... It's a acre that is identified as a managed wetland by YOLO Sub Basin groundwater. So YSGA has gone to a lot of effort to map where those wetland acres are. They use both data sources from the state. They use Ducks Unlimited.
records.notes: Speaker inferred as the HEC consultant, and Executive Committee minutes in the May packet say Tier 2 might later be collected through CDFW tenant-farmer agreements, likely not before 2028.

records.finding: At an October 2025 Board workshop, directors asked whether the GSP's Management Area committees should vote and formally recommend or only advise; 10 of 13 polled favoured revising the structure, and the group suggested an informal advisory, public-engagement model, with staff to propose a simplified design. Committee authority was still undecided in September 2026.
records.quantitative_detail: Oct 15, 2025 workshop poll: keep Board-committee model 2, revise structure 10, eliminate MA committees 1; Board participation: all listed agencies 6, one Board liaison per MA 6, public only 1.
records.speaker_role: mixed — YSGA directors and staff (workshop notes)
records.agenda_item: 4e. Receive Minutes of Special Board Workshop (Oct 15, 2025) and Executive Committee (Nov 3, 2025)
records.evidence_text: Should the Committees vote and formally recommend items to the YSGA Board, or informally advise only? ... Currently, public p articipation tends to come primarily from those experiencing acute problems. ... Revise committee structure – 10 votes ... Use an informal advisory structure to reduce formality and encourage participation
records.notes: Workshop lacked a quorum and the notes are staff-prepared; the same open question about advisory vs. other authority is in the Sept 29, 2025 Executive Committee minutes (2025-11-17 packet).

records.finding: The Hungry Hollow Working Group, a landowner advisory body chartered in 2025, voted 6-0 to recommend five priority projects and the Board approved that ranking unchanged in January 2026; a sixth WG project was added in July 2026. The WG re-reviews the ranking annually. A documented case of an advisory recommendation adopted as-is.
records.quantitative_detail: WG vote 6-0 (1 member absent), Nov 24, 2025; 5 of 16 PMAs recommended; ranking criteria score out of 36; 6th project (Western Hills) added Jul 20, 2026.
records.agenda_item: 7. Consideration: Hungry Hollow Groundwater Working Group Project Prioritization
records.evidence_text: The working group voted 6 -0 (one voting member absent for vote) in favor of recommending the following top five options to the YSGA Board of Directors ... The Hungry Hollow Groundwater Working Group will review the PMA ranking list on an annual basis to evaluate whether changes to the ranking are warranted
records.notes: Board approval is recorded in the 2026-01-12 transcript and in the Jan 12 minutes (2026-03-23 packet); all WG voting members are landowners, and staff (not the WG) scored the projects using WG-agreed criteria.

records.finding: Hungry Hollow Working Group voting seats are defined by landholding (small or large, irrigated or non-irrigated, east or west side, grower or grazer leasing land); seven landowners were appointed in November 2025 after targeted recruitment for empty categories. No seat is designated for domestic-well households or non-farming residents, extending finding 343 to this newer body.
records.quantitative_detail: 6 applications by the Oct 3, 2025 deadline; 7 appointed against a 10-landowner target; replacements appointed May, Jul and Sep 2026.
records.agenda_item: 5. Consideration: Hungry Hollow Groundwater Working Group Appointments

The YSGA Executive Officer worked with YSGA staff to identify other potential landowners that belong to the 1) Small Landowner (non-irrigated land), 2) Grower/Grazer leasing land, or 3) Large Landowner (non-irrigated land) categories ... YSGA staff will continue to make efforts to solicit landowner interest to participate as voting members of the Working Group with the goal of having ten voting members.
records.notes: Staff said the parcel breakdown used to set categories included rural residential parcels (2025-11-17 transcript), but no appointee category is residential.

records.finding: Yolo County's ag-well moratorium working group, in which YSGA staff take part, was described as having four member categories including a small domestic landowner; membership was not yet fixed. It is the only designated domestic-well seat found in the 2025-26 meetings, and it sits on a County body, not a YSGA one.
records.quantitative_detail: 4 member categories (grower, well driller, small domestic landowner, subject-matter expert).
records.speaker_role: GSA staff — YSGA Executive Officer describing the County group
records.agenda_item: 6. Presentation: Update on Yolo County's Urgency Well Ordinance
records.evidence_text: The four categories are grower, well, driller, a small domestic landowner, and then a subject matter expert who's probably going to be a professor from UC Davis. I don't think they've fully decided who the membership is going to be at this point, but those are the four groups.
records.notes: Nov 17 minutes (2026-01-12 packet) say the County group had no formal membership yet; speaker identity inferred from context.

records.finding: YSGA is reconsidering Board composition: an October 2025 workshop floated consolidating CSD votes and letting the fee structure drive Board structure; the Executive Committee (July 2026) favoured fewer voting seats; at fee adoption the Farm Bureau director asked that the Board shift toward agriculture to follow who pays. Seats that now serve DACs could be consolidated.
records.quantitative_detail: 26 voting member agencies and affiliated parties; Tier 2 fee split 95% agriculture / 5% domestic.
records.agenda_item: 4e. Receive Minutes of Special Board Workshop (Oct 15, 2025)
records.evidence_text: Consolidating Community Services District (CSD) votes and giving CSDs the option of whether to be on the Board ... Agencies may have concerns about continuing to pay into the GSA and making sure their interests are represented if they no longer have a formal Board seat. ... Potentially allowing the Board structure decisions to be driven by the fee structure.
records.notes: No decision yet; EC minutes of 2026-07-08 (2026-09-21 packet) record support for fewer voting seats; effects on DAC-serving seats were not discussed.

records.finding: The fee consultant listed Knights Landing (transcribed as 'night standing') and Cacheville CSDs as community water systems that pay nothing to YSGA today, and every 2025-26 roll call lists 26 seats without Knights Landing CSD. Finding 342 says Knights Landing CSD holds a voting Board seat; the meeting record and the finding disagree.

Those are operated by the same person. So they don't pay anything right now. They, they are community water systems.

records.finding: The Board seat of California American Water–Dunnigan, the utility serving the Dunnigan DAC, was recorded absent at 5 of 10 Board meetings from September 2025 to September 2026, including the March 2026 meeting that received fee-workshop feedback. The structural seat exists, but it is used intermittently.

records.evidence_text: Absent: City of Davis, Esparto CSD, Madison CSD, Yolo County, Cal Am Water - Dunnigan

records.finding: A concerned-citizens group asked YSGA for a subcommittee of Focus Area representatives so residents have a voice, a meeting with YSGA, and a place in YSGA–County talks; no Board response was recorded. In September 2025 YSGA's Executive Committee had chosen to work through the County's group rather than staff a citizen-led advisory committee.

records.agenda_item: 3. Public Forum

And we were wondering if a representative from the YSJ could meet with the concerned citizens to review the work plan and issues that involve the YSJ during this well moratorium extension.
records.notes: The Sept 29, 2025 EC decision is in the 2025-11-17 packet; that the 2025 and 2026 citizen groups are the same is inferred; the Board then appointed two directors to monthly 2x2 meetings with County supervisors.

records.finding: Workshop and hearing input changed the adopted fee method: the cropped-acre definition was rewritten, grazing land defined, and a corrections and appeals process added for dry-farmed land wrongly classed as cropped, which drew about 50 requests in two months. The Board also ordered a review of rangeland and Clarksburg charges before the 2028 fee.
records.quantitative_detail: About 50 correction requests covering ~5,100 acres by July 2026; ~5,000 acres corrected by the Sept 2026 minutes.
records.agenda_item: 5. Public Hearing: Adoption of Yolo Subbasin Fee Study
records.evidence_text: But the main thing that was updated in the report was to the cropped acre definition. This was something that was brought to our attention in the last board meeting. We received some great input on this. ... I'd say the other public feedback we heard most from was on the dry land farming. And what we added to the fee report is that we added the fee correction section into the executive summary stating that a fee corrections process will be developed.
records.notes: Changes favoured dry-land farmers and ranchers; written objections from domestic-well owners at the hearing did not change the domestic tier.

records.finding: In its July 2026 letter to the County, the YSGA Board cited protecting nearby domestic wells from groundwater-level decline as a community benefit of the Winters alternative-supply work, quantified only as acre-feet of pumping to be shifted to surface water. No resident-level measure of the benefit is described.
records.quantitative_detail: Over 2,000 AF/year of pumping to be shifted (planning target, annual).
records.speaker_role: mixed — YSGA Board letter drafted by the Executive Committee and staff
records.agenda_item: 4g. Approve Submitting the Letter to Yolo County Board of Supervisors
records.evidence_text: Supporting City of Winters in partnering with landowners to shift over 2,000 AF/year of groundwater pumping to surface water use to offset groundwater level declines in domestic wells nearby
records.notes: The 2,000 AF is a target in an advocacy letter; the Winters study presented the same day estimated ~2,500 AF/yr overdraft on the Yolo side.

records.finding: Hungry Hollow project ranking scores every candidate project 0-4 on benefits to small water systems and domestic wells, citing the Human Right to Water, as one of nine criteria (36 points maximum) agreed by the Working Group and used in Board-approved rankings. It is an ordinal planning score for one focus area, not a tracked outcome or a definition of meaningful benefits.
records.quantitative_detail: Criterion 6 of 9, scored 0–4, total maximum 36; e.g., Western Hills project scored 4 on this criterion, total 25 (May 2026 update).

records.agenda_item: 4f. Hungry Hollow Groundwater Working Group Consent Items (Attachment B2, PMA rankings)
records.evidence_text: Prioritization Criteria Notes Score 1 Impact to Groundwater Levels ... Benefits to small water systems/domestic wells - Benefits nearby shallow domestic wells - Addresses Human Right to Water 4
records.notes: Scope differs from finding 347 (GSP, Annual Report, Appendix J); the criterion applies to one focus area's project ranking and nothing measures the benefit after implementation. Also answers COM-3.1.2c.

records.finding: PROCEDURAL: the fee outreach plan commits to tailoring outreach for small and rural communities, minority groups and fixed-income residents, but its engagement tiers put member agencies, agriculture and water systems first, domestic well users in the second tier, and community organizations last.
records.quantitative_detail: Tier 1 engagement Oct–Nov 2025; Tier 2 Nov–Dec 2025; Tier 3 Dec 2025–Jan 2026.
records.speaker_role: consultant — Hansford Economic Consulting / Rollins PR
records.agenda_item: 8. Presentation: Update on Yolo Subbasin Fee Study Process (Fee Study Community Engagement Overview)
records.evidence_text: Outreach efforts will be tailored to reach people where they are, recognizing that small and rural communities, minority groups, and those living on fixed incomes may need different types of support to stay informed and participate. ... Tier 2 – Second Level of Engagement (November/December) ... Tier 3 – Later Engagement (December/January ) • Community organizaXons
records.notes: Tiers were reviewed with the Ad Hoc Finance Committee; residential small water systems were in Tier 1; the OCR renders 'ti' as 'X' in the packet.

records.finding: DISTRIBUTIVE: the fee adopted in May 2026 allocates SGMA costs among water users by formula. Domestic users carry 5% of Tier 2 costs and agriculture 95%; the domestic-equivalent option was chosen partly because many water systems serve disadvantaged populations and would pay least under it, and de minimis well owners are charged per developed parcel.
records.quantitative_detail: Adopted FY2027 fees: Tier 1 $1.50/parcel + $0.76/acre; Tier 2 domestic $1.36 per developed parcel (unregulated/de minimis), $0.40 per connection (state small systems), $0.80 per connection (community systems), $0.32 per person (non-community); Tier 2 ag $2.78/acre districted, $7.94/acre undistricted; Tier 2 = ~$1.159M of $1.6M/yr, split 95%/5%.
records.agenda_item: 5. Consideration: Fee Structure
records.evidence_text: So what this fee structure does on the domestic side is it charges all domestic water users, including de minimis water uses. ... many of these water systems serve disadvantaged populations. And under this methodology, they would pay the least.
records.notes: No DAC-specific exemption or hardship provision was adopted; in Nov 2025 Finance Committee members leaned 4-1 against charging de minimis users, but that view was not carried into the adopted fee.

records.finding: REPRESENTATIVE/DISTRIBUTIVE: a director objected that undistricted (white-area) parcels, charged about 2.9 times the districted Tier 2 rate, have no Board seat; staff replied that Yolo County and the Farm Bureau represent them and that fee-funded Management Area committees would give them a voice.
records.quantitative_detail: $7.94 vs $2.78 per agricultural acre (undistricted vs districted), FY2027; undistricted area stated as roughly 171,000 acres, of which ~50,000 subject to Tier 2 (spoken estimates, uncertain).
records.agenda_item: 5. Consideration: Fee Structure
records.evidence_text: I'd like to understand more about the undistricted parcels from a point of view that none of those parcels are represented here. ... I would say YOLO county and YOLO County Farm Bureau serve as their representatives. ... we want to make sure there's dedicated funding and resources to get on the ground and to connect with the landowners so that they do feel like they're being represented and their voices are kind of being heard by the board.
records.notes: Transcript is unlabelled; roles inferred from context; rural residents with domestic wells pay the domestic tier, not this agricultural rate.

records.finding: PROCEDURAL: as a Prop 26 regulatory fee, the charge carried hearing and comment rights but no landowner ballot or majority-protest right. The adopted appeal process covers only Tier 2 calculation inputs such as acreage, requires payment before appeal, and ends with a final Board decision.
records.quantitative_detail: Pre-levy data corrections by July 30; appeal after payment by July 15 of the following year; Executive Officer decision within 45 days (or 15 days after a meeting); Board appeal within 15 days.
records.agenda_item: 5. Public Hearing: Adoption of Yolo Subbasin Fee Study (Resolution 26.01, Exhibit A)
records.evidence_text: Corrections to and appeals of the calculation of Tier 2 fees under the Sustainable Groundwater Management Fee adopted by the Yolo Subbasin Groundwater Agency ... the calculation of the Tier 2 portion of the fee in that year , that person shall first be required to pay the fee as charged.
records.notes: The no-ballot point is from counsel/staff on 2026-02-09; Tier 1 charges have no appeal route under Exhibit A.

records.section: 3.1.4 Domestic Well Protection as an Equity Outcome
records.finding: YSGA's Focus Areas, which trigger extra well-permit review and now a County moratorium on new agricultural wells, were delineated from declining groundwater trends, higher concentrations of domestic wells, dry wells reported in the 2021-22 drought, and residents' information. Protection is targeted by domestic-well density and dry-well history, not DAC status; domestic wells under 2 AFY are exempt.
records.quantitative_detail: County moratorium: 45 days from Aug 26, 2025; extended through Aug 25, 2026 (Ord. 1577) and through Aug 25, 2027 (Ord. 1588); exemption for domestic wells producing <2 AFY.
records.agenda_item: 5. Presentation: Update on Yolo County's Emergency Well Ordinance
records.evidence_text: isolate the areas that we did see declining groundwater level trends, and a kind of higher concentration of domestic wells. ... As well as reported drywalls that came through in the 2021-2022 drought. ... And it has brought in information from concerned citizens along the, uh, Plainfield Ridge in the central part of Golo County
records.notes: The moratorium is a County action relying on YSGA's map; in July 2026 YSGA told the County the Focus Areas were an informational tool, not a regulatory mechanism (2026-07-20 packet). Also answers COM-3.1.1c (citizen input shaped the delineation).

records.section: 3.1.4 Domestic Well Protection as an Equity Outcome
records.finding: A Hungry Hollow rancher told the Board two of four domestic and stock wells had been replaced, said YSGA verified four new agricultural wells for a neighbouring publicly traded company despite YSGA's own estimate of 30-70 ft drawdown versus the applicant's 7-8 ft, and asked for an allocation method before the next drought. No Board response was recorded.
records.quantitative_detail: 2 of 4 wells replaced; drawdown 30–70 ft (YSGA study) vs 7–8 ft (applicant study); 4 new ag wells verified (all as stated by the commenter).
records.agenda_item: 7. Presentation: 2026 Draft Fee Study Report (public comment)
records.evidence_text: We have had replace two of our four wells on our ranch. They're domestic for stock watering. ... From what I can understand from the YSGA's own study is that the potential drawdown on groundwater levels could be anywhere from 30 to 70ft when the wells are in use. Yet this entity was able to pay for its own study, which amazingly showed there would only be a 7 to 8 foot drawdown on groundwater levels when wells are in use.
records.notes: Figures are the commenter's and were not checked by staff at the meeting; the request raises domestic-well protection without DAC framing.

records.section: 3.1.4 Domestic Well Protection as an Equity Outcome
records.finding: The draft 2027 Periodic Evaluation's well-impact analysis finds minimum thresholds protective of 95% of wells, flags about 200 wells (~5%) for follow-up, and finds higher shares in the Capay Valley and Dunnigan Hills management areas, with domestic wells most at risk. Results are broken down by management area and well type, not by DAC status.
records.quantitative_detail: WY2019–2024: 97 wells (~2%) potentially impacted; 103 more below the protective threshold; 200 wells (~5%) flagged; thresholds protect 95% of wells.
records.agenda_item: 7. Presentation: 2027 Draft Periodic Evaluation
records.evidence_text: And then our analysis looking at wells showed that our minimum thresholds are set to a level that protects 95% of the wells in the sub basin. ... There was 200 wells in total, representing about 5% of them that we considered to be something we should be focused on over the next five years ... the Cape Valley and the Donegan Hills management areas contain a higher percentage of these potentially
records.notes: 'Domestic wells most at risk' is from the Jan 12 minutes (2026-03-23 packet); the TAC chose not to rerun the analysis with corrected well-completion data before 2027; whether the Dunnigan DAC lies in Dunnigan Hills MA is not stated.

records.finding: YSGA staff hold informal coffee-shop office hours in Winters and Woodland to answer questions on YSGA, groundwater and well permitting, with about 10 attendees each at the first sessions and a plan to meet every other month; the activity is now a line item in the fee-funded five-year work plan. It is the first reach figure reported for YSGA engagement.
records.quantitative_detail: ~10 attendees per session (Winters and Woodland), summer 2025; further sessions Oct 28 and Dec 2025; planned bi-monthly.
records.agenda_item: 4e. Receive Minutes of Executive Committee Meeting (Aug 28, 2025)
records.evidence_text: Coffee Shop Hours : Kristin and Erik had a bout 10 attendees each in Winters and Woodland. They plan to c ontinue meetings every other month.
records.notes: Attendance counted only for the first sessions; no demographic data; listed as O 8.2 Coffee Shop Meetings with the Public in the 2027-2031 work plan (2026-05-18 packet).

records.finding: Fee-study outreach was the broadest engagement reported in the period: postcards to all 7,200 parcels, five in-person workshops (Clarksburg, Winters, Woodland, Dunnigan, Esparto) plus a virtual one, some with 50 or more attendees, and briefings for cattlemen, the Farm Bureau, the RCD and supervisors. Sign-ins showed mostly agricultural attendees, then rural well owners.
records.quantitative_detail: Postcards to 7,200 APNs; 5 in-person workshops Mar 11–18, 2026 + 1 virtual Mar 19; some workshops 'upwards of 50' attendees; workshop ads $600 (Daily Democrat) and $350 (Davis Enterprise); mailing service $2,933.40.
records.agenda_item: 6. Report of the Chair and Executive Officer
records.evidence_text: Hosted five in -person public workshops throughout the Yolo Subbasin to garner public feedback on the proposed YSGA fee structure and draft 5 -year budget ... The workshops were well attended ; some with upwards of 50 attendees providing thoughtful feedback and questions
records.notes: The 7,200-parcel mailing is in the 2026-07-20 packet; attendee mix by interest is the consultant's oral summary (2026-03-23 transcript); no per-workshop counts were given.

records.finding: Engagement is now funded from the fee: the FY2026-27 budget gives $196,440 to establishing Management Area committees and $92,153 to outreach and coordination, and YSGA created an Outreach Specialist post to run the committees, filled from October 2026. Earlier outreach depended on a grant-funded facilitation contract.

records.finding: YSGA still sets water-quality thresholds only for TDS. Answering DWR, the draft 2027 Periodic Evaluation commits to sampling arsenic, boron, hexavalent chromium and nitrate at more wells through 2032 to judge trends and natural occurrence before deciding whether to add them; some wells exceeded the TDS objective in WY2019-24 without an undesirable result.
records.quantitative_detail: TDS measurable objective 750 mg/L, minimum threshold 1,000 mg/L; some wells between 750 and 1,000 mg/L in WY2019–2024; decision on other constituents deferred to the 2032 evaluation.

records.notes: Which wells and who samples are not specified; the Hungry Hollow white paper (2026-07-20 packet) summarizes GAMA data for these constituents.

records.finding: Staff framed adding water-quality criteria beyond TDS as a risk question, saying doing too much could create unforeseen risk or responsibility; in September 2026 staff added that YSGA would first address only water-quality effects YSGA itself might cause. records.finding: CGA's board approved continued engagement in the seven-subbasin North Sacramento River Corridor group, whose priority is a regional ISW effort (field measurements on shared streams, refined regional modelling, guidance for each GSA to set its own ISW standards) framed as the response to DWR's ISW corrective action. No agency money is committed; a Prop 4 grant is the target.
records.quantitative_detail: 7 subbasins (Red Bluff, Antelope, Los Molinos, Corning, Vina, Colusa, Butte); 5-year implementation update covering 2026-2032; agency funding requested: $0 at this time; engagement to be documented in each subbasin's 2027 Periodic Evaluation (agenda item 4b)
records.speaker_role: GSA staff — CGA Program Manager (Carol Thomas-Keefer)

There's also refined regional modeling which is going to be important, updating those models and then the local policy support. ... There's no funding that's requested from any of the participating agencies right now. We're hoping that we're going to be able to qualify for a Prop 4 grant to cover the, the work under this program.

records.quantitative_detail: Minimum holding for demand accounting: ad hoc discussed 0-20 acres, settled near 15; joint meeting leaned to 10 acres. A speaker estimated roughly 1,800 owners at 15 acres vs about 2,200 at 10 acres (~400 more; spoken estimates).

But, but ownership is, ownership by a single entity is going to be the basis for, for the minimum.
records.notes: This is the tracking universe for subbasin-wide demand-management accounting, not a repurposing enrolment, which finding 454 says does not exist. Basin-wide rule; not specific to repurposed land.

records.finding: In April 2025 the joint boards accepted ad hoc recommendations for demand-management accounting: one subbasin-wide method, remotely sensed ET of applied groundwater as the default, certified flowmeters optional at the grower's expense, flexibility down to individual fields or parcels, and a phased pilot returning draft use data to growers in 2025/2026.
records.quantitative_detail: $500,000 to be budgeted jointly by CGA and GGA for remotely sensed ET data across the whole Colusa Subbasin (Recommendation 6; period not stated).
records.speaker_role: consultant — Davids Engineering (Jeff Davids) presenting joint ad hoc recommendations
records.meeting_body: Joint CGA/GGA Board of Directors (special meeting)
records.agenda_item: 2a. Approval of April 18, 2025 Joint Board minutes (minutes Item 5b, Groundwater Demand Management Program Development)
records.evidence_text: Recommendation 3: This accounting system needs the flexibility to potentially handle different spatial scales (large groupings of land vs. individual fields/parcels, etc.). Recommendation 4: The preferred measurement method for evapotranspiration of applied groundwater (ETAGW) is remote sensing with certified totalizing flowmeters as an option. ... Recommendation 7: Water accounting should be implemented in a phased manner with a pilot phase including provision of data to growers as soon as possible (e.g., providing draft groundwater consumption/extraction data to growers in 2025/2026).
records.notes: Evidence is the April 18, 2025 joint special-meeting minutes approved at this meeting; CGA lacked a quorum on 4/18, so consensus came from the GGA Board and the CGA members present.

records.finding: Landowner-level accounting reached growers. In August 2026 the joint boards approved draft individual water accounting statements, being mailed through Davids Engineering ahead of September 2-3 roundtable workshops. Directors framed each statement as showing whether a landowner is a net positive or net negative groundwater user; no charges attach yet because funding is undecided.
records.quantitative_detail: Draft statements approved at the 2026-08-14 joint CGA/GGA meeting; workshops 2026-09-02 and 2026-09-03 (in person and virtual).
records.speaker_role: mixed — CGA chair, GSA staff (Carol Thomas-Keefer) and a board member
records.agenda_item: Opening discussion; 5. Colusa Subbasin GSP Implementation Update; 7a. Committee Reports – Demand Management ad hoc

Their water accounting summaries already in their hands so that they could bring them and ask questions ... I'm Either a net, you know, net positive or net negative in my groundwater use.
records.notes: The water year covered and the ET product behind the statements were not stated in CGA meetings.

records.finding: Allocation remains a possible demand-management action, not a rule. In April 2026 the consultant's trigger matrix linked groundwater distress levels to actions such as penalties or allocations but was mostly empty; by May directors described tiers running to pumping fees and, last, curtailment. No discussion addressed what allocation fallowed or repurposed land would keep.
records.quantitative_detail: Program due January 2027 (stated in 2026 as next January); by 2026-08-25 staff said trigger recommendations were essentially made.
records.speaker_role: board member — CGA chair Jim Wallace reporting for the demand management ad hoc
records.agenda_item: 10a. Committee Reports – Demand Management ad hoc
records.evidence_text: presentation that we got from our consultant Jeff David was in the form of a matrix and working on developing what I would describe as checkpoints or levels of distress that are going to initiate actions for groundwater demand management. I'm going to say that the chart, the matrix is mostly empty at this point. Jeff is looking for our input and looking for our interest as to how quickly do we react. What do those reactions look like? Are they penalties or are they allocations and so forth like that.
records.notes: Chair identity inferred from context (the transcript labels the speaker CGA Board Room).

records.finding: Scoping the accounting RFQ, the CGA chair said the system should track not only extraction but surface recharge, in-lieu recharge and trading. RD108's Lewis Bair described credit rules as configurable database queries, giving the example of discounting a year-old recharge by 20%, the only decay or leave-behind idea voiced in these meetings. Nothing was adopted.
records.quantitative_detail: Illustrative rule only: recharge one year old discounted 20% (hypothetical example, not adopted).
records.speaker_role: board member — CGA chair Jim Wallace and Lewis Bair (RD108 alternate director)
records.agenda_item: 6. Discussion of Proposed FY 2025-26 Budget (groundwater demand management line)

Things like surface recharge or other kinds of recharge in-lieu recharge. um, trading, whatever the community decided. ... And then it's all the rules. that we want to apply to those queries. So… You do a recharge a year ago, that's, you know, it's discounted 20%, right?
records.notes: The transcript labels nearly every speaker Jim WALLACE; speakers were identified from the chair's hand-offs.

records.finding: The ledger that would carry any savings or credits is being procured. After an RFQ drew four proposals costed near $1 million each, the joint boards in November 2025 chose to negotiate with Davids Engineering to identify the best accounting system; a GGA-held accounting task order followed, and a demand-management task order reached the board in September 2026.
records.quantitative_detail: RFQ issued 2025-07-25, submittals due 2025-08-29; four respondents presented; chair said quotes were all about $1 million (2025-10-28); Task Order 1178.10 Groundwater Demand Management Program Development: $74,150 per GSA, $148,300 total, on the 2026-09-22 CGA agenda.
records.speaker_role: GSA staff — Carol Thomas-Keefer, CGA program manager
records.agenda_item: 8. Colusa Subbasin GSP Implementation Update
records.evidence_text: We had done the, the request for qualifications and put together a short list of those and we had presentations from them and did some reference checks. But ultimately the recommendation was made and was approved by the joint boards to, to basically just talk to David's engineering and negotiate a contract and a scope of work so that they would assist us in identifying the best water accounting system to meet our needs.
records.notes: The 2026-09-22 transcript ends before Item 7b, so approval of the $148,300 task order is not confirmed.

records.finding: Crediting is still absent and is now an explicit design question. CGA speakers agreed the voluntary south-Colusa recharge group cannot earn credit unless brought under a GSA demand-management program with accounting; counsel warned that recovering recharged imported water without GSA accounting could be a problem; one participant feared basin-wide accounting would hand recharge credits to rice fields.
records.speaker_role: mixed — board members and CGA counsel (Alan Doud)
records.agenda_item: 7b. Review and direction on funding alternatives
records.evidence_text: credit for what they're putting on the ground in skin and unless it's under a GSA demand management program with accounting, how do you do that? ... But if there's an intent to recover and use that water for their benefit and it's not being accounted for by a GSA that that could be a problem. ... if you have this wide accounting system, all of a sudden you're getting recharge credits for CP from rice fields and everybody's having to pay for that.
records.notes: Board speakers are unlabeled (CGA Board Room); on 2025-09-19 the presiding chair relayed a GCID rice grower asking when he would get credit for his recharge.

records.finding: At a Corning GSA meeting the shared consultant showed Colusa's draft statements, sent to every Colusa Subbasin landowner, as a template. The metric, net groundwater impact (rain plus applied surface water minus ET and runoff), registers recharge as a positive balance, but the statements are information-only with no financial effect, and a QR feedback form lets landowners dispute parcel data.
records.quantitative_detail: Worked example (Corning context): ET 4 AF/ac, rain 1.5 ft, applied surface water 5.5 ft, runoff 0.5 ft gives about +2 AF/ac; without surface water about -3 AF/ac (speaker corrected his arithmetic mid-example). Consultant cited OpenET accuracy of about 25% daily, 20% monthly, 15% annual.
records.speaker_role: consultant — Davids Engineering (attribution inferred; transcript speaker labels are scrambled)
records.agenda_item: Demand management program development presentation (agenda item number not available)
records.evidence_text: Basically, if you take inflows and you subtract outflows, you're going to end up with this term. And it's not exactly pumping because it includes all of the vertical exchanges. And we're just calling it a net groundwater impact. ... This is just a draft statement that actually just as of maybe today are being sent out to every single landowner in the Colusa sub basin that basically goes through and puts numbers to their, the people's lands. ... You know, this is draft, it says, you know, subject to revision for information only. So this, there's nothing you know, binding or there's no financial impacts of this. ... The left QR code is to a form where growers, landowners can say, actually this parcel of mine is missing, or actually, I don't own this parcel. These data are wrong.
records.notes: The formula was presented with Corning data; that Colusa's statements use the same metric is inferred from the consultant's comparison and CGA directors' net positive/negative framing.

records.section: 2.5 Data Source and ET Product Choice
records.finding: The ET product for demand accounting stayed open. RD108's Lewis Bair contrasted Land IQ (10 m, ground stations) with free 30 m satellite ET, describing ET as the usual uniform method with grower-paid meters optional. Later a speaker said ET overstates pumping when the soil profile is full, and a director proposed ET unless a grower has an approved, calibrated meter.
records.quantitative_detail: Land IQ ET about 10 m resolution vs free satellite ET about 30 m (as stated 2025-10-28).
records.speaker_role: board member — Lewis Bair (RD108 alternate director); other directors on later dates
records.agenda_item: 6. Discussion of Proposed FY 2025-26 Budget (groundwater demand management line)
records.evidence_text: Lamb IQ is the one, right, that has the on-the-ground stations to improve the data, so they're… ET data is, like, 10 meter spatial data, whereas the… the free satellite data is, like, 30 meter data ... offered the UT approach as a uniform sort of cost for everybody, and if you wanted to pay the. Essentially, the additional cost to do the metering, you could do that too
records.notes: Finding 465 reports OpenET ensemble in the annual report's GEEEO; no CGA meeting stated which product the 2026 statements use.

records.finding: A public commenter credited locally funded creek-water infiltration with improving water quality for the Arbuckle public utility district, and objected that the effort earns no credit. It is the only community drinking-water co-benefit of recharge named in these meetings; nobody offered a measurement.
records.agenda_item: 2. Period of Public Comment
records.evidence_text: Like I said, we have come up with some pretty good solutions to come and raise the water quality in our public. town over there in Arbuckle, the public utility district, and um… I hate to think that we're not going to get any credit for that. We not only are being taxed for it, but, you know, the locals have had to let them buy water to come down the creek, try to infiltrate our local groundwater. And, uh, surprisingly, we've been able to recover that to that level quite a bit, I believe.
records.notes: The claim is a commenter's and unverified; the transcript garbles his stated affiliation.

records.finding: Monitoring in the south-Colusa recharge hotspot belongs to others. RD108 offered CGA its monthly real-time groundwater sensor log for part of the south area, and directors noted the voluntary recharge group runs a larger network. The chair filed this under voluntarily offered data sharing; no GSA protocol ties these data to recharge outcomes.
records.quantitative_detail: RD108 sensor log reported monthly; no well counts given.
records.speaker_role: board member — RD108 representative and the CGA chair
records.agenda_item: Between 7. DWR Staff Update and 8. Committee Reports

Our whole agency footprint, but it covers, you know, a pretty good portion of the south area. ... It's just a monthly updated, you Know the real time sensors and it shows what groundwater conditions are doing in that part of the basin. ... Skinny is a larger footprint, more data points. ... That goes in the current category of voluntarily offered sharing data
records.notes: The offer concerns groundwater levels, not project-level verification of recharge volumes.

records.finding: CGA counsel set the legal limit on paying for projects after the failed Prop 218: fees under Water Code 10730 (possible under Prop 26) fund administration only, while 10730.2 extraction fees, which need a Prop 218 majority protest, can fund projects but shrink in wet years. Directors leaned toward a wellhead fee; no recharge or repurposing funding source was chosen.
records.quantitative_detail: About 1,000 domestic and 1,000 irrigation wells in the Colusa County part of the subbasin (2015 inventory, as cited); $100 per domestic well (~$100,000-150,000) and $500 per irrigation well (~$700,000) cited, with totals of $1.2-1.3 million also mentioned (garbled spoken estimates); State Water Board probation charges cited as $20/AF plus about $300 per well.
records.speaker_role: consultant — CGA legal counsel Alan Doud
records.agenda_item: 7b. Review and direction on funding alternatives
records.evidence_text: If you adopt a fee under 10730, then you can use it to administer your program. But it's generally understood that you cannot use proceeds from 10730 fees to pay for projects. ... If you do this, you can pay for all of the same things that you pay using funds from a 10730 fee, but you can also use funds from a 10.730.2 extraction fee to pay for projects.
records.notes: Counsel said on 2026-06-23 that a wellhead fee might fit under either section; no fee was adopted.

records.finding: By August 2026 the demand-management program and an accounting summary were nearly done but no funding mechanism existed. One director said a recent appellate ruling bars spreading costs over land without wells; another said the fallback without funding is regulating pumping; the FY2026-27 baseline budget funds demand management but none of the GSP's 25 projects.
records.quantitative_detail: FY2026-27 CGA budget about $631,987 expenses vs about $650,000 revenue; operations fee $1.45/acre (cap $1.48); $80,000 demand management; $50,000 domestic well mitigation fund; a director estimated demand management at $2-2.5 million over 10 years (all 2026-05-26); Lewis Bair expected fees of roughly $5-10 per acre, not $300 per acre (2026-08-25).
records.speaker_role: mixed — GSA staff (Carol Thomas-Keefer) and board members (Jeffrey Sutton; Lewis Bair, RD108)
records.agenda_item: 7a. Committee Reports – Demand Management ad hoc
