But what we really need to work on now is the program funding. ... the final step is, you know, is essentially regulation and limiting groundwater. Right. That's the only thing we can do if we don't have funding. ... I think that, you know, the idea that you can put this across all lands is now deemed unconstitutional.
records.notes: Directors called it the GARS decision (a Third District Court of Appeal ruling, county garbled in the GCID transcript); counsel had not briefed its scope in these meetings.

records.finding: A voluntary grower group (name transcribed as Skinny) runs recharge and in-lieu projects in the Arbuckle-area subsidence hotspot outside any GSA programme. A director said it may have about $750,000 for one season's recharge and treated the area as the priority for accounting; in 2026 CGA backed a USBR WaterSMART drought-response grant filed for the group by Colusa County Water District.
records.quantitative_detail: About $750,000 for the 2025 recharge season (spoken estimate); contributions cited as $24 per acre for white areas and $12.50 per acre for Tehama-Colusa Canal users (attribution uncertain).
records.meeting_body: Joint CGA/GGA Board of Directors (special meeting)
records.agenda_item: 7. Groundwater Demand Management Program Development
records.evidence_text: I think in both, both areas where we have subsidence, folks are doing a substantial amount of work with the hope that we don't need demand management. Right? Orleans, RTOS is, you know, annexing and bringing in more surface water. The skinny groups working down in our buckle may have about three quarters of million dollars for this year's recharge efforts. ... Because we're about halfway there. But yeah, that was $24 for the white areas. 1250 for the TC folks inclusive drain, so it was significantly more.
records.notes: The group's name and the per-acre rates come from a machine transcript with merged speaker labels and should be confirmed with CGA.

records.finding: Across CGA board meetings from September 2025 to September 2026, fallowing, land retirement and other repurposing never appeared as demand-management measures. Directors described the action tiers as pumping fees and, last, curtailment; the only repurposing mention was one unanswered remark about Prop 4-funded land retirement.
records.quantitative_detail: 12 CGA board meetings read, 2025-09-19 to 2026-09-22; one land-retirement remark (2026-04-28).
records.speaker_role: board member — CGA chair and directors (demand management ad hoc report)

Yeah. As instead of. And then the last year would be curtailments. Yeah. Which we're all trying to avoid.
records.notes: The absence rests on full reading and keyword searches of 12 CGA transcripts; GGA meetings, where the joint ad hoc also reports, are not in the corpus.

records.finding: The voluntary recharge group's own accounting is participant progress reports showing what each contributor's money put in the ground and their percentage share. At a GCID board meeting a director said the reports were well received and that credit within demand management would probably require coming under CGA jurisdiction. No reconciliation to the subbasin water budget was mentioned.

Yes, the progress reports went out and well received in. In the people that are participating and what has gone into the ground with their money. ... this is what you've done, this is what you've put in the ground, this is your percentage.
records.notes: Reported second-hand at a water district meeting; the reports themselves were not shown.

records.finding: In practice, programme design runs through joint ad hoc committees of directors. Boards accepted their DWM recommendations by consensus, at a meeting where CGA lacked a quorum. Eligibility decisions go to a committee of directors from each GSA. The Joint TAC appears only as a planned annual-report briefing; no community member sits in this chain.
records.quantitative_detail: 13 June 2025 joint meeting: GGA quorum present; CGA without quorum. Pilot Program Eligibility Committee: two directors appointed per GSA (CSGSA appointed 2 on 11 Dec 2025).
records.speaker_role: mixed — consultant (Davids Engineering) presenting ad hoc recommendations; boards by consensus (minutes)
records.meeting_body: Joint CGA-GGA Boards of Directors (minutes of 13 June 2025 special meeting, in 19 Sept 2025 packet)
records.agenda_item: Item 2b (approval of 13 June 2025 minutes; minutes item 4, Domestic Well Mitigation Program Development)
records.evidence_text: A quorum of members was present for GGA; CGA did not have a quorum. ... Recommendation 4: A Committee is suggested to guide CSDWM program administration and mitigation recommendations/actions at the GSA Board level. ... Following discussion, it was the consensus of the GGA Board and the CGA members present to accept the ad hoc committee’s recommendations on DWM program administration.
records.notes: The TAC's absence from 2025-26 meetings rests on searches of all 24 meetings (no TAC meeting reported); the eligibility committee's make-up comes from the 11 Dec 2025 CSGSA meeting.

records.finding: Representative: the only seat changes debated in 2025-26 were a permanent seat for Westside Water District and an extra private-pumper seat; the resolution failed on a tied vote. Directors argued over who pays. No speaker proposed a DAC, domestic-well or drinking-water seat.
records.quantitative_detail: Resolution 2026-01 failed on a 5-5 vote (transcript garbles it as '550 vote'; first split vote in CGA history per a director); a JPA amendment needs 2/3 of the 12 members (8).
records.agenda_item: Item 5, Request from Westside Water District for Full-time Board Seat / Resolution 2026-01

So I'm anxious to bring Mike and Westside in as a permanent member, but I'm not comfortable doing it unless or until we deal with what to do with the private bumpers at the same time. ... I just want to get the people that are going to be paying the bill at the table to have a discussion.
records.notes: The absence of any community-seat proposal is from reading the seat debates on 25 Nov 2025, 11 Feb 2026 and 24 Feb 2026; the July 2026 follow-up only discussed county-appointed alternates for the private-pumper seats.

records.finding: A documented case of public input changing a GSA decision. After landowners rejected CGA's Prop 218 assessment, the board cut its budget sharply. Directors redirected future funding toward charges on groundwater users (usage or wellhead fees), saying the community had made clear that users should pay.
records.quantitative_detail: Pre-ballot proposed budget about $2 million (speaker: 'I asked for $2 million'); FY2025-26 CGA revenue about $446,000 (28 Oct 2025); FY2026-27 operations fee $1.45/acre on a ~$632,000 budget (26 May 2026).
records.speaker_role: board member — CGA directors during budget discussion (speaker labels unreliable)
records.agenda_item: Item 6, Discussion of Proposed FY 2025-26 Budget
records.evidence_text: What they're gonna hear from me, Frank, is I went to my community, I asked for $2 million, the community said no. Right? That's crystal clear. So, if you want to bring an accounting system forward, don't bring it to me without a revenue stream to go with it. Right? And I expect that consultants can do that. Yeah, but I don't know what it looks like. Yeah, but the community was very clear about what. They thought that next revenue stream was going to be, which is… a, uh, a usage charge. or a wellhead charge, or a combination of the two. Because it was very clear from. The comments that we got is. We want the people that are using the groundwater. to be paying for
records.notes: The input was a weighted landowner ballot and post-ballot public meetings, not DAC or domestic-well engagement; on 24 Feb 2026 a director recalled hearing 'we don't want to subsidize that' at those meetings.

records.finding: No meeting defined, tracked or measured community benefits. Households came up only as potential fee payers. The CGA chair cited Yolo's Prop 26 fee, where engineers assessed the benefit homes receive in order to justify charging them, as a model to study.
records.quantitative_detail: Coverage: 24 meetings searched (17 CGA/GCID primary, 7 Corning secondary), 28 Aug 2025 to 22 Sept 2026.
records.agenda_item: Item 8, Committee Reports (Budget ad hoc funding discussion)

They, the engineers evaluated the benefit that they were receiving and then they applied it uniformly across the basin and it was not a very big number.
records.notes: The 6 Aug 2026 GCID board report on a Court of Appeal ruling also framed benefit only as the legal test for charging landowners; the passage describes Yolo, not a CGA decision.

records.finding: Procedural: joint CGA/GGA special meetings offered online viewing only, with public comment in person or by email. Directors relayed public complaints that special meetings on 24-hour notice are hard to attend. Staff said board packets usually go out about three calendar days ahead.
records.quantitative_detail: Special meetings on 24-hour notice; regular packets about 3 calendar days before meetings (staff, 28 Oct 2025).

records.notes: Regular CGA board agendas offer in-person or Zoom attendance; the comment restriction is on the joint special-meeting agenda. On 25 Nov 2025 directors asked to hold meetings in Colusa rather than Willows so local participants can attend.

records.finding: Distributive: CGA directors argued that GSA liability should cover only wells that fail because levels fell below minimum thresholds, and that shallow wells permitted by the county should not qualify. By Aug 2026 the pilot had set no hard depth threshold after DWR pushback, leaving review case by case.

Well mitigation, if we, as a CGA did not. mitigate well enough to keep the water. above our minimum threshold. If we get it below the minimum threshold, then. are bad. But if the well isn't. Doug, all the way to the minimum threshold. I believe that's one of the criteria that throws them out.

Yeah, they do right now, but the program is going away. The grant is ending for that program fairly soon.

And so we had a call with our group and we all felt it was the right thing to stand firm on that. And we were able to through some other county agencies get her lined up where she can get the 150 to do the application process on there.

records.finding: Distributive/procedural: CGA is weighing fees that would reach domestic users: a per-well fee (about $100 domestic vs $500 irrigation, Apr 2026) and a per-household fee for city and rural dwellings (June 2026). Counsel advised a household fee may avoid a Prop 218 vote, while an extraction fee requires a majority protest. Nothing was decided.
records.quantitative_detail: Illustrative (28 Apr 2026): ~$100 per domestic well and ~$500 per irrigation well; ~1,000 domestic and ~1,000 irrigation wells (2015 inventory); speaker's estimate ~$100,000-150,000 from domestic plus ~$700,000 from irrigation, ~$1.2-1.3M per year in total.
records.speaker_role: mixed — CGA chair and CGA legal counsel

So if you're going to, if it's clearly an extraction fee, it would be under 10.730.2 and that is where a majority protest under Prop 218 is required. ... So just you're in the basin and so you're going to pay a fee. Yeah. Unrelated to extraction amounts. Unrelated or just extractions? Yeah. Then no, you. Then 218 is not necessarily required.
records.notes: The 14 May 2026 GCID board report confirms a smaller flat domestic charge was discussed; counsel's answer is garbled in places, so the Prop 26/218 split is paraphrased with care.

records.section: 3.1.4 Domestic Well Protection as an Equity Outcome
records.finding: The joint ad hoc accepted Appendix 5E's well-impact analysis as sufficient to size the mitigation fund and split it between GSAs. The DAC-blind analysis therefore now drives money as well as thresholds. No speaker in 24 meetings mentioned DACs or disadvantaged communities, or asked for a DAC-disaggregated view.
records.quantitative_detail: Funding split CGA 45% / GGA 55%, from Appendix 5E's estimated well impacts by GSA at minimum thresholds.
records.speaker_role: mixed — consultant (Davids Engineering) presenting ad hoc recommendations; boards by consensus (minutes)
records.meeting_body: Joint CGA-GGA Boards of Directors (minutes of 13 June 2025 special meeting, in 19 Sept 2025 packet)
records.agenda_item: Item 2b (approval of 13 June 2025 minutes; minutes item 4, Domestic Well Mitigation Program Development)

records.finding: Joint ad hoc rules accepted in June 2025 turn the GSP mitigation commitment into a funding and accounting scheme. They set a $4.5M target funded linearly over 10 years and split CGA 45% / GGA 55% by Appendix 5E impacts. Contributions are tracked separately, admin is split 50/50, mitigation is charged by location, and a committee reviews funding each year.
records.quantitative_detail: $4.5M total programme target, subbasin-wide (Appendix 5E estimate including ~10% admin); 10-year linear plan = $450,000 per year combined; CGA 45% / GGA 55% of funding; admin 50/50; recommended 13 June 2025.

records.evidence_text: Recommendation 5: The CSDWM program should track CGA and GGA contributions to a shared CSDWM program fund separately. Recommendation 6: The CGA and GGA should split actual CSDWM program administrative costs equally (i.e., 50/50). Recommendation 7: The CGA and GGA should account, track, and split actual CSDWM program mitigation costs by the actual location of the mitigation actions (i.e., within CGA or GGA). Recommendation 8: The GSAs should reserve the right to adaptively adjust the annual funding of the CSDWM program within the 10-year period, as appropriate, to adequately fund actual mitigation and administration costs. Recommendation 9: Annual funding for the CSDWM program should be reviewed through an annual review process conducted by Committee. ... It was the consensus of the GGA Board and the CGA members present to accept the ad hoc committee’s recommendations on DWM program scope and funding requirements.
records.notes: The $4.5M, 10-year and 45/55 figures appear in recommendations 2-4 of the same minutes (OCR shows them with stray symbols); CGA had no quorum, so acceptance was by GGA and the CGA members present.

records.finding: The Sept 2025 joint ad hoc recommendations, given to boards as direction, set eligibility and cost rules. Dual-purpose drinking/irrigation wells may qualify, and replacements are in kind. The programme offers the most durable, cost-effective measure, and applicants pay extra for alternatives. A $150 application fee is refunded only if the well is eligible.

records.finding: At the December 2025 hearing that returned Kaweah to DWR, State Water Board staff rated the ISW minimum-threshold deficiency only partially resolved by the preliminary MTs. records.finding: State Water Board staff recommended dropping the MT's WY 2022 prerequisite: the GSAs should test every water year whether pumping caused depletions, because prolonged droughts can cause undesirable results above WY 2022 flows and cumulative impacts could be missed. This is a regulator's direct critique of the trigger design in finding 549.
records.quantitative_detail: Current MT test applies only when flows fall below WY 2022 levels (single-year reference); staff recommend a depletion test every water year
records.speaker_role: state agency — SWRCB staff (written Staff Assessment, Oct 2025, Recommendation 6)
records.meeting_body: State Water Resources Control Board (Board meeting)
records.agenda_item: 6. Consideration of a proposed Resolution to return the Kaweah Groundwater Subbasin to the jurisdiction of DWR
records.evidence_text: The GSAs should evaluate whether groundwater pumping caused depletions for each water year, regardless of whether the flows were lower than flows in Water Year 2022 , to determine if undesirable results occurred . Groundwater pumping may cause undesirable results during prolonged droughts despite flows being above Water Year 2022 levels . T here may be cumulative impacts that negatively affect beneficial uses and users which could be overlooked if the GSAs add a prerequisite for evaluating minimum thresholds .
records.notes: Also answers ISW-1.5c (staff name cumulative impacts, which finding 561 says the ISW TM never addresses); the recommendation is advisory and independent of the decision to return the basin to DWR.

records.finding: Reviewing the groundwater-level criteria, State Water Board staff found the 2024 GSPs did not thoroughly explain what groundwater-level declines to the minimum thresholds could do to ISW; staff accepted that the analysis can come in a future GSP revision. This is a regulator-identified gap next to EDF's finding that the ISW-area level MTs are never tested against ISW.

records.finding: Minutes record that during the probation response the technical team held a 22 July 2024 subbasin ISW workshop with local environmental and habitat-restoration groups on viewpoints and technologies for locating ISW, and was testing NDVI remote sensing to locate possible ISW, the same kind of screen the TM later used.

records.finding: MKGSA's two 2024 pilot auctions moved 98 AF in all: bids outran offers in May (535 AF vs 90 AF), offers outran bids in June, when 8 AF traded in two transactions. A participant told the board it 'operated like lottery rather than an auction'. EDF's documents report the auctions but no volumes or prices.
records.quantitative_detail: May 24 2024: bids 535 AF at avg $143.22/AF, offers 90 AF at avg $175/AF, 90 AF sold at avg $193.06/AF. June 14 2024: bids 166 AF at avg $131/AF (high $251), offers 258 AF at avg $238/AF (low $180), 8 AF in 2 transactions (avg price OCR-garbled as $1288.81/AF). Pilot total 98 AF at avg $192.74/AF.
records.speaker_role: consultant — Matthew Fienup (market consultant); public commenter for 'lottery' remark
records.agenda_item: ii. Transactions of the June 14, 2024 Version 1.0 Kaweah Water Market Pilot Auction
records.evidence_text: There were bids to buy 166 AF of groundwater credits at an average price of $$ 131$ per AF, with the highest bid being $$ 251$ per AF. There were offers to sell 258 AF of credits with an average price of $$ 238$ per AF, with the lowest offer at $$ 180$ per AF. A total of 8 AF of groundwater credits were transferred for an average price of $$ 1288.81$ per AF with a total of 2 transactions. ... a total of 98 AF will have sold at an average price of $$ 192.74$ for the two auctions held during the MKGSA Pilot.
records.notes: May figures and the public commenter's remark are in the 2024-05-30 minutes; the June average '$1288.81' is probably an OCR error; v1.0 rules adopted 5-0 on 2023-11-07.

records.finding: MKGSA adopted an Inter-GSA Groundwater Credit Transfer Policy with GKGSA: same water account, within 3 miles and contiguous; transfers into MKGSA carry no loss while transfers into GKGSA take GKGSA's losses; volume capped at the lower native yield, and declared 'not a water market'. EDF documents only EKGSA's inter-GSA mechanism.
records.quantitative_detail: 3-mile radius; cap = lower of GKGSA or MKGSA native yield; no transfer fee; annual transfer summary
records.speaker_role: GSA staff (Aaron Fukuda presented); board action
records.agenda_item: vi) Discussion and Consideration of Inter-GSA Groundwater Credit Transfer Policy
records.evidence_text: Transfers can only be made within the same Water Account. Transfers have to be done within a 3-mile radius and contiguous with the adjacent GSA. Water transferred into a specific GSA will assume the rules and regulations of the GSA it is transferred into. Transfers from GKGSA to MKGSA have no loss, but MKGSA to GKGSA will have losses as described in their Rules and Regulations. Initial transfer amount will be the lower of the Native Yields in GKGSA or MKGSA. ... Transfer form will acknowledge that the transfer is not a water market is only mean to balance operations.
records.notes: Earlier the Emergency Ordinance allowed transfers among common-ownership parcels within 5 miles (2022-10-25 AC minutes); in March 2025 the AC declined to recommend transfers outside MKGSA.

records.finding: GKGSA's board gave reasons for dropping zone haircuts on native sustainable yield transfers: little had traded under them, native yield is granted uniformly to every acre, and the year was framed as a pilot; tiered water kept its zone losses, and stakeholders asked only that transfers be monitored. EDF found no rationale stated.
records.quantitative_detail: Native sustainable yield revised from 0.62 to 0.83 AF/acre with deep-percolated precipitation folded in (same item); Tier 1/Tier 2 zone losses unchanged
records.speaker_role: board member (Speaker 1, apparently the chair; labels generic)
records.agenda_item: Item 10 – Rules and Regulations (transfer policy and method of allocation)
records.evidence_text: I think there's some real good thinking in freeing up a sustainable yield no one pays. ... And I think what the goal was is we had transferability here for a while, very little was transferred. But, you know, as we crank down the allocations, where some folks may need some water, and so we got as liberal as we can get with a native, which, remember, that gets spread evenly, every acre in the entire sub basin. So having zone restrictions on something that was really granted universally.
records.notes: The monitoring remark ('That should be monitored') is by other speakers in the same item; speaker identities are not given in the transcript.

records.finding: After GKGSA freed native-yield transfers, the neighbouring MKGSA/TID manager reported a landowner trying to move credits from the Farmersville area west, where pumping draws from below the Corcoran clay ('a one way ratchet'), and said GKGSA accepts it has a problem. This is the first reported leakage case under the sunset EDF describes.
records.quantitative_detail: Native safe yield of about 10 inches (0.83 AF/acre) transferable anywhere in GKGSA
records.speaker_role: GSA staff — Aaron Fukuda (TID general manager / MKGSA CEO), describing GKGSA's rule
records.meeting_body: Tulare Irrigation District Board of Directors (MKGSA member agency)

records.evidence_text: they did have a rule change in their book that allows them to transfer native safe yield. So the 10 inches anywhere within the Greater Korea, which was a reversal of their current rules which limited you could transfer but every little region you went, you lost more and more. So nobody did it because you, you only usually moved it one because you're going to lose so much going two or three. You didn't do it. This creates a big problem. And I notified them that this is a big issue for us because the reason it was brought to my attention was a landowner was trying to move groundwater credits from the Farmersville area all the way out to the west of us. records.notes: 'Greater Korea' = Greater Kaweah, 'cork and clay' = Corcoran clay; he raised it in GKGSA public comment on 2026-08-10, and on 2026-04-14 told MKGSA upper/lower-aquifer trading is unresolved.

records.finding: Like GKGSA and EKGSA, MKGSA computes no water saving for fallowed land: an approved fallow-field application replaces Land IQ ET with 80% of precipitation, giving net consumptive use of zero. This extends EDF's absence finding, which names only GKGSA and EKGSA, to MKGSA.

records.notes: History: AC recommended zeroing out fallow fields 2022-08-02, board approved a Fallow Field Approach 2022-09-13, tied to the 25-year precipitation average 2024-03-05; MKGSA has since moved to track fallowed ET (see 2.3a row).

This is an applicant's estimate with no stated method, so EDF's finding of no MLRP savings method still stands.

records.finding: MKGSA's Irrigation Efficiency Policy sets the recharge-credit haircut: surface water on fields is credited 90% in winter and 75% in summer, and on dedicated recharge basins 100% and 90%. A 2026 policy defines dedicated basins (compacted embankments, site verification, yearly application) and lets the floor be farmed.
records.quantitative_detail: Fields: 90% credit winter, 75% summer; dedicated recharge basins: 100% winter, 90% summer (adopted July 2023, retroactive to WY2023); prior EO assumption 75% consumed / 25% recharge; GSP efficiency 78% / 22%; embankments ~15-18 inches (2026)
records.agenda_item: 4. Discussion and Consideration of Irrigation Efficiency Policy
records.evidence_text: As outlined in the Emergency Ordinance, it is assumed that $7 5 %$ of surface water applied counts against Evapotranspiration (ET), with $2 5 %$ to recharge the aquifer. ... A new policy is proposed, Firstly, dedicated recharge basins will be credited with $1 0 0 %$ of surface water applied during the wintertime and $9 0 %$ during summertime. For agricultural fields, $7 5 %$ assumed in the summertime and $9 0 %$ during the wintertime.
records.notes: Dedicated Recharge Basin Policy approved 2026-06-09 after about a dozen applications; staff said fewer than a handful of true dedicated basins exist.

records.finding: DOC's December 2024 revised MLRP guidelines barred counting recharge from MLRP projects toward any future allocation or pumping. MKGSA's board signed a subbasin comment letter calling this a removal of the incentive and warning all five Kaweah projects might withdraw. EDF's documents do not record this grant rule.
records.quantitative_detail: $10 million grant; 5 projects approved early 2024
records.agenda_item: iii) Kaweah Subbasin MLRP – Department of Conservation Comment Letter
records.evidence_text: In December 2024, the DOC released the revised DOC Round 1 and 2 Guidelines for the MLRP. Upon reviewing the Guidelines in December, we discovered that the language we had worked on with DOC was not included, and in its place was a requirement that if any project conducts recharge, the amount of recharge cannot be included in any future allocation or groundwater pumping. Based on the goal and objectives of the Kaweah Subbasin MLRP, this language is very problematic and removes the incentive to pursue MLRP projects.
records.notes: Outcome unclear: EKGSA's TAC (2025-10-10) said DOC wants 'conservation with no add demand' and feedback was positive; KDWCD sent another DOC letter on MLRP challenges in May 2026.

records.section: 2.5 Data Source and ET Product Choice
records.finding: MKGSA picked Land IQ over OpenET in 2021 because OpenET lacked ground-truthing and tended to overestimate use, and after Land IQ and Davids Engineering estimates diverged sharply in citrus. This is an accuracy reason alongside the metering-delay reason in EDF 598; the comparisons were product against product, not against field measurement.
records.quantitative_detail: Land IQ monthly ET maps with ground truthing (TID approval, June 2021)
records.agenda_item: MKGSA Groundwater Allocation and Pumping Cap Proposal – comments on main issues
records.evidence_text: We will begin using ET measurements from LandIQ to start because data is complete spatially and temporally across the district. OpenET was just released this month, however, the lack of ground-truthing has resulted in higher uncertainties and a tendency of overestimate the amount of water consumed. Therefore, the MKGSA will rely on LandIQ ET measurements.
records.notes: Davids Engineering vs Land IQ citrus discrepancy is in MKGSA board minutes 2021-06-08; OpenET winter overestimate is in AC minutes 2022-01-17.

records.section: 2.5 Data Source and ET Product Choice
records.finding: MKGSA staff checked Land IQ on idle TID recharge basins and found raw ET above annual rainfall, a risk of overcharging fallowed land; Land IQ then shifted calibration to non-irrigated parcels. A local check of the ET product on idle land, not a field-measured validation, it drove the zero-out rule for fallowed fields.
records.quantitative_detail: Raw ET for 2020-2021 on TID recharge basins that received no surface water exceeded annual rainfall (values not recorded in minutes)
records.agenda_item: b. MKGSA Groundwater Allocation and Pumping Cap Proposal – i. Fallow field recommendation
records.evidence_text: Truthing expansion and related calibration of data is currently being carried out by LandIQ. The focus has shifted to calibration on non-irrigated parcels this previous year. Calibrated data for fallow fields will be provided at the end of the current water year. ... Data on TID recharge basins that did not receive any surface water for 2020-2021 were presented, displaying raw ET values for 2020-2021. Currently these values are higher than the annual rainfall, pointing to a risk of overcharging land owners with fallow fields.
records.notes: No comparison statistic is recorded; the June 2022 minutes add that fallow fields often evapotranspire about as much as annual precipitation.

records.section: 2.5 Data Source and ET Product Choice
records.finding: GKGSA heard its first Land IQ billing appeal (Bermuda pasture, Tier 3 penalties) with no appeal protocol; a director called for a 'backup methodology', Land IQ offered its checklist, and the board let the owners prove use with meter or pump data. In September they sought a 0.85 crop-coefficient variance; staff recommended denial.
records.quantitative_detail: ~$5,500 penalty adjustment over WY2024-2025; 90 days to supply data; Sept 2026 owners' claim: Land IQ over-reported 12.59 AF (WY2024) and 11.45 AF (WY2025), cumulative 24.04 AF on 22.5 acres; requested Kc factor 0.85 (>=15% error)
records.speaker_role: mixed — board member, Land IQ consultant (Joel Kimmelshue), landowners (public commenters)
records.agenda_item: Dashboard invoicing appeal (WY2024-2025 Tier 3 penalties)

records.finding: The Kaweah MLRP's bilingual call for projects requires moving irrigated land to less water-intensive uses with benefits for rural communities, economies and ecosystems, and lists habitat (pollinator, floodplain, wildlife corridor), low-water farming, low-impact solar, recharge, community recreation and tribal resource provision. EDF's co-benefit evidence is project-level only.
records.quantitative_detail: Planning funding up to $200,000, minimum $50,000 per project; deadline Aug 31, 2025; eligible applicants include landowners, GSAs, nonprofits, public agencies, local governments, tribes
records.speaker_role: GSA staff (Kaweah MLRP flyer reproduced in GKGSA packet)
records.agenda_item: Committee reports – Kaweah Multibenefit Land Repurposing Program flyer
records.evidence_text: Applications must develop projects that transition irrigated agricultural land to less waterintensive use(s) and create additional benefits for rural communities, economies, and ecosystems. Project types include: ... Habitat Restoration Pollinator Habitat Floodplain Habitat Wildlife Corridor ... Low-Impact Solar Groundwater Recharge Community Recreation Tribal Resource Provision
records.notes: 2022-10-25 MKGSA AC minutes report DAC mapping, K-12 outreach and DAC engagement under the grant; flyer points to kaweahmlrp.org.

records.finding: MLRP planning money paid for a subbasin economic-impact estimate of land leaving production, now being extended by ERA Economics, and MKGSA's CEO said a coming report compares MLRP repurposing with simply idling 25% of farmland to show smaller fiscal impacts. This is a program-level economic measure where EDF found no co-benefit quantified.
records.quantitative_detail: Baseline: 25% cut in valley agricultural footprint; CAP-funded ERA follow-on $85,000 (Dec 2025); Kaweah 'do nothing' ~ $1 billion regional economic impact, >=3,700 jobs, >$10M/yr county revenue (CWC, 2026-08-19)
records.agenda_item: Item 5 – CEO report (UC Merced land repurposing workshop)
records.evidence_text: recognizing that, you know, we're going to reduce our agricultural footprint by 25% across the valley is a daunting task. And if you just walk away from that land, we'll be left with managing those, the outcome of that. And so MLRP provides in the SGMA world a path forward where you can turn that into something. And we'll be finishing a report here soon that shows the benefits of actually doing MLRP versus the baseline of just taking 25% out of land production. You can reduce the fiscal impacts to your region.
records.notes: The report itself is not in the corpus; MLRP funding of the first estimate is at MKGSA 2025-12-09 and the CWC figure is a state-commission meeting quoting work with the Kaweah Subbasin.

records.finding: Kaweah MLRP applications pass about five review steps, including a core partner group (KDWCD, the GSA managers and Sequoia Riverlands Trust), a KDWCD board subcommittee created in May 2026 and a stakeholder committee. Reviewers added conditions (AEM and soil-data review) and dropped solar elements. Projects are scored, but no rubric was described.

records.finding: Under EKGSA's Regional Conservation Investment Strategy, MKGSA's committee heard that a CDFW mitigation credit agreement could let growers who convert farmland to habitat sell mitigation credits locally; locals worried such habitats might not save water. The only co-benefit crediting mechanism seen in Kaweah meetings; no later use appears.

records.agenda_item: d. RCIS Program
records.evidence_text: California Department of Fish and Wildlife’s program can provide a mitigation credit agreement (MCA) within a year or two. For all construction projects that destroy habitat, growers in the Kaweah Subbasin that converted ... land to habitat may sell credits to local entities, keeping both funds and land improvements local, instead of paying to a state mitigation fund that historically was distributed outside of the Kaweah Subbasin. records.finding: The Prop 68 grant that built the Okieville recharge basin, a community-driven land conversion, requires three years of post-construction monitoring and reporting, with MKGSA graded on grant administration. records.finding: MKGSA staff said MLRP projects first judged water-net-positive turned out to need groundwater or surface water to establish habitat, so long-term they must become recharge projects. Separately, the program later reopened development funds with a 'greater groundwater focus' and dropped solar; no speaker linked the two.
records.quantitative_detail: Habitat restoration estimate ~$20,000/acre (TID Seaborn Reservoir, Oct 2025); reissued planning grants $50,000-$200,000
records.agenda_item: Committee member reports – recharge discussion
records.evidence_text: The other thing, Greg, that we've been very cognizant of as we move forward with the MLRP projects that have environmental components to them. But what we found out was as we developed the habitat and the things that are, that are needed there, they actually require groundwater. ... So long term you need to turn them into a recharge project if you get the net water. Positive.
records.notes: Whether the lesson came from monitoring or construction experience is not said; 2025-10-14 is TID's restoration-cost remark and 2026-05-05 the KDWCD reissued solicitation.

records.finding: GKGSA funds its paid fallowing program from Tier 1/Tier 2 penalty revenue: the WY2026 rate resolution sets penalties to raise about $4.9 million for well mitigation plus a fallowing program of about $2 million a year, and the GSA holds a $2 million fallowing reserve. Staff expect tier revenue to dwindle within about five years.
records.quantitative_detail: ~1,200 acres/yr fallowing anticipated; ~$2,000,000/yr fallowing; ~$2,900,000/yr well mitigation; ~$4,900,000 total if Tier 1/2 fully pumped in WY2026; penalties $150/AF Tier 1, $250/AF Tier 2, $500/AF Tier 3; $2M fallowing reserve (Nov 2025); $20-30M tier income expected over next five years (June 2026)
records.agenda_item: Packet: Resolution setting Water Year 2026 penalty rates (adopted Sept 8, 2025)

The GKGSA anticipates the cost of such program could reach an amount of approximately two million dollars and zero cents ($2,000,000.00) annually; and WHEREAS, as a result of the foregoing, the GKGSA Board desires to set the annual penalty rates as set forth below. The rates below would be sufficient to collect the needed funding of approximately four million and nine hundred thousand and zero cents ($4,900,000.00) for a domestic well program and Land Fallowing Program if the Tier 1 and Tier 2 Penalty Allocation quantities were actually pumped in Water Year 2026.

That's you know, it's like double dipping.

records.finding: MKGSA itself applied for LandFlex in February 2023, missed round one and was funded in round two; staff described 'a one-time payment to remove orchards and/or purchase relief pumping indefinitely', with payments set by acreage, average crop ET and crop removed. EDF describes Kaweah's LandFlex as one-year idling with no durability instrument.
records.quantitative_detail: Payment buckets based on acreage, average crop ET and crop removed, including a 'Sustainable Yield Acceleration' bucket with permanent wording (Feb 2023 AC); no enrolled acreage reported
records.agenda_item: Resolution No. 2023-02 – MKGSA LandFlex Emergency Groundwater Reduction Program; v. LandFlex Grant Program and Criteria

Ms. Zegarra presented the LandFlex grant and scoring criteria, and recommended enrolling the MKGSA in the land flex grant.
records.notes: EDF 624 rests on a public comment; the minutes indexed 2022-02-07 describe the Feb 2023 application (date mismatch in source); whether any permanent relief was enrolled is not reported.

records.finding: GKGSA runs its own paid one-year fallowing program: a 2024 uniform-price round, then a fixed $400/acre offer in 2025 that enrolled 30 landowners and about 3,300 acres for about $1.3 million; in April 2026 the board approved up to $2 million, aiming for 5,000 acres. Eligibility: 4+ acres, member in good standing.
records.quantitative_detail: 2024: ~$500,000, ~2,000 acres applied, ~900-1,000 acres enrolled (uniform-price round); 2025: $400/acre, ~$1.3M of up to $1.5M, 30 landowners, ~3,300 acres; 2026: up to $2M at $400/acre, target 5,000 acres; 2027 round: 6 applications, ~243 acres, $97,300 (June 2026)

We had 30 landowners participate in it and about 3,300 acres involved in the program. ... It'd be nice to get about 5,000 acres involved this time. And I'd like the board to consider maybe up to $2 million for.
records.notes: Absent from EDF's file set; unlike LandFlex it is first-come first-served, not targeted near domestic wells, though its stated purpose is to reduce well mitigation; 2024 figures are from a garbled 2025-08-11 transcript.

records.finding: Through 2026 GKGSA weighed water-credit retirement as a permanent alternative to yearly fallowing: a GSA buyback modelled on the fallowing program, and a nonprofit, Water for Tomorrow, offering to retire donated credits for GSA fees. Presenters argued $2 million a year of fallowing buys only temporary cuts. No action taken.
records.quantitative_detail: Fallowing $2M/yr at $400/acre (recurring); nonprofit ask $0.25/acre base fee plus a per-AF fee, ~$55,000/yr to operate in GKGSA; illustrative cost $135/AF at 500 AF/yr or $36/AF at 5,000 AF/yr; market price $150-200/AF

It's $2 million and $2 million and $2 million. The water credit retirement creates a permanent reduction. One retired credit never comes back.
records.notes: Fee wording is garbled in the transcript; the GSA-buyback idea is at 2026-01-12 and 2026-03-09, and MKGSA (2023-08-22) also floated buying back credits with Emergency Ordinance revenue.

records.finding: Under the cities' urban groundwater plan with TID, a city-paid fallowing program on farmland at Tulare's edge is a likely early strategy: growers stop pumping, and TID surface water allocated to that land is recharged near the city instead. We're going to take you, so we're going to shut your, you're not going to pump any groundwater. And if there's an allocation of surface water by TID for that season. records.finding: Beyond its role in individual claims (637), the MKGSA Advisory Committee shaped the domestic-well protection standard itself: it rejected DWR's 20%-of-well-depth metric as arbitrary, the team adopted a 30 ft protective threshold, and the committee's 10x minimum-threshold recommendation was carried by the Board into the revised GSP.
records.quantitative_detail: Protective threshold 30 ft above well bottom (alternatives tested: 18 ft, 20 ft); DWR metric 20% of well depth; MT scenario 10x the 2014-2022 average annual decline, measurable objective 5x
records.speaker_role: consultant — Montgomery & Associates (reporting committee position in minutes)
records.agenda_item: 4.a GSP Review – Update
records.evidence_text: However, MKGSA Advisory Committee found this recommended metric arbitrary, as this would likely be too protective for deep wells and leave an insufficient head for pumps to function for shallow wells. ... The mitigation costs were insensitive to all 3 numbers simulated. Therefore, the more conservative 30 ft was deemed most appropriate for the program.
records.notes: Board adoption is recorded in the 2024-04-09 Board minutes ('The MKGSA Advisory Committee and Board of Directors agreed to proceed with the 10X'); the committee's stated rationale included operational flexibility as well as mitigation cost.

records.finding: The committee review step in 637 is used in practice. MKGSA's first domestic-well claim (PID 12072) went to the Advisory Committee, which forwarded it to the Board without a recommendation after debating attribution. The Board approved it with conditions. Staff later described claims routinely passing committee then Board, a roughly 60-day cycle.

records.finding: 634 records GKGSA board seats nominated by its two committees. In practice those committees meet as one combined committee. Staff called all committees advisory and said the Board had been 'a little bit loose' about giving the Rural Communities Committee work, such as reporting community water use. A standing agenda item to direct committees was added in June 2026.

records.finding: MKGSA's Advisory Committee has two DAC seats. One is held by Self-Help Enterprises staff (an advocate). records.finding: An engagement route into a binding agreement. The minutes do not say which were accepted; separately, the programme now delivers tanks within 72 hours and the Plan commits to English/Spanish materials (662, 657).

Some of the other comments included shortening the response time for interim drinking water to 72 hours or less, providing Spanish translations for all meetings and materials, shortening the length of the application to encourage more interest and intention, and removing SAFER funds as a funding source and outlining a more secure long-term funding source for the implementation period.

records.finding: A second land-repurposing action aimed at community wells, alongside LandFlex (647). After Self-Help found several dry wells around a small community (name garbled in the transcript), GKGSA leased about 12 acres of walnut orchard next to it to turn into a recharge basin. Later it discussed this as 'pre mitigation' instead of replacing each failing well.

records.notes: The community name is transcribed as 'Urica' and 'Hypericum' and could not be confirmed; no measured effect on well levels was reported (a director asked and staff cited an earlier model study not updated for this site), and DAC status is not stated.

records.finding: A concrete community benefit stated in money terms, which 641 finds missing from the GSPs. MKGSA's chief executive proposed backing a backup well, storage tank and fire flow for the DAC of Okieville, justified as 'complete resilience' for a community well. A roughly $600,000 cost share is compared with replacement-water costs 'well into the millions' if the community well failed.

And so in looking at that, We would need to come up with a cost share of about six hundred thousand dollars.
records.notes: Okieville is named as a DAC in MKGSA minutes of 2020-08-11; the 2025-08-05 committee minutes say the current well and storage are unreliable and lack fire flows, and the cost comparison is the speaker's estimate, not a documented analysis.

records.finding: The Kaweah MLRP's bilingual project solicitation makes community benefit an eligibility condition: projects 'must ... create additional benefits for rural communities, economies, and ecosystems', with 'Community Recreation' listed as an eligible type. Neither the flyer nor the meetings define or measure that benefit, consistent with the gap in 641.

records.finding: Narrows 645. The Mitigation Plan rule that claimants who 'contributed to overdraft' do not qualify does not apply to domestic wells. The consultant presenting the subbasin program told the MKGSA Advisory Committee that domestic wells are exempt from that third criterion, which is aimed at agricultural wells seeking technical assistance.

records.finding: Distributional. In October 2025 GKGSA let native-yield transfers move anywhere in the GSA with no distance or loss limits. Its TAC had raised monitoring of receiving parcels and 'localized management zones to protect vulnerable areas', and a speaker at the Board raised dry wells. The Rules packet still showed Community Management Areas as '[To be determined]' (642).

Tiered water transfers would remain prohibited. Discussion emphasized monitoring requirements for receiving parcels and consideration of localized management zones to protect vulnerable areas. ... Section 4.04 Community Management Areas \[To be determined\]

records.finding: Distributional. The post-2015 condition in 645 works as a pre-filter. GKGSA treats any well that appears to have been impacted before 2015 as ineligible without bringing it to the Board. That filter has disqualified a 100-ft well that went dry in August 2024 and a 42-ft well judged impacted around 2005-2008.

Asked what happens to wells GKGSA does not bring to the Board, the evaluator said they continue through the state drinking-water programme that provides interim and permanent solutions. So we would continue on through that program.

records.section: 3.1.4 Domestic Well Protection as an Equity Outcome
records.finding: The subbasin domestic-well undesirable result counts wells: more than 30 a year, at most 350 cumulative by 2040, or a GSA unable to meet mitigation needs. The committee was told 'income levels are not considered for mitigation' and every domestic well owner gets the same benefit. No DAC versus non-DAC analysis was presented, matching the lack of disaggregation noted in 650.
records.quantitative_detail: Undesirable result: more than 17 upper-aquifer RMS wells below MT AND more than 30 domestic wells needing mitigation in a water year; no more than 350 wells cumulatively by 2040 (about 10% of known domestic wells)
records.agenda_item: 4.b Sustainable Management Criteria – Subsidence / Groundwater Levels
records.evidence_text: More than 30 domestic wells in the Kaweah Subbasin are impacted due to overdraft and require mitigation in any given water year. If 30 wells require mitigation for multiple years, no more than 350 wells shall be impacted cumulatively by 2040 OR if a GSA is unable to meet mitigation needs ... Income levels are not considered for mitigation, all domestic well owners are eligible to the same benefit.
records.notes: Thresholds were chosen by trading grower flexibility against mitigation cost (5x-10x scenarios); version 3 of the threshold surface 'removed points that had dry wells or otherwise suspect data' (2024-02-20); the 646 PPAP is the only community-specific targeting found.

records.section: 3.1.4 Domestic Well Protection as an Equity Outcome

So, they're kind of on hold right now.

records.finding: The 2025 subbasin-wide 'State of the Subbasin' event and its booklet were built around growers ('Growers' Role in Implementation'). Community content was limited to the water quality notification protocol and a prompt to register domestic wells for future alerts. The agenda had no segment aimed at domestic well users or DACs.
records.speaker_role: GSA staff — joint Kaweah Subbasin booklet
records.meeting_body: Kaweah Subbasin State of the Subbasin event (MKGSA-indexed)
records.agenda_item: Event booklet
records.evidence_text: The Subbasin is committed to keeping growers informed about GSP implementation so they can stay prepared to act on SGMA issues. Maintaining good standing and local control over groundwater requires local investment and grower participation – through efforts like groundwater allocations and well registration.
records.notes: The event was held 21 Oct 2025 by all three GSAs and indexed under MKGSA; the Q&A in the transcript was dominated by growers' allocation and city-pumping questions.

records.finding: A GKGSA counterpart to EKGSA's Water Dashboard clinic (654), teaching the accounting itself. GKGSA held a workshop on how native yield is derived, how the groundwater model works and how the Groundwater Accounting Framework fits together. About 30 people attended.
records.quantitative_detail: About 30 attendees
records.meeting_body: Greater Kaweah GSA Board of Directors
records.agenda_item: GSA reports – workshop

records.notes: 'native integrated' is the transcription of native yield; the audience appears to be growers and stakeholders, not residents, and the date is shortly before the 2025-12-08 meeting.

records.finding: Supports 658 from the meeting record. No record of live interpretation appears in about 200 Kaweah GSA and member-agency meeting records (transcripts, minutes, agendas). Language access appears only in writing: English/Spanish well-registration flyers and postcards 'based on our demographic' (2025) and a website translation toggle (2026). No stipend, childcare or transport support was found either (656).
records.quantitative_detail: About 200 meeting records searched (203 primary meetings, 2020-2026)
records.agenda_item: Well registration outreach strategy
records.evidence_text: And, um, the Spanish version isn't in there, but we are developing Uh, the postcard and the flyer in English and Spanish. Based on our demographic.
records.notes: Searches covered interpret*, translat*, Spanish, stipend, childcare, transport and meals, and every hit was checked; the contrast case is the State Water Board's Kaweah hearing (separate row); a BMP tag would also fit.

records.finding: The regulator's process provided what the GSAs' own meetings did not. At its December 2025 meeting on returning Kaweah to DWR, the State Water Board ran simultaneous Spanish and Punjabi interpretation in the room and on Zoom, with translated slides, for the Kaweah item.
records.speaker_role: state agency — State Water Resources Control Board
records.agenda_item: Item 6 Kaweah Subbasin return to DWR
records.evidence_text: We're providing Spanish and Punjabi language interpretation services for this item, including the simultaneous broadcasting of this meeting in Spanish and Punjabi.
records.notes: This is a state body, a secondary meeting; the item concerns only the Kaweah Subbasin.

records.finding: The mechanism in 648 in use. MKGSA's Advisory Committee priced tiered water from mitigation funding needs against a reserve policy ($1.55M minimum, $3.0M maximum). It explicitly built the proposed WY2026 allocation from recharge credits and 'the revenue needed for the Well Mitigation Program'.
records.quantitative_detail: Mitigation reserve target minimum $1.55M (anticipated average annual expense), maximum $3.00M; tiered water $10/AF for administration and mitigation (2024); WY2026 proposed allocation 1.5 AF/acre; interim plan $50,000 for 2023 (approved 2022-12-13)
records.agenda_item: 4.b Water Year 2026 allocation
records.evidence_text: The proposed allocation of 1.5 acre-feet per acre was calculated based on the average groundwater credits afforded to agricultural areas due to recharge efforts by the Tulare Irrigation District and the revenue needed for the Well Mitigation Program.
records.notes: The reserve figures are from the 2024-07-02 committee minutes; the interim $50,000 is from the 2022-12-13 Board minutes.

records.finding: EKGSA has no dedicated mitigation funding stream like MKGSA's (649). Its draft budget held zero for well mitigation pending a Prop 218 assessment. The Executive Director said there would be no 218 for 2026 and the money on hand was 'not anywhere near' the $1.125M needed. Two weeks later a Board participant said EKGSA would be 'upside down' if claims arrived.
records.quantitative_detail: Well mitigation need cited as $1.125M (plus a second figure 'and 200' garbled); Prop 218 rate preliminary range $3-$25 per acre (2026-01-26)
records.speaker_role: mixed — EKGSA TAC member and EKGSA executive director
records.meeting_body: East Kaweah GSA Technical Advisory Committee
records.agenda_item: Budget – well mitigation and management actions
records.evidence_text: On the well mitigation, are we holding off on that until we have a 218? ... So we're telling the state we don't have any money for well mitigation. ... Yeah, we have, but not anywhere near what ... what we would need. Not 1.125 million and 200
records.notes: Speaker labels are user handles ('Board Room', 'Hags'); EKGSA reported no mitigation claims called on it by October 2025.

records.finding: GKGSA's version of the funding link in 648. Its WY2026 penalty-rate resolution states that about 800 domestic wells could go dry by 2040 at a mitigation cost of $43.5M. It sets the Tier 1, 2 and 3 penalty rates so that full use of the penalty tiers would raise the money for domestic well mitigation plus a fallowing programme.
records.quantitative_detail: About 800 domestic wells could go dry by 2040; total mitigation $43,500,000; $2,900,000 a year over 15 years; fallowing about 1,200 acres a year at about $2,000,000; target $4,900,000 in WY2026; penalties $150, $250 and $500 per AF (Tiers 1-3); Tier 1+2 penalty allocation 0.54 AF/acre, about 87,220 AF if fully pumped
records.meeting_body: Greater Kaweah GSA Board of Directors
records.agenda_item: Resolution setting WY2026 penalty rates (adopted 8 Sep 2025; in 13 Oct 2025 packet)
records.evidence_text: WHEREAS, based on the 2024 Amended GSP, it is estimated that approximately 800 domestic wells could go dry in the GKGSA if minimum thresholds were reached for groundwater levels and land subsidence during the course of the implementation period which ends in 2040; ... The rates below would be sufficient to collect the needed funding of approximately four million and nine hundred thousand and zero cents ($4,900,000.00) for a domestic well program and Land Fallowing Program if the Tier 1 and Tier 2 Penalty Allocation quantities were actually pumped in Water Year 2026.
records.notes: The resolution was adopted 8-0 with 1 absent at the 2025-09-08 Board meeting; the 800-well figure is the GSA's GSP-based estimate, not a count.

records.finding: Terms set as the first claims were handled. MKGSA pays for a replacement well only down to the depth its minimum-threshold maps justify, and owners who want a deeper well pay the difference. Working tanks and pumps are reused, liability rests with Self-Help and the owner, and the GSA only reimburses Self-Help.
records.agenda_item: 3. Well mitigation – Self-Help Enterprises update
records.evidence_text: Self help is working on a approach where we're going to use our minimum threshold maps to help establish those depths, And so we don't exceed pay for wells that are deeper than a minimum threshold.
records.notes: The 2025-10-14 Board debate set the depth, equipment-reuse and liability conditions; on 2026-04-14 (Tulare ID Board) the same manager said 'if you want one you can pay the difference'.

records.finding: A proactive mitigation step beyond the notification in 664. MKGSA proposed paying a one-time incentive to re-drill a domestic well to the minimum threshold before it goes dry, avoiding interim tanks and hauled water. Staff said no other agency does this and the State has not considered it.
records.quantitative_detail: Interim water supply and tanks about $20,000 per year per dry well (staff estimate)
records.agenda_item: 3. Mitigation plan update
records.evidence_text: we are looking at what we call an incentive program where we would make a one time payment. It's. It's provided re drill the well below or at the minimum threshold like we're currently doing. ... If the well went dry right up front you would avoid all the interim water supply and tanks that are required and that's about $20,000 a year. ... Nobody is doing it. We'd be going out on a limb again as usual.
records.notes: This is a concept, not adopted; GKGSA discussed a similar capped 'pre mitigation' scenario on 2026-08-10, where a garbled passage also floats a state revolving fund to help lower-income owners.

records.finding: Updates 650 for MKGSA. The Board hears counts of households on interim water, wells with data-sharing consent and claims in evaluation, and these are far below plan. Staff had expected 20-30 claims a year, but said Self-Help reported no new dry wells in MKGSA in the last two years. Staff proposed returning mitigation money to growers or not collecting it.
records.quantitative_detail: Dec 2024: 9 households and 7 wells on interim services; Oct 2025: 10 homes on interim water, 6 consenting to data sharing, 2 in evaluation; expected 20-30 claims a year; no new dry wells in 2 years per SHE (transcript 'don't have any drywalls popped up'); Sept 2026: 4 claims on docket; SHE admin fees $900 per six months (2026)
records.speaker_role: GSA staff — MKGSA interim general manager
records.agenda_item: Mitigation plan; reserves
records.evidence_text: So we only have 6 wells now that we're looking at, not 10. ... We were envisioning, like, 20, 30 per year. ... we're not seeing the mitigation we once thought we were going to have to do. So we should be returning this money back to the growers, or not collecting it at all.
records.notes: The counts are interim-water households, not the 'mitigation evaluations' tallied in the WY2025 Annual Report (650: MKGSA 1), so the two measure different things.

records.finding: Planned versus actual spending at GKGSA. In 2025 the Board budgeted $3M for well mitigation, with at least 24 wells identified by Self-Help in the pipeline. By August 2026 staff reported $1M placed with Self-Help and only about $170,000-$200,000 billed over three years, against a planning assumption of $3M a year.
records.quantitative_detail: 2026 budget $3,000,000 for well mitigation (2025-11-10); 24 wells identified by SHE (Aug 2025); $1,000,000 deposited with SHE; billed about $170,000-$200,000 over about 3 years versus about $3,000,000 a year anticipated
records.speaker_role: GSA staff — GKGSA (speaker unlabelled; probably general manager)
records.meeting_body: Greater Kaweah GSA Board of Directors
records.agenda_item: 11. Mitigation plan – dry wells
records.evidence_text: We put a million dollars in self help. When we first started this three years ago, they built us for $170,000 total. We anticipated when we first did this we'd be spending 3 million a year. That's all we've spent. We've been billed about 200,000.
records.notes: 'built us' is the transcription of 'billed us'; the 24 wells are SHE-identified cases, not claims evaluated (650 reports 5 GKGSA evaluations and 3 funded), so the counts are not directly comparable.

records.finding: Infrastructure behind the hauled-water service in 662. GKGSA had been buying City of Farmersville water from a hydrant at the KDWCD office to fill haul trucks. It designed a permanent fill station on KDWCD land, with service agreements from LAFCo and Farmersville, construction help from Ivanhoe ID and then Exeter ID, run with Self-Help under a site agreement to 2031.
records.quantitative_detail: Site agreement to 18 Dec 2031, automatically renewed for 5 years
records.meeting_body: Greater Kaweah GSA Board of Directors
records.agenda_item: Mitigation plan – Haul Water Fill Station
records.evidence_text: we've had now designed these all water fill stations so they fill up anchor trucks to go out and order water to those who have dry wells and have those large green flash tanks in front that fill station design completed. ... The agreement would last till December 18th of 2031 and then automatically renewed for 5 years if everyone's happy
records.notes: The 2025-10-13 packet minutes record the interim Farmersville-water arrangement; on 2026-08-10 the Board took up a mutual aid agreement with Exeter ID and a construction agreement, and the station was still not operating.

records.finding: Names the constituents behind 666's 'expanded list'. The subbasin samples eight constituents of concern at 70+ representative sites each spring and fall, with GSA-funded sampling coordinated through the Kaweah Water Foundation. Results so far show MCL exceedances of nitrate, arsenic and uranium, with 1,2,3-TCP under the cities. Some homeowners withdrew sampling access.
records.quantitative_detail: 8 COCs; 70+ RMS (71 per GKGSA TAC notes Sept 2025 and the event transcript); spring (Feb-Apr) and fall (Sep-Oct) sampling; MKGSA testing costs about $15,000-$20,000 per round
records.meeting_body: Kaweah Subbasin State of the Subbasin event (MKGSA-indexed)
records.agenda_item: Implementation priority: groundwater quality
records.evidence_text: 70+ designated represented monitoring sites sampled for all listed COCs ... Constituents of Concern (COCs) Nitrate as N 1,2,3-Trichloropropane (1,2,3 TCP) Gross Alpha Uranium Arsenic 1,2-Dibromo-3-chloropropane (DBCP) Perchlorate Tetrachloroethene (PCE) ... Subbasin-wide sampling coordinated via partnership with Kaweah Water Foundation
records.notes: The site count differs from 666's 75 RMS (spring 2026) and may reflect later replacements; exceedance constituents are from MKGSA staff on 2025-09-09 and 2025-10-14 and the Tulare ID Board on 2026-04-14.

records.finding: Adds to 670's roadmap. Today notification means seasonal reports on websites, email blasts and social media, plus semi-annual notices to landowner and invoicing lists. Next, shorter letters will be mailed to households near exceeding monitoring sites, but only those enrolled in well registration. The draft report also went to Self-Help, the Kaweah Water Foundation and the cities for review.
records.meeting_body: Kaweah Subbasin State of the Subbasin event (MKGSA-indexed)
records.agenda_item: Exceedance Policy: Notification
records.evidence_text: Current Notification C Seasonal Groundwater Quality Reports C Posted on websites C Email blasts C Shared on social media C Future Notification Shorter letters mailed to households near monitoring sites that exceed water quality standards ... Notification of an exceedance will be released to all households enrolled in the Well Registration Program near the RMS site.
records.notes: Draft-report review by SHE, KWF and the Cities of Visalia and Tulare is from MKGSA's 2025-08-12 Board meeting; tying letters to registration means unregistered domestic well households get only the general report.

records.finding: Shows what sits behind the free-testing route in 668. The Kaweah Water Foundation's emergency and interim drinking-water programme reported 737 applications, 354 wells tested (271 above the nitrate standard) and free bottled water to dozens of homes. It runs weekly community outreach, a monthly newsletter and fill stations, and has a $5.1M SAFER grant.
records.quantitative_detail: 737 applications; 354 wells tested; 271 above nitrate standard; bottled water to 59 homes (June 2026; May 2026 transcript reads 'nine'); SAFER grant about $5.1M over 3 years; fill stations at KDWCD and Okieville
records.speaker_role: consultant — presenter for the Kaweah Water Foundation programme
records.meeting_body: Kaweah Delta Water Conservation District Board of Directors
records.agenda_item: Kaweah Water Foundation update
records.evidence_text: Jacob that works at the district here, he does all our outreach, so he's in the community every week spreading the word about our program. ... we've got 737 applications to date. We've tested 354 wells, 271 of those above the nitrate standard, and then we provide free bottled water delivery to 59 homes.
records.notes: This is a CV-SALTS nitrate programme, not a GSA programme, reported to a GKGSA member agency; the counts are cumulative to date and the bottled-water count differs between the two monthly reports.

records.finding: Adds to 671. The subbasin exceedance policy uses the water-quality data to decide responsibility. Exceedances judged due to GSA activity after 2015 trigger mitigation projects, with a one-year goal for a long-term fix. Others are referred to CV-SALTS or other programmes. MKGSA's chief executive said exceedances seen so far have 'been there forever'.
records.quantitative_detail: Resample within 1 month (primary MCL), 3 months (secondary MCL), 6 months (agricultural standards); desktop evaluation within 6 months; long-term solution within 1 year
records.meeting_body: Kaweah Subbasin State of the Subbasin event (MKGSA-indexed)
records.agenda_item: Exceedance Policy
records.evidence_text: Deemed a significant and unreasonable impact in the scope of the GSAs' responsibility. PMAs commence to mitigate. ... Goal: Complete long-term solution within 1- year of resampling ... Deemed not a significant and unreasonable impact in the scope of the GSAs' responsibility to mitigate. GSAs notify and support CV-SALTS entities or other applicable programs to upport action within their scope f services.
records.notes: 'upport' and 'f' are as printed; the 'been there forever' remark is from the MKGSA chief executive at the Tulare ID Board on 2026-04-14 (followed by 'Legacy stuff' from an unidentified speaker).

records.finding: A water-quality condition enters MKGSA's dedicated recharge basin policy, though not as a siting criterion (671). Staff checked dairy-order setbacks and made the landowner responsible if a nitrate plume forms, on the view that 'dilution is the key'. Earlier, the subbasin said recharge that pushes nitrate into a well can trigger GSA mitigation.
records.agenda_item: Dedicated recharge basin policy
records.evidence_text: So all these questions we asked of Aaron and we talked about it internally and we thought the, the main. The mindset of Mid Kui GSA is dilution is the key and that's. That's the way we kind of look at all this. So we just put that a landowner is responsible in the case that a nitrate flu kind of forms.
records.notes: 'nitrate flu' is the transcription of 'nitrate plume'; the Board approved the Dedicated Recharge Basin Policy on 2026-06-09; no water-quality screening criterion for siting is described.

records.finding: The subbasin is starting to tie its water-quality work to the nitrate and salt programmes it currently refers cases to. In 2026 it joined a CV-SALTS and Kaweah Water Foundation nitrate management plan pilot to inventory its nitrate situation, and was put forward as a CV-SALTS salt pilot area.
records.speaker_role: GSA staff — MKGSA chief executive reporting to Tulare ID
records.meeting_body: Tulare Irrigation District Board of Directors
records.agenda_item: Kaweah Subbasin update
records.evidence_text: an opportunity has come up to partner with the CV Salts Program and I think the Cuya Water Foundation to work on a nitrate management plan pilot study. So we're one of the unique subbasins that will be doing an inventory of our nitrate situation, looking at solutions in preparation for ongoing salt-related issues in the subbasin.
records.notes: This is a member-agency meeting, used because the item is a Kaweah Subbasin SGMA update; the salt-pilot presentation by CV-SALTS counsel was at the GKGSA Board on 2026-06-08.

records.section: 3.3.3 Domestic Wells and Community Water System Consolidation
records.finding: The trust problem 672 anticipated has shown up in the mitigation programme. MKGSA evaluates only households that authorise data sharing (6 of 10 on interim water). At GKGSA, one household on a shared well was not enrolled 'due to fear of public information'. At registration events staff promised the data would not be public.
records.quantitative_detail: MKGSA: 10 homes on interim water, 6 consenting to data sharing (Oct 2025)
records.speaker_role: GSA staff — MKGSA interim general manager
records.agenda_item: Mitigation plan
records.evidence_text: We have 6 authorized landowners that are willing to share their data with us. If you're not willing to share your data with us, and you don't give self-help the authorization, you don't qualify.
records.notes: The GKGSA quote ('One is not enrolled in the program due to fear of public information') is from 2026-07-13; the no-public-release assurance is from the 2025-10-21 subbasin event; the MKGSA committee asked for a privacy statement on 2025-07-01.

records.section: 3.3.3 Domestic Wells and Community Water System Consolidation
records.finding: Updates 673. MKGSA's registration rose from 79 wells (December 2025) to 358 against a roughly 1,300 target (July 2026). The mandatory policy adopted in May 2026 enforces only agricultural and industrial wells, and staff do not actively push domestic registration. The per-household alerts in 670 therefore still depend on voluntary domestic enrolment.
records.quantitative_detail: Well inventory 1,542 (725 agricultural); registered 79 (Dec 2025), 199 (Mar 2026), 227 (Apr 2026), 358 of about 1,300 target (Jul 2026); 58 of 725 agricultural wells (8%) in Dec 2025
records.agenda_item: Well registration status
records.evidence_text: The total wells we've registered is 79. And as a, as a baseline foundation, when we did the well inventory, we had 1,540, 42. ... And then domestic wells, we don't necessarily actively push to get domestic wells registered, but there we get them either way and helps us with our numbers.
records.notes: On 2026-05-12 staff said enforcement would apply 'to agricultural wells and industrial wells'; door-to-door domestic registration was floated on 2025-10-02 but not reported as done.

records.section: 3.3.3 Domestic Wells and Community Water System Consolidation
records.finding: Updates 673 differently from MKGSA. GKGSA amended its Rules in March 2026 to require registration of all extraction facilities including de minimis and domestic wells. Non-compliance costs good standing for carryover and transfers and may bring a civil penalty, with a July 2026 deadline.
records.quantitative_detail: Civil penalty up to $1,000 plus $100 per additional day; new wells registered within 30 days; deadline 1 July 2026; about 2,000 wells (AI summary 2026-02-09)
records.meeting_body: Greater Kaweah GSA Board of Directors
records.agenda_item: Rules and Regulations amendment – well registration
records.evidence_text: So this is in state regulations that all groundwater extracting facilities including the minimus extractors shall be registered with the greater FIA DSA. ... we've added the item of that these are for both agricultural domestic and retired non destroyed wells ... in a civil penalty not to exceed $1,000 plus $100 for each additional day on which the violation continues.
records.notes: The AI summary says the amendments were approved; an MKGSA committee member on 2026-05-05 believed GKGSA covered only ag wells, which conflicts with this Rules text, so EDF should check the adopted Fifth Amended Rules.

records.section: 3.3.3 Domestic Wells and Community Water System Consolidation
records.finding: Consolidation moves from a checklist line (674) to a live option. MKGSA staff said a pending claim might be resolved by connecting the home to the City of Visalia and Cal Water systems. GKGSA leaders called connection to a neighbouring system a valid remedy for clusters of dry wells, but slow: expanding a service area can take about five years.
records.quantitative_detail: GKGSA estimate: about five years to expand a service area
records.agenda_item: Task order amendment for well evaluations
records.evidence_text: We have one other well that is on our tail plate right now, but we're evaluating that. That may not need much evaluation because we may just. It may be one of those what they call consolidation where it gets just hooked up to the city of Visalia and Cal Water.
records.notes: No consolidation is reported as completed; MKGSA's first claim in the City of Tulare instead got a new well under a city ordinance waiver, with a future city hook-up anticipated (2025-04-08, 2025-10-02).

records.finding: Community-relevant well data feeds decision support. The GIS well inventory sets the well counts that drive each year's mitigation cost budgets and is stored in the shared data management system. Montgomery & Associates is building an attribution tool that splits a well's impact between GSAs and between agricultural and urban pumping.
records.meeting_body: Kaweah Subbasin State of the Subbasin event (MKGSA-indexed)
records.agenda_item: Groundwater levels – well inventory
records.evidence_text: It's not fully complete, but it does help firm up well counts, which largely drives mitigation cost budgets that is used for GSA budgeting each year. So that's compiled into our data management system used by the various consultants and trying to help estimate those costs
records.notes: The attribution tool ('GSA vs GSA, Ag vs Urban') is from MKGSA Board minutes of 2025-06-10 and 2025-07-08; no output from it was reported in the meetings reviewed.

records.finding: Adds a third, public data tier to 678. The subbasin data management system is the public online tool for groundwater levels and water quality. It was rebuilt in 2024 and is meant to become the single clearinghouse all three GSAs use, and the well-registration app runs as a subdirectory of its website.
records.quantitative_detail: DMS rebuild budget about $113,000, spent about $82,000; original MKGSA task order $123,500 (Dec 2022)
records.agenda_item: Task Order 10 amendment – Data Management System
records.evidence_text: So our data management system is our online tool for public access to GSA data, groundwater levels, water quality. ... Focal point or clearinghouse for all data, so all three GSAs are inputting data and taking data out of only one place.
records.notes: GKGSA described the registration platform as 'a subdirectory of the data management system website' on 2025-08-11; none of the named state tools (CalEnviroScreen, DWR dry well system, Drinking Water Tool, StoryMap, SGMA Data Viewer) came up in any meeting.

records.finding: Parallel data streams are not joined. SGMA and the CV-SALTS nitrate programme run separate well registrations and separate water-quality sampling, sometimes with the same sampler. In 2026 MKGSA, through a Self-Help-arranged meeting with the State Water Board chair, proposed a pilot to let one programme's data satisfy several regulatory frameworks.
records.agenda_item: Key meetings
records.evidence_text: We met thanks to Self Help Enterprises, coordinated a meeting with Joaquin Esquivel at the State Water Resource Control Board where we talked a lot about well mitigation. And really what we looked at is the, the multitude of programs that are out there and how they overlap each other and we may be double funding things and it's not very efficient. ... The CV Salts program is also doing a well registration. Why are we doing two well registration processes? So can we just point to one?
records.notes: GKGSA staff on 2026-03-09 described water-quality programmes operating 'from kind of different silos' and a shared sampler (Jacob Salinas) working for both the Foundation and the GSAs.

records.finding: Community Water Center's 2023 data requests to all three GSAs: base domestic-well analysis on wells drilled since 1990, add PFOA/PFOS, close water-quality data gaps, identify DACs with the April 2023 census, and keep SAFER out of mitigation. Results were mixed: the 2025 constituent list omits PFOA/PFOS, and GKGSA's GSP still uses 2016 census data (676).
records.quantitative_detail: Requested well-age cutoff 1990; requested census vintage April 2023
records.speaker_role: NGO/advocate — Community Water Center (summarised in minutes)
records.agenda_item: 5. Well Mitigation Comment Letter
records.evidence_text: Tien Tran of the Community Water Center wrote a comment letter to all 3 GSAs in the Kaweah Subbasin. Tien listed several comments, including. (1) For the domestic well reliability analysis, the GSP should set the Sustainable Management Criteria (SMC) based on wells drilled from at least 1990, not the abbreviated time-period used. (2) Water quality SMCs should include more constituents of concern, such as PFOAs and PFOS. ... (4) Disadvantaged Communities should be identified using the most recent census dataset published in April 2023. (5) SWRCB’s SAFER funds should not be used for mitigation.
records.notes: The GSA responses are in the comment matrix approved by the committee on 2023-10-10, which these meetings do not reproduce, and the outcomes are set side by side without causation; SHE, Leadership Council and CWC commented again on water quality in October 2024 (2024-11-05 minutes).

records.finding: In the water year 2025 annual report highlights, ISW depletion is judged by the percent of time wells are connected, and all wells are reported as below the SMC except one with limited data. Several representative monitoring wells lack enough data to assess ISW at all.
records.quantitative_detail: Percent-of-time-connected measure, 'below the SMC' (threshold value not given); one well with limited data; annual report for water year 2025
records.speaker_role: GSA staff (agenda item summary; presented by Davids Engineering consultant)
records.agenda_item: Item 4c: Review Madera and Chowchilla annual report highlights
records.evidence_text: For depletion of Interconnected Surface Water (ISW), percent of time connected at all wells are below the SMC, except for one well with limited data. Several RMS wells also lack sufficient data to fully assess ISW conditions.
records.notes: The ISW paragraph follows the Chowchilla highlights without its own heading, so the subbasin is inferred; the presenter did not discuss ISW aloud, and the packet does not say what 'below the SMC' means for a percent-connected metric.

records.finding: Madera County GSA describes itself as a participant in the Department of Conservation MLRP and says it has worked since 2023 with the County, Resource Conservation Districts and local partners on program criteria, workshops and project solicitation. The report names no block-grant holder, grant amount or day-to-day administrator.
records.quantitative_detail: Work with County and RCDs since 2023 (start year as stated in draft GDM report, April 2026)
records.agenda_item: 4f. Review of draft Chowchilla Subbasin Groundwater Demand Management Programs and Subsidence Mitigation Measures Report (GDM report, April 2026, in agenda packet)
records.evidence_text: Madera County GSA participates in the Multi -Benefit Land Repurposing Program (MLRP), a California Department of Conservation grant -funded initiative that supports voluntary transitions of irrigated agricultural lands to alternative uses that require substa ntially less water. ... Since 2023, the Madera County GSA has worked closely with the County, Resource Conservation Districts, and local partners to design and implement program criteria, conduct public workshops, and solicit project applications.
records.notes: Text is from the draft GDM report in the April 2026 agenda packet, not from a spoken statement; it describes Madera County GSA activity across its own areas. Most denials from the district resulted from incomplete or ineligible applications, often from uninhabitable properties such as mobile homes with no electricity.
