records.finding: PV Water reports annual sustainable management criteria for water quality degradation using three constituents (TDS, chloride, nitrate) in coastal and inland management zones. A nitrate minimum-threshold exceedance persists in the coastal zone.
records.quantitative_detail: TDS threshold 1,000 mg/L; chloride threshold 150 mg/L; nitrate threshold = drinking water MCL; coastal-zone nitrate 53 mg/L (2021-2025 five-year average), down from a high of 62 mg/L (2019-2023 period); coastal chloride 307 mg/L (five-year average, evaluated under the seawater-intrusion criterion instead)
records.agenda_item: Annual report / water year 2025 sustainability status
records.evidence_text: There's three analytes or parameters that we use and it set sustainable management criteria for and that's total dissolved solids, tds, chloride and nitrate. And we have this minimum threshold set of 1000mg per liter for TDS, 150mg per liter for chloride. And then the drinking water level, maximum containment level threshold for nitrate. ... We did have a continued minimum threshold exceedance. So a concentration of 53 milligrams per liter for nitrate in the coastal zone. It's something that's been occurring for a number of years, but we actually are seeing declines. Had a high of 62 milligrams per liter in 2019 through the 2023 period
records.notes: Presenter is not named in the transcript; role inferred as consultant presenting the annual report, and the nitrate MCL basis (nitrate as NO3 vs N) is not stated.

records.finding: The Tule Subbasin groundwater flow model currently carries river infiltration as externally reported recharge values, not as simulated stream-aquifer exchange. The consultant's April 2025 update scope adds a Streamflow Routing (SFR) package for the Tule River, Porter Slough, Deer Creek and White River, intended later for pumping/no-pumping depletion runs.
records.quantitative_detail: Model calibrated through September 2019; update adds October 2019 to September 2024 data; 2026 model-update tasks 3-6 estimated at $163,740 (subbasin-wide); scope dated 22 Apr 2025.
records.speaker_role: consultant — Thomas Harder & Co. (scope document in GSA board agenda)
records.meeting_body: Porterville Irrigation District GSA Board of Directors
records.agenda_item: Tule Subbasin 2026 hydrogeological services scope and cost estimate (Attachment A: model update scope)
records.evidence_text: TH&Co will incorporate the Tule River, Porter Slough, Deer Creek, and White River into model with the Streamflow Routing (SFR) Package. ... It is envisioned that the updated model with the SFR package will be used later to conduct pumping/no pumping scenarios to estimate potential depletions of interconnected surface water (ISW) due to pumping which will inform ISW SMC development.
records.notes: Scope is a Tule Subbasin TAC document attached to the PID board agenda; the draft model name (MODFLOW-based, uses the Farm Process) is not stated in the text; updated model was still expected late Oct/early Nov 2026 per the 2026-10-01 PID staff report.

records.finding: Planned ISW inputs are named: stage and flow at three USGS or dam gaging points feed the first reach of each stream segment, and up to 30 new groundwater-level calibration wells in the Upper Tule River and Upper Deer Creek areas are added specifically for future depletion analysis.
records.quantitative_detail: Up to 30 new calibration wells (Upper Tule River, Upper Deer Creek); up to 100 further new wells from the Tule Subbasin Monitoring Plan for general head calibration; gaging points: Success Dam, Fountain Springs, East of Ducor.
records.speaker_role: consultant — Thomas Harder & Co. (scope document in GSA board agenda)
records.meeting_body: Porterville Irrigation District GSA Board of Directors
records.agenda_item: Tule Subbasin 2026 hydrogeological services scope and cost estimate (Attachment A: Tasks 5-6)
records.evidence_text: Add groundwater elevation calibration targets with up to 30 new wells in the Upper Tule River and Upper Deer Creek areas in support of future analyses of depletions of ISW due to pumping. ... Flow terms to the Subbasin for the Tule River, Deer Creek, and White River will be that reported at Success Dam, Fountain Springs, and East of Ducor gaging stations , respectively
records.notes: Streambed conductance, roughness and thickness are to come from literature values refined in calibration, i.e. no field streambed data are planned in this scope.

records.finding: Staff describe the draft PID GSP as establishing sustainable management criteria that include interconnected surface water, but give no ISW threshold, proxy or measurable objective. Subbasin ISW SMC development is still a funded work item elsewhere in the same period.

records.evidence_text: The GSP establishes Sustainable Management Criteria addressing applicable sustainability indicators, including groundwater levels, groundwater storage, groundwater quality, land subsidence, and interconnected surface water.
records.notes: One-line staff summary of the draft GSP; the criteria themselves were not in the meeting materials, so no value could be recorded.

records.finding: The proposed Tule River monitoring well is designed with separate completions in the shallow upper aquifer and the lower aquifer, so that surface water-groundwater interaction can be read by depth.

records.notes: Design intent only; no thresholds or depth-specific ISW criteria were described, and the well is a proposal, not yet installed.

records.finding: A PID GSA presenter says the Tule River-groundwater connection is not fully described in existing GSPs and is a recognised data gap. PID proposes a new multi-completion monitoring well along the Tule River (as one of its new project and management actions) to fill it.

records.finding: A Lower Tule speaker described converting floodplain ground along the Tule River and Deer Creek into a flexible land-use area (flood protection, recharge, dryland farming, habitat) as a way to cut deep-aquifer pumping, and said Pixley would roll out a voluntary programme with the Tule Trust and Lower Tule might follow.

And then you have environmental and other stakeholders in this group. ... a lot of that is just due to the Department of Conservation, you know, issuing this grant, and all the criteria that goes along with, you know, all the streams, in other words, that come along with, like, you have to have all of these people involved for us to, you know, send this money down to you guys.
records.notes: Speaker 3 unlabeled; the committee's membership, decisions and meeting dates are not given. A separate Ag Advisory Committee meeting on Oct 23, 2025 was announced in the same meeting by the Tule Basin Land and Water Conservation Trust.

records.finding: Pixley's Groundwater Planning Commission has an at-large sixth seat that the board opened to applications; none had come in, and staff described the commission as informal group discussions. The seat is open to any applicant, with no designated seat for disadvantaged-community or domestic-well users.
records.agenda_item: Other: GPC Open Seat
records.evidence_text: So you do have an open seat on the GPC. We put the applications out after the last board meeting, but we haven't received any back. ... the GPC meetings are kind of more informal group discussions anyway.
records.notes: Draft Oct 9 minutes in the same packet say the open seat is at-large and applications were to be sent out. The reader should confirm whether GPC voting seats carry any community criteria.

records.finding: A Pixley staff member said community pushback that the MLRP grant had no direct benefit for residents led to setting aside leftover grant money for projects with a direct community benefit, such as a walkway or school curriculum on repurposed land. A floodplain project may also benefit communities. This is a documented case of community input changing a land-repurposing programme's design.
records.agenda_item: MLRP grant update (task 2 / community projects)
records.evidence_text: when we had a lot of pushback from the communities, they felt that there wasn't a project that had direct benefits to them, so there is going to be money left over for some type of community, a landowner can he believed that project, it just has to be your community, direct benefit to the community, so something like a walkway around the basin ... there's hope that we'll have a floodplain project, kind of idea that could either have benefits for communities as well, or landowners too.
records.notes: Account is secondhand ('when we had pushback from the communities'); the date and the community bodies involved are not given. Speaker 7 unlabeled. Which communities and how much money is left over is not stated.

records.finding: Pixley staff said that after feedback from the Pixley and Lower Tule committees, the Groundwater Planning Commission decided to meet monthly with its consultant, who would analyze shallow and deep pumping by zone. The feedback pushed the options toward GSA-wide allocation changes instead of chasing high-risk zones. Advisory input changed meeting frequency and the analysis scope.
records.agenda_item: Groundwater Planning Commission update
records.evidence_text: we decided to start meeting monthly eki based on feedback we got that day from both the Pixley and lower two league committees. Is eki students and further analysis, we have a meeting next Friday to talk about some of that. We'll have by zone. You know, what's what's shallow pumping, what's deep pumping by zone, that's one of the things. And then some options on next steps. Because some of the feedback we got was, you know, our current policy reads that, you know, if you get into a high risk zone, and transitional goes away, and certain things happen. But what we've seen is like, if we don't start acting more on a GSA wide level, you're just constantly chasing zones across the GSA until everybody's impacted, right? And so we're looking at options of what can we do next year, as far as allocations GSA wide that might make a difference or not.
records.notes: 'eki' is EKI Environment and Water (the consultant). Makeup of the committees is not described in the excerpt; on 2026-05-14 staff again said the GPC would move from quarterly to monthly meetings.

records.finding: PID GSA's stakeholder committee recommended retiring all past Tier 1 transitional allocation, and the board's motion followed, carving out prepaid water. The discussion also produced an idea of a bankers-and-rechargers market to backfill small prepaid holdings. This is documented stakeholder input changing an allocation rule; no disadvantaged-community role in the committee is described.
records.quantitative_detail: About 200 acre-feet of prepaid Tier 1 water excluded from retirement; one grower holding about 300 acre-feet (speaker figures)
records.agenda_item: 5.c Tier 1 transitional allocation
records.evidence_text: The, the committee was in favor of Retiring all past Tier 1 allocation stakeholders, the stakeholder committee. Yes that was pretty fairly unanimous and we had pretty robust discussion. ... We are excluding those prepaid from retirement.
records.notes: Board adoption is inferred from 'Before I make the motion' and 'we are excluding those prepaid'; the vote is not in the excerpt. Stakeholder Committee members were appointed on Oct 2, 2025 (Oct 16 transcript).

records.finding: A concern raised in public engagement at the Tule probationary hearing, that small pumpers (often disadvantaged, linguistically isolated and BIPOC farmers) bear reporting fees out of proportion to their pumping, led board members to direct staff to study an exclusion. Staff now proposed excluding pumpers of 20 AF per year or less.
records.quantitative_detail: Fee: $300 per well base plus $20 per acre-foot; about 2,100 extractors (roughly 50%) pump 20 AF or less; cumulatively about 4,400 AF in water year 2022 (stated as roughly 2% of extractions); Tule extractions about 719,000 AF vs sustainable yield 408,000 AF in water year 2022
records.meeting_body: State Water Board hearing (Delta-Mendota return to DWR; Tule and Tulare Lake minimal-impact exclusions)
records.agenda_item: Item 4 Tule Subbasin minimal impact exclusion
records.evidence_text: A concern was raised during public engagement for the Tuley sub basin probationary hearing that smaller groundwater extractors have a minimal impact on pumping in the sub basin and may be disproportionately affected by the reporting and fee requirements. This category of pumpers includes small scale farmers, many of whom are often disadvantaged, linguistically isolated and black, indigenous people of color or bipoc
records.notes: Spoken figures are inconsistent (4,400 AF is not 2% of 719,000 AF); do not rely on the percentage. Also answers COM-3.1.3 (distributive). Some GSAs wrote letters against the proposal.

records.finding: A Tule Trust representative told Tri-County that, unlike earlier programs paid from other sources, MLRP funding requires long-term, multi-benefit projects with some community benefit. The benefit is described only in general terms; no examples, definition or metric are given here.
records.speaker_role: NGO/advocate: Tule Basin Land and Water Conservation Trust
records.agenda_item: Reports: MLRP / Trust update
records.evidence_text: long-term, multi-benefit with some community benefit as well
records.notes: Speaker is the Trust's executive director per context (Tri-County Water Authority label, Oct 9, 2025 'updates from the trust'); the transcript has mojibake around the quoted phrase. Related Pixley statements on what counts as a direct community benefit are in the 2025-09-16 and 2025-10-09 Pixley meetings.

records.finding: A Pixley MLRP partner said the Department of Conservation's idea of a 'direct benefit to a community' (parks, walkways) fits big cities poorly. Pixley has many small communities without public works, and staff had spent three years educating DOC and having it redefine the term. The definition is being negotiated case by case, not written down.
records.quantitative_detail: Three years of education with DOC (speaker estimate)
records.agenda_item: MLRP program update
records.evidence_text: we've done a pretty solid education job with Doc about understanding how unique our sub basin is, especially when it comes to communities, because we don't have one big, giant community like almost every other sub basin does? We have a bunch of smaller communities that take place, and a lot of them don't have the public works they can keep things going that are a direct benefit to the communities. And that's the education part that we're having to put forth with them, is they are having to redefine what is a direct benefit to a community.
records.notes: Speaker 8 is unlabeled; context is the $10M DOC block grant administered by Pixley/LTRID with Tule Basin Land and Water Conservation Trust. No written definition quoted.

records.finding: Pixley's draft surface-water operating guideline has the district set aside a first block of water to recharge in and around the Severely Disadvantaged Communities in its GSA, and that recharge counts toward the district's annual groundwater credit allocation. It is the one place found where benefit to disadvantaged communities is tied to the accounting system.
records.agenda_item: Packet: Surface Water Delivery Operational Guidelines (draft)
records.evidence_text: Under this stage, the District sets aside a block of water to recharge in the areas > in and around the Severely Disadvantage Communities (SDAC) located within > the GSA. • The District recharges all the surface water available. All deliveries are made through the District owned canal and facilities. Delivery of water is for recharge > purposes. > • The water recharged in this stage becomes part of calculation of the District's annual District Groundwater Credit allocation.
records.notes: Draft 'Surface Water Delivery Operational Guidelines' dated November 2025 in the Nov 13 packet; no measurement of well or community benefit is described, and the share of credits is not stated.

records.finding: A public commenter told the board a lien for unpaid extraction fees had landed on her residential parcel, whose well serves only the household. Staff said the opt-out exemption requires the account to be compliant, so past-due fees still owe, and the item was deferred to closed session and a later agenda. This shows a fee-hardship route (distributive/procedural) conditioned on paying arrears.
records.quantitative_detail: 9.75 acres (two residential parcels); household of four; income stated as Social Security
records.agenda_item: Public Comment
records.evidence_text: We are on increased income. And we're a household of four. ... To be able to brush our teeth and take a shower. ... We do, and just in the… we do just in order for any account to be exempted from future charges, it would need to be compliant. ... So, she would still owe if her previous extraction fees, and once those are… once her balance is clear.
records.notes: Transcript renders 'fixed income' as 'increased income'; speaker is a public commenter and the staff reply is not labelled; no outcome shown in this meeting.

records.finding: A State Water Board notice reproduced in PID's packet offers an extraction-fee waiver to low-income households, to public or state-small water systems serving disadvantaged communities, and to public schools, but only if the annual extraction report is filed by May 1, 2026. This is the main equity safeguard in the probation reporting fees.
records.quantitative_detail: Base fee $300 per well; $20 per acre-foot; 25% monthly late fee; waiver threshold household income at or below 200 percent of the federal poverty level
records.agenda_item: Packet: State Water Board probation notice
records.evidence_text: The State Water Board may waive extraction fees, upon request, for certain extractors. 1 Groundwater extractors may qualify for a fee waiver if they meet any of the following criteria: 1. You qualify as a low-income resident: a. Your household income is 200 percent or less of the federal poverty level. For more details, visit U.S. Department of Health and Human Services ; or b. You are enrolled in a qualified income-based public assistance program. ... To qualify for a fee waiver, you must submit your annual groundwater extraction report by May 1, 2026.
records.notes: State Board probation notice (dated Mar 10, 2026) included in the PID GSA packet; the GSA itself did not adopt it. Domestic wells are described as de minimis in other passages.

records.finding: PID staff reported that other districts complained about the transparency of the subbasin policy-group meetings and that the group was moving to let other participants monitor the proceedings. It is a procedural-access issue in the body making subbasin-wide mitigation decisions.
records.agenda_item: Reports: Tule Subbasin Policy Group
records.evidence_text: There was some comments by other districts on which the transparency of the policy group meeting. So they are working on allowing other participants to kind of monitor what's going on and be more involved with some of the distribution of information.
records.notes: The manager adds that the group is 'not the Dark web meeting anymore'; the text of how access will be given is not stated. The policy group is a subbasin body of GSA directors.

records.finding: PID GSA's manager told the stakeholder committee that State Board hearings draw many disadvantaged-community speakers, expecting about three for each grower, and that this is why a full mitigation plan matters to the Board. It shows community testimony shaping the GSA's mitigation design.
records.meeting_body: Porterville Irrigation District GSA Stakeholder Meeting
records.agenda_item: Policy discussion: Tule Subbasin Domestic Well Mitigation Reserve Fund (Stakeholder Committee)
records.evidence_text: for every one grower that's going to talk in front of that at the hearing in front of them at the hearing, there's going to be three from disadvantaged communities rebutting basically our, our story so it's obviously important to them is a full mitigation plan.
records.notes: Prediction attributed to the staff speaker (unlabeled) about the State Board hearing; not a measured count. Same discussion records the 2015 pre-SGMA claim cutoff.

records.finding: The State Water Board's draft probation order, reproduced in PID's stakeholder packet, cites the human right to water and makes racial equity and environmental justice central considerations. It proposes that individuals pumping up to 20 acre-feet a year, and not within two miles of the Friant-Kern Canal, be excluded from reporting. This is the State's framing of equity in the Tule probation.
records.quantitative_detail: Reporting exclusion: 20 acre-feet per year or less and not within 2 miles of the Friant-Kern Canal
records.meeting_body: Porterville Irrigation District GSA Stakeholder Meeting
records.agenda_item: Packet: Draft State Water Board order, Tule Subbasin
records.evidence_text: The State Water Board recognizes the established Human Right to Water policy of the state that every human being has the right to safe, clean, D R A F T > 3 affordable, and accessible water adequate for human consumption, cooking, and sanitary purposes. 12. The State Water Board is committed to upholding California’s human right to water and making racial equity, diversity, inclusion, and environmental justice a central consideration in the Board’s decision. ... proposes that in the Tule Subbasin extractions by individuals who extract no more than 20 acre-feet of groundwater annually and do not extract groundwater within two miles of the Friant-Kern Canal should be excluded from the reporting requirement.
records.notes: Draft State Board order text in the PID packet (labelled DRAFT); the final adopted threshold should be checked. Small and domestic pumpers excluded from reporting means less State data on them.

records.finding: Tri-County directors raised a distributional concern about the pooled mitigation fund: Tule East, which has the most private domestic wells outside districts and cities, may be least able to fund its share. Claims draw only from the GSA where the impact is attributed, so the burden follows pumping area and local financial capacity.
records.agenda_item: 1 Tule Subbasin drinking water well mitigation program reserve fund
records.evidence_text: I think the only concern is that Tula east is not going to be able to fund that. ... Their population and their domestic wells that are not within DIS or city csds. And so they just have a lot more than. Than we have. We've always been fortunate in that we've talked about that quite a bit that we just don't have that amount of domestic wells. And there's no doubt this is a heavy lift for them,
records.notes: Speakers unlabeled; one director raises the concern and the manager answers. Tule East GSA had started a Prop 218 fee process (LTRID 2026-04-14).

records.finding: At Pixley's board, a director asked whether every domestic well owes the State's $300 probation fee. Staff said all wells are listed but most domestic wells should be excluded under the new 20-acre-foot threshold, and that the State has not clarified this. Residents' fee exposure depends on an unclear State rule.
records.quantitative_detail: $300 per well annual base fee; exemption threshold 20 AF/yr; most domestic wells expected to fall under it
records.agenda_item: Groundwater extraction reporting and fees
records.evidence_text: did I read that right now we're gonna have to pay $300 on every domestic well, too. Is I was reading through that. It's been a while when it first came out. Did anybody catch that? Yes. So all wells, all wells, every domestic Well, 300 bucks to the state. Yes, it's less than 20 acre feet. Most domestic wells are going to end up being excluded through that meter.
records.notes: Exchange between a director and staff; staff note that they 'have no idea' how the State will treat domestic wells.

records.finding: At an LTRID communications session, a participant said SGMA implementation affects not just farmers but surrounding disadvantaged communities when the farming footprint shrinks, and that assistance to lessen that impact should be part of the story told in Sacramento. Distributional impacts on communities are named, but no measure or remedy is stated.
records.meeting_body: Lower Tule River Irrigation District Meeting
records.agenda_item: Communications strategy session
records.evidence_text: there's a big impact to this implementation, not only to farmers, but the communities, and, you know, the assistance needed to lessen that impact has got to start getting in front of Sacramento. You know, the DACs, you know, we're surrounded by DACs. They have a big impact from when we reduce our footprint.
records.notes: Speaker unlabeled; probably a district director. No data or programme attached.

records.finding: At the public hearing on the 2026 extraction fee, two small residential well owners objected that fixed-income households that grow nothing bear the fee while large growers can write it off, and one asked to be excluded. The board's reply was a protest process (a majority protest stops the fee), explicitly not an exemption.
records.quantitative_detail: Proposed 2026 GSA budget about $785,343 (per Aug 20 packet summary); protest filed by APN, address and signature during hearing
records.agenda_item: Public hearing: 2026 extraction fee
records.evidence_text: as an individual that is on a fixed income, I'm totally being impacted by all this and nobody's going to come and rescue my well. ... is there a way that we can get excluded from being charged? ... And you could submit a protest against the fee implementation. But that's different than an exemption. That's not an exemption.
records.notes: Hearing under Proposition 218; commenters unnamed. A board member answered that wells have funding; the PID manager was to give details. The State Board low-income fee waiver (see PID 2026-03-20) is for the State's own fee, not the GSA fee.

records.section: 3.1.4 Domestic Well Protection as an Equity Outcome
records.finding: LTRID staff reported spring 2026 releases used to recharge around communities and shut off wells in the surrounding area: 208 acre-feet to idle wells in March and 976 in basins around the communities. Staff say the community wells are shallow, so these operations are the district's way of protecting them, and the volumes are tracked.
records.quantitative_detail: March 2026: 208 AF used to shut wells off around communities; 976 AF in basins around communities; 359 AF channel loss recharge; total release about 7,826 AF
records.meeting_body: Lower Tule River Irrigation District Board
records.agenda_item: Water supply and operations
records.evidence_text: So what we're doing with that water is delivering it, recharging it around the communities, as well as shutting off wells around the community. So there was about 208 acre feet used to shut wells off in March, and then 976 in basins around the communities. 359 acre feet recharged as channel fruit.
records.notes: Staff statement; 'channel fruit' in the transcript is channel loss. A district manager says on 2026-08-11 that community wells are about 150 feet deep and wells within a mile are shut off. Which communities are meant is not named.

records.section: 3.1.4 Domestic Well Protection as an Equity Outcome
records.finding: The reserve-fund tables estimate impacted wells by GSA, but not by disadvantaged versus other communities. Tea Pot Dome showed no wells projected dry from water levels and about six from water quality, giving a $15,000 contribution. A speaker said a State Board member's top priority is domestic and disadvantaged-community well protection.
records.quantitative_detail: Tea Pot Dome: 0 wells projected dry at minimum thresholds; potentially 6 water-quality impacts (12.5% of up to 45 wells); initial contribution $15,000
records.meeting_body: Tea Pot Dome Water Dist Board
records.agenda_item: Subbasin mitigation plan reserve fund
records.evidence_text: So teapot again, zero on the projected to go dry, Potentially six to be affected by ground water quality. So it's the $15,000 number ... But this is like her number one, top, top top priority is domestic well and disadvantaged community well protection.
records.notes: Speaker unlabeled (consultant or manager presenting); the State Board member is named in the transcript. The analysis is by GSA area; no DAC/non-DAC split is shown.

records.section: 3.1.4 Domestic Well Protection as an Equity Outcome
records.finding: A Pixley director warned that shifting pumping to shallow wells to reduce subsidence would put small individual domestic-well owners and disadvantaged communities back at risk, and said a water-level trigger to stop shallow pumping would be needed. Protection of shallow domestic wells is treated as a constraint on subsidence policy but no analysis is shown.
records.agenda_item: Subsidence policy / allocations discussion
records.evidence_text: Is one of the reasons we got in this mess is because of the shallow well pumping and the socio economic, economically disadvantaged communities, and why we got to be careful not to deplete the upper aquifer. But now we're back to talking about, hey, we got to do shallow well pumping, or is, this is kind of a double edged sword. We're going to have to have some sort of trigger that says, hey, you know, water levels get at the shallow. Forget below this thing. You've got to stop pumping, right? Because then we're back to square one with with the individual submersible landowner. That's not a farmer. That's a concern of mine.
records.notes: Quote has the phrase 'socio economic, economically disadvantaged communities'; speaker unlabeled (a director). A related trigger concept appears in the GPC's monthly subsidence discussions.

records.section: 3.1.4 Domestic Well Protection as an Equity Outcome
records.finding: Pixley staff said protecting domestic and community wells was the State Board's first priority and that well readings show Pixley's allocation system met it. No breakdown by disadvantaged versus other communities is shown, and a subbasin-wide domestic and small-community well mitigation plan is still being finalized.
records.agenda_item: Groundwater conditions and allocation update
records.evidence_text: This was priority number one originally to the State Board. It was protecting domestic wells and community wells. And I think what we'll see in a little bit is our original plan for that has worked. And we achieved that goal. We now have a new issue, obviously. It's subsidence. But this is an upper aquifer. This was initially an upper aquifer issue. And over the last several years, we've performed pretty well here. And we're close to having a finalized mitigation plan for domestic and small community wells. ... And we saw earlier with those domestic well readings, so far the system was successful in achieving its overall goal.
records.notes: Staff assertion based on upper-aquifer readings; the wells shown are community-supply wells, not individual domestic wells. See also 2025-10-09 community wells.

records.finding: ETGSA gives the board a standing monthly 'stakeholder outreach and community engagement' report that counts participants at its own meetings. For August 2025 it counted 21 online at the board meeting and 35 listening to a land-subsidence committee meeting. This is reach reporting for GSA meetings, not a separate community outreach programme.

records.agenda_item: 6a Report on ongoing ETGSA outreach efforts
records.evidence_text: for the board meeting, um, we had 21 participants online. ... For that land subsidence monitoring and measurement, we had 35 participants listening in.
records.notes: Speaker unlabeled (ETGSA staff reading the outreach item); the 31-participant October figure is in the 2025-12-04 transcript.

records.finding: Pixley's treasurer reported MLRP grant spending to date on outreach, education and workshops with residents, farmers and landowners, about $765,000 on task four as transcribed. records.finding: Tri-County added a consultant task order for outreach support because Kern's experience showed the State wants specific outreach, and Kern reportedly spent about half a million dollars on its own outreach. records.finding: At an LTRID board meeting a speaker said a district staff member has attended all the meetings of the community water systems, which raised some customer issues the district tries to help with. records.finding: LTRID/Pixley managers described an earlier professionally made video on what SGMA means for Pixley, costing about $10,000, and asked whether to commission more storytelling. records.finding: Pixley staff explained that Self-Help used to cover dry wells with state SAFER money, but under SGMA the state expects GSAs to pay for impacts caused by GSA-related activity, so each claim must be screened for GSA causation before Self-Help can use SAFER funds instead. The funding split depends on an attribution test.

If it's GSA related activities, they need to mitigate for it. And so we have to go through this to determine is it our fault or not, and if not now, this now self help can still work with this landowner, use those safer funds to mitigate their well, either get them a new one, or whatever they need to do, rehab the well, whatever they need to do to get it back into service so that, like this, part of it is Just to determine who pays to do that.

records.finding: Pixley handles domestic-well claims through Self-Help Enterprises, which files the claim, visits the site and interviews the owner; consultants then judge whether GSA activity caused the dry well, ignoring impacts before January 2015.
