records.finding: Pixley staff said its ramp-down calculation rested on upper-aquifer water levels because domestic wells had to be protected, and that the GSP's original intent (the State Board's 2021-23 domestic-well argument) was met. LTRID staff separately said its accounting system is not good enough for the lower aquifer and subsidence.
records.quantitative_detail: Years referenced: State Board argument 2021-2023; no quantities
records.agenda_item: Subbasin coordination / allocation discussion
records.evidence_text: The calculation was mostly on the effects of upper aquifer ground levels, because that was the name of the game, because we were having to protect the domestic wells. ... generally speaking, we have achieved the original intent of our GSP, ironically, because if you guys recall, 2021, 2022, 2023, what was the state board argument? Domestic wells.
records.notes: LTRID's 2026-06-29 committee says its accounting targets upper groundwater and 'isn't good enough right now' for the lower aquifer; the two statements are the same design logic across the two districts, not a single quantity.

records.finding: Of the named public tools, the only one found in Tule meetings is DWR's SGMA Data Viewer, listed by the modeling consultant as a source of groundwater-level data for the subbasin flow model. It is a staff and consultant input; no meeting mentions using it, or the Dry Well Reporting System, SAFER dashboard or CalEnviroScreen, with or for residents.
records.agenda_item: Model update scope: data compilation
records.evidence_text: Groundwater levels o Tule Subbasin TAC o Irrigation and Water Districts o City of Porterville o SGMA Data Viewer
records.notes: Thomas Harder & Co. data-needs list in the draft model scope (Apr 2025) in the Jan 15, 2026 packet. Absence of the other named tools is from keyword searches of 87 meetings, not a full read.

records.finding: PID GSA staff said they had not mailed well-registration notices, had used a login pop-up and one-on-one calls, and that most landowners never log into their BasinSAFE account and call instead unless a bill arrives. The accounting portal is thus used by a small share of account holders, and staff planned electronic and district-wide mailer notices once a deadline is set.
records.meeting_body: Porterville Irrigation District GSA Stakeholder Meeting
records.agenda_item: Well registration deadline and outreach
records.evidence_text: We've not sent mailers out. There was a pop up on the login if you logged in that it would direct you to, to register, you know, the, the public meetings and stuff. Of course the, that we've tried to do but we've not sent out a direct mailer. But I didn't want to send mailers out at such a point till we set a deadline so we have something to push against. I will tell you a large majority of folks within the district don't even log into their basis safe account and they just, they call and do a transaction for orders unless they receive a bill.
records.notes: Landowner accounts, not DAC or domestic well users. The statement 'a large majority' is a staff impression, not a count.

records.finding: During PID's move from the Eastern Tule account system to its own BasinSAFE, staff said landowners could not see their groundwater pumping history in the online account, only surface-water deliveries, until a new data set was loaded. The online accounting portal is the main way landowners see their data, and it was incomplete during the transition.
records.meeting_body: Porterville Irrigation District GSA Stakeholder Meeting
records.agenda_item: Announcements: BasinSAFE migration
records.evidence_text: Right now, any previous reporting on well pumping is not available. And under the exist the existing PID Basin Safe account, you can't see your groundwater. You can only see the surface water deliveries that have transacted.
records.notes: Landowner-facing portal, not community or well-impact data. Staff said the Eastern Tule dataset was static and had been updated only on specific actions.

records.finding: At Tri-County, staff pointed growers to the State's open data portal where extraction (GEARS) reports are public, offered the link on request, and flagged errors in the revised State dataset. Residents and the public could look up neighbors' reported pumping there, but the GSA does not host or interpret the data.
records.agenda_item: GEARS / State reporting update
records.evidence_text: I think most of you are aware that it is available to everyone on the Calpurna open data portal. And if any of you would like the link, just contact me or Deanna and we'll get you the link for that.
records.notes: Speaker is the consultant giving the GEARS update (unlabeled); 'Calpurna' is the transcription of CalPortal or the California open data portal. Tri-County's own web tools are not described.

records.finding: At the PID fee hearing, residents with small parcels said they did not know a service existed for dry domestic wells and asked where to find a holding tank. Staff said they would connect them with providers in the subbasin. The exchange shows an awareness gap and an ad hoc referral rather than a published programme or tool.
records.agenda_item: Public hearing: 2026 extraction fee
records.evidence_text: I didn't know there was services, like if your well out so we can come to you. ... do you guys happen to know anybody too that provides holding tanks ... But we can, we can connect you with individuals that provide that assistance within the Tulisa Basin
records.notes: Commenters unnamed; one says a holding tank came from another programme (possibly Self-Help). The GSA reply is paraphrased by staff; the referral outcome is not recorded.

records.finding: Westlands holds the DOC grant agreement and, once DOC conditionally approved four projects, its board authorized staff to sign sub-agreements with the applicants: two district-led projects, one grower (a director's relative, recused) and the Central California Environmental Justice Network.
records.quantitative_detail: $8.9 million DOC grant agreement; four projects approved
records.meeting_body: Westlands Water District Board of Directors (acting as Westlands WD GSA)
records.agenda_item: Item 8C: approve Westside MLRP projects and authorize sub-agreements
records.evidence_text: This is to for your consideration in approving the west side Subbasin Multi benefit land repurposing program projects and authorizing the general manager or designee to execute agreements with those applicants. So the district entered into a grant agreement with the California Department of conservation for $8.9 million
records.notes: One director recused himself because an applicant is a relative; the approval was by voice vote.

records.finding: Westlands Water District, as the Westside Subbasin GSA, is the DOC MLRP grantee and runs the programme through a staff programme manager, with EKI as technical consultant, CeresCollab for outreach and a steering committee that includes community, justice and land-trust partners.
records.meeting_body: Westside Subbasin MLRP community meeting (Westlands WD)
records.agenda_item: Community meeting: programme introduction
records.evidence_text: My name is Shelly Ruiz. I work for Westlands Water District. I am the program manager for the west side Sub Basin Multi Benefit Land repurposing Program. ... I'm the Deputy General Manager of Resources for Westlands Water District, and I just want to thank the Department of Conservation for awarding Westlands Water District this grant.
records.notes: Consultants and partners (EKI, CeresCollab, CCEJN, Sequoia Riverlands Trust, LEAP Institute) are named in this and the committee transcripts and the 2025-09-17 agenda, not in the quoted lines.

records.finding: Westlands tells its GSA board the DOC grant is $8.9 million and that it pays for the MLRP plan, a community engagement plan and implementation of aligned projects. Of this, about $7.7M was later described as available for projects.
records.quantitative_detail: $8.9 million total DOC MLRP grant (Aug 2025); covers plan, engagement plan and project implementation
records.meeting_body: Westlands Water District Board of Directors (acting as Westlands WD GSA)
records.agenda_item: Item 7B: update on the Multi-Benefit Land Repurposing Program
records.evidence_text: Funded by an $8.9 million grant from the California Department of Conservation. ... The grant funding covers the development of the MLRP plan, community engagement plan, and implementation of projects that align with the goals and objectives of the plan.
records.notes: Other sources round the award to $8.89M (PV Water's packet); the split between plan, engagement and projects is not itemized.

records.finding: Staff report that proposed MLRP projects request about $18.7 million against $7.7 million available, of which about $7.3 million is for implementation and $0.4 million for project development and permitting, so priorities must be ranked.
records.quantitative_detail: $18.7M requested; $7.7M available (about $7.3M implementation + $0.4M development/permitting), March 2026
records.meeting_body: Westside Subbasin MLRP Steering and Outreach Advisory Committee (Westlands WD)
records.agenda_item: Funding summary and project overview
records.evidence_text: the total funding requested by pilot projects and prior and projects applications that were submitted by the priority deadline was approximately $18.7 million. And as you can see here, available funds that we have for our MLRP is 7.7 million. Of that 7.7 million, roughly 7.3 million is allocated for project implementation. So that's the actual funding that gets to fund, you know, the construction of the project, basically. And 400,000 is for development and permitting.
records.notes: Block grant total is not stated in this passage; $7.7M is the project-funding portion available to the committee. The 2026-02-18 meeting gives the same $7.3M/$0.4M split.

records.finding: The four projects advancing to DOC exhaust available MLRP implementation money; the district is sending three alternates to DOC in the hope of additional Prop 4 funding.
records.quantitative_detail: Requests: Pasajero Ph.2 ~$4.5M, Los Gatos ~$1.6M, Westside Community Cooling Center ~$0.2M, Section 21 ~$0.4M; alternates Rock'n JK ~$1.7M, Panoche Creek ~$3.7M, Papas solar ~$0.1M (June 2026)
records.meeting_body: Westside Subbasin MLRP Steering and Outreach Advisory Committee (Westlands WD)
records.agenda_item: Project update
records.evidence_text: the Passahero Phase 2 project, which is a groundwater recharge project, requesting around 4.5 million of the MLRP funding. There's also the Los Gatos groundwater recharge pilot project requesting around 1.6 million. ... with those four projects, that utilizes all the available funding at the moment, the district is trying to be proactive with the hopes that potentially there might be additional funding over through Prop 4, an extension of the program.
records.notes: Speaker is the EKI consultant presenting; Pasajero request here ($4.5M) differs from the ~$5M requested in the 2026-03-24 meeting, and Panoche Creek is ~$3.7M here vs ~$4M then.

records.finding: Westlands expects DOC approval of all projects in one to two months and then roughly a one-year extension to the implementation deadline, which was December 31, 2026 under the grant agreement; DOC has appeared receptive.
records.quantitative_detail: Original implementation deadline 2026-12-31; extension of about one year expected
records.meeting_body: Westside Subbasin MLRP Steering and Outreach Advisory Committee (Westlands WD)
records.agenda_item: Project update: DOC review of packets
records.evidence_text: generally one to two months hoping to get approval and then we'll get probably a year long extension on completing all the projects.
records.notes: Speaker is Peter Maraccini (Westlands) describing a same-day DOC call; extension not yet granted.

records.finding: DOC told Westlands that Prop 4 guidelines for a third round of MLRP funding are due within a month or two, so the district keeps alternate projects ready. All current implementation money is already committed.
records.quantitative_detail: Round 3 MLRP guidelines expected within about 1-2 months of 2026-08-19
records.meeting_body: Westside Subbasin MLRP Steering and Outreach Advisory Committee (Westlands WD)
records.agenda_item: Project updates
records.evidence_text: We got an update today from the Department of Conservation that, you know, Prop 4 guidelines for their Round 3 of MLRP funding will be coming out in the next month or so or two months. And so there possibly could be more funding coming our way.

records.finding: A district staff member says eligible projects must have a water-savings component, which means finding a landowner currently farming the land, so savings are counted only where irrigated agriculture is removed.
records.meeting_body: Westside Subbasin MLRP Steering and Outreach Advisory Committee (Westlands WD)
records.agenda_item: Project concept form eligibility discussion
records.evidence_text: It needs to have that water savings component, which means finding kind of like you said, that landowner who is currently using it for agriculture. And therefore you're seeing a water savings on top of the other community benefits.
records.notes: Describes eligibility, not a tracking programme; scope of ongoing savings tracking is not stated.

records.finding: Westlands tracks cropped and fallowed land district-wide through an annual grower survey, now separating fallow land with solar from other fallow. It reports a 40,000-acre rise in fallowing in 2025. This is acreage tracking, not ET or savings tracking.
records.quantitative_detail: Fallowing up about 40,000 acres in 2025 vs 2024 (annual, district-wide)
records.meeting_body: Westlands Water District Board of Directors
records.agenda_item: Item 8: Receive update on the 2025 crop report
records.evidence_text: So we send out a survey to all the farmers to report on their. Their acres of what is being farmed, what crops and what has been fallowed. ... We are now just differentiating between what is fallow and what is fallow with solar on it. ... you'll see an overall increase of fallowing in the district over the past year of 40,000 acres.
records.notes: Survey unit is acreage by crop (grower-reported, annual); parcel-level ET tracking is not mentioned. The 2025-11-18 meeting notes a satellite-based acreage estimate was revised after survey data.

records.finding: Under the Westside GSP, land enrolled in MLRP will not apply for a groundwater allocation, so there is no pumping from that parcel and the allocation is preserved. Staff describe it as a rule of the GSP applied to enrolled parcels.
records.meeting_body: Westside Subbasin MLRP Steering and Outreach Advisory Committee (Westlands WD)
records.agenda_item: Project overview: Los Gatos pilot project (benefit: preservation of groundwater allocation)
records.evidence_text: So essentially the preservation of groundwater allocation is in regards to the west side subbasin groundwater system sustainability plan. So in there there's rules of how much land in the district or in the sub basin can receive a groundwater allocation. So if this pro land is enrolled into the mlrp, there will, they will not apply for the groundwater allocation. So there won't be any groundwater use on that land.
records.notes: Transcript garbles 'pro land' (likely 'project land') and 'groundwater system sustainability plan'; the allocation rules themselves are in the GSP, not described here.

records.finding: Staff cite district rule changes (Article 2) that let temporarily converted land, including land converted to solar via VSIP or private developer deals, keep eligible-land status, among efforts to support growers who must repurpose land under SGMA.
records.meeting_body: Westlands Water District Board of Directors
records.agenda_item: Item 10: Land stewardship rule changes
records.evidence_text: such as the district's changes to Article 2 that allow, you know, maintaining eligible land status for temporarily converted lands, including those that are converted to solar, not just through VSIP, but through other private arrangements with developers.
records.notes: Staff speaker is Russ Freeman (counsel/staff, per the item introduction); allocation consequences of 'eligible land status' are inferred from the 2026-07-21 meeting.

records.finding: For land set fallow or abandoned, staff proposed rules that withhold surface-water and groundwater allocation, including groundwater credits, if harmful weeds and pests are not removed within 30 days of district notice. A director noted the penalty would come after allocations are made in March.
records.quantitative_detail: 30-day cure period after district notice; allocations made at start of year (March)
records.meeting_body: Westlands Water District Board of Directors
records.agenda_item: Item 9: rule revisions for land stewardship (Articles 1.5 E and 2.4 F)
records.evidence_text: These changes would preclude land from receiving allocations of surface or groundwater, including groundwater credits, if the user has not removed harmful weeds and pests within 30 days after receiving notice from the District.
records.notes: Concerns weeds and pests on abandoned or fallow land, not dust; a revised version was approved on 2026-07-21.

records.finding: For the grower-led Section 21 recharge project, the grower has agreed to stop requesting 'transitional allocation' on the converted land, so less pumping. This shows a project-level allocation give-up as the repurposing commitment.
records.quantitative_detail: ~50 acre recharge basin on land formerly in almonds and wheat
records.meeting_body: Westside Subbasin MLRP community meeting (Westlands WD)
records.agenda_item: Project updates: Section 21 recharge
records.evidence_text: the grower has agreed to no longer request transitional allocation. That is to say they will no longer be utilizing their full groundwater credits. And so less pumping out of the groundwater, that groundwater stays there for the benefit of the rest of the sub basin.
records.notes: Speaker is a WWD staff presenter (Peter, presumably Peter Maraccini); 'transitional allocation' is a GSP term not explained here; 'groundwater credits' here seems to mean allocation, not recharge credits.

records.finding: Staff say enrolled parcels cannot be given pumping by shifting allocation from another parcel, since landowners otherwise move allocation among their parcels. This is an anti-leakage limit but the movement rules themselves are not described.
records.meeting_body: Westside Subbasin MLRP Steering and Outreach Advisory Committee (Westlands WD)
records.agenda_item: Project overview: Los Gatos pilot project
records.evidence_text: And they're not going to be allowed to because a lot of other, a lot of landowners own different land in the district. And so they will move around their groundwater allocation to parcels that are, you know, are more productive, I guess you could say, so that they wouldn't be allowed to take groundwater from a different parcel and place it here.
records.notes: Sentence structure is garbled by transcription; read as: owners may move allocation between parcels in general, but not onto the enrolled parcel.

records.finding: Under the GSP, Westlands credits can be stored and transferred. This is cited among the programmes supporting land repurposing, but no geographic limit, anti-leakage or transfer-price rule is described in the meeting.
records.meeting_body: Westlands Water District Board of Directors
records.agenda_item: Item 10: Land stewardship rule changes
records.evidence_text: We have the groundwater sustainability plan, Article 1 credits allowing for storage and transfer of credits.
records.notes: Credits here are recharge/storage credits; whether freed allocation from repurposed land is transferable is not stated.

records.finding: For recharge projects Westlands credits water at about 80 to 90 percent of recharged volume after a 10 percent vadose-zone loss and evaporative loss that depends on wetted area and ET data. The credit is allocated to the upper or lower aquifer according to the Corcoran Clay. This is recharge crediting, not a fallowing savings method.
records.quantitative_detail: Credit typically 80-90% of recharged water; ~10% vadose-zone loss; evaporative loss depends on wetted area and ET (no ET product named)
records.meeting_body: Westside Subbasin MLRP Steering and Outreach Advisory Committee (Westlands WD)
records.agenda_item: Pilot projects: Panoche Creek and credit question from Huron mayor
records.evidence_text: all of our credits are generated through active recharge. They go through the vados zone, so they will experience a 10% loss. But prior to going through the theta zone, they also will have evaporative losses, which I believe Peter mentioned as well. And that just depends on what the wetted area is of the basins as well as the ET data available for the time we're recharging. Based on that, we will typically calculate a credit somewhere between 90 and 80%.
records.notes: Speaker is Westlands staff Kiti Campbell (named in the transcript); the method is for recharge credits under the GSP, which the MLRP recharge projects rely on.

records.finding: Staff note rising groundwater levels in the core subsidence-prone areas and credit both recharge and retired land, with growers' own recharge, as the cause together. No separate effect of retired land is quantified.
records.meeting_body: Westlands Water District Board of Directors
records.agenda_item: Item: SGMA groundwater conditions update
records.evidence_text: You'll see that along the core, particularly in subsidence prone areas where we have a lot of recharge efforts, where we have some retired land, you're seeing those groundwater levels go up. And that's both because of the efforts that staff have done to try to get as much recharge in the ground as well as growers try to get as much water into the ground.
records.notes: Recharge and retirement are listed side by side; no one separates their contributions.

records.finding: Benefit figures presented for the Section 21 recharge pond are inconsistent: 150-200 AF/yr 'recharge', corrected to 150-200 AF/yr 'groundwater savings' while the grower says the pond can take 25 AF/day. No method for turning a retired acreage or pond capacity into savings is given.
records.quantitative_detail: Section 21 (~50 acre pond): 150-200 AF/yr (Feb 2026); applicant capacity 25 AF/day; later 700 AF/yr recharge (March 2026 meeting); application first read as 7,000 AF
records.meeting_body: Westside Subbasin MLRP Steering and Outreach Advisory Committee (Westlands WD)
records.agenda_item: Project overview: Section 21 recharge project (applicant Gary commenting)
records.evidence_text: Well, that still is a benefit, but the benefit should say 150 to 200 acre feet of groundwater savings.
records.notes: Section 21 identified by the 50-acre pond and $400,000 budget matching the 2026-03-24 slide (700 AF/yr); the 25 AF/day figure is from the grower-applicant; unit and time basis uncertain because the exchange is garbled.

records.finding: The committee reviews a ~300 acre solar farm alternate project with a claimed 1,000 AF/yr benefit 'through avoided pumping', but nobody states how avoided pumping is calculated (baseline crop, ET or metered use).
records.quantitative_detail: ~1,000 AF/yr claimed avoided pumping; ~300 acre solar farm; MLRP request ~$100,000
records.meeting_body: Westside Subbasin MLRP Steering and Outreach Advisory Committee (Westlands WD)
records.agenda_item: Alternate project: Papa's solar farm
records.evidence_text: The project proposes to develop a roughly 300 acre solar farm. Benefits include reduced groundwater use, sustainable renewable energy and diversified economic opportunities. The estimated water supply benefit is approximately 1000 acre feet per year through avoided pumping.
records.notes: The method may sit in the application packet; none is described in the meeting. Applicant name garbled in transcript.

records.finding: Credits from MLRP recharge projects go to whoever manages the project; Westlands has historically held them in its accounts for the next dry year, though it could share them with a community or landowner by arrangement.
records.meeting_body: Westside Subbasin MLRP Steering and Outreach Advisory Committee (Westlands WD)
records.agenda_item: Pilot projects: who receives recharge credits
records.evidence_text: Those credits are then allocated to whoever's managing the project. So in this example, it'd be Westland. Westlands could have an arrangement with a community, we could have an arrangement with a, a landowner, or we could have just an arrangement with ourselves for the benefit of the sub basin to allocate those credits out. What we've been doing historically is we've been holding onto the credits and hanging on to them for the next dry year, and then we have those credits sitting in accounts.
records.notes: Speaker is Westlands staff (Kiti Campbell per transcript). A Huron mayor asked whether credits could benefit communities; staff said the GSP does not limit community pumping.

records.finding: Westlands staff say the GSP allocates groundwater to all gross acres, so land retired with MLRP funds can be repurposed to generate credits through recharge or reduced demand. A partner urged staff to confirm with DOC that MLRP funds may create groundwater credits; staff said they are eligible.
records.meeting_body: Westside Subbasin MLRP Steering and Outreach Advisory Committee (Westlands WD)
records.agenda_item: Project overview: groundwater credits for recharge projects
records.evidence_text: I think any project that's included in this slideshow package is in the spirit of MLRP because as Shelley mentioned that our JSP allocates groundwater to all gross acres in the district. So all of these projects are technically eligible for groundwater allocation. And if we fund these projects with the MLRP money, then that will potentially be retired and then repurposed to generate more credits either through a recharge project or. Or intentionally reduce the demand on the groundwater aquifer to prevent from undesirable results which are all within the spirit of our gsp.
records.notes: The question about DOC's position on credits came from a partner (Emily Boettger); no DOC confirmation appears in this meeting. 'JSP' is the transcription of 'GSP'.

records.section: 2.5 Data Source and ET Product Choice
records.finding: Westlands added an ET calculator to its SGMA website so water users can estimate ET when planning recharge. The ET data product behind it and any validation are not named.
records.meeting_body: Westlands Water District Board of Directors
records.agenda_item: Item 7A: SGMA/GSP implementation update
records.evidence_text: we do have an ET calculator on our Sigma website that has been added so it would assist water users in advising how they plan to use their water. In this case, how they would plan to recharge and what that ET would be.
records.notes: Speaker not labelled (SGMA staff report by the deputy GM's team); the tool is described for planning recharge and water use, not for crediting fallowing savings. Basin-wide rule; not specific to repurposed land.

records.finding: The consultant says habitat is not one of the top opportunities in the Westside Subbasin (limited waterways, existing land uses), so habitat co-benefits are to be included only where feasible. Recharge, solar and community projects dominate.
records.meeting_body: Westside Subbasin MLRP Steering and Outreach Advisory Committee (Westlands WD)
records.agenda_item: Regional goals: habitat and ecosystem goal
records.evidence_text: we wish there was an opportunity to do some kind of like flood flow reconnection and you know, a larger habitat and ecosystem project. But you know, due to the unique state of the basin and you know, the land use types that are currently in the basin, you know, we started with where feasible. So identifying that, you know, unfortunately habitat and ecosystem isn't one of the top goals and top opportunities for the basin.

records.finding: Five community listening sessions (Kettleman City, Huron, Mendota, Five Points, Cantua Creek) surfaced co-benefits residents want from repurposing: safe affordable drinking water, residential solar and lower energy costs, less pesticide and dust exposure, and jobs.
records.quantitative_detail: 5 listening sessions
records.meeting_body: Westside Subbasin MLRP community meeting (Westlands WD)
records.agenda_item: Community meeting: community needs themes
records.evidence_text: What we heard was that folks really, really care about access to safe, affordable drinking water, that they are interested in residential, solar and lower energy costs, that they wanted to be to have reduced exposure to pesticides and dust. That they wanted economic resiliency and opportunity.
records.notes: Speaker is the outreach facilitator (Grace Person, CeresCollab) inferred from context.

records.finding: Projects are ranked on a three-part rubric: spatial suitability (EKI maps), feasibility (implementation readiness) and a qualitative alignment with DOC and GSP goals. The steering committee dropped the cost-effectiveness factor after the first round of scoring.
records.meeting_body: Westside Subbasin MLRP Steering and Outreach Advisory Committee (Westlands WD)
records.agenda_item: Project scoring rubric
records.evidence_text: The total project score is made up of three components which include the Suitability, feasibility and qualitative evaluation. The suitability factor includes spatial and non spatial factors derived from suitability maps that were developed by eki and Visibility focuses on implementation readiness. ... And then qualitative evaluation allows consideration for alignment with the California Department of Conservation's MLRP goals and including the goals of the West Site Sub Basin, MLRP and our Groundwater Sustainability Plan
records.notes: Co-benefit weights are not given in the meeting. The rubric scores expected co-benefits at application; no post-implementation co-benefit metric is described.

records.finding: Staff say applications were scored on suitability, groundwater-sustainability benefit, benefit to disadvantaged communities, habitat, local economy and feasibility. These are co-benefit scores at application, not post-project measurements.
records.meeting_body: Westlands Water District Board of Directors (acting as Westlands WD GSA)
records.agenda_item: Item 8C: approve Westside MLRP projects
records.evidence_text: From those applications, we score them based on suitability, benefits to groundwater sustainability, whether they had benefits, disadvantaged communities, habitat, local economy, their feasibility, so on and so forth.

records.finding: When a participant asked for metrics on how many workers would be affected, staff said they had no such estimate and would have to calculate it, so job impacts of land repurposing are a stated goal without a quantified measure.
records.meeting_body: Westside Subbasin MLRP community meeting (Westlands WD)
records.agenda_item: Community meeting: economic well-being breakout report-out
records.evidence_text: Is there any estimated amounts of people that would more than likely be impacted in terms of workforce at the moment? We will have to go back and actually do that ourselves. Do that calculation ourselves. We don't have that number prepared at the moment.
records.notes: Question asker and answerer share one transcript turn; the answer is by WWD staff.

records.finding: Residents at the August 4 meeting asked for metrics to measure the impact of agricultural land displaced by solar. Staff plan a deeper look at monitoring and tracked benefit metrics for the four funded projects at the next committee meeting.
records.quantitative_detail: Four funded projects; no metric values stated
records.meeting_body: Westside Subbasin MLRP Steering and Outreach Advisory Committee (Westlands WD)
records.agenda_item: Community meeting report-out
records.evidence_text: requests to develop metrics to measure the impact of agricultural. Agricultural land displacement by solar.
records.notes: Outreach partner relaying community comments; the metrics promised for the four projects are not described in this meeting.

records.finding: Co-benefits link to funding only through scoring: staff say projects that offer more benefits generally score higher, with a 10-year minimum commitment to maintain the benefit. No price, credit or weighting of co-benefits in allocation is described.
records.quantitative_detail: 10-year minimum maintenance of project benefits
records.meeting_body: Westside Subbasin MLRP Steering and Outreach Advisory Committee (Westlands WD)
records.agenda_item: Project process and incentives
records.evidence_text: the benefit that the project provides has to be maintained for a minimum of 10 years and that projects that offer more benefits will generally score higher, but the program requires it to be maintained for a minimum of 10 years.
records.notes: A consultant in the same meeting said the 10-year commitment is deterring applicants in other subbasins she works in; this passage is staff (Shelly Ruiz) answering.

records.finding: A GIS suitability tool weights local benefit categories into one suitability value, and land scoring above 50 percent is designated a priority area for repurposing. This is the closest link between co-benefits and project ranking; it does not set payments or allocations.
records.quantitative_detail: Priority areas = weighted suitability value above 50%
records.meeting_body: Westside Subbasin MLRP Steering and Outreach Advisory Committee (Westlands WD)
records.agenda_item: Plan update: DOC program priority definitions
records.evidence_text: it went through and weighted all of the suitability values into a single suitability value. And anything over 50% was highlighted in blue and became our land repurposing priority areas.
records.notes: The weights for each benefit category are not stated in this meeting.

records.finding: After the Westlands board approved four projects (July 21), contracts depend on DOC approving each project's monitoring plan. Monitoring plans are therefore a DOC-gated requirement before work starts.
records.quantitative_detail: Four projects approved by Westlands board 2026-07-21
records.meeting_body: Westside Subbasin MLRP Steering and Outreach Advisory Committee (Westlands WD)
records.agenda_item: Project update: contracting phase
records.evidence_text: we are hoping that we get contracts signed, you know, the next couple of weeks, and the DOC also approves their monitoring plans.
records.notes: The monitoring plans' content (frequency, duration) is not described at this meeting.

records.finding: For the recharge projects, groundwater benefit is to be monitored with the district's existing deep-well network, read twice a year, and not with project-specific meters. Nothing is said about monitoring water savings from retired land.
records.quantitative_detail: Deep-well groundwater levels read twice per year (biannual)
records.meeting_body: Westside Subbasin MLRP Steering and Outreach Advisory Committee (Westlands WD)
records.agenda_item: Pasajero Phase 2 project review; question on domestic well monitoring
records.evidence_text: we do actually have that factor in our project monitoring plan. So we do plan to monitor ground levels through our existing deep ground water well network. So the district does go out on a biannual basis to collect groundwater readings on every deep groundwater well that's registered with the district. And so that's how we'll be tracking the groundwater level surrounding the project area.
records.notes: Answer to a CCEJN representative asking about domestic wells near the site; 'biannual' is read as twice a year.

records.finding: DOC asked Westlands to describe how its top land-repurposing strategies will include adaptive management to avoid adverse impacts on neighbouring or repurposed lands. This is a stated feedback mechanism; no monitoring result has yet changed the programme.
records.meeting_body: Westside Subbasin MLRP Steering and Outreach Advisory Committee (Westlands WD)
records.agenda_item: DOC comments on draft plan
records.evidence_text: And then another key aspect that they wanted to see is to describe how those top land repurposing strategies will provide adaptive management strategies to avoid adverse impacts on neighboring properties or repurposed lands. ... And so they really want this to be, you know, an adaptive management program.
records.notes: Consultant relaying DOC's comment on the draft plan; no instance of results changing a decision.

records.finding: Staff say that once state grant money is gone, Westlands will look for other funding for programmes like this one and is keeping a project list to target it. Nothing was said at this meeting about funding post-grant monitoring or accounting.
records.meeting_body: Westside Subbasin MLRP Steering and Outreach Advisory Committee (Westlands WD)
records.agenda_item: Project process: concept forms and future funding
records.evidence_text: Even when the funding is all said and done, the grant, there's no more funding through the current grant through the state. You know, Westlands is always looking for other funding opportunities to keep funding, you know, programs that we have implemented, which would be one of these.
records.notes: Refers to funding projects, not to funding monitoring; in 2025-09-17 staff said DOC's review step ends when the grant agreement terminates in 2027.

records.finding: For land kept as eligible cropland under a modified use such as solar, Westlands will require a land maintenance plan backed by financial assurances, modelled on decommissioning assurances. This is a post-conversion funding guarantee, though not for MLRP projects.
records.meeting_body: Westlands Water District Board of Directors
records.agenda_item: Item 14: rules and regulations for allocation and use of agricultural water (land stewardship)
records.evidence_text: For those landowners that are participating in retaining their eligible cropland status for modified uses, there will be required a development of a land maintenance plan supported by financial assurances similar to what we provide require for decommissioning of projects at the end of their life.
records.notes: Speaker is district staff (Russ Freeman) presenting the revised rules; applies to eligible-cropland conversions, not to DOC MLRP grantees.

records.finding: A neighbouring grower told the board that dust and air-quality problems come from retired drainage-impaired land that is disked each summer to control weeds, and said converting it to solar would end the soil disturbance. This is a landowner view, not a staff or measured finding.
records.quantitative_detail: ~4,000 acres of retired land next to the commenter; commenter says ~92,000 acres permanently retired district-wide (unverified)
records.meeting_body: Westlands Water District Board of Directors
records.agenda_item: Items 9-10: public comment on Valley Clean Infrastructure Plan
records.evidence_text: The number one being the air quality issues associated with all the retired ground. ... And so to improve air quality, I would love to see that turned into something more permanent solution which is to me, solar, which would remove disturbing the soil and kicking up the dust and everything that comes up out here every summer when everybody has to go start disking it.
records.notes: Comment is by a grower (family farming since 1949), not the board; acreage figures are the commenter's own.

records.finding: A resident speaker opposing the same solar plan said approval would bring years of traffic and dust, so repurposing to solar is itself raised as a dust source. Dust is raised by residents on both sides, with no measurement offered.
records.meeting_body: Westlands Water District Board of Directors
records.agenda_item: Items 9-10: public comment on Valley Clean Infrastructure Plan
records.evidence_text: If this project is approved, we cannot repeat the same story of benefits for a few and consequences for the communities. Approval would mean years of increased traffic, dust and risks that we yet fully do not understand.
records.notes: Commenter name and organisation are not clear from the transcript; speaker is a resident opposing VSIP.

records.finding: Dust exposure was raised by residents in the listening sessions and is written into the community health goal. Staff and the outreach partner say repurposing high-dust, high-pesticide cropland could reduce it.
records.meeting_body: Westside Subbasin MLRP Steering and Outreach Advisory Committee (Westlands WD)
records.agenda_item: Regional goals: community health goal
records.evidence_text: I think what we'll need to do is incorporate it into the main bullet, you know, because that ties back to one of the key things that you heard from the listening sessions. Right. Is that the communities were wanting reduced exposure to dust and pesticides. ... And that's very possible if ag land that's used, that has a crop that has a high pesticide or high dust component is no longer being used as that.
records.notes: Both speakers are consultants/partners, not the board; the goal text 'reduce exposure to dust and pesticides through strategic land repurposing and vegetative cover establishment' recurs in the 2026-07-15 and 2026-08-19 meetings.

records.finding: Residents at the August 4 meeting tied valley fever in schools to soil disruption, extending the dust concern from pesticides to disease. Staff say the existing goal wording on exposure to dust and pesticides already covers it, with valley fever possibly named in the plan.
records.quantitative_detail: Concern raised at 2026-08-04 community meeting; no figures
records.meeting_body: Westside Subbasin MLRP Steering and Outreach Advisory Committee (Westlands WD)
records.agenda_item: Report-out of August 4 community meeting: community health goal
records.evidence_text: They noted valley fever in schools as something that, that they're really concerned about the impact of soil disruption and they get, you know, exposed to valley fever and then they have cases of it.
records.notes: Speaker is the outreach partner (Grace Person) relaying residents' comments; no air-quality metric or control is attached.

records.finding: Advocates for west Fresno residents asked the board to require publicly accessible air and heat monitoring around solar project sites as a condition of approval. Whether the adopted plan includes any such monitoring is not stated in the meeting.
records.speaker_role: NGO/advocate - Central California Environmental Justice Network (for Futuro Justo)
records.meeting_body: Westlands Water District Board of Directors
records.agenda_item: Items 9-10: public comment on Valley Clean Infrastructure Plan
records.evidence_text: providing publicly accessible air and heat monitoring around the project sites
records.notes: Board adopted Resolution 12325 the same day; no staff reply on air monitoring is in the transcript. This is solar on retired/fallow land, not MLRP projects.

records.finding: Dust gets several meetings of wordsmithing as a goal but is not quantified, monitored or tied to a control. Participants note it is really an air-quality issue and that the district sees it as only partly within its reach.
records.meeting_body: Westside Subbasin MLRP Steering and Outreach Advisory Committee (Westlands WD)
records.agenda_item: Regional goals: community health goal
records.evidence_text: we wanted to acknowledge it, but we also knew that the district has a little bit of. It's a little bit outside of the. The reach.
records.notes: Speaker is the outreach partner (Grace Person); another partner (Emily Boettger) said exposure to dust and pesticides is more about air quality than water.

records.finding: The Westlands board approved the Valley Clean Infrastructure Plan, a master-planned solar build-out on up to 136,000 acres of retired and fallow land. Staff frame it as a use for drainage-impaired and SGMA-retired land.
records.quantitative_detail: Up to 136,000 acres of solar; 35-40 year project life (public comment); 10-year phased implementation (AI summary)
records.meeting_body: Westlands Water District Board of Directors
records.agenda_item: Items 9-10: certify program EIR; approve Valley Clean Infrastructure Plan (Resolutions 12225 and 12325)
records.evidence_text: VSIP allows for conversion of retired and fallow land to a beneficial use. It also provides our growers the flexibility to plan long term and create sufficient and stable water supply for a portion of their land while putting the remainder of that land that must be followed to a beneficial use.
records.notes: Both resolutions passed by voice vote (non-conflicted directors only). Water savings and groundwater accounting for solar land are not discussed in this passage.

records.finding: Westlands' general manager traces its retired land to unmet drainage service and later SGMA-driven retirement of subsidence-prone land. Prior retirements were not part of any savings accounting discussed in these meetings.
records.quantitative_detail: A public commenter put permanently retired land at about 92,000 acres (not a staff figure)
records.meeting_body: Westlands Water District Board of Directors
records.agenda_item: Items 9-10: opening remarks on VSIP background
records.evidence_text: the appropriate drainage services were not provided as promised by Bureau of Reclamation, leading to necessary retiring and fallowing of drainage impaired lands. ... And then the Sustainable Groundwater Management act was implemented which severely limited our access to groundwater and resulted in additional retirement of subsidence prone land.
records.notes: The 92,000-acre figure comes from a grower commenter at the same meeting, not staff; no retired-acreage baseline appears in any staff report.

records.finding: Staff list Westlands' programmes for growers repurposing land: recharge on eligible cropland, LandFlex, low-interest leases for irrigation and recharge equipment, and metering upgrades for real-time water use reporting.
records.meeting_body: Westlands Water District Board of Directors
records.agenda_item: Item 10: Land stewardship rule changes
records.evidence_text: We have the district's groundwater recharge programs that include eligible cropland. Land flex has been implemented. We have the district's low interest lease programs for irrigation equipment and recharge. And we've done upgrades to metering to support real time report of water use.
records.notes: No accounting method for any of these programmes is described.

records.finding: In the Westside MLRP, the steering committee scores proposed projects; outreach-committee members and the public leave the call during scoring and get a report-out at the next meeting. After scoring, the Department of Conservation and then the Westlands board give approval, so scoring is a required step.
records.meeting_body: Westside Subbasin MLRP Steering and Outreach Advisory Committee
records.agenda_item: Overview of combined committee meeting structure
records.evidence_text: Once we start receiving projects, you know through our project process we will score them. But once we, and that's going to be up to the steering committee to score. ... when we have a meeting the steering committee scores the new projects, we will report out on that scoring process at the next meeting with everyone in the room.
records.notes: Speakers are the programme manager and the plan consultant; the transcript does not list which members sit on the steering committee versus the outreach advisory committee.

records.finding: Steering committee members pre-score each project, staff consolidates and flags large disagreements, and the committee settles them in discussion. The committee itself decided to drop the cost-effectiveness factor from the rubric after scoring the first set of applications.
records.meeting_body: Westside Subbasin MLRP Steering and Outreach Advisory Committee
records.agenda_item: Project scoring rubric and process
records.evidence_text: I sent the scoring rubric to our steering committee members. They completed their scores beforehand and then after they give me back their rubrics, I basically go in and consolidate all their scores into one scoring rubric spreadsheet. And if there are any discrepancies in the scoring, for example, if someone scored it a zero and another person scored a five, I would flag that as something that we would need to discuss further with the committee so they can reach a final agreed upon score. ... they have decided to remove the cost effectiveness from the scoring rubric.
records.notes: Shows a committee decision (rubric change) adopted by the programme; no dissent is recorded.

records.finding: Committee members critiqued the draft process flyer on October 15, asking for a sentence naming eligible project types, hosting all flyers on the website, and an audience-specific headline. The flyer shown November 19 includes examples of fundable project types and the website hosts flyers.
records.quantitative_detail: Flyer feedback 2025-10-15; flyer shown 2025-11-19
records.agenda_item: Feedback on flyer
records.evidence_text: it might be helpful. to just add, like, an intro sentence, identifying the types of projects that are eligible.
records.notes: Change is to an outreach document, not a GSA rule; Nov 19 flyer description is from staff in that meeting. No speaker links the revision to this feedback.

records.finding: The plan consultant says the scoring criteria and project application were revised in response to steering committee scoring feedback and to comments at recent meetings, including public comments. The specific public comment is not named in this passage.
records.meeting_body: Westside Subbasin MLRP Steering and Outreach Advisory Committee
records.agenda_item: Update on revisions to the plan
records.evidence_text: we revised the scoring criteria and the MLRP project application per feedback from the steering committee while they were scoring, while they were doing the scoring process. And then also feedback from the past couple meetings that we've had here which also included some public comments.
records.notes: Before/after wording of the criteria is not shown; asks in 2026-03-24 were a pre-application checklist and a glossary of terminology.

records.finding: Committee input in May (a Huron city official asked about supporting small businesses) was followed in June by a revised economic well-being goal that now names small businesses. The consultant says the change reflects what was heard the month before.
records.meeting_body: Westside Subbasin MLRP Steering and Outreach Advisory Committee
records.agenda_item: Revised regional goals (economic well-being)
records.evidence_text: our revised goal is preserve the long term viability of the regional agricultural economy to continue to support local employment and small businesses while advancing workforce transition, job training and employment Opportunities connected to land repurposing projects. ... one thing that we heard from our meeting last month was to somehow incorporate small businesses and then really focusing on that workforce transition.
records.notes: May 20 draft goal had no small-business wording; speaker links the change to last month's meeting. Role of the May 20 commenter inferred from the 2026-09-15 board remark "Mayor Leon in Huron".

records.finding: After the August 4 community meeting, the consultant reviewed attendee feedback against the draft community-health goal. Items such as protective crops for solar EMF and rainwater capture would go into plan text rather than the goal wording, so the goal stays unchanged.
records.quantitative_detail: No quantities; considers feedback from the 2026-08-04 community meeting
records.meeting_body: Westside Subbasin MLRP Steering and Outreach Advisory Committee
records.agenda_item: Community meeting report-out and regional goals
records.evidence_text: after looking back through this feedback and looking at our community health goal, I'm thinking we've captured most of them. You know, I think the crops to protect EMF emitted from solar, I think that's something that we can touch on within the description of the top land repurposing strategies. I don't think it needs to explicitly be incorporated into the goal itself.
records.notes: Records input considered and mostly placed elsewhere in the plan; CCEJN said the goals reflected its feedback.

records.finding: Westlands' benefit write-up for recharge projects names water reliability, water quality, flood risk and recreation as community benefits. An LCJA staffer added that recharge near a community water system could buffer it from nearby high-production wells.
records.meeting_body: Westside Subbasin MLRP Steering and Outreach Advisory Committee
records.agenda_item: Responses to DOC comments (strategy benefits)
records.evidence_text: for meaningful benefits to community. These projects improve water reliability and water quality. You know, especially if your community is dependent on groundwater, it can help reduce flood risk and then also supports agricultural and local recreation. ... especially if it is near like a community's water system, it could act as a, also like as a buffer between the system and other high production wells. So that could be another direct benefit to community.
records.notes: Consultant gave the first quote; the second is an advocate's suggestion, welcomed by the consultant but not confirmed for inclusion.

records.finding: A Westlands speaker (transcript unlabelled; likely staff presenting the plan, possibly a director) said community benefits should account for existing needs, including domestic water service in remote communities that county services cannot cover, suggesting the plan's funding could assist the county though Westlands would not provide the service.
records.meeting_body: Westlands Water District Board of Directors
records.agenda_item: Valley Clean Infrastructure Plan update: Community Benefits Agreement plan
records.evidence_text: some of the local communities certainly have domestic water needs that the county services that I don't know that it's possible for the county to charge enough to offset the cost. And so some of the existing needs, I think. Would you Know, certainly need to be factored in if maybe that's a domestic water service for some of these desperate communities. Not that we would provide it, but maybe that some of the funding would assist the county and something like that.
records.notes: Speaker unclear: the passage continues the staff presenter's remarks ('what I was saying earlier') but includes 'just me speaking'; speculation, not a programme term.

records.finding: The one community-led MLRP project, a solar and battery system for the Westside Community Center, a designated cooling center in Five Points, is the programme's concrete community benefit (heat resilience). It was proposed by residents with CCEJN support; the board approved it July 21, 2026.
records.quantitative_detail: About $200,000 total, $190,000 MLRP request; land under 5 acres (staff, 2026-03-24) vs about 2,500 sq ft (staff, 2026-06-17)
records.meeting_body: Westside Subbasin MLRP Steering and Outreach Advisory Committee
records.agenda_item: Priority project review: Westside Community Cooling and Resilience Center
records.evidence_text: This project proposes installation of a ground mounted solar photovoltaic system with battery storage. The goal is to offset electricity demand and provide reliable backup power to the Westside Community center, which serves as a designated cooling center. This project improves improves community resilience during extreme heat and power outages.
records.notes: Board approval is stated in the 2026-08-19 meeting; size figures conflict between meetings.

records.finding: The initial Westside MLRP eligibility screen asked whether a project's benefits would serve a DAC or severely disadvantaged community for at least 10 years, with a map of DAC/SDAC places. Staff noted that on a census-tract basis the whole subbasin counts as disadvantaged.
records.quantitative_detail: Benefit duration test: minimum 10 years
records.meeting_body: Westside Subbasin MLRP Steering and Outreach Advisory Committee
records.agenda_item: MLRP project process overview (step 1 screening)
records.evidence_text: will these benefits serve a disadvantaged community or severely disadvantaged community for a minimum of 10 years? So one big aspect of the state's guideline for the program is that the benefits must, you know, translate to a minimum of 10 years. So if you look at this map and based on the legend, essentially the whole basin is a disadvantaged community.
records.notes: This screening question was later reworded (see 2026-01-21).

records.finding: Westlands will adopt, in the plan, a definition of "meaningful benefits to communities" modelled on the Department of Conservation appendix: measurable benefits to DAC residents, better water supply, quality and affordability, reduced air and noise impacts, projects reflecting community-identified needs, and avoiding long-term harm.
records.meeting_body: Westside Subbasin MLRP Steering and Outreach Advisory Committee
records.agenda_item: Responses to DOC comments on draft plan
records.evidence_text: just the definition in a nutshell for you all is, you know, promoting projects that deliver measurable benefits to residents of disadvantaged communities. Projects that improve community resources and quality of life, including water supply, water quality and water affordability. Projects that improve air noise quality, community assets or other community identified impacts. Projects that also directly reflect community identified needs with meaningful opportunities for engagement and participation in project development and decisions. And then also projects that avoid long term harm to community resources and if there are potential impacts from the project, you know, having clear mitigation or mediation commitments.
records.notes: Speaker paraphrases the DOC definition ("in a nutshell"); the DOC appendix itself is not in the corpus.

records.finding: Two advocacy groups (LCJA, CCEJN) asked that solar-project benefits be stated as local, quantified (for example number of local jobs) and monitored. The consultant called it critical feedback; no benefit metric or tracking method was committed in the meeting.
records.meeting_body: Westside Subbasin MLRP Steering and Outreach Advisory Committee
records.agenda_item: Responses to DOC comments (meaningful benefits)
records.evidence_text: I'd just be a little bit more clear about like clean energy directly to community, adjacent to project for local jobs. Like it will create like X amount of jobs for, for like local residents. ... we would just really hope that the MA LRP is able to monitor as much as possible how like we can actually like streamline that full benefit.
records.notes: Speakers are staff of Leadership Counsel for Justice and Accountability ("Nataly (LCJA)") and CCEJN; the DOC definition quoted that day does use the word "measurable".

records.finding: Westlands described a community benefits plan for its solar programme: an 18-month-plus needs assessment scoped by a working group of communities and benefit organisations, then a framework "with metrics" and funding rules. Funding starts only at commercial operation, several years out.
records.quantitative_detail: Needs assessment up to about 18 months; plan implementation roughly 60 months out, at commercial operation
records.meeting_body: Westlands Water District Board of Directors
records.agenda_item: Valley Clean Infrastructure Plan update: Community Benefits Agreement plan
records.evidence_text: we're going to be conducting a community engagement and needs assessment that's going to occur through what we envision to be a series of multiple meetings covering various topics to assess the needs of the community. We plan to scope those meetings through a working group that will establish that includes local communities and community benefit organizations so we know what to cover in the meetings. ... we're adopting a framework and then having metrics and kind of rules around how things are funded
records.notes: Metrics are stated as intended, not defined. Two speakers: a district staffer (needs assessment) and the general manager (framework with metrics).

records.finding: Huron's mayor, who leads the LEAP Institute (Westlands' MLRP workforce partner), reported counts for a construction class in Huron: 15 in the current cohort and 12 in the prior one, half of whom work in solar fields. He did not say whether this class is the MLRP-funded course.
records.quantitative_detail: 15 participants (current cohort); 12 (previous cohort), 6 of 12 working in solar fields; spoken figures, May 2026
records.speaker_role: advisory committee member — Huron / LEAP Institute
records.meeting_body: Westside Subbasin MLRP Steering and Outreach Advisory Committee
records.agenda_item: Draft economic well-being goal discussion
records.evidence_text: we have a construction class going on in Huron. First time ever that we've had something in these neck of the woods. There's 15 people that are part of it. The previous cohort had 12 people. Six of those, 50% of those are working in solar fields right now.
records.notes: Self-reported by the partner; "Rey Leon" is the speaker label and the 2026-09-15 board refers to a Mayor Leon of Huron.

records.finding: Asked by Huron's representative who receives the groundwater credits from MLRP recharge, Westlands staff said credits go to the project manager (Westlands, a community or a landowner by arrangement) and Westlands has been holding them for dry years. The GSP does not limit community pumping, so a community credit benefit would have to be designed.
records.quantitative_detail: Recharge credit about 80-90% of water recharged after 10% vadose-zone loss plus evaporation (staff estimate)
records.meeting_body: Westside Subbasin MLRP Steering and Outreach Advisory Committee
records.agenda_item: Pilot project updates (Panoche Creek) / credits Q&A
records.evidence_text: Those credits are then allocated to whoever's managing the project. So in this example, it'd be Westland. Westlands could have an arrangement with a community, we could have an arrangement with a, a landowner, or we could have just an arrangement with ourselves for the benefit of the sub basin to allocate those credits out. What we've been doing historically is we've been holding onto the credits and hanging on to them for the next dry year ... currently the way our groundwater sustainability plan has been implemented and adopted, we do not limit communities use of groundwater. So we would have to figure out how to develop those credits and then create it as a benefit to the communities.
records.notes: Distributive question raised by a local official (Rey Leon, Huron) who also suggested credits as a community benefit during drought; credits-as-benefit is not adopted. Speaker for the credit rules is the Westlands consultant/staff (Kiti Campbell).

records.finding: A Rural Communities RISE representative (the group reports 21 elected board members representing 36 rural communities) read a letter asking Westlands to help form a master Community Benefits Agreement authority for the Valley Clean Infrastructure Plan, with at least 80% of benefit resources going to the most impacted rural communities. No response to the 80% figure was recorded.
records.quantitative_detail: At least 80% of community benefit resources requested to go to most impacted rural communities; commenter's organisation: 21 board members, 36 rural communities
records.meeting_body: Westlands Water District Board of Directors
records.agenda_item: Valley Clean Infrastructure Plan update: public comment
records.evidence_text: most community benefit resources, at least 80% should flow directly to the rural communities most impacted. ... Rural Communities RISE is ready to partner with Western's Water District
records.notes: Speaker labels are unclear (a farmworker and a RISE board member both speak around this point); the letter is RISE's position. Earlier in the item a speaker cautioned against new bureaucracy.

records.finding: Westlands dropped the rule that every MLRP project directly benefit a disadvantaged community; only the project suite must include direct community benefits. Staff explains the best recharge sites are far from communities, so the single Five Points community project covers the community-benefit requirement for the portfolio (distributive dimension).
records.meeting_body: Westside Subbasin MLRP Steering and Outreach Advisory Committee
records.agenda_item: Update on revisions to the plan
records.evidence_text: we also remove the requirement that every project has to provide direct meaningful benefits to disadvantaged community in order to be funded. That also was a change that I think DOC has made over, you know, their experience with these grantees. The suite of projects must include direct meaningful benefits to a dac, but not every individual project. I think one thing that they really struggled with is that a lot of the areas that had the poor groundwater conditions are far away from communities.
records.notes: Jan 21: the website screening question was reworded from "serve a DAC ... for 10 years" to "provide benefits for a minimum of 10 years" after DOC clarified; no public comment drove this change.

records.section: 3.1.4 Domestic Well Protection as an Equity Outcome
records.finding: A CCEJN organizer asked how the Pasajero recharge project would show benefits to nearby domestic wells and small community systems. Westlands answered that its project monitoring plan uses the district's deep-well network, read twice a year; no domestic-well-specific monitoring was described.
records.meeting_body: Westside Subbasin MLRP Steering and Outreach Advisory Committee
records.agenda_item: Priority project review: Pasajero Phase 2
records.evidence_text: the domestic well piece, like, I was just kind of curious as to how this project would be monitoring groundwater improvements with, you know, domestic wells that are maybe near this project site. Because I know that dealing with water conservation, you would want to see domestic wells or even small community systems benefit like through the project. ... So we do plan to monitor ground levels through our existing deep ground water well network. So the district does go out on a biannual basis to collect groundwater readings on every deep groundwater well that's registered with the district. And so that's how we'll be tracking the groundwater level surrounding the project area.
records.notes: Question raised by the public; no DAC versus non-DAC well analysis presented. The two quotes are from different speakers (organizer, then programme manager).

records.finding: Westlands planned to join Leadership Counsel's standing meeting with Cantua Creek residents to give MLRP updates, using a community partner's existing forum. On 2026-05-20 staff said it could not attend the May 6 meeting and instead planned its own July community meeting.
records.quantitative_detail: Planned Cantua Creek residents' meeting 2026-05-06, 6:00-7:30 pm; Westlands did not attend
records.meeting_body: Westside Subbasin MLRP Steering and Outreach Advisory Committee
records.agenda_item: Upcoming outreach
