records.finding: Each MLRP applicant receives, with its pre-filled implementation packet and monitoring plan, a disadvantaged-community engagement checklist, so project-level community engagement is tracked as an application item. Staff separately said projects must be opened to public input once approved by the state.
records.meeting_body: Westside Subbasin MLRP Steering and Outreach Advisory Committee
records.agenda_item: Priority project schedule
records.evidence_text: during this past month we have provided all applicants their pre filled implementation packets, their monitoring plans, the disadvantaged community engagement checklist for review and feedback.
records.notes: The checklist itself is not shown or quoted; the public-input requirement is stated on 2026-02-18 (staff reply to a youth-involvement suggestion).

records.finding: In early 2025 the outreach partner ran five community listening sessions (Kettleman City, Huron, Mendota, Cantua Creek, Five Points) without Westlands staff present so residents could speak freely, and also gathered survey responses and interviews. Per-session reach figures are not given.
records.quantitative_detail: Five listening sessions in early 2025; per-session attendance not stated
records.meeting_body: Westside Subbasin MLRP Steering and Outreach Advisory Committee
records.agenda_item: Listening session themes
records.evidence_text: what we did in early 2025 was a series of listening sessions around the basin to talk with community members, residents and others about what they saw as the need of their community, what were their pressing issues and things that they want to see addressed, et cetera. And so these listening sessions was an opportunity for them to tell us what they needed. And it was me in the room. I had spent time with Shelly and Kristen developing questions and then also, you know, an agenda. But it was really just Westlands was not at the listening sessions because we wanted people in residence to feel safe, to be able to tell us what they saw as their needs were. ... And we had some great turnout at the 5 that we did in Kettleman City, Huron, Mendota, Cantua Creek and Five Points.
records.notes: Grace Person (CeresCollab) describes the sessions; she also mentions two later community meetings in May (Huron, Cantua) in the 2026-05-20 transcript, year not stated.

records.finding: The August 4, 2026 Westside MLRP community meeting at the Five Points field office, run in breakout stations on the five regional goals, drew 28 community and public participants. Department of Conservation staff and about 10 Westlands staff also attended.
records.quantitative_detail: 28 public participants (18 in person, 10 online), meeting 6:00-7:30 pm, August 4, 2026; excludes partner agencies and about 10 district staff
records.meeting_body: Westside Subbasin MLRP Steering and Outreach Advisory Committee
records.agenda_item: Community meeting report-out
records.evidence_text: we had a community outreach meeting on August 4th. So earlier this month, it was from 6 to 7:30. It was at the Westlands field office in Five Points. So in the middle of the field, in the middle of the basin and accessible to. The goal was to be accessible to several communities and have them attend. So we had 28 participants in total. That was 18 people online and, excuse me, 10 people online and 18 in person.
records.notes: Speaker is the outreach partner consultant (CeresCollab) who reported out; the transcript misstates then corrects the in-person/online split ("18 people online and, excuse me, 10 people online and 18 in person").

records.finding: For its community benefits needs assessment, Westlands has run English and Spanish focus groups with elected officials and community leaders, with open community meetings and resident phone surveys planned next. Participants were mostly past commenters or known leaders.
records.quantitative_detail: Up to about 20 focus-group participants (staff estimate), first week of September 2026
records.meeting_body: Westlands Water District Board of Directors
records.agenda_item: Valley Clean Infrastructure Plan update: community benefits plan
records.evidence_text: our consultants conducted focus group studies with elected officials and community leaders in English and Spanish the first week of September. I understand that there are probably up to 20 participants in total. ... Then following the other two steps for the needs assessment will be those more traditional open community meetings with the residents and then a final step of direct communication through phone surveys to the residents as well.
records.notes: Results of the focus groups not yet received by the board. "Phone surveys" are resident polling, not geologic surveys.

records.finding: An MLRP-funded partner, the LEAP Institute in Huron, runs a training course preparing residents for plumbing apprenticeships and gray water system certification. Westlands circulated its flyer in English and Spanish through newsletters and its MLRP contact list.
records.quantitative_detail: Up to 20 enrollees; classes begin late February 2026, held in Huron
records.meeting_body: Westside Subbasin MLRP Steering and Outreach Advisory Committee
records.agenda_item: MLRP outreach update
records.evidence_text: we also met with our MLRP partner, the LEAP Institute, this past month to review their progress to date. And currently they are in the recruitment phase and finalizing their curriculum to ensure participants are well prepared to apply for and enter into a plumbing apprenticeship program. ... they're planning to enroll up to 20 people in their course
records.notes: Workforce/education programme rather than materials about groundwater.

records.finding: For the Five Points community cooling-center project, a Department of Conservation staffer suggested pairing the solar project with workshops (extreme heat training, solar maintenance workforce training), and committee members suggested MLRP signage. Westlands said it would pass the ideas to the applicant.
records.meeting_body: Westside Subbasin MLRP Steering and Outreach Advisory Committee
records.agenda_item: Priority project review: Westside Community Cooling and Resilience Center
records.evidence_text: Other things that we've seen from other grantees and other block grantees and projects is maybe like some sort of workshops too, could be tagged along with the project as well. Like for example, maybe like a extreme heat training since this is a cooling center and like that could be tagged along with it as well as just maybe like workforce development to maintain the solar Some sort of trainings to train staff or volunteers to maintain those systems.
records.notes: Suggestions only; not a funded programme. DOC attended the meeting as a funder.

records.finding: Westside MLRP programme meetings run with simultaneous Spanish interpretation by a contracted vendor (Linguistica), and the draft plan's executive summary is posted in Spanish. The same interpreter introduction opens every monthly committee meeting in the corpus.
records.agenda_item: Meeting start / MLRP timeline
records.evidence_text:
Good morning, everyone. Today, we will be having Spanish interpretation.

Spanish Interpreter, Emilia, Linguistica:
If you would like to hear any comments or questions made in Spanish, interpreted directly into English, then we ask that you join the interpretation channel. ... there was also an executive summary of the plan. That was translated into Spanish, which you can also find on.
records.notes: Sep 17 transcript labels the meeting a steering committee meeting; its agenda page is titled for the Outreach Advisory Committee.

records.finding: A committee member from the listening-session work asked whether technical assistance exists to help residents write project concepts, noting most community members do not own land in the target areas. Staff planned to learn from Tule Subbasin's MLRP, which paid partners including Self-Help Enterprises for technical support.
records.agenda_item: Outreach strategy for project process
records.evidence_text: most community members do not own land in the areas that, you know, we went out and did the listening sessions at. ... I don't know if there's any TA available for community to put together a potential concept.
records.notes: Tule/Valley Eco/Self-Help detail is said by Sequoia Riverlands Trust on the same call; Westlands agreed to call Valley Eco. By 2025-11-19 the process lets residents file land-less concepts that staff post and share monthly with landowners.

records.finding: The Westside MLRP web page has a one-click Spanish version, and the Spanish contact block lists separate phone numbers for Spanish speakers. Staff says the project concept form is also offered in Spanish on request.
records.meeting_body: Westside Subbasin MLRP Steering and Outreach Advisory Committee
records.agenda_item: MLRP project process overview
records.evidence_text: And one big thing to note is this Spanish, this website is all translated into Spanish as well. So if you click this green button here, this is Spanish, it will translate everything that's on the English version into Spanish. ... On the Spanish one we have, you know, two different numbers for those that want to reach out and speak Spanish. We have a phone number designated for that.
records.notes: Concept-form availability in Spanish is stated in the 2026-08-05 programme description, not in this passage.

records.finding: Westlands' December 2025 board meeting on the Valley Clean Infrastructure Plan provided in-person and Zoom Spanish interpretation, and took Zoom comments from people needing interpretation first.
records.quantitative_detail: Public comment limit: 2 minutes per person
records.meeting_body: Westlands Water District Board of Directors
records.agenda_item: Valley Clean Infrastructure Plan EIR certification and public comment
records.evidence_text: Everybody at the dais, we do want to remind you that we do have interpretation in person as well. ... We will take comments starting on Zoom first, starting with those who need interpretation services, then move to those who do not need interpretation services online.
records.notes: The transcript also shows an interpretation mix-up (a comment was heard in Spanish and the commenter was asked to repeat in English), so delivery was imperfect. Public comment limit was two minutes.

records.finding: For the August 4 community meeting, Westlands planned an evening hybrid format with Spanish interpretation on Zoom and in person, an English and Spanish feedback survey, plus food, children's activities and prizes. Staff says earlier meetings also offered food and children's activities.
records.quantitative_detail: Meeting 6:00-7:30 pm, August 4, 2026; survey open through August 7, 2026
records.meeting_body: Westside Subbasin MLRP Steering and Outreach Advisory Committee
records.agenda_item: Upcoming outreach: community meeting
records.evidence_text: The meeting will take place in a hybrid format from 6pm to 7:30pm allowing participants to attend either in person or virtually. And please note that interpretation services will be available both on Zoom and at the in person meeting. ... we've had children's activities and food. The only main difference I would say this time around is we're giving prizes and probably going to play a bingo game
records.notes: Raffle prizes had been floated on 2026-05-20 pending DOC approval; the 2026-08-05 recording shows gift-card and hat prizes drawn.

records.finding: Near-final Westside MLRP regional goals list "protect domestic wells" and affordable drinking water for rural and disadvantaged communities under the community health goal. No domestic-well mitigation programme, eligibility rule, funding amount or administrator is described in the meetings.
records.meeting_body: Westside Subbasin MLRP Steering and Outreach Advisory Committee
records.agenda_item: Regional goals (near-final)
records.evidence_text: for our community health goal, we came up with improve access to clean, reliable and affordable drinking water for rural and disadvantaged communities, support sustainable groundwater management, protect domestic wells, reduce exposure to dust and pesticides through strategic land repurposing and vegetative cover establishment, strengthen community infrastructure and economic well being and provide community and landowner education opportunities.
records.notes: Goal-level language only; whether the Westside GSP contains a well-mitigation policy is not discussed in these meetings. "Dry wells" in MLRP project talk means recharge injection wells.

records.finding: Westside MLRP uses an ArcGIS-based suitability tool to delineate priority areas for land repurposing, built from regional and local data with disadvantaged communities as one of five weighted local benefit categories. Community meetings in Huron and Cantua Creek helped shape it (per staff on 2025-11-19).
records.quantitative_detail: Weighted suitability above 50% = priority area (staff, 2026-07-15); 5 local benefit categories
records.meeting_body: Westside Subbasin MLRP Steering and Outreach Advisory Committee
records.agenda_item: Responses to DOC comments (priority areas)
records.evidence_text: the suitability tool is a geospatial analysis tool developed using ArcGIS, the best available regional and local data, and the west side MLRP local benefit categories, which you can see up in the top corner, you know, we identified five local benefit categories. Groundwater sustainability, habitat, disadvantaged community, communities, local economy, and additional criteria.
records.notes: Community input into the tool is stated by staff on 2025-11-19; weights are not given in this passage. Which DAC dataset feeds the category is not stated.

records.finding: When a Huron official asked where to see recharge and subsidence results, Westlands staff pointed to the DWR SGMA Data Viewer (InSAR subsidence layer) as well as the district website. This is the only named public tool used with the community in the Westside meetings.
records.meeting_body: Westside Subbasin MLRP Steering and Outreach Advisory Committee
records.agenda_item: Draft water supply goal discussion
records.evidence_text: They have what's known the SGMA Data Viewer, which they have multiple different tools. And so one of the ones that they use to present subsidence data is called nsar. So you could go on the website there and click the tool you're looking for. But if you're interested in subsidence, I would encourage you to take a look at the NSAR data, which shows subsidence.
records.notes: Tool is for subsidence data, not for domestic-well, DAC or water-quality data; the rest of the quote names "NSAR" for InSAR in the transcript.

records.finding: The Westside MLRP web page hosts a PDF map (Figure 1) of disadvantaged and severely disadvantaged communities in the subbasin, used by applicants to check project location, with a Spanish version of the map legend.
records.quantitative_detail: One map (Figure 1) in 2 languages (English, Spanish)
records.meeting_body: Westside Subbasin MLRP Steering and Outreach Advisory Committee
records.agenda_item: MLRP project process overview
records.evidence_text: we have a reference here to look at Figure 1 of DAC's and SDAC communities within the Westside subbasin for boundary details. This just means disadvantaged communities and severely disadvantaged communities. But if you wanted to see what your answer is, you just go down here. This is figure one. And essentially if your project is located within this boundary here and you could actually click on the PDF to zoom in, if you can't really see, you know, from that screen, you can zoom in and see if your project's located within this boundary. This is translated as well in English and Spanish. So you could see what all the symbols mean on this map.
records.notes: A static PDF, not an interactive tool; data source for the DAC/SDAC boundaries is not named.

records.finding: A Leadership Counsel staffer asked who proposed a pilot project and for plain-language explanation of a technical term; Westlands' resources supervisor explained it on the call. Later (2026-03-24) applicants were offered a glossary of terms.
records.quantitative_detail: No quantities; dates only
records.speaker_role: NGO/advocate — Leadership Counsel for Justice and Accountability
records.meeting_body: Westside Subbasin MLRP Steering and Outreach Advisory Committee
records.agenda_item: Pilot project updates (Los Gatos)
records.evidence_text: a lot of these words are very technical for me. And so I was wondering if you can explain, for example, what traveling trash screen means just to kind of understand this project better.
records.notes: Speaker affiliation inferred from the 2025-09-17 exchange ("Leadership Council for Justice and Accountability ... Mariana"); glossary is for applicants, not residents.

records.finding: Futuro Justo, through CCEJN, asked the board to adopt community mitigation measures (setbacks, publicly accessible air and heat monitoring, a valley fever plan) and a collaborative benefits process before approving the solar plan. Staff said the comments did not alter the EIR conclusions; the board proceeded and committed to a collaborative process.
records.meeting_body: Westlands Water District Board of Directors
records.agenda_item: Valley Clean Infrastructure Plan EIR certification and public comment
records.evidence_text: At a minimum, the FPO must adopt all of community identified mitigation measures such as adopting increased setbacks between homes and solar panels incorporating vegetative barriers to mitigate visual and noise impacts reroute routing vehicle and truck traffic away from communities, schools and other sensitive receptors during the construction and decommissioning of the project modifying mitigation measure MPS1 to ensure that funding is available for adequate and effective fire protection providing publicly accessible air and heat monitoring around the project sites as well as ensuring all homes and schools have air purification and cooling improving homes to mitigate visual visual air quality, heat and noise impacts and lastly implementing a valley fever mitigation plan that includes awareness workshops and respiratory protection measures specifically for residents. ... staff determined that the comments do not reflect the adequacy of the program EIR and do not alter any of its conclusions. ... we are committed to a community benefit program and if the board does approve moving forward with the project, we will begin a collaborative and inclusive process soon
records.notes: Parts come from three speakers: CCEJN policy associate, district staff counsel and the general manager. The monitoring request is for air and heat near solar sites, not groundwater. The EIR vote passed; the plan resolution followed.

records.finding: A Five Points community organizer (CCEJN) asked that the planned community meeting be held on a weekday after 6 pm, indoors, hybrid and with interpretation. Staff was considering its Five Points office; the July 15 plan matched these terms (6 pm, hybrid, interpretation on Zoom and in person).
records.quantitative_detail: Requested: weekday meeting after 6 pm; set meeting 6:00-7:30 pm on 2026-08-04
records.speaker_role: NGO/advocate — Central California Environmental Justice Network
records.meeting_body: Westside Subbasin MLRP Steering and Outreach Advisory Committee
records.agenda_item: Outreach: July community meeting
records.evidence_text: residents had let me know that 6pm is a good time throughout the weekday for them to be able to attend. And then obviously, of course, as long as it's indoors. ... making sure also that this meeting includes translation or interpretation services would be awesome.
records.notes: No speaker says the request caused the later format; facts shown side by side. Org name in the speaker label is CCEJN/CCJN (transcript varies).

records.finding: Five listening-session communities asked for clean drinking water and lower water bills, residential solar and lower energy bills, less pesticide and dust exposure, and economic resilience including job training. Westlands says MLRP will address the first four themes but cannot fund community infrastructure improvements.
records.meeting_body: Westside Subbasin MLRP Steering and Outreach Advisory Committee
records.agenda_item: Community listening-session themes and draft regional goals
records.evidence_text: across the board the key themes was clean drinking water and low water bills. So community members and residents need clean drinking water and lower water bills. The theme along the lines of residential solar energy projects and lower energy bills. So there's strong interest in residential solar projects and, and there's a need for lower energy bills, reduced pesticide and dust exposure. Many residents want less pesticide and dust exposure within their communities. And a really key one is economic resiliency. You know, I feel like every community meeting we had, you know, there was a very strong concern about the loss of jobs from land use changes near the communities. And you know, on top of that, community members are really interested in job training, job placement and other work opportunities in the ag industry and other sectors. ... This funding opportunity and this program are going to be mostly focused on the first four that we talked about, you know, because unfortunately there's just not enough money to get into the community infrastructure improvements
records.notes: Themes are summarised by the consultant from sessions run by the outreach partner; no data product (e.g. well or water-quality map) was requested in this passage.

records.finding: A CCEJN organizer asked that the regional water-supply goal address groundwater quality, noting uncertainty about solar's long-term effects. The consultant said water quality could be incorporated and that recharge improves quality over time. The July near-final goal text read in the meeting does not show a water-quality clause.
records.meeting_body: Westside Subbasin MLRP Steering and Outreach Advisory Committee
records.agenda_item: Draft water supply and groundwater sustainability goal
records.evidence_text: I think groundwater quality is still sort of like a big component that I'm maybe trying to see like how much the MALRP can address. ... I think we'll have to think on this one about the water quality, but I don't think it should be an issue to incorporate that in as well
records.notes: Final wording of the water supply goal was only partly read in the transcript; outcome unconfirmed. Evidence joins an advocate's statement and the consultant's reply.

records.finding: At the August 4 breakout, residents raised concern about electromagnetic fields from large solar projects and whether they can be monitored, and about valley fever in schools. The consultant relaying them said the district would look into them; no data product was promised.
records.quantitative_detail: No quantities; concerns raised at 2026-08-04 breakout
records.meeting_body: Westside Subbasin MLRP Steering and Outreach Advisory Committee
records.agenda_item: Breakout report-out: community health goal
records.evidence_text: There is quite some concern about the large solar projects and specifically the EMF that's admitted through it, and if there's a way to treat that or monitor it. And a recommendation that was provided was agave and sunflower help reduce those EMFs. So that's a really good segue into what was just discussed, you know, utilizing if you do have a solar field, bringing in other practices and kind of combining everything together. So something that we can highlight there is agave and sunflowers. Again, along the same lines that Shelly already Brought up the importance of keeping employment within the district, especially for the lands that are being repurposed, making sure that the folks that work on those lands have another employment opportunity. There was also discussion about valley fever within the schools and, you know, making sure our practices are preventative of any, you know, detrimental health aspects.
records.notes: Report is by a table facilitator, not the residents themselves; on 2026-08-19 the consultant said such items would go in plan text, not the goal.

records.finding: Community members at the August 4 meeting asked for metrics measuring the impact of agricultural land displaced by solar, citing a garlic processor that moved to Gilroy. The goal text was left unchanged, with job-retention language kept in the economic well-being goal; no metric was committed.
records.quantitative_detail: No quantities; request is for new metrics
records.meeting_body: Westside Subbasin MLRP Steering and Outreach Advisory Committee
records.agenda_item: Community meeting report-out
records.evidence_text: there were requests to develop metrics to measure the impact of agricultural. Agricultural land displacement by solar. Folks are really, really aware and concerned about agricultural lands being taken out of production.
records.notes: Report-out by the outreach partner (CeresCollab); original comments are on the 2026-08-05 recording.

records.finding: Packet minutes of the January 2026 meeting show the consultant listing five possible Cuyama model improvements, two of them about streamflow inputs and stream geometry, at an estimated $160,000 to $280,000. Stream geometry comes from 2023 LiDAR flown in dry conditions, which a director questioned. This concerns the Ventucopa water balance, not an ISW depletion analysis.
records.quantitative_detail: $160,000-$280,000 estimated cost range (one-time, depending on scope); LiDAR flown 2023 during dry conditions
records.meeting_body: Cuyama Basin GSA Board (minutes of 2026-01-14 meeting in the packet)
records.agenda_item: Approval of minutes, January 14, 2026 meeting (Ventucopa model recalibration)
records.evidence_text: Mr. Ceyhan outlined five potential model improvements, including incorporating updated fault information, refining streamflow inputs, evaluating subsurface inflows, improving stream geometry representation, and recalibrating the model. He estimated costs ranging from approximately $160,000 to $280,000 depending on scope. ... Mr. Van Lienden responded that LiDAR was flown in 2023 during dry conditions and acknowledged that stream channels are dynamic but the data remains useful.
records.notes: The streamflow inputs matter to Cuyama River recharge and the water balance; no stream depletion figure is discussed. The discussion took place on 2026-01-14 and is quoted from the later packet.

records.finding: DWR's letter on its periodic review, put in the board packet, says it is still reviewing the Cuyama GSA's approach to interconnected surface water and may take it up at a meeting with the GSA. The approach itself is not described at this meeting.
records.quantitative_detail: Meeting request deadline in the letter: January 23, 2026
records.speaker_role: state agency (DWR letter in board packet)
records.meeting_body: Cuyama Basin GSA Board of Directors
records.agenda_item: Receive DWR additional information request on the GSP (periodic review)
records.evidence_text: In addition, the Department is still reviewing GSA’s approach to interconnected surface water, which may require interconnected surface water to be a topic of discussion in the meeting as well.
records.notes: Letter text is in the 2026-03-04 packet; the transcript of this meeting does not mention ISW, so what the GSA's ISW approach is stays unstated.

records.finding: The consultant proposed a budget task to review DWR's forthcoming ISW guidance and technical papers and develop an approach for the basin; a board member backed it as preparation every GSA will need. DWR was said to be promising the guidance by end of June or July 2026.
records.quantitative_detail: No cost for the ISW task stated in the passage; DWR guidance expected end of June or July 2026
records.agenda_item: FY 2026-27 budget: proposed items 3.6 and 3.7
records.evidence_text: So 3.6 would basically be looking at the guidance that comes from DWR and right now they're saying end of June or July that the guidance for interconnected surface water is going to come out. And so basically what this would be would be for us what it incurin to review that guidance, kind of review the technical papers that are already out there and develop a approach that the basin can take going forward to comply with DWR's requirements. ... And definitely with ISW. I mean, we're all, every, every GSA is going to have to deal with that at some point. So having been prepared for that, I think is a good idea.
records.notes: Speaker names are not tied to roles by the transcript; the first speaker is the GSA's technical consultant by context. Whether item 3.6 survived into the adopted budget was not traced.

records.finding: Staff's fiscal-year schedule lists a 'developing ISW approach' and says an ISW depletion study and ISW sustainable management criteria are planned after the 2028 model update and recalibration, ahead of 2030 allocations and the next periodic evaluation. DWR's ISW best-management-practices document was said to be coming in fall 2026.
records.quantitative_detail: Model update/calibration planned 2028; results early 2029; allocations for 2030-2034; next periodic evaluation due 2030
records.agenda_item: Fiscal year 2026-27 work schedule
records.evidence_text: we have a developing ISW approach in this next period here. We did hear from DWR recently that the ISW BMP will be released in the fall. ... And then I mentioned we would be doing the ISW depletion study and setting SMCs potentially based on that new guidance once the model is updated and calibrated during that process, allocations for 2030 through 2034 and then the five year period eval development.
records.notes: Speaker is unnamed; presenting staff or consultant inferred from context. The study is described as 'potential', not funded or contracted.

records.finding: A director or committee member said DWR's long delay in issuing ISW best management practices is very problematic for everyone; staff agreed to look into whether another GSA had received the guidance. The remark is about state timing, not Cuyama data.
records.agenda_item: Fiscal year 2026-27 work schedule (discussion)
records.evidence_text: Yeah, I was like, wow, that just to me is very problematic for everybody. Yeah, it just speaks volumes that they're taking so long to come out with best management practices for two.
records.notes: Speaker not identified; the transcript is garbled around 'White Wolf' and 'for two' (likely ISW), so intent is partly inferred.

records.finding: Public commenters said landowners who bought fallow land have little or no allocation because the allocation rests on historical use. One said they received about 13 AF/yr for 40 acres of newly planted trees, that no one is selling, and that no process exists to buy.
records.quantitative_detail: Commenter: about 13 AF/yr allocation for 40 acres of pistachio and lavender trees (their figure)
records.evidence_text: We bought fallow land and now we are being permanently halted for having bought fallow land because there was no historical use on us. ... no one has brought forward any transfers.
records.notes: Commenters' account of how Cuyama's historical-use allocation treats previously fallow parcels; this is the reverse of retired land, but shows what the rule does to idle land. Not a GSA statement.

records.finding: In June 26, 2025 minutes carried in this packet, Cuyama's advisory committee reached consensus on a free market with buyers and sellers in good standing, staff (not board) approval of trades and a carryover policy. The chair favoured limiting trade distance and several members favoured reserving allocation for small farmers; members split on trading only sustainable yield or whole allocations.
records.quantitative_detail: Minutes of the 2025-06-26 SAC meeting
records.agenda_item: 6. Approval of June 26, 2025 Minutes (item 7d market discussion)
records.evidence_text: SAC consensus in favor of Free market, but concerned about ... Landowner Participant Eligibility - SAC consensus of requiring buyers and sellers be in good standing with the CBGSA. ... Chair Kelly commented in favor of limiting trade distance ... In favor of reserving allocations for small farmers ... SAC consensus in support of a carryover policy. ... SAC consensus that trades should be handled administratively by staff rather than requiring Board approval.
records.notes: These are minutes of the June 26, 2025 SAC meeting, attached to the 2025-08-28 packet as the approved prior minutes; the index date of this meeting is 2025-08-28. Basin-wide rule; not specific to repurposed land.

records.finding: Cuyama's draft allocation exchange policy lets a Central Management Area landowner transfer allocation to another CMA landowner for use inside the CMA only. Transfers end by 2029, unused transferred water cannot be carried over, and a transfer must not cause a minimum-threshold exceedance. Staff approve on a form; price stays private.
records.quantitative_detail: Transfer term ends on or before 2029-12-31 (allocations are set only through 2029); no carryover of unused transferred water
records.agenda_item: 9b. CMA Allocation Exchange Policy (water market)
records.evidence_text: The intent of this policy is to simply allow one landowner from the central management area to transfer. ... Their allocation to another landowner within the Central Management area for use within the Central Management area. ... transferred groundwater allocation shall be used solely within the central management area. ... the transfer shall terminate on or before December 31st, 2029. ... We're not allowing the carry over of that unused water. ... that the transfer shall not cause an exceedance of any minimum threshold.
records.notes: The transcript labels every speaker 'Grace Bianchi'; the presenter appears to be legal counsel or staff walking through the draft policy. The Board later approved a one-year pilot (per the 2026-03-04 packet), so this is the draft, not the final text. Basin-wide rule; not specific to repurposed land.

records.finding: Board members and counsel discussed a leakage risk: a landowner outside the CMA who has stopped farming could join a farming unit and sell a paper allocation into the CMA. Staff replied that farming units cannot be joined mid-cycle, so this could not happen before allocations expire.
records.agenda_item: 9b. CMA Allocation Exchange Policy (water market)
records.evidence_text: They've quit farming, but they have an allocation or whatever. ... That farm might say, oh, I know what I'll do. Let me join a farming unit and I'll sell that allocation into the central management area, which we might not want to happen. ... That might be bad because that's basically now gaming your way to pumping into the central management area. ... you can't join a farming unit mid cycle on allocations, right?
records.notes: Speakers are unlabeled (transcript attributes all lines to one name); the speakers appear to be a board member or counsel raising the scenario and staff answering.

records.finding: For possible new pumping outside Cuyama's Central Management Area, staff proposed tracking land-use change with annual landowner reports and the LandIQ dataset plus new-well permits, then, if needed, a watch area, more monitoring, localized allocations or well restrictions. This addresses pumping shifting to unregulated land.
records.agenda_item: Options to address new pumping outside management areas
records.evidence_text: Map changes in land use (annual landowner reports and current State/Land IQ data set) and new wells including well size/capacity (from County permitting). ... Establishing a “watch area”. ... Implementing localized allocations.
records.notes: Agenda-packet slides; this deals with new irrigation outside the CMA (an outside-the-boundary leakage risk), not with repurposed land. No decision recorded in the packet. Basin-wide rule; not specific to repurposed land.

records.finding: Two public commenters (a family farmer and a representative) told the Cuyama board the pilot allocation market is not working: a farm with an allocation shortfall cannot find a seller. They blamed the historical-use allocation and asked the board to stay enforcement until adjudication. Staff's reply did not describe any completed trade.
records.quantitative_detail: Commenter cites a nearly 90% single-year allocation reduction for one farm (their figure, not verified)
records.agenda_item: Public comment / allocation exchange
records.evidence_text: the difficulties that we're having trying to find someone to sell us water. ... this market's not functioning. There's no buyers, I mean, excuse me, there's no sellers. ... the only reason why we have this market is because your allocation process is flawed. ... ask the board to stay enforcement of the current allocation until the adjudication process can resolve the underlying water rights issues.
records.notes: Commenters describe the market; this is not the GSA's own account. Names are in the transcript (a landowner and a supporter or advocate) but roles are inferred. Basin-wide rule; not specific to repurposed land.

records.finding: After a one-year pilot allocation exchange, Cuyama staff and an ad hoc proposed an opt-in seller list for the 14 CMA landowners (buyers could not reach sellers) and a mid-February deadline for trading prior-year unused allocation, and kept the rule that every farming-unit participant sign off. One advisory committee member asked for limits on where traded pumping moves.
records.quantitative_detail: 14 landowners eligible as sellers in the CMA; trade deadline mid-February for prior calendar year unused allocation
records.agenda_item: Allocation Exchange Program (pilot evaluation)
records.evidence_text: an allocation exchange pilot program was enacted for this current calendar year as a one year pilot program. ... going to the 14 folks in the CMA saying, Do you want to be on the seller's list? ... allowing transfers up to mid February before the board reporting makes sense to the ad hoc. ... leave it as is where currently everyone in a farming unit, if they want to do a trade, has to sign off on the trade. ... expressed a need for regulating where exchange allocations are, removing the pumping from and to within the basin to avoid possible increased pumping in sensitive areas.
records.notes: The advisory-committee view is relayed by staff from the SAC's 2026-09 discussion and the term 'stakeholder policemen' in the transcript is garbled. The number of completed trades was not stated in the passages read. Basin-wide rule; not specific to repurposed land.

records.finding: Cuyama's consultant models fallowed land as follows: land fallowed for a few consecutive recent years is classed as permanently fallowed and receives no water in the Cuyama model, while temporarily fallowed land is tracked separately. This is how fallowing enters the basin water budget.

records.section: 3.1.4 Domestic Well Protection as an Equity Outcome
records.finding: Cuyama's groundwater-level minimum thresholds use a well protection depth calculated for each active production and domestic well, from pump depth, screen midpoint or a regional median. Wells too far from the representative network or already dry in 2015 are screened out; DWR asked how domestic wells were selected and excluded. The excerpts read show no comparison by community.
records.quantitative_detail: Pump depth plus 10 ft where pump depth is known; wells already dry in 2015 excluded
records.meeting_body: Cuyama Basin GSA Board of Directors
records.agenda_item: Agenda packet: 2024-2025 WY annual report and DWR periodic review comments
records.evidence_text: The well protection depth is used to ensure that active production and domestic wells within the Basin are protected from harm to their beneficial uses. The well protection depth is a numerical value representing the approximate depth at which, if exceeded, beneficial uses could be impacted in a well. This value is unique and calculated for each active production and domestic well within the Basin where there is available data. Where data is not available, generalized or regional proxy data is utilized. Some wells are screened from this analysis either because they are too far removed from the representative well network (and therefore conditions at the nearest RMW are not indicative of conditions at the active well because of distance and/or other conditions such as geology or topology) or wells were already dry in 2015. ... Does not provide explanation for how wells were selected at individual RMS, i.e., how far from the RMS well; how more than one well type were handled in the process; and if any wells (domestic, production) were excluded.
records.notes: Method text is from the draft annual report in the packet; the DWR request is a slide quoting DWR staff comments in the same packet. The packet does not say how domestic wells were located or whether the approach treats the community of New Cuyama differently.

records.finding: The ESJ ISW depletion analysis uses the integrated Eastern San Joaquin Water Resources Model (ESJWRM) Version 3.0. Seven pumping-reduction runs approximate a no-pumping case and one pumping-pulse run tests the lag of stream response; DWR's fourth ISW guidance document is still pending.
records.quantitative_detail: 8 simulations run June-August 2024 (7 reduced-pumping, 1 pulse); historical model WY 1995-2023 (29 years); PCBL variants simulate 55 years (WY 1969-2023 hydrology)
records.agenda_item: IV.B.v Interconnected Surface Water - Sustainable Management Criteria (Technical Memorandum, Woodard & Curran, Aug 27, 2026)
records.evidence_text: Eight model simulations were conducted in 2024 as part of the effort to better understand ISW depletions in ESJ Subbasin: seven simulations with varying degrees of pumping reduction intended to approximate a without-pumping condition (discussed in Section 1.1.1 ), and a pulse-pumping simulation designed to identify the lag between pumping and the resulting stream depletions (discussed in Section 1.1.2 ). ... The Historical ESJWRM Version 3.0 represents the With-Pumping scenario for the purpose of calculating depletions.
records.notes: Technical memorandum on Woodard & Curran letterhead included in the board packet; the memo describes 2024 modeling re-explained in 2026 for DWR.

records.finding: The ESJ no-pumping runs are built by converting irrigated land to unirrigated land and removing urban population in ESJWRM. The memo says data scarcity before WY 1995 limits extending the simulation backward.
records.quantitative_detail: Without-pumping case removed ~231,000-294,000 irrigated acres (61-76% of irrigated acreage) and ~223,000-362,000 people, depending on year
records.agenda_item: IV.B.v Interconnected Surface Water - Sustainable Management Criteria (Technical Memorandum, Woodard & Curran, Aug 27, 2026)
records.evidence_text: Extending the simulation period is possible, but extending it backward before WY 1995 is limited by data scarcity, and extending it forward would require projecting beyond the present day, reducing the reliability of a current Subbasin depletion estimate. ... In order to reduce pumping in the model, non-rice irrigated land use was converted to unirrigated land (called native vegetation in the model).
records.notes: Input list is inferred from the modelling description; the memo does not provide a single list of inputs.

records.finding: Modelled pumping depletion in ESJ is reported by stream. Over WY 2013-2023 the Mokelumne carries 33 percent, Stanislaus 28, San Joaquin 20, Calaveras 17 and Dry Creek 2. Half of Dry Creek and Stanislaus depletion is assigned to ESJ because those streams are shared with the Cosumnes and Modesto subbasins.
records.quantitative_detail: Share of ESJ modelled depletion, 11-year average WY 2013-2023: Mokelumne 33%, Stanislaus 28%, San Joaquin 20%, Calaveras 17%, Dry Creek 2%; 50% of Dry Creek and Stanislaus simulated depletion attributed to ESJ
records.agenda_item: IV.B.v Interconnected Surface Water - Sustainable Management Criteria (Technical Memorandum, Woodard & Curran, Aug 27, 2026)
records.evidence_text: Because Dry Creek and the Stanislaus River are represented in ESJWRM as shared between ESJ Subbasin and Cosumnes and Modesto Subbasins, respectively, an estimated 50 percent of the simulated depletions of each are attributed to the ESJ Subbasin. Averaged over the most recent 11 years of the simulation period (WY 2013 –2023), depletions within the ESJ Subbasin are approximately distributed as follows ( Figure 15 ): • Mokelumne River: 33 percent ... Dry Creek: 2 percent
records.notes: Dry Creek is shared with Cosumnes Subbasin, but the memo gives no Cosumnes-side figure.

records.finding: A one-year pumping-pulse run shows ESJ streams respond slowly: a 650 TAF cut in WY 1995 produced about 20 TAF of stream response in year one and still 2.5 to 4 TAF per year in WY 2023.
records.quantitative_detail: 650 TAF single-year pumping reduction (WY 1995); ~20 TAF stream response in year 1 (~3% of removed pumping); 2.5-4 TAF/yr by WY 2023; ~36% of reduced pumping expressed as stream change cumulatively over 28 years
records.agenda_item: IV.B.v Interconnected Surface Water - Sustainable Management Criteria (Technical Memorandum, Woodard & Curran, Aug 27, 2026)
records.evidence_text: The one-year reduction of 650 thousand acre-feet (TAF) of groundwater pumping in WY 1995 produced a positive stream response of approximately 20 TAF in the first year (about 3 percent of the removed pumping), declining gradually to approximately 2.5 to 4 TAF per year by WY 2023. In other words, a measurable stream response remained for the entire 28-year simulation period following the single-year pulse, with no indication of having fully disappeared by the end of the simulation.
records.notes: Pumping-pulse scenario; not a current-conditions depletion figure.

records.finding: The WY 2025 annual report presented to the ESJ board found no ISW undesirable result, using a new ISW monitoring network set up in the 2024 GSP amendment.
records.quantitative_detail: ISW network of 21 monitoring wells (6 overlapping the groundwater level network) per the presenter; WY 2025
records.agenda_item: Water Year 2025 Annual Report
records.evidence_text: For interconnected surface water, we have a new network that was established as part of the 2024 GSP. It now consists of 21 monitoring wells, six of which overlap with the groundwater level monitoring network. There were no undesirable results related to depletions of ISWs that were identified based on the data that we were able to collect for this annual report.
records.notes: Presenter unnamed in transcript; role inferred. The "21 wells" count differs from the 12-well ISW RMN described in the Aug 2026 technical memo (possible garble or different counting).

records.finding: South San Joaquin GSA board members heard that DWR's comment letter on the ESJ five-year update asks how the basin handles interconnected surface water, with responses due in October and a DWR adequacy ruling possible by January. A board member said a negative ruling could put the basin on probation.
records.quantitative_detail: $167,000 ESJGWA budget increase approved the prior week; responses due October 1, 2026; ruling possible by January 2027
records.agenda_item: Discussion on recent Groundwater Authority meetings (DWR comments on 5-year GSP update)
records.evidence_text: How are you approaching groundwater dependent ecosystems and integrated interconnected surface water? So these are very, very hard questions to answer, very technical questions to answer. Immediately. DWA goes to our consultant with her cran and starts to talk through how do we answer this? How do we answer it by October, which is what DWR has said. So the ER could come out with a ruling on our adequacy of our plan by January. ... And if we get a negative ruling out of them, we could be on probation.
records.notes: Speakers unlabeled (SSJID/SSJ GSA staff and chair). The $167,000 figure is from the same item ("there was $167,000 budget increase") but not in the quoted excerpt.

records.finding: ESJ defines an ISW undesirable result as 25 percent of a 12-well ISW monitoring network below minimum thresholds for two consecutive years (three wells). Only six of the 12 wells have thresholds, so groundwater-level criteria stand in as the proxy for now.
records.quantitative_detail: 25% of 12 ISW RMN wells = 3 wells below MT for 2 consecutive years; 6 of 12 wells have established MTs; new wells need about 4+ years of data including a dry or critical year to set SMCs
records.agenda_item: IV.B.v Interconnected Surface Water - Sustainable Management Criteria (Technical Memorandum, Woodard & Curran, Aug 27, 2026)
records.evidence_text: The undesirable result for the ISW sustainability indicator is 25 percent of the ISW RMN (not the GWL RMN) falling below minimum thresholds for two consecutive years. Applied to the full 12-well ISW network, this indicator translates to three wells needing to be below their respective MTs. ... Until SMCs are established at all six new wells, the groundwater level SMC will be used as a proxy
records.notes: In its answer to DWR the memo confirms the 25% GWL-based definition applies "in the interim"; the board approved the memo on 2026-09-09.

records.finding: To defend using groundwater levels as the ISW proxy, ESJ modelled a basin-wide pumping increase (15 percent less agricultural surface water) that triggers a groundwater-level undesirable result. Depletion in that case, about 457 TAF per year, is only modestly above the current ~430 TAF per year.
records.quantitative_detail: 15% cut in ag surface water deliveries -> +41-51 TAF/yr pumping; MT exceeded at 6 GWL RMN wells; depletion ~457 TAF/yr (average of final 5 of 55 simulated years), ~40% capture; compare ~430 TAF/yr, 38% capture in historical runs; PCBL-CC-MT incremental ~6,600 AFY (~1.5% of current depletion)
records.agenda_item: IV.B.v Interconnected Surface Water - Sustainable Management Criteria (Technical Memorandum, Woodard & Curran, Aug 27, 2026)
records.evidence_text: Retaining 85 percent of the Subbasin's agricultural surface water diversions (a 15 percent reduction in agricultural deliveries) produced undesirable results for GWL, with minimum thresholds exceeded at six GWL RMN wells for two consecutive years; this scenario is referred to as PCBL-SW85 Version 3.0. ... The simulated depletion of approximately 457 TAF per year over the final five simulated years from the PCBL-SW85 scenarios, capturing approximately 40 percent of cumulative pumping, is only modestly larger than the approximately 430 TAF per year and 38 percent cumulative capture estimated in Section 1
records.notes: Scenario results are modelled projections (~2040 demands, climate change), not measured depletion.

records.finding: ESJ now states a pumping-attributable ISW depletion estimate from with- versus without-pumping model runs: about 430 TAF per year averaged over WY 2019-2023, which the memo itself calls a low estimate because the model had not reached equilibrium.
records.quantitative_detail: Cumulative ~7,900 TAF over 29 years (WY 1995-2023), average ~270 TAF/yr; ~430 TAF/yr average WY 2019-2023; ~490 TAF in WY 2023; ~58% of annual pumping difference in WY 2023; all modelled, flows in thousand acre-feet
records.agenda_item: IV.B.v Interconnected Surface Water - Sustainable Management Criteria (Technical Memorandum, Woodard & Curran, Aug 27, 2026)
records.evidence_text: Comparing the With-Pumping and Without-Pumping scenarios, groundwater pumping is estimated to have depleted ISW in the Subbasin by a cumulative total of approximately 7,900 TAF over the 29-year simulation period (WY 1995 –2023) ( Figure 8), an average annual depletion of approximately 270 TAF. ... The estimated depletion for the Subbasin based on the scenarios is 430 TAF (average of the last five years).
records.notes: Depletion is expressed against a "pumping difference" that includes deep percolation, so the 58% is not a share of consumptive use.

records.finding: The 2024 GSP amendment reported no depletion quantity because the model had not stabilised; the 2026 memo now gives about 430 TAF per year. The memo says annual depletion is still rising at the end of the run, so the number is a floor, and ESJ may revise it once DWR guidance is out.
records.quantitative_detail: 2024 amendment: no quantity reported; 2026 memo: ~430 TAF/yr (mean of WY 2019-2023, historical with/without-pumping runs), ~490 TAF in WY 2023; separate projected PCBL-SW85 scenario: ~457 TAF/yr averaged over the final five of 55 simulated years (not a historical figure)
records.agenda_item: IV.B.v Interconnected Surface Water - Sustainable Management Criteria (Technical Memorandum, Woodard & Curran, Aug 27, 2026)
records.evidence_text: Because the results did not stabilize, no depletion quantity was reported in Appendix 3-G as the ESJGWA did not have a sufficient basis to report a defensible depletion quantity based on best available science at the time. This is the basis for the statement in Appendix 3-G that the analysis was inconclusive. ... Because the annual depletion series is still increasing at the end of the simulation, these values likely represent a low estimate of the depletion associated with current levels of pumping rather than an equilibrium value.
records.notes: Figures reflect the same model re-analysed, not new measurements.

records.finding: The ESJ depletion figure is attributed to essentially all subbasin pumping: the no-pumping run removes 93-99 percent of agricultural pumping and all urban pumping. No well counts or near-stream subsets are used.
records.quantitative_detail: Agricultural pumping reduced 93-99%; urban groundwater pumping reduced 100%; irrigated acreage reduced 61-76%
records.agenda_item: IV.B.v Interconnected Surface Water - Sustainable Management Criteria (Technical Memorandum, Woodard & Curran, Aug 27, 2026)
records.evidence_text: For groundwater pumping, this translated to a reduction between 93 and 99 percent of the annual agricultural pumping as compared to the With-Pumping scenario; the reduction is not 100 percent due to the targeting of groundwater-pumping dependent model elements while leaving elements predominantly supplied by surface water unconverted and with a small amount of pumping. ... For urban demand, the population reduction ranged from about 223,000 to 362,000 people, based on the year, and removed 100 percent of the urban groundwater pumping in every year of the scenario.
records.notes: Attribution scope is stated in modelling terms; no per-well or pump count appears.

records.finding: ESJ pairs modelling with a new 12-well ISW monitoring network: six new shallow wells sited at connected reaches and the Delta, plus six existing wells. The new wells have a single spring 2026 reading, so they cannot yet support thresholds.
records.quantitative_detail: 12-well ISW RMN: 6 new shallow wells + 6 existing GWL RMN wells; 1 measurement per new well (spring 2026); monitored in biannual subbasin-wide events
records.agenda_item: IV.B.v Interconnected Surface Water - Sustainable Management Criteria (Technical Memorandum, Woodard & Curran, Aug 27, 2026)
records.evidence_text: Six newly constructed shallow monitoring wells (Well A, Well B, Well C, Well E, Well G, and the Delta Well) were sited specifically to close the shallow well monitoring data gap near interconnected reaches and the Sacramento-San Joaquin River Delta (Delta). ... These wells currently only have one data measurement from spring 2026.
records.notes: The memo says the ISW RMN is "not yet used to actively manage depletions".

records.section: 1.5 Per-well Attribution and the Cumulative Pumping Problem
records.finding: ESJ uses a five-mile distance from connected surface waters as the spatial rule for choosing existing groundwater-level wells for its ISW monitoring network, adding six new shallow wells where gaps remain.
records.quantitative_detail: Existing wells within 5 miles of connected streams: 6; new shallow wells: 6
records.agenda_item: IV.B.i Groundwater Level - Sustainable Management Criteria (Technical Memorandum, Woodard & Curran, Sept 2, 2026)
records.evidence_text: The ISW RMN currently consists of a subset of six groundwater level RMN wells located within five miles of connected surface waters, plus six recently constructed shallow monitoring wells specifically sited to fill data gaps in understanding of stream-aquifer interactions.
records.notes: Spatial rule governs monitoring-well selection, not attribution of depletion to wells; only one Mokelumne well is included because new wells cover other segments.

records.section: 1.5 Per-well Attribution and the Cumulative Pumping Problem
records.finding: The ESJ memo recognises that modelled stream depletion in any month or year reflects pumping over many earlier years, i.e. a cumulative, lagged effect. It offers no method to apportion it to individual wells or pumpers.
records.quantitative_detail: Modelled monthly average depletion: Oct-Jan 34 to almost 36, Jun-Aug 31 to almost 32, printed in the memo as 'TAF per year' (11-year average period WY 2013-2023; the unit label appears to be a memo error for monthly volumes)
records.agenda_item: IV.B.v Interconnected Surface Water - Sustainable Management Criteria (Technical Memorandum, Woodard & Curran, Aug 27, 2026)
records.evidence_text: The limited seasonality in the data points to the lagged nature of the stream response demonstrated by the Pumping Pulse test scenario (Section 1.1.2); depletions in any given month or water year reflect pumping over many prior years, not just the pumping occurring in that month.
records.notes: Cumulative effect is described in time, not across many small wells; the no-apportionment statement reflects the passages read, not an explicit memo statement.

records.finding: ESJ recognises that the shallow, near-stream aquifer is the depth that matters for stream-aquifer interaction and that its general groundwater-level network had too few shallow wells, so it built a separate ISW network.
records.agenda_item: IV.B.v Interconnected Surface Water - Sustainable Management Criteria (Technical Memorandum, Woodard & Curran, Aug 27, 2026)
records.evidence_text: The groundwater level (GWL) RMN on its own did not include enough shallow wells to characterize near-stream, shallow aquifer dynamics, which is the depth interval most directly relevant to stream-aquifer interaction. For this reason, a separate ISW RMN was established.
records.notes: Depth recognition is in monitoring design; no depth-specific depletion estimate is given.

records.finding: ESJ handles depth in its ISW network by using only shallow completions: five single-completion shallow wells plus the shallower side of the dual-completion Delta well.
records.quantitative_detail: 5 shallow single-completion wells + 1 dual-completion Delta well (shallow only used)
records.agenda_item: IV.B.v Interconnected Surface Water - Sustainable Management Criteria (Technical Memorandum, Woodard & Curran, Aug 27, 2026)
records.evidence_text: Five of the new wells are shallow single-completion wells, and the Delta Well is a dual-completion well with only the shallower of the two completed wells utilized in the ISW RMN.

records.finding: A consultant told the ESJ board that interconnected surface water and groundwater-dependent ecosystems are named data gaps, and that new wells are being sited near streams to close them.

And so we're focusing on trying to get monitoring wells near streams and identifying the natural communities commonly associated with groundwater and which can lead to reclassifying as GDEs also groundwater levels.

But it fulfills the data gap of groundwater levels, groundwater levels near streams, in this case Calaveras river, and also water quality.

records.finding: The ESJ board packet budgets a dedicated "ISW Response" phase of the DWR-comment scope: quantify depletions from the current model, and determine incremental depletions, at $35,245.

records.finding: ESJ says it will redo its ISW modelling, undesirable-result definition and thresholds once DWR issues its fourth ISW guidance document, which was still unreleased in August 2026. DWR staff had told the board in February it expected the guidance in the first quarter.

records.finding: ESJ communicates uncertainty by saying its depletion runs did not converge, so the 430 TAF per year figure likely understates depletion; the memo does not give a numeric range.

Based on the analysis completed, the 29-year historical simulation period may simply be too short for the stream-aquifer system to reach a new equilibrium following a reduction in groundwater pumping
records.notes: No confidence interval or calibration statistic appears in the excerpts read.

records.finding: The ESJ board unanimously approved submitting six technical memoranda to DWR, one on the ISW sustainable management criteria. No ISW-specific pumping action was taken.

records.section: 2.5 Data Source and ET Product Choice
records.finding: South San Joaquin GSA staff said they will compare the consultant's satellite ET estimates with landowner-provided applied-water data already used for the district's groundwater charge, to see how close the estimates are.

records.agenda_item: Presentation: Greg Young, Zanjero (satellite ET)

records.finding: South San Joaquin GSA approved a satellite-ET contract with Zanjero as a third pumping estimate beside SSJID's water balance and the basin model, so the three can be cross-checked. Staff said satellite ET is becoming the industry norm for accounting and for growers tracking reductions.

records.section: 2.5 Data Source and ET Product Choice
records.finding: Zanjero chose OpenET (free, public remote-sensing data) for field-level ET and contrasted it with the subbasin GSP model, which gives all vineyards one ET coefficient. He said the approach is a trend proxy, not field-exact.

It's a open source free service that can get remote sensing data so we can pull this, the gridded data for each one of those field parcels that gets us total evapotranspiration number. ... So your current model is a land use base. It has multiple crop acres by monthly general ET value. So it treats like vineyards are just vineyards. They all have an et a KC factor and there's one value regardless of whether you're operating in a deficit irrigation or not or what your soil and management practices might be. All vines have the same number.

records.finding: The board adopted (11 yes, 1 no) an amended and restated domestic well mitigation program. Owners whose wells failed from local pumping drawdown, or whose well water quality degraded, can apply for interim measures such as bottled or hauled water. A technical committee recommends and the executive director issues a final opinion; claims reach back to 2015.
records.quantitative_detail: $200,000 mitigation fund (stated at meeting); technical committee recommendation 15 days amended to 30 days; executive director opinion within 60 days; six-month window to file for past dry wells; eligibility from 2015
records.agenda_item: Well mitigation program: resolution approving amended and restated Eastern Subbasin program for domestic well mitigation
records.evidence_text: Any private well owner, domestic well owner, who believes that their well has failed or has gone dry as a result of low local area pumping, meaning the drawdown of groundwater levels due to local groundwater pumping or if they've seen a degradation in their water quality in their drinking water well, they can submit an application to the authority for interim measures. ... the technical committee can will review that and then make a recommendation within 15 days of receiving the application, which will then be given to the executive director and then the executive director is required to issue a final opinion within 60 days and bring it to the board of directors.
records.notes: Original program was initiated by resolution in September 2024; the 200,000 figure is from staff and board discussion at this meeting and in the 2026-04-08 budget talk.

records.finding: A water-district speaker pointed out that the program sets no cap per applicant and does not require the least costly fix. The board then directed staff to convene the technical committee to propose a per-claim cap.

records.finding: South San Joaquin GSA staff described the well mitigation program as a claims process: a well owner with evidence that overdraft dried the well may recover drilling cost, from a $200,000 revolving fund paid by the GSAs. records.evidence_text: if you have a well that went dry and you have some evidence showing that it's due to overdraft or somebody else pumping, you know, or other people around you pumping at a rate that's unsustainable, perhaps you're entitled to getting your well drilling cost back maybe $20,000, which is the number that we had thought of at the time. So we funded it at a $200,000 sort of revolving fund ... The director, executive director has the ability to disqualify, you know, because if, if it clearly was an electrical issue or mechanical issue, we throw it out and we reject the claim outright.
records.notes: Speaker is unlabelled, likely SSJID/GSA management; this describes the same Authority-wide program ESJGWA relaunched on 2026-08-12.

records.finding: At the Kern County Subbasin probation hearing a State Water Board member said the oversight agencies are still working out what SGMA expects for interconnected groundwater and that fact-finding and gaps remain to be addressed in different basins, Kern included.

records.finding: Semitropic screens every field's ET-based demand before charging. Properties under two acres, or with demand under about 1.55 AF/acre, are treated as de minimis or not irrigated and screened out, cutting proposed 2025 charges from about $3.6M to $1.8M.
