records.agenda_item: Preliminary 2025 water budget exceedance charges
records.evidence_text: if it's a property is less than two acres, they're screened out as small. If the demand of the property aggregates less than two acre feet. I screened them out so small, that's our de minimis definition. And then I have another category that for from a water use standpoint, is the demand is less than I think I used, 1.55 acre feet per acre
records.notes: Speaker is a district consultant or manager presenting a worksheet (role inferred). Describes the scope of ET-based accounting (all fields, with a floor), not a repurposing programme. Basin-wide rule; not specific to repurposed land.

records.finding: Only 15 percent of Cawelo's fields had signed up for the Land IQ daily ET tool by March 2026, and results reached the district's administrative dashboard only for fields landowners had claimed. Coverage of field-level ET tracking is therefore partial and voluntary.
records.quantitative_detail: 15% of district fields signed up (March 2026)
records.agenda_item: SGMA update: Land IQ Daily ET tool
records.evidence_text: We only have 15% of the fields within the district signed up right now and we don't. The information isn't aggregated to the administration form unless the fields are clear.
records.notes: 'clear' in the transcript is likely 'claimed'. Staff spoke of sending monthly letters to encourage sign-up. Basin-wide rule; not specific to repurposed land.

records.finding: By September 2026 Land IQ changed its back end so Cawelo landowners no longer need to claim fields for the district to aggregate their daily ET. Data is up to date within about 48 to 72 hours; the district can trend monthly but not yet daily data.
records.quantitative_detail: Data latency 48-72 hours; first year of daily data
records.agenda_item: SGMA update: Land IQ Daily ET tool
records.evidence_text: landiq did change their process on the back end so landowners don't have to claim their fields for it to get aggregated. So we, at least at the district side, we could, we could get all that aggregated information now. But. Yeah, yeah. Oh, it's, it's. I mean, it's up to date within 48 hours. I mean, you're. 48. 72 hours.
records.notes: Follows the March 2026 report that only 15% of fields had signed up. Basin-wide rule; not specific to repurposed land.

records.finding: Cawelo is buying Land IQ's daily ET tool for all managed lands in the district and its GSA at 55 cents per acre. Staff describe daily ET by parcel and crop with a one to two day lag and a year-end forecast, offered to growers as a planning tool.
records.quantitative_detail: $0.55/acre/year (first year) for about 37,468 managed acres, escalating $0.02/yr; about $1,700-$1,850/month for 3 years; 1-2 day data lag
records.agenda_item: SGMA: Land IQ Daily ET tool
records.evidence_text: includes all the managed lands within the district and the GSA. Um, the cost is 55 cents an acre. Um, just for managed lands. ... 37,468 acres at 55 cents an acre.
records.notes: Speaker is Cawelo's SGMA staff member (role inferred); a board member says it is a water planning tool, not an irrigation scheduling tool.

records.finding: KNDLA's year-end Land IQ ET report shows monthly GSA-wide cropped and uncropped ET, and cropped ET both including and excluding fallowed land. Fallow is defined as only what has not had land disruption in the last year or so.
records.quantitative_detail: Monthly, GSA-wide; water year 2025 report
records.meeting_body: Kern Non-Districted Land Authority GSA Board
records.agenda_item: Land IQ water year report
records.evidence_text: Our monthly GSA wide cropped and uncropped ET and how that kind of cumulatively looks at and month to month and then it breaks it down by our monthly cropped et. So you can see of our cropped acres there's including our fallowed and then excluding fallowed and they. The excluding fallow is still anything that has had land disruption in the last year or so.
records.notes: Aggregate-level reporting, not parcel by parcel; speaker is the KNDLA executive director.

records.finding: Semitropic is rolling out Land IQ's daily ET tool, which tracks consumptive use by hand-delineated managed field rather than by parcel, including fallowed fields. The daily numbers are meant to reconcile to the monthly ET the district uses for its water budgets.
records.quantitative_detail: Daily field-level ET; reconciled to the district's monthly ET (monthly vs daily frequency)
records.agenda_item: Land IQ daily ET tool presentation
records.evidence_text: providing kind of real time et information that will be reconciled with our monthly information ... as part of the deliverable that we provide with our ET is we also provide annual crop mapping, so every field is hand delineated. ... So these are non parcel boundaries. They're what you irrigate or fallow or what have you.
records.notes: The first sentence is from district staff (Speaker 4) and the delineation description from the Land IQ presenter (Speaker 5); the roles are inferred from the Land IQ introduction.

records.finding: Buena Vista's draft rules create a District Landowner Fallowing Program in which an enrolled landowner gives up the right to apply District water and native yield to the enrolled land for the term. In exchange the landowner is credited the District water that would otherwise have been used.
records.meeting_body: Buena Vista Water Storage District Board
records.agenda_item: Rules and Regulations Update (draft Rule 17(b))
records.evidence_text: The participant relinquishes the right to apply water to enrolled lands for the term. For clarity, this relinquishment includes District water and native yield. ... In exchange for the land fallowing activity, the participating landowner shall be credited with the amount of District water that would otherwise have been utilized by the landowner.
records.notes: Board-packet draft of revised Rules and Regulations (Rule 17(b)); staff said the rules would return for approval at the next meeting, so adoption is not confirmed. Package text is OCR-damaged in places. Role is the board rules committee draft, not a named speaker.

records.finding: KNDLA's goal is a gradual ramp-down of groundwater use to native yield by 2040, with a groundwater allocation policy first. Open design questions include whether irrigated, range and urban land get the same native-yield allocation. Treatment of fallowed or retired land is not addressed.
records.quantitative_detail: Target: ramp down to native yield by 2040; policy start date discussed as perhaps 2027
records.meeting_body: Kern Non-Districted Land Authority GSA Board
records.agenda_item: Groundwater allocation options analysis (Phase 1) proposal
records.evidence_text: Kindler's, their main goal is really a gradual long term ramp down of groundwater use to native yield by the year 2040, something they want to start as soon as possible. ... there's the native yield allocation for the different land use types. Irrigated range, land, urban. Are they all going to get the same native date of yield?
records.notes: Machine transcript renders KNDLA as 'Kindler'/'Kindle'; presenter is the Provost & Pritchard project manager. No decision on allocations yet.

records.finding: Shafter-Wasco waived a penalty in exchange for the grower removing almond orchards on 53 acres and keeping them out of production, plus buying credit from other landowners to reach a zero cumulative balance by end of 2027. Any surplus from the removed acres goes back to the district, not to be traded.
records.quantitative_detail: Penalty about $31,000 (62 AF overage, 2025); 53 acres removed (33 + 20 acres on two APNs); 110 AF credit transfer; about 45 AF short at end of 2026, about 45-46 AF surplus in 2027; zero cumulative balance by end of 2027
records.agenda_item: Waiver of enforcement (penalty settlement agreement)
records.evidence_text: remove almond orchards on 53 acres of property within the switch GSA boundaries identified on these APNS in the fall of 2026 and to keep such property out of production thereafter, and to acquire groundwater credit from other MIT landowners, such that the cumulative balance. ... cumulative account balance of zero by the end of 2027
records.notes: Staff walks through the agreement; transcript is uneven. Whether the removed land keeps any allocation beyond the glide path is not stated.

records.finding: A WaterOne summary reports that Semitropic's board approved new landowner banking agreements that widen storage eligibility and allow a water-budget deficit to be offset by ledger entry without physically recovering the banked water.
records.agenda_item: Landowner banking agreement amendments
records.evidence_text: New landowner banking agreements were approved to expand water storage eligibility and allow ledger-based deficit offsetting without physical water recovery.
records.notes: AI-written recap; the meeting's 'transcript' document is a podcast script, not a real transcript, so no verbatim source was available. Not specific to retired land. Basin-wide rule; not specific to repurposed land.

records.finding: Under the same draft rules, water credited for fallowed land can be transferred within Buena Vista. It can also move out of district in-ground subject to a 20 percent leave-behind after losses; the receiving district must approve.
records.quantitative_detail: 20 percent leave-behind (after losses) on in-ground transfers out of the district; no extra leave-behind if used within BVWSD
records.meeting_body: Buena Vista Water Storage District Board
records.agenda_item: Rules and Regulations Update (draft Rule 17(b))
records.evidence_text: Water allocated to fallowed lands may be transferred within the District. ... In-ground water allocated to fallow lands under this program may be transferred outside of the District in-ground, with a $20 %$ leave behind for the District after losses. If water created under this program is utilized entirely within BVWSD, there will be no additional leave-behind deducted beyond losses.
records.notes: Draft rule text (Rule 17(b)(iv)-(v)); also Rule 2(d) lets users who fallowed or did not exhaust their pumping limit sell water to other District water users. The out-of-district transfer needs approval from the receiving district. OCR garbles '$20 %$'.

records.finding: Shafter-Wasco amended its water budget rules: precipitation credits cannot be transferred or carried over, temporary pumping credit cannot be carried over year to year, and growers choose which water type they transfer on a form. Purchased supplemental water is used last.
records.quantitative_detail: Use order: native yield, precipitation, temporary pumping credit, then supplemental water last
records.agenda_item: Water budget policy revisions
records.evidence_text: the last one precipitation credits cannot be transferred or carried over. Precipitation can only be consumed. ... the grower irrigates parcel, the first water yield, then precipitation, then temporary, finally, supplemental water
records.notes: Transcript is garbled; the editor notes in the recap triage confirm the direction (purchased water used last). Motion to approve passed. Basin-wide rule; not specific to repurposed land.

records.finding: KNDLA's consultant (Provost & Pritchard) told the board its allocation options analysis will weigh carryover of unused groundwater, groundwater transfers, maximum limits and whether transfers must stay on contiguous property. The board approved only the options phase; no policy was selected.
records.quantitative_detail: Phase 1 draft report estimated 10 to 14 weeks after approval
records.meeting_body: Kern Non-Districted Land Authority GSA Board
records.agenda_item: Groundwater allocation options analysis (Phase 1) proposal; vote to engage Provost & Pritchard
records.evidence_text: There's also carryover water. If you don't use your groundwater one year, can you carry it over to the next? How long can you carry it over? Are there annual losses? We also have groundwater transfers. Can you transfer your groundwater to someone else? What are the rules? Are there maximum limits? Does it have to be a contiguous property?
records.notes: Provost & Pritchard presenter (introduced as principal water resources engineer); Phase 1 only was approved, with one abstention. Basin-wide rule; not specific to repurposed land.

records.finding: At Shafter-Wasco, leftover groundwater credit from land its owner stopped farming was transferred to a neighbouring grower to cover an overage. The precipitation portion could not be moved, and the GM called it a win because demand fell. Whether such transfers can be made after the fact was left unresolved.
records.quantitative_detail: About 180 AF leftover credit, of which about 40 AF was precipitation (not transferable); overage covered about 118-119 AF; calendar year 2025
records.agenda_item: GSA hearing: penalties for groundwater extraction above allocation
records.evidence_text: the Wilson AG, property, ended up working on a deal. So Aaron said, we're not going to farm this property, and the water that we have left over will transfer it to the Mosley's, so it'll help the Mosley's kind of avoid the feed and then keep farming until the trees come out. ... Wilson, AG, they have, they have about 180 left over, and then 40 was precipitation, right? So they couldn't transfer the whole 180
records.notes: Names of the growers involved are garbled by the machine transcript. A banked credit transfer into MA-2 and the 10% loss treatment are also discussed in the same item. Retroactive transfers were questioned and later described as off the table.

records.finding: Semitropic lets landowners combine commonly owned parcels and LLCs each year so supplies and demand are pooled across their holdings. The district stresses the request must be renewed annually, because charges start from the county assessor's owner of record.
records.agenda_item: Public hearing: civil penalties for 2025 water budget exceedances
records.evidence_text: the district allows for the application amenities for common ownership, so that a farming operation is full time for property and multiple names and LLCs. And aggregate your property, such as the water supplies and demand can be aggregated to allow the farming operation the flexibility to focus their available water supplies where farming operation this ... You have to do this annually.
records.notes: Machine transcript garbles 'application amenities' (likely 'applications for combination'). Pooling is within an ownership group, not a basin market or transfer. Basin-wide rule; not specific to repurposed land.

records.finding: In the same settlement the grower buys a 110 AF credit transfer from another landowner, but surplus created by the removed acres would not be sold: it would be turned back to the district so the cumulative balance reaches zero. This limits monetising freed-up credit.
records.quantitative_detail: 110 AF transferred in; about 45-46 AF expected surplus in 2027 returned to the district
records.agenda_item: Waiver of enforcement (penalty settlement agreement)
records.evidence_text: So rather than him being able to, like, monetize that and trade it to someone, he would be turning that back into us, basically. So by the end of 2027, it would all be, it would all be, the cumulative balance would be zero.
records.notes: Attribution is to the district manager answering a director's question; the first speaker's exact role is unlabeled.

records.finding: An East Side Water Management Area representative told KNDLA that landowners there enrolled significant acreage so a water market can later move water to existing irrigators while the enrolled land stays unplanted. He also reported about 3,000 AF a year of produced water and some irrigated land retired in the last couple of years.
records.quantitative_detail: About 3,000 AF per year of produced water (average); irrigated acreage reduction described only as 'limited'
records.speaker_role: public commenter — East Side Water Management Area
records.meeting_body: Kern Non-Districted Land Authority GSA Board
records.agenda_item: Public comment / EWMA update
records.evidence_text: that have enrolled significant acreage. And part of that is the we've always said, you know, we're going to form a water market at some point. And so for a lot of those acreages the concept is to not plant more acres but to provide water markets so that again that water could then go to some of the existing irrigators but some of that land then would not be planted so again would prevent additional demand for agriculture.
records.notes: Speaker is a representative of the Kern Subbasin's East Side Water Management Area reporting to KNDLA (role inferred from context); 'enrolled' is not defined and the water market is a concept, not a rule.

records.finding: Semitropic staff said contract water follows the property and growers cannot sell or transfer contract water between landowners; charges follow the land. Staff think transfers are inevitable and that the district should act as clearinghouse for physical water but not handle payments.
records.agenda_item: Water transfer policy discussion
records.evidence_text: you cannot just transfer water from one landowner to another. Basically, water follows property. ... as far as like, if you've got five acre feet of table layer contract water this year that you want to sell to somebody those transfer that's that those are not permitted.
records.notes: Speakers are unlabeled; the answer is by district staff in response to a board question. A lease/water use authorization form is the current workaround. Basin-wide rule; not specific to repurposed land.

records.finding: Cawelo staff summarised KNDLA's draft groundwater allocation options analysis (first phase, presented June 15, 2026): it covers native-yield allocation, groundwater transfers, imported-water ramp-down schedules and compliance. It sets no policy; Cawelo urged that choices be coordinated subbasin-wide.
records.quantitative_detail: First phase of a four-phase allocation process; special meeting date 2026-06-15
records.agenda_item: SGMA: Kern Subbasin and KNDLA update
records.evidence_text: It evaluates key policy options or decisions to support the development of a future groundwater allocation program and eventual funding structure. ... outlines implementation strategies for policies such as native yield allocation, groundwater transfers, imported water ramp down schedules and compliance. This is solely an options analysis and doesn't establish any policy
records.notes: Second-hand description by Cawelo staff of a KNDLA special meeting on 2026-06-15 that is not in this corpus; the options-analysis memo itself should be requested. Row concerns KNDLA policy. Basin-wide rule; not specific to repurposed land.

records.finding: KNDLA's board committee reviewed buckets of demand-management policy options: native yield, carryover water, water transfers, a leave-behind, and others. These were judged the less controversial ones to narrow first. Nothing was decided.
records.meeting_body: Kern Non-Districted Land Authority GSA Board
records.agenda_item: Demand management update (ad hoc committee report)
records.evidence_text: And then we native yield carryover water, water transfers, leave behind contingency and our curing policy seems to be more or less. Less controversial perhaps that we could decide on some options to narrow down what the work PMP did.
records.notes: Speaker is the KNDLA executive director or committee chair summarizing an ad hoc committee report; 'curing' may be a garble. The committee report itself is not in the corpus text read. Basin-wide rule; not specific to repurposed land.

records.finding: Semitropic reports its demand-reduction and land-retirement results against a 2017 reference point, not the 2020 SGMA start. Staff counted just over 54,000 AF of demand reduction and almost 19,000 retired acres since then, calculated from end of calendar year 2017.
records.quantitative_detail: Just over 54,000 AF demand reduction (cumulative, end of CY2017 through WY2025, per annual-report table); almost 19,000 acres retired (cumulative); baseline: end of calendar year 2017
records.agenda_item: Annual report (WY2025) review
records.evidence_text: we also track from 2017 It begins in 2020 because that's when sigma implementation started. But we the district began its its demand reduction efforts in 20, essentially 2017 and so that's our, our kind of reference point. ... we reduce our demand by 54,000 acre feet, a little over 54,000 acre feet, and retire land. Retirement is about almost 19,000 acres within the district.
records.notes: Speaker label unclear (Speaker 9, presenting the annual report table); whether the 54,000 AF is a cumulative or annual figure is not stated precisely, so treat as cumulative.

records.finding: Wheeler Ridge-Maricopa's manager said district deliveries fell to 130,000 AF in 2025 from a historical 180,000 to 185,000 AF, citing land-use changes in the district. He asked whether the change is permanent and whether landowners are using wells when surface supply is available. No fallowing figure or accounting was offered.
records.quantitative_detail: 130,000 AF delivered (2025) vs 180,000-185,000 AF historical delivery schedule; 10-year average 141,000 AF per the AI recap
records.meeting_body: Wheeler Ridge-Maricopa Water Storage District Board
records.agenda_item: Engineer-Manager report
records.evidence_text: On this chart here on the first page of the M report, it shows our total deliveries for the year of 130,000. ... I mean we can all see the land use changes that have happened within the district. But it's just another thing that we need to be mindful of. And you know, is this a permanent or is this, you know, guys that have changed and hopefully we're not having landowners using wells when we have surface supplies available.
records.notes: Speaker is the engineer-manager. The remark connects the decline to land use, but no acreage, ET or pumping figures are given at this meeting.

records.finding: In its MA-2 management area, Shafter-Wasco fines pumping above an ET allowance: allowable ET is 3 AF/acre times total acreage (ramping down linearly over the remaining SGMA period) minus Land IQ ET on farmed acres, at up to $500/AF. The district frames the fee as a way to take ground out of production.
records.quantitative_detail: ET limit 3 AF/acre at start, ramping down linearly over about 15 years (end value garbled in transcript); penalty $500/AF of overage; three invoices (about $1,250, $32,000 and $88,000 per the 2026-04-08 meeting)
records.agenda_item: GSA hearing: penalties for groundwater extraction above allocation
records.evidence_text: We started the ET limitation at three, ramping it down 2.5 700 feet acre in a linear fashion over the 15 years that remain of the sigma implementation period ... you would get the total allowable et, which will be three times the total acreage, and then the total et consumed would be the basically this, this total multiplied by the farmed acreage. Then we calculate a surplus or a deficit for each of those APs.
records.notes: Speaker is the district general manager at a GSA penalty hearing; the ramp-down end value reads '2.5 700' in the transcript (the AI summary says toward 2 AF/acre), so the end value is uncertain. 'MA-2' is the management area name used by the district.

records.finding: The Shafter-Wasco GM proposed letting penalised growers repay by taking ground out of production, sized so ET falls under the limit and repays the overage; he calculated 4, 44 and 108 acres for the three growers. The board approved only sending the invoices, deferring any acreage settlement.
records.quantitative_detail: Acres to remove: about 4 (38-acre operation), about 44, about 108; example overage 62 AF; limit stepping from 3 AF/acre
records.agenda_item: GSA hearing: penalties for groundwater extraction above allocation
records.evidence_text: if you take ground out of production, and the amount of ground you take out is enough to stay under the limit next year, and also for pay back the water. So rather than being charged with a 62 acre feet for example, you would essentially pay that back through demand reduction. ... for GP farms, it'd be about 108 acres.
records.notes: Motion passed 'just to approve sending the invoice' with no options; one grower already planned to remove 54 acres. See 2026-04-08 for the settlement actually adopted.

records.finding: Wheeler Ridge-Maricopa tracks the retreat of cropped land through crop surveys: irrigated acreage fell by about 13,000 acres to about 68,000 acres in 2025, and ET fell with it. Groundwater use is then backed out as ET minus deliveries, about 45,000 AF, or 0.7 AF/acre.
records.quantitative_detail: About 68,000 irrigated acres (2025 crop survey), described as down about 13,000 from 2018-2019 (speaker also said 'from a 90 ... down to 68' and 'my math is bad', so the drop is uncertain); ET about 183,000 AF; ET minus deliveries about 45,000 AF (about 0.7 AF/acre, high-level); water year 2025
records.meeting_body: Wheeler Ridge-Maricopa Water Storage District Board
records.agenda_item: 2025 Agricultural Water Management Plan update
records.evidence_text: We're currently as of 2025, as of those crop surveys, we're at about 68,000 acre total irrigated. It's 2019, 2018. We've lost about 13,000 acres acres farm cropping within the district. ... So if we say I'm just high level, the difference would be about 45000 acre feet.
records.notes: Excludes fallow land, rangeland and solar from 'irrigated'; the acreage drop is stated inconsistently in the transcript, and the 45,000 AF is a high-level ET-minus-deliveries difference, not measured pumping.

records.finding: Semitropic tracks an acreage target for fallowing: irrigated acreage fell from 135,397 acres (2015) to 109,571 acres (spring 2026), reaching the acreage the plan assumed supplies could support. Staff say the demand on those acres is a separate metric not yet known.
records.quantitative_detail: Irrigated acres 135,397 (2015) to 109,571 (spring 2026 crop survey), a drop of over 25,000 acres; plan supply assumed to support about 110,000 irrigated acres; demand check at end of 2026
records.agenda_item: GSA: Preliminary results of 2026 Spring Crop Survey
records.evidence_text: We've had a target of how many acres need to be fouled for us to reach sustainability, and with this most recent crop survey, we're there about just less than 110,000 acres, that's only one metric that we need to wait to see is what's the demand associated with that 110,000 acres to see how our demand matches up with our supply. ... Now it's what's happening on the irrigated acres. Is the demand going above the average so we still have the demand metric to meet, which we won't know that until the end of this year.
records.notes: Two-part metric (acreage then ET demand) is a measurement design EDF may want to compare with other GSAs; 'fouled' = fallowed in the machine transcript.

records.finding: Shafter-Wasco's GM modelled that a grower removing trees by end of October 2026 will be over the limit this year and then far enough under it for the next three years to repay the overage by 2029, apart from an $88,000 penalty. A similar payback approach was used for an earlier penalty settlement.
records.quantitative_detail: $88,000 penalty; trees out by end of October 2026; overage repaid by 2029 (cumulative balance basis)
records.agenda_item: Penalty settlement agreement (GP Farms)
records.evidence_text: this year he will be basically over the limit, and there would be a penalty, and then the next through the next three years he will be so far under the limit that it'll pay back all of the water that was owed, except for the $88,000 penalty that he's paying, so with the penalty and the acres coming out by 2029 he has, he will have sort of made us whole
records.notes: Speaker is the district GM; acreage and AF figures for this grower were on slides not in the transcript.

records.finding: At the State Water Board's Kern hearing, the subbasin's GSAs said implementation is mainly taking farmland out of production. They use standardized procedures and consistent consumptive-use data sets to calculate benefits and report them in annual reports to DWR. No ET product is named.
records.quantitative_detail: 31% of planned demand reduction achieved by water year 2024 (cumulative against target); estimated deficit 372,120 AF/yr under the 2030 climate change scenario
records.agenda_item: Kern Subbasin hearing: return to DWR (Resolution)
records.evidence_text: Now, let's talk about what implementation looks like very simply, it's land use changes, taking agricultural lands out of production through the course of implementation. The current GSAs have developed standardized procedures for reporting implementation progress and calculating the benefits the impressive demand reduction and water supply augmentation. Benefits reported today come from the sun basins. Annual Reports to DWR ... the GSAs are using consistent data sets to track consumptive use, and are collectively participating in the basin study to gain a better understanding of the current sub basin and how best to manage for sustainability, native yield, subsurface flow and evapotranspiration.
records.notes: Transcript calls the basin the 'current' sub basin (a transcription of Kern; hearing agenda URL is the Kern hearing); speaker is a Kern GSA presenter, name not captured. The 31% figure was said earlier in the same hearing.

records.finding: Semitropic's new landowner dashboard computes a water budget variance as account ET minus total supply (contract, supplemental, precipitation, native groundwater and a declining temporary allowance). Landowners can submit a field as fallowed after removing trees, with district verification; groundwater bank accounts are not yet in it.
records.agenda_item: SGMA Dashboard demonstration
records.evidence_text: the total water supply subtracted from the consumptive use is how we get the water Budget Variance ... there's a fallow field. ... You can basically submit that there's a step for us to go through and actually kind of validate, yes, it was actually knocked over. We marked as a fallow field, no longer almonds, that we have a verification. ... these groundwater bank accounts are not in here.
records.notes: Several district staff speak without labels; the fallow example is a hypothetical (80 acres of almonds removed on October 1). The dashboard was approved for public release at this meeting.

records.section: 2.5 Data Source and ET Product Choice
records.finding: At Wheeler Ridge-Maricopa, a speaker asked whether Land IQ has ever proved its accuracy and answered no. Staff said growers who dispute the Land IQ-based groundwater service charge can install their own meter, and a comparison with meter data was under way but too early to call.
records.quantitative_detail: Land IQ cost estimated at $65,000 to $72,000 per year (district/GSA share; speaker self-corrected)
records.meeting_body: Wheeler Ridge-Maricopa Water Storage District Board
records.agenda_item: Land IQ ET monitoring contract; groundwater service charge
records.evidence_text: Has land IQ ever proved its accuracy? No. No. I can give them five years of my water usage and tell them to tell me what I gave and all. ... if a landowner says it's not accurate, they can, they can install their own meter. We'll use that meter ... it's too early to tell because timing is a big issue
records.notes: Speakers are unlabeled; the first is a director or landowner skeptic, the reply is the engineer-manager or a colleague. Another passage says Semitropic and Kern Delta have analyzed Land IQ and 'we have not done that and we need to'. Applies to the district's groundwater service charge in the Kern Subbasin; the district also overlies White Wolf. In the same exchange a caller reported Land IQ 8 AF (0.7%) below his own meter readings in his heaviest pumping month on drip (one data point). Basin-wide rule; not specific to repurposed land.

records.section: 2.5 Data Source and ET Product Choice
records.finding: Staff say Land IQ is used because the subbasin needs one consistent ET method and the groundwater service charge must be calculated from it. They noted that GSAs can require meters but a water storage district cannot.
records.meeting_body: Wheeler Ridge-Maricopa Water Storage District Board
records.agenda_item: Land IQ ET monitoring contract; groundwater service charge
records.evidence_text: the issue that we have is that one, we have to have a consistent methodology throughout the sub basin. ... It's my understanding a district cannot require meters. Sure we can. The GSA can require meters, but the water storage district cannot.
records.notes: Exchange between unlabeled speakers (a director and the engineer-manager). In the same exchange he says he does not want meters in White Wolf for now, so ET data are still needed there. Basin-wide rule; not specific to repurposed land.

records.section: 2.5 Data Source and ET Product Choice
records.finding: Wheeler Ridge-Maricopa approved Land IQ for one year and expected a December 2025 presentation comparing Land IQ ET with metered use in the valley and district. This is a planned local validation exercise; its results were not found in the meetings read.
records.quantitative_detail: One-year Land IQ approval; December 2025 comparison presentation planned
records.meeting_body: Wheeler Ridge-Maricopa Water Storage District Board
records.agenda_item: Land IQ ET monitoring contract (WRMGSA)
records.evidence_text: last month we Talked about land IQ and we approved for one year I had a conversation with Mr. Kimmelshoe he was agreeable to that but I think in December Joel and Tom will be working on a presentation about comparisons of their ET measurements versus metering within the valley and within the district
records.notes: Speaker is the general manager or counsel at the board meeting (role inferred). The December meeting is not in the corpus read for this scope, so the comparison's results are unknown. Basin-wide rule; not specific to repurposed land.

records.section: 2.5 Data Source and ET Product Choice
records.finding: Arvin-Edison's board approved a $271,000 three-year Land IQ contract for the basin-wide ET used in the SGMA water budget. The manager called Land IQ's method proprietary and said no competitor was available during the three years to test cost or data quality.
records.quantitative_detail: $271,000 for a three-year contract (2025 to 2028)

records.section: 2.5 Data Source and ET Product Choice
records.finding: Kern River GSA's scope for the Kern Subbasin annual report model update says water-year ET rates, precipitation and crop acreages for the whole subbasin will be provided by Land IQ, run through the C2VSimFG-Kern model. records.notes: From a Todd Groundwater task-order scope in the board packet (Kern Subbasin annual report), not a statement by a KRGSA speaker. Basin-wide rule; not specific to repurposed land.

records.section: 2.5 Data Source and ET Product Choice
records.finding: Land IQ's presenter acknowledged that its ET models were built for irrigated systems and were being applied to fallow fields, after a board member noted fallow-ground ET above rainfall. Land IQ added stations in fallow fields, but no local validation figure was given.

records.evidence_text: I'll be completely honest with you. We, our models were developed for irrigated systems, and we were using those for fallow fields. And that, and we have a we put some more stations in fallow fields, and we're we're never now our system is never higher than preset.
records.notes: Presenter is Land IQ (a vendor); transcript wording around 'preset' (precipitation) is garbled. Relevant to whether fallowed-land ET savings can be trusted.

records.section: 2.5 Data Source and ET Product Choice
records.finding: Shafter-Wasco bills against Land IQ remotely sensed ET, which its manager calls the best available data. But the monthly data posted to growers ran about two months late, and one penalised grower said he could not get current ET. The district now offers Land IQ's daily view.
records.quantitative_detail: Monthly ET posting about 2 months behind; penalty owed by that grower about $31,000; $500/AF
records.agenda_item: GSA hearing: penalties for groundwater extraction above allocation
records.evidence_text: this is remotely sensed data from land IQ is the best available data that we know of. ... when I went on, it said the data was two months behind on et So, and I really didn't irrigate in the fall, so I figured I was okay, and it's my fault.
records.notes: First sentence is the district GM; second is a penalised landowner during the hearing. Land IQ ET is based on farmed acreage while the allowance uses total acreage, which the GM says favours the grower. Basin-wide rule; not specific to repurposed land.

records.section: 2.5 Data Source and ET Product Choice

records.section: 2.5 Data Source and ET Product Choice
records.finding: During Kern Subbasin basin-study calibration, modelled groundwater levels did not match observations, so the technical team proposed raising assumed ET rather than altering surface-water deliveries, because ET data across the subbasin are not consistent over time and come from different datasets. A subcommittee is re-checking each GSA's data for six months.

records.finding: Semitropic staff say critics of its demand-management programme want no net loss of wetlands. The spring crop survey now separately tracks exempt wetlands, including the federal refuge, whereas the programme had focused only on private wetlands.

records.finding: An Agricultural Energy Consumers Association presenter told Cawelo's board that SGMA-driven fallowing and reduced pumping will cut agricultural energy use, citing a preliminary economist estimate of roughly 14 to 20 percent, and will reduce food-processing capacity. records.finding: Distributive equity: Semitropic's groundwater charge for use above a water budget screens out parcels under two acres or using under two acre-feet as de minimis, which spares small and rural-residential users. The charge is aimed at irrigated use, not at communities.

records.notes: Speaker unlabelled; the intermediate figure after the 2 AF screen is garbled in the transcript, so only the thresholds and the two clear totals are recorded.

records.evidence_text: On February 20, 2025, the State Water Board opened a hearing to determine whether to place the Kern County Subbasin on probation. In recognition of the substantial progress the Kern County Subbasin GSAs made in revising the GSPs since the Department issued its 2023 Inadequate Determination , the Board adopted Resolution 2025 -0007 continuing the hearing to September 17, 2025 so that remaining deficiencies might be resolved without the need for the Board to designate the subbasin probationary , and directing the GSAs to increase community engagement to assist in the resolution of outstanding issues ... records.finding: EKI explained Arvin GSA's water-quality exceedance process: a subbasin consultant flags exceedances, an investigation decides whether GSA activity caused them, and domestic well owners within three miles get notices; nitrate notices point to free testing through the Kern Water Collaborative.
records.quantitative_detail: 5 Arvin GSA representative WQ wells, 3 with spring 2026 exceedances (RMW004: 1,2,3-TCP, nitrate, TDS; RMW224: 1,2,3-TCP; RMW225: arsenic, nitrate); 3-mile notice radius; 3 notices (RMW225) and 16 notices (RMW004 nitrate) sent; TDS is not noticed
records.agenda_item: Water quality network exceedance update
records.evidence_text: And so the spring sampling event was completed back in March and there is a sub basin wide consultant that reviews that data and alerts the GSAs when there's exceedance of the minimum threshold and that triggers action. Both an exceedance investigation, very similar to the subsidence process we just talked about, as well as specific notices to domestic wells within a radius of influence of that well. And there's actually two pathways, one for nitrate and one for non nitrate. And so for those wells that have a nitrate exceedance, the notice is provided to the domestic well owners that alerts them of the Kern Water Collaborative program and that they may be eligible for free testing through the Kern Water Collaborative for their domestic well. Specifically for all the other constituents, there is an exceedance investigation report that is being conducted by a selected qualified professional team that is conducted sub basin wide. Todd Groundwater is the firm that's doing those. And the result of that investigation would be a finding of whether the exceedance is due to groundwater management activities being groundwater pumping or groundwater recharge or not due to groundwater Management activities. And then each of those results have a notice that would be notified to the domestic well owners on in the vicinity. And we're using a three mile radius. ... notices have gone out to three domestic wells on record. And for RMW004, there was 16 notices that went out for those nitrate exceedances.
records.notes: Also answers COM-3.3.2a (constituents, locations, method). Speaker is Christina Lucero (EKI) per transcript label.

records.section: 3.3.3 Domestic Wells and Community Water System Consolidation
records.finding: North Kings GSA made registration of all wells, including domestic wells, mandatory so it can see every extraction in an area and know which wells a decline could affect. Registered counts are published by well type; the stated aim is not to meter domestic wells.
records.quantitative_detail: 1,225 domestic wells and 978 agricultural wells registered as of 2025-11-06, of 2,500+ total; deadline 2025-11-30; no registration fee before deadline
records.meeting_body: North Kings GSA Board of Directors

records.evidence_text: As you know, we have a lot of domestic wells in our GSA boundary. A lot. Individually they don't account for much. Collectively, they account for a lot. And it is impossible to make good management decisions without knowing all the straws in the ground at a particular location. And so we are trying to gather that information so that we can then utilize that not to put a meter and require extraction reporting on domestic wells, but so that we know what exactly could be impacted in a particular area ... you can see already to date we have 1225 domestic wells registered. We have 978 agricultural wells and then a scattering of other wells.
records.notes: Speaker is inferred as the GSA executive officer from context; a public commenter objected to registering domestic wells at this meeting.

records.section: 3.3.3 Domestic Wells and Community Water System Consolidation
records.finding: Staff justify registering rural domestic wells by the duty to protect all users: without knowing small wells exist, the GSA cannot show it is not harming them. Staff say de minimis users (under 2 AF/yr) would not have to meter or report.

So we've got to have that accounting in place. So that we're accounting for that as we're moving towards, you know, our water budget. Especially because how can we make sure we're not negatively impacting those low users if we don't know they're out there, right? Like that's what our charge is. DWR has said you have to protect all the groundwater users and uses. So, how can we do that if we don't have a good account of them? ... We would not get to a point where these folks are going to have to monitor and or report their usage as long as it's less than two acre feet

records.finding: Procedural equity (notice): during the late-reporting penalty backlog debate, directors said stale or incomplete owner and contact data in FCGMA's database means people are penalised without having been told, and asked for a periodic outreach and verification programme. Maybe that's an ongoing exercise, maybe it's a limited exercise, maybe it's got a six month lifespan where every stakeholder gets touched to make sure that the data that we have is accurate or as accurate as we can make it because, you know, otherwise. We often wind up in the position of folks complaining, I didn't know and for good reason. Because we didn't tell them because we had bad information, we had old information, we didn't complete information. The correct information's in a drawer somewhere. ... it was brought up in public comment that landowner versus leasee, the bill does not go to both. So for one reason or the other, the lease doesn't get it or there doesn't get it. And there are some complications I'm looking to see from staff's point of view as to how we can improve this process.

records.finding: Distributive equity (penalties): FCGMA staff cited safeguards such as caps, ability to pay, hardship, appeal and separation of powers, and proposed a backlog schedule with a first-violation waiver and second-violation amounts scaled by pumping size. Staff said $50 a day escalates quickly.
records.quantitative_detail: Existing penalty $50 per day; proposed backlog second violation $25 (under 2 AF), $50 (2-50 AF), $100 (over 50 AF) per reporting period; first violation $0; $11.5 million assessed to date (cumulative, staff, 2026-09-23)
records.agenda_item: 14. Civil penalty collection procedures and late-reporting backlog
records.evidence_text: it's good practice for public agencies to have safeguards on civil penalty to prevent unfair punishment, specifically putting caps on the assessment, making sure that the violation is in line with the offense and ability to pay. And it also needs to be they have the ability to adjust for inflation and we don't want to have a situation where the fee is growing much larger than the original infraction. There needs to be fairness. And we need to be able to consider first time mistakes and look at the financial hardship. There also needs to be clear noticing from the agency ability to appeal and a separation of powers, meaning that the staff that apply the penalties are not the same staff that are actually determining whether or not a waiver occurs. ... Any second violation would be reduced to, excuse me, to $25 for accounts that extract less than 2 acre feet, $50 for accounts that extract 2 to 50 acre feet or $100 per reporting period for accounts that extract more than 50 acre feet
records.notes: Staff speaker is the business process coordinator by self-introduction; penalties fall on water-right holders and operators across FCGMA basins, not specifically on DACs; the schedule was a staff suggestion and the chair's 30-day cure idea was not adopted per the AI recap (not verified in transcript).

records.finding: San Luis Obispo County approved the Paso fallow land registry on Feb 3, 2026 and revised its Ag Offset Ordinance so enrolled land keeps protection from the ordinance's 'look back' pumping restrictions. It also revised Williamson Act procedures so enrolled land gets the same protection as land not fallowed.

records.meeting_body: Paso Robles Area Groundwater Authority Board

That choose to enroll their followed lands in the registry. ... What we call the look back provisions or there was those future pumping restrictions that are currently in the Ag Offset Ordinance so that those protections are now baked into the. The revised Ag Offset ordinance. ... They also voted to revise the rules and procedures of the Williamson act to, to ensure that if growers or landowners enroll their farming units in the the fellow land registry, they are afforded the same protections under the Williamson act as they would have had they not chosen to follow.

records.section: 2.5 Data Source and ET Product Choice
records.finding: PRAGA's draft volumetric fee measures agricultural consumptive use with LandIQ ET, net of effective precipitation, on an October-September water year. Staff adopted the water year after reviewing ET data with LandIQ and the GSA staff group, to align rain with crop demand.

So this is measured by land iq. ... we have removed effective precipitation from this total. ... the Water year data is used here from October to September as opposed to calendar year. ... When we looked at the ET data with the GSA staff group representatives from the GSA group and Landiq, again with a higher pre set period at the end of 2025, it really resulted in us recognizing that it makes more sense to use a water year where the precipitation for that period more directly aligns to the crop demands

records.finding: PRAGA staff expect DOC's MLRP guidelines (Prop 4 money) in fall-winter 2026 and see them as a way to turn fallowed land into long-term or permanent fallowing, with repurposing that could benefit the community or wildlife. records.finding: The County of San Luis Obispo and PRAGA are building a voluntary multi-benefit irrigated land repurposing (MILR) programme. Its first phase is a fallowed land registry where irrigators enroll land they plan not to irrigate, with an enabling ordinance and CEQA review under way. LandIQ is the lead consultant.

records.agenda_item: Update on DWR grant projects (MILR / fallowed land registry)

Plan to not irrigate into the program, into the followed land registry. ... the primary consultant on this is Land IQ. ... Developing of the enabling Ordinance so that the program. Can actually be launched and deployed. ... the consultant is undergoing. A CEQA review of the various component elements

records.finding: PRAGA's counsel explained that a formal advisory committee would be a Brown Act body while an informal one would not. The board voted without objection to direct the executive director to set up informal stakeholder feedback, such as periodic workshops. A public commenter said advisory committees have no power and their recommendations are mostly ignored.

records.agenda_item: 9A. Improving stakeholder representation at PRAGA
records.evidence_text: Because it wasn't established by the board, it's not subject to the Brown Act. That's really the big distinction, if it's established formally by the board, in a vote of this board, it will be a Brown act organization. ... Direction to the Executive Director to establish public stakeholder feedback mechanisms. And maybe that's in the form of a standing group that advises him. It may be in the form of. Of quarterly or. Or semi regular workshops, but it would be this sort of informal stakeholder feedback mechanism. ... So we have a motion and a second. Any further discussion or questions? Okay. Do we need a roll call vote for this? We don't need a roll call. All in favor? Aye. Any opposed? Abstentions. None. ... so people need to understand that advisory committee has no power. So whether it's formal or informal, all you're doing is recommending to the board what they think should be done. And you know, I've been on advisory committee now for almost 10 years and essentially probably more than half the time, at least if not more recommendations that have been submitted by that advisory group have been totally virtually ignored.
records.notes: Evidence joins four passages in a different order from the transcript. The commenter's 10-year advisory experience probably concerns another body, not PRAGA. Counsel's distinction between formal and informal bodies was confusing to some in the room.

records.finding: In September 2026 PRAGA's executive director used an informal advisory committee of basin stakeholders, including representatives of each GSA staff group, to review draft project priorities. Staff reported its feedback to the board; the committee is advisory only.

records.finding: A local stakeholder group's written report in the PRAGA packet recommended that a new management entity include ranching and rural residential landowners on its board, and create advisory committees (de minimis users, non-irrigated and irrigated agriculture) each with one seat on the governing board. It was a recommendation, not an adopted seat.
records.meeting_body: Paso Robles Area Groundwater Authority Board
records.agenda_item: Stakeholder group findings and recommendations on PRAGA funding and governance (packet)
records.evidence_text: the board should include someone from ranching, as that is the largest land use overlying the Basin, and rural residential landowners, who face the greatest risk from groundwater declines. Agricultural organizations should be represented. Unless the management is under a single, unified GSA, there should be at least one representative from each involved GSA, and possibly two representatives, but those representatives shouldn’t have to be an elected person. Irrigated agriculture should have a majority of its representatives personally engaged in farming. ... we believe that the new management entity should create advisory committees of stakeholders. The committees could consist of de minimis users, non-irrigated agriculture, irrigated agriculture or some combination of those and others. The point is to give overlying landowners a real voice, so perhaps each advisory committee could have one seat on the governing Board.
records.notes: Authored by an informal local stakeholder group facilitated by Steve Sinton, not by PRAGA. The 2026-02-18 board chose informal stakeholder feedback over added seats.

records.finding: PRAGA staff laid out four ways to improve stakeholder representation, including adding three board seats assigned to user categories such as residential and small or large pumpers. Some stakeholders wanted a de minimis seat; a director said formally expanding the board did not make sense now because of cost and JPA renegotiation. No designated seat was created.
records.quantitative_detail: About 47 stakeholders attended or gave feedback across the survey and two workshops (Feb 2026); options: +4 seats, or +3 category seats
records.meeting_body: Paso Robles Area Groundwater Authority Board
records.agenda_item: 9A. Improving stakeholder representation at PRAGA
records.evidence_text: So the three four options. One was again the formal advisory committee. This would be a Brown act compliant committee and again there's some considerations there. There would be incur new ongoing costs. It's possible that that could be covered by the DWR grant. So there's may potentially a way to mitigate the cost there stakeholder feedback for that item. There was significant support for this option. Comments were raised that cost shouldn't prevent structural improvements. Number two was an informal advisory committee and this would be more of a committee or group that staff myself would would convene as needed to discuss relevant topics. Again this would be a more of a minimal implementation cost. There was also a majority expressed support and interest in this option and again encouraged the providing input to the board before board meetings. So there was a preference for these two. Item number three was increase the board by four seats. Again these next two options would require a change to the joint powers agreement which again can will incur costs and would take several months if not longer to finalize as discussions would need to be negotiated by each of the four GSAs going to their GSA board. So it could be a process that takes a bit of time again and money lawyers would need to be involved as well on that. So the Stakeholder feedback was minimal support for that option. There were some concerns that the GSA seats wouldn't improve overall representation. So generally stakeholders did not like that option. And then lastly, option number four was to increase the board by three seats and assign seats to specific user categories, for example residential, small, large pumpers, grazers. Again, same issue of requiring a change to the JPA and incurring costs and taking time. The stakeholder feedback was there were stakeholders that supported this option with interest, specific interest in having de minimis representation. ... Then I think given the, the logistical complexities, the time, the money and elsewhere, to formally expand the board to include their voice doesn't make sense at this time.
records.notes: First passage is staff (executive director); second is a director (speaker inferred from labels, likely Director Gibson). No vote on a designated seat was taken.

records.evidence_text: not a single one of the solar farms that's in the GSA have registered. So, they're obviously not farming that ground. You know, from what I understand, there's really no wells on there other than. Possibly the wash panels, if even that.
