records.finding: MKR's presenter says transitional water goes to land in production at any time 2015-2024, not to fallow land, with eligibility set from Land IQ crop data and an appeal to the board.
records.quantitative_detail: Transitional eligibility window 2015-2024 (production in any year)
records.agenda_item: Draft Groundwater Allocation Policy for 45-day comment
records.evidence_text: the idea here is that it's going to areas that have been in production and not just a fow land. we don't need to give transitional water to to follow land. Um we're going to look at land IQ data for those years and based on that will uh assign uh transitional allocation to those lands.
records.notes: Transcription renders "fallow" as "fow land" and "follow land"; read as fallow from context.

records.finding: SFK's public draft allocation policy lets a parcel that gets a sustainable-yield allocation but is not irrigated (fallowed) keep it and move it to irrigated acreage in the GSA. Transitional allocations cannot be transferred. The draft does not say whether payment or a repurposing programme changes this.
records.agenda_item: Draft Groundwater Allocation Policy (public draft ver. 16) - Transfers
records.evidence_text: Parcels that receive a sustainable yield allocation but do not irrigate that acreage may transfer that allocation to other acreage within the SFK GSA. This will enable landowners who fallow some of their parcels to move allocation for that year to parcels that are actively irrigated. ... Only sustainable yield and recharge credit are eligible for transfer; transitional allocations are prohibited from being transferred across water accounts.
records.notes: Public draft released for comment; the 2026-01-16 adopted version was not in the extracted text, so the clause may have changed. Same clause appears in MKR GSA drafts.

records.finding: SFK adopted transitional (temporary) allocation only for land in agricultural production at any time 2015-2024, not for land never farmed; denied owners can appeal to the board. Land idle across that whole period would receive no transitional water.
records.quantitative_detail: Eligibility window 2015-2024 (agricultural production in any year)
records.agenda_item: Groundwater Allocation Policy (approved this meeting)
records.evidence_text: On the transitional allocation, what the land that's been in production anytime between 2015 and 2024 is going to be eligible for the transitional water. If you are. If that land has never been in production in that time period, then it does not qualify for transitional water. ... Anybody who is denying that eligibility can always appeal their decision to the board.
records.notes: Speaker is the unlabeled presenter of the policy (manager or consultant). The 2040 date is from the MKR policy text; SFK recap says transitional pumping decreases to 2040.

records.finding: El Rico's draft allocation covers only parcels in the irrigated-lands programme, a banking site or the dairy order; solar farms and never-farmed land get none. Land now in non-agricultural use therefore carries no entitlement.
records.agenda_item: Allocation map update
records.evidence_text: if you're in ilrp, or if you're a banking site, or if you're in the dairy order, there's an allocation. We're just figuring out what all those parcels are. So like the solar farms don't get one.
records.notes: Speaker unlabeled. Draft map, parcels still being sorted; the 2026-08-11 meeting adds "if you don't claim your parcels, you don't get an allocation".

records.finding: SFK staff set conditions for moving sustainable yield across the GSA boundary: both GSAs approve, neighbours only, contiguous parcel in the same farm unit, metered well reported to both, receiving parcel in active farming, no more than 1 mile out, annual registration, revocable.
records.quantitative_detail: Maximum 1 mile from SFK boundary; sustainable yield only (not transitional); registered annually
records.agenda_item: Draft Allocation Policy: transfers across GSA boundary
records.evidence_text: We also very much specify exactly what and whom you can transfer to, and which GSAs and sub-basins. I'm making sure that we're clear it's only our neighbors. The parcel receiving must be contiguous. Um, and it has to be part of the same farm unit. Um, we're only talking about transferring the amount of the sustainable yield, not transitional pumping. Um, the pump and the well that's pumping has to be metered. The metered data that needs to be reported to both GSAs. The parcel receiving the water must be. Active agricultural production. Um, under no circumstances can the water be moved more than 1 mile from our boundary. And the GSA can revoke this at any time, and you have to register with us every year that you're going to continue to do that.
records.notes: Presenter unlabeled. Same meeting: a director calls the restrictions good ideas but hard to police, and the presenter says a westside group told SFK it would not allow such transfers (group not identified). The 2026-06-19 row shows these export restrictions were later rolled back. Basin-wide rule; not specific to repurposed land.

records.finding: SFK's draft policy keeps a share of any landowner recharge or banking project in the subbasin as a leave-behind, set in the Groundwater Recharge Policy, and requires approval by both GSAs for credits bought from outside SFK.
records.agenda_item: Draft Allocation Policy ver. 14 - Landowner Developed Credits
records.evidence_text: a percentage of any landowner water banking or recharge projects will remain with SFK. The amount of leave behind is defined in the Groundwater Recharge Policy" ... All transfers purchased from outside of SFK boundaries must be approved by both GSAs with jurisdiction
records.notes: The percentage is in the separate Groundwater Recharge Policy, not in this document. The same draft's Transfers section also lets landowners who fallow parcels move that year's allocation to irrigated parcels within SFK. Basin-wide rule; not specific to repurposed land.

records.finding: MKR's draft allocation policy lets sustainable yield move penalty-free among registered parcels in the GSA, and out only to bordering GSAs under conditions: both GSAs approve each year, contiguous parcel in the same farm unit, only the border parcel's yield, metered well, and revocation if the well sits in a management-plan area.
records.agenda_item: Draft Allocation Policy - Use of Sustainable Yield
records.evidence_text: The sustainable yield may be transferred outside of the MKR GSA once all of the following conditions are met: 1. The Sustainable Yield can only be transferred into the GSAs bordering MKR GSA . 2. All transfers must be registered with and approved by both MKR GSA and the receiving GSA on an annual basis . ... 4. Only the sustainable yield amount for the registered parcel within MKR GSA that directly borders the surrounding GSA is eligible for transfer. ... 9. The MKR GSA may revoke, at its sole discretion, the ability to transfer water out of the GSA, if the pumping well is located in an area subject to actions identified in the Management Plans.
records.notes: Draft policy out for 45-day comment; neighbouring agencies criticised the methodology per the recap. Basin-wide rule; not specific to repurposed land.

records.finding: MKR's subsidence policy blocks transfers of groundwater credits into an affected subsidence management area once 50% of allowable subsidence is reached, and bars new lower-aquifer wells. This is a geographic limit on moving freed or banked water.
records.quantitative_detail: Trigger: 50% of allowable cumulative subsidence (75% and 100% tiers follow in the policy)
records.agenda_item: Early Action / Subsidence Management Plan, section 4.3.2
records.evidence_text: (1) When 50% of the allowable cumulative subsidence in a subsidence management area has been documented to have occurred or impacts to critical infrastructure are noted that cannot be mitigated , no recharge credits pumping will be allowed in the lower aquifer. No transfers of groundwater credits into the affected area will be allowed. If surface water is available to the areas that receive groundwater irrigation, it must be used first, prior to any groundwater pumping. No new wells will be permitted in the lower aquifer.
records.notes: South Fork Kings explained the same triggers at its 2026-02-20 meeting; per the recap MKR adopted the subsidence policy at this meeting. Basin-wide rule; not specific to repurposed land.

records.finding: SFK plans a future electronic trading platform for water; for now trades are by notifying the GSA. Staff note Reclamation grants have funded platforms in the area and the GSA intends to apply.
records.agenda_item: Draft Groundwater Allocation Policy: response to public comments
records.evidence_text: we were going to have a future trading platform at some point allow people to trade water back and forth. Right now we're going to do it where you notified the gsa. But in the future we're going to go to probably some kind of electronic platform that hasn't been selected yet. ... there's also the Bureau of Reclamation has grant money that some of our GSAs and the surrounding sub basin have used to develop those as well.
records.notes: Presenter unlabeled. The platform is for allocation trading generally, not repurposed land specifically. Basin-wide rule; not specific to repurposed land.

records.finding: In SFK, landowners may transfer sustainable yield or landowner-developed credits by notifying the GSA, which debits and credits both accounts; price stays private. Unused sustainable yield can be carried over, credits retire on a five-year rolling basis, and combined use is capped at 3 AF/acre, 4 AF/acre with credits.
records.quantitative_detail: Combined cap 3 AF/acre (4 AF/acre with credits), annual; carryover and credits expire on a five-year rolling basis
records.agenda_item: Groundwater Allocation Policy (approved this meeting)
records.evidence_text: you can transfer your sustainable yield. Meaning if I wanted, you know, John wants to transfer his sustainable to me. That's between the two of us. All you have to do is notify Johnny and the gsa. He'll, he'll take it out of both accounts and make sure that it gets subtracted out of yours and credit mine. And then whatever deal you and I cut between us is just between the two of us. And GSA doesn't care or doesn't need to know, I should say, but we do need to know how much water got transferred between the two of us. You can also transfer landowner develop credits. So again, if John sinks an acre foot of water, you know, 10 acre feet of water, he wants to transfer that credit to me. We can do that again. We just let the GSA know. ... Again, your credits don't, they are rolling up on a five year retirement.
records.notes: Speaker unlabeled. Transfers apply within the SFK GSA; movement to a neighbouring GSA needs that GSA's approval (answer to a question in the same meeting). The 3 and 4 AF/acre figures come from adjacent passages in the same transcript. Basin-wide rule; not specific to repurposed land.

records.finding: At a Tulare Lake hearing, a Kings County supervisor (also a GSA director) recalled a land retirement programme about 20 years earlier where West Side farmers carved out 20 acres around their wells, kept pumping and moved the water. It is a leakage example: retirement without retiring the wells.
records.quantitative_detail: 20 acres carved out around wells (speaker's figure); programme about 20 years old
records.speaker_role: board member — Kings County supervisor (GSA director)
records.agenda_item: Resolution: exclusion of small pumpers in the Tulare Lake Subbasin from probationary reporting
records.evidence_text: There was a program about 20 years ago, a land retirement program, and some of the West Side farmers retired their ground, but they never retired where the wells were at. They carved out 20 acres where the wells were at. And they never stopped pumping. Instead of pumping for their crop, they started moving water, 24/7, all the time moving it, because that's where the money was at.
records.notes: Transcript labels the speaker 'Unknown Speaker' but the Board replies 'Thank you, supervisor' (preceding turns identify Doug Verboon, Mid-Kings River GSA, which is in the Tulare Lake Subbasin); the programme's name and location ('West Side') are not given.

records.finding: At an MKR board meeting a speaker asked how many acres have been fallowed because surface water was sold out of the area. The responder said surface water rights are private property and there is no vehicle to track where the water goes, so no count of such fallowing was available.
records.quantitative_detail: A speaker cites unsourced estimates as low as 2% of water rights sold; no acreage figure given
records.agenda_item: Public comment / questions
records.evidence_text: How many acres or how many if we were to take and compute out by APNs slash acreage, how much those areas, the water is being sold out of the area, how many acres basically have been chosen to become fallow in our area so the water's not sinking? Surface water rights, we don't manage them. It's a personal property. Right. You handle it within your own business and there's no vehicle to track where it goes.
records.notes: Questioner and answerer unlabeled; the Kings County Water District is said to restrict sales out of its district.

records.finding: SFK's counsel recommended rolling back the export restrictions in its allocation policy and replacing them with reporting and GSA-to-GSA coordination, because the GSA did not know who moves water, where, or when. Reporting covers exports and transfers within the GSA.
records.agenda_item: Amendment to Groundwater Allocation Policy (export wells)
records.evidence_text: Became apparent to me through that evaluation that we did not know nearly enough information about who was engaged in this activity, where they were doing it, where the water was going to, when these activities were occurring. And so without actually understanding the nature of the activities and how that might relate to our obligations under sgma, I felt it prudent to roll those particular restrictions back to substitute provisions that require the reporting of information that we needed to understand how that activity is occurring
records.notes: Speaker is the GSA's legal counsel by context ("I felt it prudent"). This later date updates the 2025-09-18 conditions; kept as new_basin because no prior-finding link applies in Mode B. Basin-wide rule; not specific to repurposed land.

records.finding: An MKR director demands enforcement against large landowners moving groundwater and surface water out of the county, naming South Fork Kings, and says no water should leave the GSA without permission. This is a leakage concern about moving freed or sold water.
records.agenda_item: Public hearing / Prop 218 fee discussion
records.evidence_text: we have the same thing happening here by other large landlords moving water out of here. So if we're all complying, I better see some actions to stop the exit of groundwater out of our county and also the exit of surface water out of our county too. ... No water leaves the GSA without permission.
records.notes: Speaker is addressed as Mr. Verboon and matches director Doug Ver Boone in the roll call; this is an enforcement demand, not an adopted rule. On 2025-11-18 another MKR speaker also complained about people who bought ground and farm the water, not the ground. Basin-wide rule; not specific to repurposed land.

records.finding: SFK changed its allocation policy so ET-based pumping estimates do not charge non-irrigated (fallow) fields; such land is zeroed out through a landowner affidavit process still to be set up. The passage does not describe crediting any water saved by fallowing.
records.agenda_item: Draft Groundwater Allocation Policy: response to public comments
records.evidence_text: one of the questions that came up is when we use evapotranspiration as a method to back calculate pumping if we have a foul field, the E.T. the satellites will pick up E.T. off those fields. We wanted to make sure that people's accounts weren't being subtracted and being impacted by that. So we made it clear that those non irrigated lands would be zeroed out and just you know there's going to be a process for that. There'll be an affidavit, people have to sign things of that nature.
records.notes: Speaker unlabeled (policy presenter). Transcript says "foul field" for fallow field. Affidavit process is described as still to be built.

records.section: 2.5 Data Source and ET Product Choice
records.finding: MKR staff say the GSA has used Land IQ for four years for monthly field-level ET, that ET is an allowed pumping-measurement method under its 2025 policy, and recommend a three-year contract at about $70,000-$75,000 a year. No local validation or landowner dispute is described.
records.quantitative_detail: $70,332 year 1; $72,444 year 2; $74,616 year 3 (annual service fee, three-year contract); ET service used about four years before 2025-08
records.agenda_item: Consider agreement with Land IQ for ET services
records.evidence_text: OK, so mid Kings River GSA has utilized land IQ for developing monthly field by field estimate of actual evapotranspiration or ET that occurs within the GSA for the last four years ... ET is one of those allowed methods. ... The cost for this consulting service will run $70,332.00 in year one, $72,444 in year 2.
records.notes: Transcript attributes every line to one clerk label; read as the manager's report. Same passage says the cost is paid by Kings County and the City of Hanford until GSA fees exist. Whether the board voted is not shown in these lines. Basin-wide rule; not specific to repurposed land.

records.section: 2.5 Data Source and ET Product Choice
records.finding: MKR's Land IQ scope of work calibrates its ET models with GSA-area eddy-covariance or surface-renewal ground stations, delivers monthly field-by-field ET and precipitation within about 30 days, and runs April 2025 to March 2028. Stations need grower cooperation for siting.
records.quantitative_detail: Monthly field-by-field ET and precipitation, delivered about 30 days after month end; annual crop map; contract period April 2025-March 2028
records.agenda_item: Land IQ agreement for ET services - Scope of work, Tasks 2-3
records.evidence_text: This effort continues the management and continuous maintenance of ground truthing climatic stations of eddy covariance and/or surface renewal approaches to collect instantaneous ET ground data at select locations representing crop production within MKRGSA. ... The data collected by these stations will be used to calibrate the Land IQ ET RS models and create ET estimates across all fields within MKRGSA ... This scope of work is for a three-year time-frame from April 2025 through March 2028.
records.notes: Scope document authored by Land IQ and attached to the board packet; shows local ground-truthing, but no validation results or landowner disputes were discussed. Basin-wide rule; not specific to repurposed land.

records.section: 2.5 Data Source and ET Product Choice
records.finding: SFK's draft meter policy would estimate unmetered wells from Land IQ ET and add a 5% surcharge, partly recovering Land IQ's cost to the GSA of roughly $60,000-$70,000 a year.
records.quantitative_detail: 5% surcharge on ET-estimated pumping; Land IQ cost about $60,000-$70,000+ per year (speaker unsure)
records.agenda_item: Proposed flow meter policy
records.evidence_text: if we have to go through and you don't install the meter and we have to use land IQ, we're going to charge you 5% surcharge on top of your pumping. So Atlanta IQ estimates you pumped 100 acre feed. We're going to charge you at 105 acre feet. So that's there's additional cost with a GSA to maintain. It's like $60,000 a year. Like yeah, close to 70. Close to 70,000 actually that I just got an email saying that the price is going to go up a nickel. Oh so over $70,000 a year or land IQ. So if we have to pay to keep land IQ, we're going to recover some of those costs from folks that don't put meters in and that cost is going to be charged the surcharge on those accounts.
records.notes: Meter policy failed to pass this meeting per the recap; a revised version was expected in June. A later passage in the same meeting notes ET needs surface-water delivery data to be accurate. Basin-wide rule; not specific to repurposed land.

records.section: 2.5 Data Source and ET Product Choice
records.finding: MKR's Prop 26 fee study says pumping is either metered or estimated from ET with precipitation, surface-water application and a crop-based irrigation efficiency. Landowners may challenge an ET estimate only with calibrated, properly installed meter data.
records.quantitative_detail: Land IQ ET subscription $71,000 in the first column of the five-year budget table in the same packet
records.agenda_item: Prop 26 Cost of Service Study - Groundwater pumping estimates
records.evidence_text: Groundwater pumping within the MKRGSA is determined either by reporting direct meter values or estimated using evapotranspiration (ET). Well owners may choose t o report either meter data or have their groundwater pumping estimated using the ET method. ... Landowners seeking to challenge groundwater pumping estimates using well meter data may do so provided they demonstrate that the meter data are accurate and reliable.
records.notes: Engineer's fee memo dated 2026-07-22; the ET product is not named in this passage (Land IQ is named elsewhere in the packet budget at about $71,000 a year). Basin-wide rule; not specific to repurposed land.

records.finding: In SFK's draft implementation-cost estimate, land fallowing is a $0 placeholder because MLRP grants might fund it, and recharge basins are also $0 because the GSA does not want to own basins. The total is about $1.82 million a year, with no repurposing programme costed.
records.quantitative_detail: Land fallowing $0 placeholder; recharge basins $0; total about $1.82 million per year, about $28 per AF at 65,000 AF average pumping (staff figures, same meeting)
records.agenda_item: Preliminary implementation cost estimate (fees)
records.evidence_text: put a zero in there, but I have a placeholder for it, because there are grant fundings out there for the MLRP program. ... recharge basins, the consensus is that the GSA doesn't want to own any bases, so we're putting a zero in there for that.
records.notes: Transcript renders fallowing as "land following". Presenter unlabeled; role read as GSA staff or consultant. The $1.82 million and $28 figures come from later in the same passage.

records.finding: MKR's subsidence management plan names land repurposing programs in some areas as a priority action to investigate, coordinated with the Kings County Planning Department and funded from pumping fees and any grants. No programme design or savings accounting is given.
records.agenda_item: Early Action Management Plan, section 3.3.2 GSA-initiated actions
records.evidence_text: Priority actions that will be investigated by MKR GSA include: • Land repurposing programs in some areas. These actions will be coordinated with Kings County Planning Department.
records.notes: The same section says funding is intended to come from pumping fees and grants. Policy was adopted at this meeting per the recap summary; no meeting discussion of repurposing was found in the transcript.

records.finding: A speaker at SFK's allocation-policy adoption said perhaps 5,000-6,000 acres of the GSA may have to be permanently retired, probably to solar as in Westlands. No retirement programme, funding or accounting was discussed.
records.quantitative_detail: 5,000-6,000 acres possibly permanently retired (speaker's estimate, no time basis); preceding figure garbled in transcript ("two 20,000 acre fee")
records.agenda_item: Groundwater Allocation Policy (approved this meeting)
records.evidence_text: two 20,000 acre fee is probably, you know, maybe 5 to 6,000 acres may have to be permanently retired, sadly. Probably going to turn into solar like we see over Westlands
records.notes: Speaker unlabeled; role inferred (references the growers committee and "we"). A public commenter later in the meeting also objected to farmland going to solar.

records.finding: A grower commenting at El Rico says growers are spending millions to buy ground and fallow it to move water, and asks for credit for banked water. The GSA says banking credit is not yet legally clear.
records.agenda_item: Private water banking discussion (item 10.5)
records.evidence_text: We're buying ground, just a fallow, you know, it's getting very, very expensive, and we're trying to play within these rules, spending millions upon millions of dollars buying ground and never going to farm out.
records.notes: Commenter identifies himself as representing a farming company (Warren Ag Service); no acreage figure given.

records.finding: A GSA consultant told Kings County WD's board that the GSA is 'very seriously thinking' of applying for an MLRP subbasin award to fund a fallowing program taking land out of production where pumping causes subsidence near ditches. Prospective only; no application, amounts or accounting described.
records.quantitative_detail: Potential MLRP award cited as $10 million per subbasin
records.speaker_role: consultant — GSA consultant (inferred Geosyntec, working for Mid-Kings River GSA)
records.meeting_body: Kings County Water District Board of Directors
records.agenda_item: GSA / project funding discussion
records.evidence_text: The last thing I was going to mention is the additional funding. Is the mlrp, the multi benefit land repurposing. So the potential that's $10 million for a basin, or $10 million if you know some of the GSA don't want to participate, we can still split it amongst those who do, and to Larry lake. ... Maybe we can use some of that money to say, look, we're going to take some of that land out of production. We're going to come up with a fouling and we can fund that following program through that $10 million something like that.
records.notes: Subbasin inferred from 'Larry lake' (Tulare Lake) and the area 'south of 198'; GSA and speaker identity inferred from context, so attribution is uncertain.

records.finding: TLBWSD's staff review a county-circulated solar and battery project that would convert ag land in the floodplain, and the district plans a letter asking for a full EIR. Land conversion to energy is raised as a CEQA and water-use issue, not as an accounting question.
records.meeting_body: Tulare Lake Basin Water Storage District Board
records.agenda_item: County project notice / government affairs
records.evidence_text: Again, I think there's solar fields are through here and then some potential substations there. ... So again, they're going to convert some ag land.
records.notes: Project sponsor and acreage are not stated in the transcript; speaker unlabeled. Part of the transcript contains stray model prompt text; only the project description was used.

records.finding: El Rico's advisers say private recharge banking earns no allocation credit unless officially documented, for example a CEQA-approved bank or an MLRP project, and note that many MLRP-funded projects were recharge projects. The GSA is researching this.
records.agenda_item: Private water banking discussion (item 10.5)
records.evidence_text: Remember the mlrp program as it got that Department of Conservation started getting out a lot of the projects that were going to be part of the multi benefit land reproach program were recharge projects, ... you need some official documentation that you've gone through some either CEQA hoops or mlrp or a banking CEQA report that makes it a bank that works
records.notes: Speaker unlabeled; read as counsel or consultant. Second excerpt spans a line break in the transcript. This is not an adopted rule; the board said legal findings would come next month.

records.finding: Mid-Kings has a grower-led stakeholder advisory committee, open to the public, that drafts policy for the board. A board member said the board will approve policy brought to it by growers; staff also route public comments and vendor selection through the committee before the board decides.
records.meeting_body: Mid-Kings River GSA Board of Directors
records.agenda_item: Regular Calendar A: Stakeholder Advisory Committee update
records.evidence_text: one of the things, having the grower stakeholder committee, I mean, those are open to the public. ... We're not going to make the policy up here. We're going to prove the policy brought to us by the growers.
records.notes: Two speakers (the committee chair and a director) are joined; composition of the committee (growers versus residents or DAC members) is not described.

records.finding: South Fork Kings' well mitigation policy went through several revisions with its grower advisory committee and the board's advisory committee before the committee recommended it to the board, showing a committee step ahead of the board vote.
records.meeting_body: South Fork Kings GSA Board of Directors
records.agenda_item: Item 15: Well mitigation policy
records.evidence_text: the policy went through several revisions with the Wise View Committee, the Grower advisory committee and the board Advisory committee did recommend this version to take back to the board.
records.notes: The committee is a grower committee; no domestic-well-owner or DAC member is named. Transcript garbles the committee's name ('Wise View Committee').

records.finding: A resident who uses shallow water told the South Fork Kings board that his area has no representation; staff reported a JPA amendment to add two board seats signed by three of five member agencies. By June four of five had signed, with Empire West Side still tabling it.
records.quantitative_detail: 2 board seats proposed; 3 of 5 member agencies signed by 2026-05-22; 4 of 5 by 2026-06-19; unanimous JPA approval required
records.meeting_body: South Fork Kings GSA Board of Directors (public comment and staff update)
records.agenda_item: Public comment; JPA amendment status
records.evidence_text: in our area, when we use shallow water, we have nobody to represent those. ... We have three of the five JPA seats have signed the amendment to add two board seats.
records.notes: The commenter's statement is partly garbled and his area, and whether 'shallow water' means domestic wells, is not defined. Later staff describe the two seats as added for farmers in the northern part of the GSA, not for residents.

records.finding: Mid-Kings' stakeholder committee asked that the well mitigation program not be considered in isolation from the budget, and raised reaching renters; staff said they stepped back and added a separate funding presentation, and said they would also contact renters.
records.meeting_body: Mid-Kings River GSA Board of Directors
records.agenda_item: Regular Calendar B-C: Domestic Well Mitigation Program; Study Session on fees
records.evidence_text: That was one of the questions that the stakeholder committee kept asking is like, hey, you're asking us to talk about and approve a program, but it's being done a little bit in isolation. ... We do want to make sure we're reaching out to the renters as well
records.notes: Speaker is staff relaying committee input; the committee is largely growers (see 2025-11-18). The change is to process and presentation, not to a program term.

records.finding: Mid-Kings dropped a proposed 35-year well-age limit from its mitigation plan after advisory committee discussion and after State Water Board staff called age caps a non-starter in Tulare Lake. The board still asked about proration and repayment.
records.quantitative_detail: 35-year well-age limit proposed (EPA capital life 25 to 35 years cited) and removed; pilot of up to $360,000 approved the same day
records.meeting_body: Mid-Kings River GSA Board of Directors
records.agenda_item: Regular Calendar E: Updated well mitigation plan
records.evidence_text: we went back to the advisory committee and said, guys, we, we don't think this is going to fly. ... the state has rejected all of that and made it very clear that that's a non starter
records.notes: Contrast: Kings Subbasin GSAs under DWR kept a 50-year age limit; staff made that comparison here. The change followed state input and committee agreement, not public comment.

records.finding: South Fork Kings dropped the well-age limit after State Board staff called it a non-starter, and its grower committee asked for wording making landowners document that water quality worsened; the committee accepted the revised policy.
records.meeting_body: South Fork Kings GSA Board of Directors
records.agenda_item: Item 12: Well mitigation policy
records.evidence_text: We had a discussion with state water board, we mentioned that and it was a non starter with them. They made it clear. We then brought that back to the committee. We all felt like, hey, this is not the hill we want to die on. ... The BUR committee specifically asks us to add some language that, that talks about the fact that the landowner has some responsibility on the water quality as well. And they need to show us some supporting documentation that that water quality has gotten worse over the years before it would qualify for our eligible eligibility under this program.
records.notes: 'BUR committee' is read as the grower committee. The age-limit change followed state input; the water-quality change followed committee input.

records.finding: The same small-pumper exclusion was brought to the Tulare Lake Subbasin: staff recalled that at the Tule hearing board members directed staff to examine excluding small farms from probationary reporting fees. Staff found no unsupportive comment letters there.
records.quantitative_detail: About 1,058 extractors (about 44%) pump under 20 AF; Tulare Lake extractions about 549,000 AF vs sustainable yield 299,000 AF in water year 2022; 5 public comment letters

records.section: 3.1.4 Domestic Well Protection as an Equity Outcome
records.finding: Rural domestic wells would get emergency water and a replacement well, while community and municipal wells get only technical assistance up to a fixed dollar amount, not a new well. Impacts already fixed before the program, or before 2015, are not covered.
records.quantitative_detail: Technical assistance capped at $30,000 for community and municipal wells; eligible impacts from 2015-01-01
records.meeting_body: Mid-Kings River GSA Board of Directors
records.agenda_item: Regular Calendar B: Domestic Well Mitigation Program
records.evidence_text: The technical assistance track is intended for the other wells, the Community wells, the municipal wells and in that case we are just providing a technical assistance up to a fixed dollar amount ... To drill a brand new municipal well.
records.notes: This differential treatment is by well type (rural domestic vs community or municipal), not an analysis by DAC status; no DAC-versus-non-DAC comparison is presented.

records.section: 3.1.4 Domestic Well Protection as an Equity Outcome
records.finding: South Fork Kings staff tied domestic-well protection to threshold choice: because the plan lets levels fall below 2015 drought levels (about 30 feet in places), more wells will go dry and a mitigation plan is required; flat thresholds at today's levels might avoid it.
records.quantitative_detail: Minimum thresholds allow levels below 2015 drought levels by about 30 feet in some cases (speaker's recollection)
records.meeting_body: South Fork Kings GSA Board of Directors
records.agenda_item: Administrative Consultant Report: well mitigation
records.evidence_text:
because we are, in our plan, allowing the water levels to drop below the 2015 drought levels.

South Fork Kings GSA:
I think 30 feet in some cases. Um, you know, we know for a fact that more wells will go dry along the way.
records.notes: Staff do not break the impact down by DAC versus non-DAC; the link is between thresholds and the need for mitigation.

records.section: 3.1.4 Domestic Well Protection as an Equity Outcome
records.finding: South Fork Kings staff are asking Kings County to let the GSA review new well permits so that new wells, including domestic ones, are drilled below minimum thresholds. Otherwise the GSA could be liable to replace them if water levels drop.

records.evidence_text: the county would respect an ordinance or a resolution from. From this board, if we would put something together so that we could actually look at those well permits to make sure that. Um… that those wells are being drilled past our minimum thresholds?
records.notes: Domestic wells are named later in the same passage; a county policy example from the North Fork Kings area is mentioned but not described.

records.section: 3.1.4 Domestic Well Protection as an Equity Outcome
records.finding: State Water Board staff pressed Kaweah and Kern to quantify dry wells both per year and cumulatively, so South Fork Kings is modelling how many more wells go dry if thresholds are set lower; staff note most dry wells fall in South Fork and Mid-Kings.
records.meeting_body: South Fork Kings GSA Board of Directors
records.agenda_item: Item 11: Sustainable management criteria

So the state essentially said, yeah, you're going to allow so many wells to go dry in a year. Or we also want to put a limit on the total number of wells that go dry because you can't just 145 wells is still 145 households that have been impacted. ... between South Fork and Mid Kings, that's where the vast majority of the wells actually are located
records.notes: The '145' figure refers to a state example, not a South Fork count; the analysis is by threshold, not by DAC.

records.section: 3.1.4 Domestic Well Protection as an Equity Outcome
records.finding: South Fork Kings' policy treats rural domestic wells and community systems differently: domestic wells can get a replacement or other fix, while municipal, small community and industrial wells get technical assistance capped at $30,000 one time and no well drilled.

We're not doing, you know, we're not, we're not responsible for that. We basically say, look, all we're going to do is provide technical assistance to those communities or those agencies and limit that our exposure there to no more than $30,000. ... 30,000 is one time.
records.notes: Same structure as Mid-Kings. The comparison is by well type, not DAC status; no outcome analysis for disadvantaged communities is given.

records.finding: Mid-Kings outreach in spring 2026 combined one-on-one registration workshops, verification mailers, weekly emails, social media, and direct outreach to small communities, small water systems and schools. Reach is tracked: about 22 at a follow-up session, 420 on the email list, 250 Instagram followers.

records.meeting_body: Mid-Kings River GSA Board of Directors

Our email list now is up to 420 people which we're very happy to see that number growing. And our Instagram followers now are up to 250
records.notes: Second excerpt begins mid-sentence in the transcript; figures are verbal.

records.finding: Mid-Kings River GSA adopted a domestic well mitigation program (6 votes for) with two tracks: replacement or other physical fixes for rural domestic wells, and technical assistance capped at $30,000 for small community and municipal wells. Impacts must date from 2015 and be caused by pumping conditions.

records.meeting_body: Mid-Kings River GSA Board of Directors

Groundwater management activities for purposes of this Mitigation Program equate to GSA groundwater management policies. The Technical Assistance Track includes up to $$ 30,000$ reimbursement funding for grant application development, contingency planning, feasibility study, or well design. ... The impact must have occurred after January 1, 2015

we figured up to about 90 potential wells could go dry.

records.finding: South Fork Kings projected well mitigation costs from its threshold maps: 41 domestic wells would go dry, plus 7 already served by Self-Help, or 48 wells, at about $60,000 each over a three-year drought, roughly $960,000 per year, with a $1.2 million cap.

records.notes: Estimates are preliminary; transcript has the cap figure as '$1.2 million or $1.25'.

records.finding: Self-Help's programs turn some households away on income, but State Water Board staff told South Fork Kings that income limits are not allowed for GSA mitigation; if it is a GSA problem the GSA is responsible. This differs from the Kings Subbasin program, which has an income limit.

And I don't know the exact details on what their criteria are, but I know there are people that have applied with them and did not qualify because their income level is too high. ... the state board staff in discussions with Atule and with the KUIA sub basin have basically said no, you can't do income limitations on that. If it's a GSA problem, it's a GSA problem and you're on the hook.

records.finding: The consultant presenting the annual report told the board that interconnected surface water depletion does not apply to the Carpinteria basin, because the GSP found the creeks hydraulically disconnected from the aquifer, so there is no ISW threshold or management by the GSA.
records.agenda_item: Water year 2025 annual report presentation
records.evidence_text: Now note that in the Carpinteria groundwater basin, interconnected surface water depletions don't apply. The GSP was able to demonstrate that although we have surface water bodies in the basin, the creeks are one of the main sources of recharge to the basin. Those creeks are hydraulically disconnected from the aquifer system and therefore are not subject to management by the GSA or the GSP.
records.notes: Presenter is unnamed; role inferred from the annual report presentation. The disconnection finding is attributed to the GSP, not shown here.

records.finding: Answering a board question, the consultant tied the creek-aquifer disconnection to depth: a clay cap in the confined area limits communication with creeks, and creek beds sit above the water table, with 10 ft to 100+ ft of unsaturated zone. The consultant added that pumping can deplete streams where aquifers connect, but only the recharge area could be affected here.
records.quantitative_detail: Water table about 10 ft below creek bottoms in the shallowest places, 100 ft or more in upland areas (consultant's description, no date or source figure given)
records.agenda_item: Water year 2025 annual report presentation (board questions)
records.evidence_text: the only areas where creeks could be potentially affected by groundwater pumping is in that recharge area. Right. Because that clay cap in the confined Area limits any hydraulic communication between where the aquifers are and pumping that's going on there and the creeks. ... depending on where you are in the basin, the distance of that separation, you know, can vary between maybe as little as 10ft of separation to in the upland areas, you know, the water table is, you know, 100ft or more below the bottom of the creeks.
records.notes: Reasoning is conceptual; no seepage or depletion measurement is cited. The same passage mentions a garbled word ('thou wags', likely thalweg).

records.finding: Corning consultants weighed using the finer, nine-layer SVSIM or the four-layer C2VSim as the single regional model for demand-management scenarios and future interconnected surface water evaluation. And so we have one modeling platform that could be utilized for the entire region. And we're kind of thinking really on two primary fronts. Demand management. We know it's going to happen. There's going to be, there's going to be model scenarios that are needed to kind of run through these demand management scenarios and sort of, you know, whatever happens up in the Red Bluff sub basin is going to have an effect in the Corning sub basin. records.notes: Monitoring wells here serve the GSP generally, not specifically ISW; included because it is a funding mechanism for data-gap wells. Speaker is the district manager (unlabelled).

records.finding: After a director relayed residents' concerns that over-pumping is changing private-well water quality, a district speaker (unlabelled, counsel or manager) said the GSP is supply-oriented rather than quality-focused, the district has no obligation for private-well quality, and residents should consult the county health department.

records.notes: Speaker unlabelled (counsel or manager); the GSA's own water-quality monitoring network is not discussed in this exchange.

records.finding: Presenters hope groundwater and linked surface-water model outputs can feed the Lost Creek habitat mapping, but said the current modeling trajectory may not allow it, in which case the work would be done empirically.

records.finding: Presenters outlined how Lost Creek thresholds might be set: map habitat at high and low groundwater levels, then extrapolate downward to pick thresholds that mark an undesirable effect. No threshold exists yet.
records.speaker_role: mixed — United Water scientist and Stillwater consultant
records.meeting_body: Fillmore and Piru Basins Groundwater Sustainability Agency Board
records.agenda_item: 4C East Grove GDE status report and study plan

records.notes: Speaker is a consultant or United Water scientist; no name given for this answer.

records.finding: The GSA's East Grove GDE (Lost Creek) study, prompted by NMFS and CDFW comments on the draft GSP, tests whether pumping could affect rising groundwater that supports steelhead/rainbow trout habitat. FY2026 work added habitat typing, eDNA, snorkel surveys, temperature loggers and stage-discharge loggers; O. mykiss was detected by eDNA and one juvenile was observed.
records.quantitative_detail: One juvenile O. mykiss (about 6 inches) observed and eDNA detections at lower Lost Creek, FY2026 survey; run habitat 78%, riffle 19% of surveyed habitat units
records.speaker_role: consultant (Stillwater Sciences) and United Water staff
records.meeting_body: Fillmore and Piru Basins Groundwater Sustainability Agency Board
records.agenda_item: 4C Biological data gaps, East Grove GDE status report and study plan
records.evidence_text: Early drafts of the GSP receives comments from outside organizations, including the National Reef Fisheries Service and the California Department of Fish and Wildlife with regard to addressing potential data gaps and evaluating the potential for pumping effects on interconnected water that support groundwater dependent ecosystems. ... in this year's survey we actually detected Omicus in the EDNA surveys, that kind of the lower end of Lost Creek, the furthest downstream reaches.
records.notes: Transcript spells O. mykiss as 'Omicus'; East Grove GDE is described as near the Santa Paula Basin and is attributed here to Fillmore, but could touch Piru GDE work.

records.finding: Presenters said drought-year flow and habitat data are the missing piece for Lost Creek, and that it may take many years of dry conditions before the GSA can map habitat at the key low point. A presenter raised setting money aside so the GSA can act when those conditions arrive.
records.speaker_role: mixed — United Water scientist and Stillwater consultant
records.meeting_body: Fillmore and Piru Basins Groundwater Sustainability Agency Board
records.agenda_item: 4C East Grove GDE status report and study plan

Ultimately what this all kind of speaks to is that long term monitoring is needed or longer term approaches. ... it may be years, many years before we see conditions seed to a point where we get to that point of interest. We want to get out and map again. And so figuring out a way that this organization can have Money set aside to do that when conditions arise
records.notes: Two excerpts from the same discussion; speaker identity not named.

records.finding: Staff said the next scope of work will build a long-term Lost Creek monitoring plan, and a board member suggested sharing GDE and ISW monitoring costs across GSAs through a revived watershed committee (dues of about $500 to $1,000 a year were mentioned).

records.finding: The GSA's consultant told the board that DWR's long-awaited surface water-groundwater interaction guidance document has again been pushed back, now to fall 2026.

So there's a seat for the Tavium and Chumash if we can get somebody to participate.

records.section: 3.1.4 Domestic Well Protection as an Equity Outcome
records.finding: The GSA's consultant is preparing a domestic well drought vulnerability evaluation to be bundled as an appendix to the periodic evaluation, with no policy content. On 2026-09-17 he said release was delayed for further refinement. Whether it separates DAC from non-DAC wells is not said.
records.meeting_body: Fillmore and Piru Basins GSA Board of Directors
records.agenda_item: Consultant update (DBS&A) on technical documents
records.evidence_text: Draft reports are being prepared for the periodic evaluations, the domestic well drought vulnerability evaluation, and the land subsidence revised tech memo. ... There's no policy in there, so we thought we don't need to necessarily have the board consider it for adoption. At that point in time, you actually will end up adopting it because it will be an appendix in the periodic evaluations.
records.notes: Fillmore (4-004.05) and Piru (4-004.06) are both covered; the evaluation's method, data and findings are not described in any meeting examined; the 2026-05-21 agenda lists a DBS&A presentation (item 4D) but the transcript has no content on it; on 2026-09-17 the consultant said the evaluation 'is still in progress' and needed 'additional refinements' before release.

records.finding: A GSA speaker said stakeholder communication was cut short in the original GSPs because of COVID, noted that the basins have many lower-income and underrepresented people and that Prop 4 scoring gives points for them, and said DWR has money and a Glendale office to help with outreach to disadvantaged communities. The speaker doubted the public would engage.

records.finding: The general manager described, in words and without a map or numbers, where the Arroyo Seco river is and is not connected to groundwater: essentially not until near the Salinas River, because the river bed percolates so fast the watershed is separated from groundwater levels.
records.agenda_item: General manager's report: GSP five-year update
records.evidence_text: In fact, there's really no integrated surface water to speak of until we get closer to the Salinas River. Most of the watershed is separated from the groundwater elevation. Yeah. And the percolation rates are so high that it just pushes through. So it's really not integrated.
records.notes: Verbal characterisation only; no modelled or measured output is shown. A similar statement was made on 2026-09-22. Transcript garbles river names ('Aroma Cycle').

records.finding: The general manager said the GSP update for DWR's deficiencies on water quality and interconnected surface water needs plan amendments, with draft chapters out for review and a public hearing targeted for early January 2027; the manager also said a model used for the work still has errors.
records.quantitative_detail: GSP update due to the state end of January 2027; public hearing targeted for first week of January 2027
records.agenda_item: General manager's report: draft GSP update chapters
records.evidence_text: And remember there are, there are some modifications that were associated with deficiencies that the state had indicated we had in our gsp. Those being items on water quality and in the integrated surface water. So those will take amendments and those draft chapters and elements are out there for review.
records.notes: The content of the proposed ISW amendment is not described. The model with errors may be the Salinas Valley model shared with SVBGSA (case-study basin).

records.finding: The same superposition runs show that turning off Forebay pumping increases flow by about 25,000 AF and flow from the Forebay into 180/400 by about 40,000 AF. The Coalition's consultant agreed upstream pumping mainly reduces Salinas River flow but argued this should not be called an impact on water availability.
records.quantitative_detail: Forebay pumping off, average 1980-2022: flow +~25,000 AF (as stated); flow Forebay to 180/400 +~40,000 AF
records.speaker_role: mixed — Bob Abrams (consultant to Salinas Basin Water Alliance) and Dwight Smith (consultant to Salinas Valley Water Coalition), interpreting M&A model runs
records.agenda_item: 2.1 Interbasin Flow Modeling Results
records.evidence_text: Moving on to the four bay, you see a similar thing. Turn off pumping in the four bay flow increases by about 25,000 acre feet. And flow between the four bay and the 18400 increases by about 40,000 acre feet. ... The biggest things affecting is flows in the Salinas River. However, it should not be characterized as an effect to availability.
records.notes: Whether the 25,000 AF figure is river or groundwater flow is unclear in the transcript, and staff said the runs will not be used directly in GSP work.

records.finding: Grant-funded ISW monitoring wells were screened at the water table and placed near stream gauges or MCWRA river-series sites so groundwater levels can be related to river flow: three were added in the Forebay and an older ISW well was replaced because it sat too far from the river. Staff said this fills the ISW network's data gaps.
records.quantitative_detail: 3 ISW wells added in the Forebay and 2 in the Upper Valley; 1 Forebay ISW well replaced
records.speaker_role: mixed — GSA staff and M&A presenters (no speaker labels)
records.meeting_body: SVBGSA Forebay and Upper Valley Aquifer Subbasin Committees (joint special meeting)
records.agenda_item: 4.2 Periodic Evaluation - New Information Collected/Data Gaps Filled
records.evidence_text: So these were for interconnected surface water. So for these we were really trying to screen right about where the water table is. That was the goal. And trying to locate them close to either screen gauges or where Water Resource Agency does a river series. So we can look at that relationship between groundwater levels and river or stream. So there were three added to the forebay, two added to the upper valley. We also run from your network in the Fore Bay. It was a bit far from the river to monitor what we wanted it to. So this mean well replaced it. Yeah. So these fill all of your data gaps for those two monitoring networks.
records.notes: Joint meeting with unlabeled speakers; 'screen gauges' is a transcription garble of stream gauges.

records.finding: The Arroyo Seco GSA manager said Forebay GDEs have only been identified, with no monitoring or assessment of extraction impacts, and that the state has given no ISW guidance. He warned guidance could become an unfunded mandate to restrict pumping and said Russian River approaches do not fit the reservoir-managed Salinas.
records.speaker_role: GSA staff — Curtis Weeks, General Manager, Arroyo Seco GSA
records.meeting_body: Arroyo Seco GSA Board of Directors
records.agenda_item: General Manager's report
records.evidence_text: The one that I'm concerned about is the whole discussion about integrated surface water and groundwater dependent ecosystems. You guys have heard me, I know I'm a broken record, but the state still hasn't provided guidance to us about what that means. And at its worst it could be an unfunded mandate to protect habitat by restricting pumping in areas. ... We have been participants in the GDE work thus far. ... But nevertheless, you know, we just have kind of identified where they are. We haven't talked about monitoring or if they have any impacts due to groundwater extractions, what that might look like in terms of management.
records.notes: Secondary meeting (Arroyo Seco GSA co-adopts the Forebay GSP); on 2026-09-22 the same manager said the Arroyo Seco River is not interconnected until near the Salinas confluence.

records.finding: The Arroyo Seco GSA general manager said DWR has not issued ISW guidance in five years, that every basin differs, and that the GSA has therefore taken on providing more detail itself in its GSP update, for the Arroyo Seco Cone.
records.quantitative_detail: DWR guidance said to have been awaited for five years (as of June 2026)
records.agenda_item: General manager's report: GSP five-year update
records.evidence_text: Integrated surface water is a difficult thing for the DWR to, to come to grips with in terms of how do they write guidance. We've been waiting for guidance for five years. ... And we've yet to receive direction. So we have taken upon ourselves to provide more detail, go into a little bit more look
records.notes: Transcript has no speaker labels; the general manager is inferred from the report format and the triage summary. Basin attribution to the Forebay (Arroyo Seco Cone) relies on the speaker's remarks.

records.finding: The framework warns that land repurposing may move crop production and contracts to other parts of the Salinas Valley instead of reducing overall production, and that a fallow bank only cuts pumping if crop contracts do not shift elsewhere. It names this leakage but sets no rule to prevent it.
records.agenda_item: F1/F2. Salinas Valley Basin GSA Demand Management Framework (Oct 2025)
records.evidence_text: Land repurposing incentivizes land to come out of agriculture in some areas. This will affect the market for crops, contracts, and land. As such, this program may not reduce overall agricultural production but instead shift where it occurs within the region. ... Market forces are likely to push contracts toward other parts of the Salinas Valley where land and water remain available. ... Fallowing agricultural land directly reduces pumping if crop contracts on that land do not shift to other areas in the Valley.
records.notes: Text is from the SVBGSA Demand Management Framework (October 2025) included in the Arroyo Seco GSA board packet; the Framework covers the whole Salinas Valley (including the 180/400-Foot subbasin) and does not activate any measure, so it describes options, not practice in the Forebay.

records.finding: The framework says the existing county pumping systems (GEMS and the new Groundwater Monitoring Program) record only wellhead pumping and may not suit a fallow bank because they cannot show savings at field or parcel level. It also says fallow banks work better where accounting is defined.
records.agenda_item: F1/F2. Salinas Valley Basin GSA Demand Management Framework (Oct 2025) - fallow bank feasibility
records.evidence_text: GEMS or the new GMP may not be suitable because it only tracks pumping at the well head and this limits the ability to measure groundwater savings at the field or parcel level. ... Fallow banks can be implemented in areas without a groundwater accounting system, but are more effective in areas with defined accounting because it is easier to measure groundwater savings.
records.notes: Text is from the SVBGSA Demand Management Framework (October 2025) included in the Arroyo Seco GSA board packet; the Framework covers the whole Salinas Valley (including the 180/400-Foot subbasin) and does not activate any measure, so it describes options, not practice in the Forebay.

records.finding: A scope of work for Arroyo Seco GSA's demand management asks, as open governance questions, how a pumping reduction would be quantified and verified (against each user's historical baseline, or by fallowing a set amount of land) and whether voluntary reducers should be paid, as under USDA's CRP.
records.agenda_item: F1. Scope of work to integrate demand management into the SMC-TAC annual review
records.evidence_text: How should a reduction in pumping be quantified and verified? By comparison with a historical baseline of pumping by each user? By fallowing a certain amount of land? ... If voluntary, should people who reduce pumping be compensated financially by those who do not? This is somewhat analogous to USDA’s Conservation Reserve Program. ... M&A found no correlation between historical pumping and historical water levels
records.notes: Scope drafted by the GSA's consultant; the pumping-correlation finding is the consultant's and concerns the Upper Valley/Forebay. Whether the board adopted the scope is outside this excerpt (it was item F1 on 2026-01-28).

records.finding: The framework proposes a groundwater 'bank account' accounting system, by subbasin and by parcel, well or user, to credit, debit and track water use and to quantify pumping reductions from demand management measures such as fallowing. Components and methods are left to future SVBGSA workplans.
records.agenda_item: F1/F2. Salinas Valley Basin GSA Demand Management Framework (Oct 2025)
records.evidence_text: A water accounting system is like a bank account and ledger for water, and in particular groundwater. ... Quantify reductions in pumping achieved through DM measures. ... The components of the water budget, tracking system and methods, and approach would be defined as part of future DM measure policies and programs, as specified in future SVBGSA workplans.
records.notes: Text is from the SVBGSA Demand Management Framework (October 2025) included in the Arroyo Seco GSA board packet; the Framework covers the whole Salinas Valley (including the 180/400-Foot subbasin) and does not activate any measure, so it describes options, not practice in the Forebay.

records.section: 2.5 Data Source and ET Product Choice
records.finding: The framework judges remote sensing and meters the best measurement options (remote sensing cheapest, meters more precise and consistent with MCWRA's GEMS system). It lists Salinas Valley limits on satellite ET: small mixed rotating fields, plastic mulch and coastal fog; remote sensing does not give total pumping. It names OpenET among providers.
records.agenda_item: F1/F2. Salinas Valley Basin GSA Demand Management Framework (Oct 2025) - measurement
records.evidence_text: Remotely sensed data does not represent total groundwater pumped. In the Salinas Valley, relatively small farm sizes with mixed and rotating crops also presents a challenge for remotely sensed data collection. In addition, the use of plastic mulches and the coastal fog is another challenge for remote sensing. ... the best approaches to measuring groundwater use generally remote sensing and meters. The former is the most cost effective, while the latter is more precise (when maintained correctly) and, importantly, consistent with the existing MCWRA GEMS system and new Groundwater Monitoring Program (GMP). ... OpenET, UCCE CropManage
records.notes: Text is from the SVBGSA Demand Management Framework (October 2025) included in the Arroyo Seco GSA board packet; the Framework covers the whole Salinas Valley (including the 180/400-Foot subbasin) and does not activate any measure, so it describes options, not practice in the Forebay. No local validation of an ET product against field measurement is reported. Basin-wide rule; not specific to repurposed land.

records.finding: The framework says repurposing projects with added public benefits (air and water quality, habitat, flood risk, open space) are often prioritized for supplemental grants, and restates DOC's MLRP rule that repurposed land must reduce groundwater use and deliver at least one additional benefit from a listed set.
records.agenda_item: F1/F2. Salinas Valley Basin GSA Demand Management Framework (Oct 2025)
records.evidence_text: Projects that provide additional public benefits—such as improved air and water quality, habitat creation, flood risk mitigation, or community open space—are often prioritized or eligible for supplemental grant funding. ... The repurposed land must reduce groundwater use and generate at least one additional benefit including employment opportunities, flood risk mitigation, habitat creation, recreation opportunities, renewable energy, tribal or cultural benefits, air quality improvement, water quality improvement, and/or soil quality enhancement.
records.notes: Text is from the SVBGSA Demand Management Framework (October 2025) included in the Arroyo Seco GSA board packet; the Framework covers the whole Salinas Valley (including the 180/400-Foot subbasin) and does not activate any measure, so it describes options, not practice in the Forebay. Tracking or quantifying co-benefits is not described.

records.finding: The framework says verification of a repurposing or fallow-bank programme typically uses remote sensing, site inspections and grower reporting, with the rules defining a monitoring process (site visits for visual inspection or satellite imagery). Enforcement uses fines.
records.agenda_item: F1/F2. Salinas Valley Basin GSA Demand Management Framework (Oct 2025)
records.evidence_text: Remote sensing, site inspections, and grower reporting are used to verify compliance. ... Define the process for monitoring to ensure that the parcels are repurposed according to the terms. This typically includes site visits for visual inspection, or satellite imagery can be used. ... Fines would be established to disincentivize noncompliance.
records.notes: Text is from the SVBGSA Demand Management Framework (October 2025) included in the Arroyo Seco GSA board packet; the Framework covers the whole Salinas Valley (including the 180/400-Foot subbasin) and does not activate any measure, so it describes options, not practice in the Forebay.

records.finding: The framework says a land repurposing programme needs a stable funding source, from grants or, failing that, local fees or the general fund that need stakeholder support. It names no funding plan for the Forebay or Upper Valley.
records.agenda_item: F1/F2. Salinas Valley Basin GSA Demand Management Framework (Oct 2025)
records.evidence_text: Funding. A land repurposing program requires a stable source of funding. This can come from grant programs. If grant programs are not available it would come from local sources (e.g., general fund or fees), which require support from stakeholders.
records.notes: Text is from the SVBGSA Demand Management Framework (October 2025) included in the Arroyo Seco GSA board packet; the Framework covers the whole Salinas Valley (including the 180/400-Foot subbasin) and does not activate any measure, so it describes options, not practice in the Forebay.

records.finding: The framework notes that fallow agricultural land still needs management against weeds, pests and dust, and that these costs are typically paid under a fallow bank programme. It does not say how dust would be measured or controlled.
records.agenda_item: F1/F2. Salinas Valley Basin GSA Demand Management Framework (Oct 2025)
records.evidence_text: Fallow agricultural land still requires management to prevent weeds, pests, dust, and other issues. Land repurposing avoids widespread unmanaged fallowing. ... Fallow agricultural land still requires management to prevent weeds, pests, dust, and other issues. These costs are typically paid as part of a fallow bank program.
records.notes: Text is from the SVBGSA Demand Management Framework (October 2025) included in the Arroyo Seco GSA board packet; the Framework covers the whole Salinas Valley (including the 180/400-Foot subbasin) and does not activate any measure, so it describes options, not practice in the Forebay. The same sentence appears for both the land repurposing and fallow bank sections; the only dust reference in this scope tied to fallowed land.

records.finding: A demand management framework in Arroyo Seco GSA's packet lists targeted land repurposing and fallow-bank programmes as options, citing DOC's MLRP (about $10M block grants per subbasin), DWR LandFlex, Madera's Voluntary Land Repurposing Program and IID fallowing. It describes land repurposing as voluntary, bid-based and needing careful accounting of groundwater savings.
records.quantitative_detail: MLRP block grants of about $10 million per subbasin (framework's description, statewide); LandFlex block grants about $10 million to SJV GSAs
records.agenda_item: F1/F2. Salinas Valley Basin GSA Demand Management Framework (Oct 2025) - land repurposing and fallow bank measures
records.evidence_text: Land repurposing is voluntary, typically solicits interest through a defined bid, offer, or solicitation package, and includes careful accounting to measure resulting groundwater savings. ... MLRP is a grant program that covers the cost of transitioning agricultural lands to less water intensive uses that also provide other co-benefits. Block grants of approximately $$ 10$ million were awarded to subbasin across the state, and each subbasin is developing its own local land repurposing program. ... LandFlex was a DWR grant program that offered growers payments to idle land for one year, remove any trees/vines, and forgo any overdraft allocation (sometimes called supplemental water allocation) on those lands for all future years. ... The VLRP is a fallow bank program that was developed, in concept, in the GSP and then refined and implemented as part of GSP implementation.
records.notes: Text is from the SVBGSA Demand Management Framework (October 2025) included in the Arroyo Seco GSA board packet; the Framework covers the whole Salinas Valley (including the 180/400-Foot subbasin) and does not activate any measure, so it describes options, not practice in the Forebay. The SVBGSA, not Arroyo Seco GSA, authored the framework.

records.finding: Arroyo Seco's general manager walked the board through agricultural demand-management measures and said fallow or land banking is best done at subbasin scale, and land repurposing (he cited the Williamson Act as an analogy) 'needs to be developed'. He said the how has not yet been addressed.
records.agenda_item: Demand management framework briefing
records.evidence_text: following land and a land banking program gets kind of the next level up. That's actually going in and thinking about how we might use less water in a larger area like a sub base. And that's probably best implemented as sub basin scale, ... Land repurposing. You know, thinking about what that looks like, I think Williamson act is a, you know, something that kind of pops into my mind where a agricultural guy once upon a time ago says, I'm going to give up my development rights and just grow crops for a reduced tax burden. Right, that's, that's a re. Land repurposing to you. So I'm not going to, I'm not going to grow houses or condominiums. I'm going to grow. Well, now we got to think about do we have different kind of crops, do we repurpose that land? You know, do we put it into, you know, a fallow setting? I, you know, that needs to be developed. ... this is a what we haven't, haven't got to the how yet.
records.notes: Speaker is the board's general manager (unnamed in the transcript excerpt); 'following' stands for fallowing in the machine transcript.

records.finding: Arroyo Seco GSA's manager said its advisory committee has existed since about 2017 with uneven participation, so staff drew up a roster of seven regular participants, including a city member, Clark Colony, and two board members, staffed by GSA and city staff. records.agenda_item: Approval of Arroyo Seco GSA Advisory Committee roster

records.finding: Arroyo Seco GSA's manager recalled earlier demand-management workshops, one or two held in Greenfield, in which participants role-played trade-offs among strategies. The framework had moved from concepts to a draft needing board direction.

records.finding: For DWR's corrective action the SMC Technical Advisory Committee reviewed nitrate trends in Forebay and Upper Valley wells: 23 of 51 were rising, but trends showed no significant correlation with groundwater levels or extraction, so the analysis sent to DWR will show no basis for managing pumping to manage nitrate.
records.quantitative_detail: 51 wells with nitrate data: 23 increasing, 13 decreasing, 15 no trend; nitrate data from GAMA and the irrigated lands program
records.meeting_body: SVBGSA Sustainable Management Criteria Technical Advisory Committee (Forebay and Upper Valley)
records.agenda_item: 4.2 Water Quality Action Levels
records.evidence_text: So, uh, 23 of the 51 wells that have. Nitrate data have increasing trends in nitrate. ... We see increases in nitrate concentrations are not significantly correlated to changes in groundwater levels. And increases in nitrate concentrations are not significantly correlated to average annual extraction.
records.notes: Covers Forebay and Upper Valley (3-004.05), hence MULTI; on June 12, 2026 the joint Forebay/Upper Valley meeting heard nitrate and gross alpha results with no significant relationships and a recommendation for periodic reassessment.

records.finding: An IID board speaker (unlabelled; a director or water manager) said the only fallowing in the district is a temporary solar fallowing programme for county-permitted solar fields, and that a QSA provision lets IID claim that water so it stays available if the fields return to production. records.quantitative_detail: Deficit irrigation programme (a separate temporary programme) had about 75,000 acres left, winding down within about two weeks (September 2026)

There is a QSA legislative loophole that lets us claim that water. And for good reason, because at some point in time, if those fields go back into production, we want to make sure that that water is then available for their use. So it's not IID-directed fallowing.

records.finding: IID staff reported 2025 conservation of almost 714,000 AF against about 470,000 AF of transfer obligations, with the surplus left in Lake Mead. The mix includes canal lining, solar fallowing, deficit irrigation and an on-farm efficiency programme, and staff called the 9.15 million AF cumulative total 'documented, verified'. The verification method is not described.
records.quantitative_detail: About 470,000 AF obligations and almost 714,000 AF generated in 2025 (speaker's 'last year'); excess over 243,000 AF; on-farm efficiency a little over 196,000 AF; valley deliveries 2.187 million AF; cumulative over 9.15 million AF since 2003
records.agenda_item: Water conservation program annual update
records.evidence_text: we had about 470,000 acre feet of conservation obligations to fulfill for the various transfers. The Cotella Valley Water District transfer was at 98,000. But we ended up generating almost 714,000. And that excess conservation of over 243,000 will be left in Lake Mead to add elevation ... So our total is now over 9.15 million acre feet generated of documented, verified conservation since 2003.

records.finding: The draft Langley GSP amendment adds Management Action 5, a study of rural-residential well mitigation.
