records.finding: Las Posas Valley allocation transfers need Watermaster approval and a finding of no material injury, must be within the basin, and cannot be made by domestic users. Staff said there was no active water market or facilitation mechanism, only a service list of rights holders.
records.quantitative_detail: Transfer requests due 2025-10-31 for year-end closeout; about 56% of rights holders held carryover at end of water year 2023
records.meeting_body: FCGMA Board of Directors (also Las Posas Valley Watermaster)
records.agenda_item: Overuse, carryover and transfers update (Las Posas Valley)
records.evidence_text: We do not have an active water market at this point in time. So, the agency does not, nor does Water Master, have a mechanism. That, uh, to facilitate that. ... A domestic user may not transfer their allocation. They may receive a transfer, but they may not transfer their allocation. Uh, all the transfers must be. Within the basin. So, both the transferring party and the receiving party must be. Within LPV. ... We must find that there is no material injury or undesirable condition caused by the transfer.
records.notes: Transfers are of annual allocation for overuse cures, not tied to land repurposing; the Oct 22 date is the board debate on the transfer deadline. Basin-wide rule; not specific to repurposed land.

records.finding: Staff said unused allocation can be carried over, capped at 150% of a holder's allocation with carryover sunsetting after five years; a director said the agency's earlier credit system let some holders accumulate 'massive' amounts and a carryover must not recreate that.
records.quantitative_detail: Carryover cap 150% of annual allocation; sunset after 5 years (staff recalled, 'I'd have to check'); 56% of rights holders in carryover and 17% in overuse at end of water year 2023
records.meeting_body: FCGMA Board of Directors (also Las Posas Valley Watermaster)
records.agenda_item: Overuse, carryover and transfers update (Las Posas Valley)
records.evidence_text: A carryover, which is a word, but it is equal to the word credit. And I'm not looking to reinstitute. Credits, but the credit process that we had at this agency allowed certain entities. To amass, massive amounts of credits. ... if it sunsets after 5 years, so you don't get to… doesn't get to last perpetually. And in fact, if the… if… I would also add that the max that any one water right holder can accrue is 150% of their allocation.
records.notes: Sunset period was stated tentatively by staff; speaker roles are inferred without labels. Basin-wide rule; not specific to repurposed land.

records.finding: By July 2026 staff said there was still no Watermaster water market but one was being considered, while a private Las Posas Valley water market already connected buyers and sellers with transfers subject to Watermaster approval. Staff said pricing was the main difficulty.
records.quantitative_detail: Overuse cure transfers for water year 2024 due 2026-10-01; 140 water-right accounts (WY2023) and 141 (WY2024); 22 of 141 WY2024 accounts (about 15.6%) could not be calculated for lack of reports (transcript figures garbled, so approximate)
records.meeting_body: FCGMA Board of Directors (also Las Posas Valley Watermaster)
records.agenda_item: 20. Update on carryover, overuse and transfers
records.evidence_text: Watermarket does not have an active water market. That is something that we're actively looking into and like to develop. ... There's also another option which is the Las Cosas Valley Water Market, which is a private water market, which connects sellers and buyers. Again, it's a private thing that's happening out there. Watermaster still has oversight or transfers are still subject to Watermaster for approval. ... I think what people are struggling with is I'd say the pricing of the water. Nobody knows what price to pay for water.
records.notes: 'Watermarket' and 'Las Cosas Valley Water Market' are transcription errors; the Sept 2025 statement and this one differ only in a private market now being named. Basin-wide rule; not specific to repurposed land.

records.section: 2.5 Data Source and ET Product Choice
records.finding: FCGMA approved a $62,240 consultant pilot in its groundwater accounting platform for Las Posas Valley to compare meter (AMI) data, self-reports and ET estimates, with the aim that ET and AMI replace self-reporting. No ET product is named.
records.quantitative_detail: $62,240 contract, about 6 months; about 80% of reports in a month after the deadline
records.meeting_body: FCGMA Board of Directors (also Las Posas Valley Watermaster)
records.agenda_item: 14. Contract with Environmental Science Associates, groundwater accounting pilot (Las Posas Valley)
records.evidence_text: because we've moved to a parcel based system within lpv, it allows the ready use of evapotranspiration data because that is all delivered from the providers, at least all the ones I've ever seen delivered on a parcel basis ... the key cross source analysis to compare our AMI data to what's self reporting, to compare metered extraction to the ET estimates and to compare allocation usage to water availability. The intent of this is to provide multiple sources of extraction data, AMI self reported and et.

records.finding: In the Las Posas Valley Watermaster process the judgment sends the draft Basin Optimization Plan and yield study to the Policy Advisory Committee (PAC) for review before board adoption, and staff respond in writing to every PAC and TAC comment. A director asked that staff flag where the PAC agrees or disagrees.
records.agenda_item: Item 22 (Las Posas Valley draft Basin Optimization Yield Study); PAC/TAC discussion
records.evidence_text: the judgment calls for the draft Basin Optimization plan and yield study to come before the PAC for review and comment to then inform the revisions and presentation ultimately to the board for adoption. And that has happened. We have reviewed a draft and submitted our comments. Those comments are structured such that we kind of synthesize them into a handful of key themes, but then also include a table of every detailed comment that each PAC member submitted to the PAC for discussion and on prior occasions, the Basin optimization plan. The annual report staff has been very receptive to those, to that approach, and they have responded to every comment that PAC and TAC have made. ... Can I ask one thing is in the information that you provide us to just make a note that the PAC intact, what they agree with or don't agree with. I think that's good that it's just one more reference point that people know we're listening to them and that we agree or something.
records.notes: Speaker is the PAC vice chair per self-introduction (Rob Grether); the PAC is a Watermaster body, so this is the Las Posas Valley Basin (4-008) rather than Oxnard; the PAC and its Technical Advisory Committee (TAC) are Watermaster stakeholder bodies of Las Posas Valley water-right holders, not community or DAC committees; the board request was by an unnamed director.

records.finding: Distributive equity: Watermaster put to its Policy Advisory Committee whether water-right holders who already pay United Water Conservation District assessments should be exempted or given a reduction on Las Posas project assessments. The board directed staff to carve them out of only the imported-water Project 2 costs; the PAC proposed 500 AF of deliveries and the board set 1,000 AF with FCGMA funding half.
records.quantitative_detail: 1,000 AF/year of imported water in the first year; PAC recommended 500 AF; FCGMA funds about half (500 AF); projected annual Watermaster revenue need about $2.3 million (FY 2026-27)
records.agenda_item: LPV Watermaster FY 2026-27 budget and basin assessments
records.evidence_text: One was to basically put equity question judgment 7.9 before the PAC and they have their recommendation report which is exhibit 19C. The second part was to have incorporate that feedback following the board's direction and further develop the drug budget. And then we also got another recommendation. So in exhibit C I'm just going to summarize this the recommendation we submitted this for consultation and we asked I think two questions really which was as a matter of equity to the water right holders in the United Water Conservation District. Pay an assessment to your United Water Conservation District the exempt from project assessments and if so if they should have a reduction how much that reduction should be. ... your board directed that we examine water right holders in United Water Conservation District service area from the cost of only Basin Optimization Project 2 which is the purchase of imported water from Cuyagis.
records.notes: The affected parties are pumpers inside and outside the UWCD service area, not DACs; the transcript is garbled in places ('PAD', 'Cuyagis' for Calleguas) and the staff speaker swaps assessment figures, so per-acre-foot amounts are not used; the 2025-09-24 meeting introduces the equity question as concerns raised by Las Posas water-right holders about duplicative fees.

The consultant said mountain-front recharge is a placeholder, a 10-year average from the 2020 model, until the next model; he agreed replacement would help and a letter from the three GSAs would not hurt.

records.agenda_item: 8. Mission Creek Subbasin Annual Report for Water Year 2425
records.evidence_text: on page 25 it's discussing about how the Hillary storm destroyed the stream gauge and that both United States Geological Survey as well as the Riverside County Flood Control and Water Conservation District have no intentions of replacing that stream gauge. ... we used the groundwater model that we did in 2020 for the 2021 alternative update, and we took an average of that over 10 years. And it's kind of a placeholder until we do the next model, which we're working on now, and then we'll actually get actual numbers for that and replace them. records.section: 3.3.3 Domestic Wells and Community Water System Consolidation
records.finding: Mission Springs staff presented a State Water Board grant request to consolidate the CVWD Improvement District 8 domestic water system, whose four wells exceed the hexavalent chromium limit. Staff cited $25 million to treat at the wells or $40 million to connect, up to $85 per month per customer, and said the action is not a divestiture decision.
records.quantitative_detail: Four wells at 10.4 to 12.5 ppb hexavalent chromium vs 10 ppb limit; $25 million (treatment) or $40 million (connection); up to $85 per month per customer
records.agenda_item: 10. Resolution 2026-03: State Water Board funding agreement for consolidation of the ID8 domestic water system
records.evidence_text: The four wells all have Chrome 6 ranging between 10.4 to 12.5, which is above the California's 10 parts per billion standard for hexavalent chromium. The cost to comply with the state standards is $25 million if they were due treatment at the well locations or if they were to connect to the main system with $40 million. With $40 million of capital improvements, the treatment could cost up to $85 per month per customer. ... the action presented to the MSWD board is a grant funding request and not to be viewed as a decision on the ID8 divestiture or annexation. Any possible ID8 divestiture or annexation effort will be initiated by CBWD.
records.notes: Subbasin is the index default for MSWD; ID8 (Desert Edge, Sky Valley, Indio Hills) may overlie more than one subbasin; 'CBWD' is CVWD in the transcript.

records.finding: The Modesto water budget model has been developed and extended for about eight to ten years; the water year 2025 update only extends it, with no recalibration, and a more detailed refinement is planned in the periodic evaluation.
records.quantitative_detail: Model in development about 8-10 years; extended through water year 2025
records.agenda_item: Water year 2025 annual report: model update
records.evidence_text: we are extending a lot of the time series and input files from the model that we have been developing over the past many years. I think we're, we're going on about eight to 10 years now that this model has been being continuously developed, revised, extended, improved. It's kind of a living model and we'd like to kind of continue that process. ... we do not make any fundamental changes to the model structure we parameters. This is not a recalibration. It is simply an extension of the previous model at this time.
records.notes: Item is the annual water budget update, not an ISW item as such; the same model is used for the ISW depletion work later (2026-08-12).

records.finding: STRGBA's consultant quantifies ISW depletion by differencing two runs of the GSA's numerical model: a baseline with all basin pumping turned off versus the historical run, plus a one-year pumping pulse to build a time-response curve. The model is named in other STRGBA documents as C2VSim.
records.quantitative_detail: Historical simulation period about 35 years; baseline run about 50 years (1969-2018 hydrology per 2026-09-23 agenda)
records.agenda_item: 2027 periodic evaluation and five year GSP update (topic: interconnected surface water)
records.evidence_text: And so that's exactly what we're doing. We're utilizing the model that we have available to us to be able to quantify and characterize the what, what do those depletions look like if there were no pumping, and what does that do to our stream system? ... So what we've done in this case is we've developed two different scenarios. On one hand, we're looking kind of at a, what we call a baseline. In this case, this a baseline, no pumping scenario, right? So effectively, what happens if we just turn off all the groundwater production in the basin, and effectively, we just simply just didn't meet the demand within it? Within the basin, we still have our surface water supply, we still have our urban centers, but we just don't supply any of those needs with applied water.
records.notes: Model name (C2VSimTM) comes from the 2026-07-08 and 2026-09-23 agendas, not from this transcript; presenter is Woodard & Curran.

records.finding: Model inputs named for streams: dam releases at Goodwin (Stanislaus) and La Grange (Tuolumne) set the river flow, with extra downstream flow points on the Tuolumne, Stanislaus and San Joaquin used to check calibration.
records.agenda_item: Water year 2025 annual report: model update
records.evidence_text: we also look at several state and federal agencies to estimate our stream flow and really govern what kind of water, particularly water that goes into the model here at Goodwin Dam and at Lagrange Dam. This is what feeds the Stanislaus and Tuolumne rivers. And so that we can input what that flow is. And in addition to that, we also make sure that we grab a couple data points here, further downstream, both along the Tuolumne, Stanislaus and even the San Joaquin rivers to make sure that the model is well calibrated right.
records.notes: Source agencies are described only generally as state and federal.

records.finding: Inputs to the GDE and ISW check named at the meeting: Nature Conservancy GDE polygons screened by depth to water within 30 ft, a field survey by a biologist at one ranch that removed some polygons, and model stream-node riverbed elevations.
records.quantitative_detail: GDE screen: depth to water within 30 ft; stream nodes about 0.5 mile apart
records.agenda_item: Periodic evaluation / GSP update: GDE analysis
records.evidence_text: started out with polygons from, they're called the NCOG polygons from the Nature Conservancy that had polygons throughout the sub basin. And we determined that in fall 2015. The potential GDEs vegetation and wetland GDEs are along river boundaries and the downstream reach of Dry Creek. And that's what you're seeing on the map. On the left, the red and the orange are the wetland and vegetation GDEs. The polygons that are left, these are potential GDEs. We don't know for sure that they all are. This was based on a paper study where we looked at potential GDEs in fall 2015 in areas with depth to water within 30ft, which is the potential rooting depths. ... The stream note invert elevations are coming from the model. There are stream nodes spaced about a half a mile apart along each of the rivers in the model.
records.notes: 'NCOG' in the transcript is likely TNC's NCCAG dataset (garbled); the field study covered only the far western subbasin.

records.finding: Model output shown to the board is a time-response curve for a single year of pumping: about 32% of the pumped volume ends up as stream depletion in the long run, with most of the rest filled by subsurface inflow. About 85% of depletion appears within 10 years and about 97% within 20 years.
records.quantitative_detail: 32% of pumped volume becomes stream depletion cumulatively (long-term, one-year pumping pulse); 85% of depletion within 10 years and 97% within 20 years of that pulse
records.agenda_item: 2027 periodic evaluation and five year GSP update (topic: interconnected surface water)
records.evidence_text: And so even on a long term basis, we see that approximately one third of the pumping volume that is taken out of the system, about 32% of whatever that volume is, is directly impacting the stream system. ... we can see about 97%, right. Or the vast majority of those depletions occur within a 20 years of a singular pumping event. And there is a kind of, you can see kind of here a breakdown here, right? So even within the first 10 years, we do still see the bulk of it, the 85%.
records.notes: Percentages are the presenter's spoken figures read off a chart.

records.finding: The sustainable-yield modelling uses three indicators the model can simulate, including depletion of interconnected surface water. Consultants report a revised yield of 235,000 AF/yr and say that, at that pumping level without new projects, there would be no undesirable results for storage, groundwater levels or ISW.
records.quantitative_detail: Sustainable yield 235,000 AF/yr (about 157,000 agricultural, about 78,000 urban) vs 267,000 AF/yr in the GSP; annual
records.agenda_item: 2027 periodic evaluation: sustainable yield
records.evidence_text: our focus for this conversation is to really target three of these six topics. The chronic lowering of groundwater levels, reduction in groundwater storage, and depletions of interconnected surface water. Fortunately, each of these three are very available in the modeling tools that we have. ... overall the total sustainable, sustainable yield of the sub basin is estimated 235,000 acre feet. ... So in the absence of projects, we will be able to meet our sustainability objectives. We were able to mitigate and have no undesirable results when it comes to aquifer storage, groundwater levels or interconnected surface water dynamics.
records.notes: The 'no undesirable results' statement for ISW has no ISW output figures behind it in this meeting; sustainable-yield runs cover the next 50 years.

records.finding: A consultant's project-scenario model output charts a decrease in the 'gain from stream' term, alongside higher groundwater storage, when about 65,000 AF/yr of projects are modelled. The meeting does not say whether that is read as less stream depletion, and no ISW threshold result is shown.
records.quantitative_detail: About 65,000 AF/yr of project yield at full buildout (about 2042)
records.agenda_item: 2027 periodic evaluation: project modelling
records.evidence_text: So we see an increase of groundwater storage in the aquifer and we see a decrease in the gain from stream which is represented in the in the blue bar.
records.notes: 'Gain from stream' direction is ambiguous in the transcript; the agenda says projects avoid ISW undesirable results absent new projects.

records.finding: Fall 2025 monitoring showed 3 of 8 Stanislaus River ISW wells (38%) below their minimum thresholds, above the 33% trigger, for the first fall exceedance on that river since fall 2022. An undesirable result still needs three consecutive fall exceedances, so none is declared.
records.quantitative_detail: Fall 2025: Stanislaus 3 of 8 wells (38%), Tuolumne 1 of 9 (11%), San Joaquin 0 of 2; spring 2026 (2026-05-13): Stanislaus 3 of 8 (38%), Tuolumne 3 of 10 (30%); 33% trigger on Stanislaus/Tuolumne, 50% on San Joaquin
records.agenda_item: Fall 2025 monitoring results and annual report
records.evidence_text: In the fall for interconnected surface water along the San Joaquin river, both wells had water levels above the minimum threshold, 0%. Along the Stenoslaus, three of the eight wells had water levels that were below the minimum threshold. And that's a 38% MT exceedance. So that's slightly above the 33% threshold, which is why that's highlighted pink. ... So this does not mean that we are in undesirable results because of the fall 2025 monitoring event. It just means that this is the first fall event that could potentially lead to undesirable results.
records.notes: Speaker is the GSA's technical lead presenting the water year 2025 monitoring update; spring 2026 results repeated at the 2026-05-13 board meeting.

records.finding: Staff and consultants analysed whether letting ISW-network water levels fall from the minimum threshold to the 2027 interim milestone would harm groundwater-dependent ecosystems, responding to a DWR recommended corrective action. Five wells (three on the Stanislaus, two on the Tuolumne) have interim milestones below their thresholds; the analysis found effects unlikely.
records.quantitative_detail: 5 ISW wells with 2027 IM below MT (3 Stanislaus, 2 Tuolumne); MT-to-IM drop 13-14 ft at two Stanislaus wells more than 1 mile from river
records.agenda_item: Periodic evaluation / GSP update: GDE analysis for temporary lowering below minimum thresholds
records.evidence_text: So what did we do for this analysis, we focused on the representative monitoring wells with 2027 IMS below MTS in the interconnected surface water monitoring network. Why in this network? Because they are along the GDEs that we know. The potential GDEs that we know of are along the rivers along the San Joaquin River. There are no representative monitoring wells that have IMs below MTs along the Stanislaus river three wells, and Tuolumne river two. ... Two wells that are more than a mile from the Stanislaus river have MT&IM elevations below the nearest stream node elevation. The Change in groundwater elevation from the MT to The IM is 13 or 14ft at these wells.
records.notes: Speaker is the GSA's technical lead (named Liz Elliott elsewhere in the transcript set); this transcript lacks labels. Transcript garbles the San Joaquin sentence; agenda confirms no San Joaquin wells.

records.finding: For the five-year update the consultant recommends keeping groundwater levels as the ISW proxy and the existing minimum threshold of about 57 ft (average across the ISW network), arguing model runs show it protects against exceeding the roughly 60,000 AF/yr historical depletion. The GSA does not have to reduce pre-2015 depletion, only avoid worsening it.
records.quantitative_detail: 60,000 AF/yr = modelled average annual stream depletion over the ~35-year historical simulation (full-pumping vs no-pumping runs), the pre-2015 condition the GSA must not worsen; minimum threshold about 57 ft (average groundwater level across ISW network); about 53-54 ft stated as sufficient for 60,000 AF/yr after a model-uncertainty adjustment; five pumping scenarios at 100/75/50/25/0% of existing pumping, groundwater levels range about 10-15 ft
records.agenda_item: 2027 periodic evaluation and five year GSP update (topic: interconnected surface water)
records.evidence_text: what we're going to recommend moving forward as part of the five year update is to continue to use groundwater levels as a proxy. ... we say if we're targeting that no more than that 60,000 acre feet of depletions, that we should be able to achieve that so long as the, the average groundwater level across our ISW wells is higher than about 53 or 54ft. ... 57ft here is this is what we have currently set as our groundwater level threshold for our ISW SMCs, right? This is what we currently are, this is what have, have been within the GSP for the past five years was at 57ft. And what we've were able to prove by utilizing this and some of the modeling tools that we have is that is that 57ft is protective. If as long as we kind of our groundwater levels across that ISW network average about 57ft, we are protective of the STRE system of that 60,000 acre foot target.
records.notes: The same talk gives about 53-54 ft as the average level needed to hold depletion to 60,000 AF/yr after a model-uncertainty adjustment, and 57 ft as the current threshold; the transcript does not reconcile the two. The AI summary says no board action was taken.

records.finding: The consultant reports a pumping-attributable stream depletion for the Modesto Subbasin of about 60,000 acre-feet per year on average over the historical simulation period, obtained by comparing the full-pumping run with the no-pumping run. This is a depletion figure, not total stream seepage.
records.quantitative_detail: About 60,000 AF per year, average over about 35-year historical period; scenario range about 55,000-65,000 AF per year (see ISW-1.8a)
records.agenda_item: 2027 periodic evaluation and five year GSP update (topic: interconnected surface water)
records.evidence_text: comparatively to a full, comparing a full and no pumping scenario, we can see that stream depletions are estimated under that historical period of about 60,000 acre feet per year on average across that, across that period.
records.notes: Presenter calls this the average historical depletion estimate; no per-river split is given in the transcript.

records.finding: Depletion is attributed to all pumping in the subbasin taken together: the no-pumping run switches off every groundwater supply in the basin. No pump counts, near-stream well sets or per-well attribution are mentioned.
records.quantitative_detail: About 32% of pumped volume depletes streams (long-term cumulative response, modelled, all subbasin pumping)
records.agenda_item: 2027 periodic evaluation and five year GSP update (topic: interconnected surface water)
records.evidence_text: So effectively, what happens if we just turn off all the groundwater production in the basin, and effectively, we just simply just didn't meet the demand within it? ... approximately one third of the pumping volume that is taken out of the system, about 32% of whatever that volume is, is directly impacting the stream system.
records.notes: The basin-wide reading follows from the no-pumping run switching off all groundwater production; the presenter does not discuss subsets of wells.

records.finding: STRGBA's consultant says stream depletion cannot be measured directly, so the GSA proposes to keep its network of ISW wells as a groundwater-level proxy and to use model runs to correlate those water levels with stream depletion.
records.agenda_item: 2027 periodic evaluation and five year GSP update (topic: interconnected surface water)
records.evidence_text: our recommendation again is to use the ground, the existing groundwater network as a proxy, continue to build on that, that ISW network and to make sure that we take that, you know, the data that we do have and we do have access to continue to use that monitor and then to be able to utilize the modeling to develop that correlation between stream depletions and the observed data that we have to estimate a defensible proxy.
records.notes: The proxy-justification model runs are described in the ISW-1.2 row; a direct measurement approach was explicitly set aside as outside the update's scope.

records.section: 1.5 Per-well Attribution and the Cumulative Pumping Problem
records.finding: At the MID board, a public commenter argued that the replenishment program's rule limiting it to parcels solely dependent on groundwater is awkward for ISW, because pumping on parcels next to the river is the source of ISW undesirable results in the Modesto GSP.
records.agenda_item: Groundwater Replenishment Program draft: public comment
records.evidence_text: So why that matters in the eyes of SGMA is because we have to watch the interconnected surface waters issue. The undesirable results that come from potentially pumping too much water from parcels that are adjacent to the river. And that is an issue in the GSP for the Modesto sub basin.
records.notes: Speaker is a consultant speaking for a grower ('I have a client'), so this is a commenter's view, not MID's; MID is a member of the Modesto GSA.

records.section: 1.5 Per-well Attribution and the Cumulative Pumping Problem
records.finding: The Modesto GSP sets the ISW undesirable-result trigger river by river: it occurs when 33% (Stanislaus, Tuolumne) or 50% (San Joaquin) of that river's representative wells exceed the minimum threshold in three consecutive fall events.
records.quantitative_detail: 33% of wells on Stanislaus and Tuolumne, 50% on San Joaquin, three consecutive fall events
records.agenda_item: Fall 2025 monitoring results and annual report
records.evidence_text: for interconnected surface water, an undesirable result will occur on one of the rivers when 33% to 50% of the representative monitoring wells for that river exceed the MT in three consecutive fall events, it's 33% on the San Jose and Tuolumne rivers and 50% on the San Joaquin.
records.notes: Transcript renders 'Stanislaus' as 'San Jose'; the agenda for 2026-03-11 confirms the river names.

records.section: 1.5 Per-well Attribution and the Cumulative Pumping Problem
records.finding: The ISW check is spatial: each monitoring well's minimum-threshold and interim-milestone elevations are compared with the model's nearest stream-node riverbed elevation and its distance from the river. The five wells sit roughly 4,000 to over 7,000 ft from the river.
records.quantitative_detail: Stream nodes about 0.5 mile apart; wells about 4,000-7,200 ft from river
records.agenda_item: Periodic evaluation / GSP update: GDE analysis
records.evidence_text: the distance from the well to the nearest stream node. And this is very important because you can see that These wells are 4,4000ft from the river. At the closest one, the furthest one is over 7,000ft.
records.notes: Speaker unlabelled; role inferred from the technical presentation. Stream nodes are in the model (C2VSimTM per agenda); transcript garbles '4,000 ft' as '4,4000ft'.

records.finding: In response, an MID speaker said the district has wrestled with ISW in many areas, does not fully understand how it works, and that much of the science is unproven, but treated the commenter's point as valid and a board policy question.
records.agenda_item: Groundwater Replenishment Program draft: board discussion
records.evidence_text: I think interconnected surface water is one of those things that we've wrestled with in a lot of areas. We don't quite understand how it all works. There's a lot of science that's unproven out there
records.notes: Speaker unlabelled (possibly district counsel or the general manager); role guessed.

records.finding: Two representative monitoring wells in the combined network, one of them also in the ISW network, could not be measured for several years because of casing obstructions.
records.quantitative_detail: 2 of 59 representative wells unmeasured, fall 2025
records.agenda_item: Fall 2025 monitoring results and annual report
records.evidence_text: Two of the wells were not measured because they had casing obstructions. And this has been the case for several years now.
records.notes: The sentence covers the 59-well network for both indicators; the well named as also in the ISW network comes later in the same presentation.

records.finding: GSA technical staff say there is little monitoring data right next to the rivers, which is where the groundwater-dependent ecosystems are, and call it a data gap that DWR accepted in the revised GSP.
records.agenda_item: Periodic evaluation / GSP update: GDE analysis
records.evidence_text: But we also said there's uncertainty. We don't have a lot of data right next to the river. Right. This is a data gap that we have. We don't have a ton of data next to the rivers.
records.notes: Speaker unlabelled; role inferred. No fix, funding or schedule for adding near-river wells is stated at this meeting.

records.finding: The consultant acknowledges that a full stream-by-stream measurement of flows, diversions and inflows is not feasible in this planning cycle: stage, flow and diversion data for every diverter would be a very large lift beyond the scope and timeline of the five-year update.
records.agenda_item: 2027 periodic evaluation and five year GSP update (topic: interconnected surface water)
records.evidence_text: And first and foremost, it is not possible to directly measure stream depletions. And obviously, as we've been doing over the past several years now, groundwater levels can be measured. ... We could measure all flows, all diversions from every, you know, diverter, riparian user. We can and also look at every, you know, inflow to the system to really heavily understand the dynamics within the system and create an estimate. But with that, that is a huge lift and the amount of data and analysis that would need to go into that would be, is well beyond kind of the scope and timeline of this, this five year update.
records.notes: This is a stated scope limitation, not a funding amount; no plan to remedy it is given.

records.finding: GSA staff replaced the two obstructed monitoring wells with new wells starting with the spring 2026 event, with thanks to MID for helping locate replacements.
records.quantitative_detail: 2 replacement wells for 2 obstructed wells (spring 2026 event)
records.agenda_item: Fall 2025 monitoring results and annual report
records.evidence_text: And since the fall event, we have found replacement wells for these. So starting during the spring 2026 event, which took just a couple weeks ago, both Wood and Cuisine Berry have been removed and the replacement wells have been added
records.notes: Well names are garbled in the transcript; no cost given.

records.finding: Uncertainty is shown as scenario bounds: if neighbouring subbasins set lower or higher thresholds, average depletion runs about 55,000 to 65,000 AF/yr around the 60,000 central figure. The curve linking water levels to depletion is also shifted by a correction factor from modelled versus observed data.
records.quantitative_detail: Depletion about 60,000 AF/yr (central), about 65,000 AF/yr (neighbours at lower levels), about 55,000 AF/yr (neighbours at measurable objectives); annual averages
records.agenda_item: 2027 periodic evaluation and five year GSP update (topic: interconnected surface water)
records.evidence_text: So this is kind of more of a worst case scenario where we average about 65,000 acre feet. If our neighbors have particularly low water levels on the other hand, I've also run other scenarios where if our, our neighbors are up at their measurable objectives, what does that look like in that? In any case it drops about 55,000. But you know, overall we're in a pretty, a pretty tight response. Right. They all float around that 60,000 acre foot mark, plus or minus a few thousand acre feet. ... we certainly want also want to make sure that we acknowledge that there is uncertainty with any model. And so what we've done is we've done a slight adjustment of Kind of looking at modeled, modeled data versus observed data and we've kind of drawn kind of this, a correlation factor to kind of shift or adjust our this curve to be able to account for that model uncertainty.
records.notes: Neighbour scenarios concern the shared Stanislaus (Eastern San Joaquin side) and Tuolumne (Turlock side) boundaries; the correction factor value is not stated.

records.finding: The ISW depletion result is being turned into proposed GSP language, but at this meeting the board only gave feedback and no action was taken. The loop from the 60,000 AF/yr estimate to an adopted threshold and policy depends on the later GSP amendment.
records.quantitative_detail: Historical average depletion estimate about 60,000 AF/yr proposed for adoption; threshold about 57 ft
records.agenda_item: 2027 periodic evaluation and five year GSP update (topic: interconnected surface water)
records.evidence_text: we're also looking for feedback here across the, from the gsa. And then we, our goal is to kind of, after we had that conversation, to be able to draft this language for the gsp, the periodic evaluation and the GSP amendment.
records.notes: 'No board action was taken' comes from the AI summary, not the transcript; the transcript shows the consultant seeking feedback ahead of drafting.

records.finding: A Stanislaus County Department of Environmental Resources speaker invited landowners across the county's 'white area' lands to submit projects for a coming DOC multi-benefit land repurposing call for projects. The county would collect proposals and wants wider participation to strengthen the grant bid.
records.meeting_body: Stanislaus and Tuolumne Rivers Groundwater Basin Association GSA Board
records.agenda_item: Stanislaus County / member agency updates
records.evidence_text: just want to let everybody know that the Department of Environmental Resources is open to receipt of additional projects and all our white area lands we oversee within the county. We're looking forward to finding ways where we can try to get a hold of some of that popcorn money, maybe specifically in the multi benefit land repurposing program. So if anybody has some ideas or wants to be put on a list for the call for projects, I can give you a project proposal form to start working on.
records.notes: Speaker not named in the passage (appears to be the county staff presenter on groundwater programs); the sub-basin(s) covered by the 'call for projects' are not stated, and Stanislaus County's white-area lands also span other subbasins. Who would hold the grant is not stated.

records.finding: Stanislaus County staff are considering a county application for Prop 4 MLRP block-grant funding covering its subbasins outside Turlock, with the county as likely coordinator; its consultant described $200M of Prop 4 MLRP money, regional block grants of up to about $17M, and a 40% disadvantaged-community benefit requirement.
records.quantitative_detail: Prop 4 MLRP allocation $200M; block grants 'up to $17 million' (pre-guidelines estimate), existing grants ≈ $8.9M; Prop 4 requirement that 40% of funds benefit disadvantaged or vulnerable communities; guidelines expected by October 2026, applications early 2027.
records.speaker_role: mixed — consultant to Stanislaus County (EKI) and county staff (inferred)
records.agenda_item: Prop 4 funding programs and county project concepts

Again, here we have this, this sort of global Prop 4 requirement that 40% of funds go to projects that benefit disadvantaged communities or vulnerable communities. ... I am really interested in the idea of pursuing receiving funding for the multi benefit land repurposing program in a county application that wouldn't include the term up sub basis.
records.notes: Mode B row (gsa_entity MULTI): item spans Stanislaus County portions of the Modesto, Eastern San Joaquin and Delta-Mendota subbasins ('term up sub basis' = Turlock subbasins); county speaker unlabelled; intent only; also answers MLRP-2.1b.

records.finding: Stanislaus County staff said it wants to apply for the Department of Conservation's $200M Prop 4 multi-benefit land repurposing money, with partner agencies and its consultants. No application had been filed and no match or tranche is discussed.
records.quantitative_detail: $200 million, DOC Prop 4 set-aside for multi-benefit land repurposing, as stated by county staff (statewide total, not Modesto-specific; per-basin cap not stated)
records.meeting_body: Stanislaus and Tuolumne Rivers Groundwater Basin Association GSA Board
records.agenda_item: Stanislaus County update: Non-District East action plan
records.evidence_text: So I also would like to, and I'll work with, you know, our consultant team in house and also Geosyntech to see how maybe we could submit an application to get some funding for multi benefit land repurchase because there's $200 million available from the Department of Conservation.
records.notes: Transcript says 'multi benefit land repurchase', read as repurposing. The $200M figure is the speaker's, not checked against DOC. On 2026-05-13 county staff made the same $200M point.

records.finding: County staff described how the Non-District East accounting platform would likely work, modelled on East Turlock: field-level ET data showing groundwater use, with tiered categories and high fees above the limit. Staff said phase-two support programmes such as incentivized fallowing or land repurposing would follow. Nothing is decided.
records.meeting_body: Stanislaus and Tuolumne Rivers Groundwater Basin Association GSA Board
records.agenda_item: Stanislaus County update: Non-District East action plan
records.evidence_text: So once we have that specific recipe that'll go into the groundwater accounting platform we'll use. I mean it hasn't been decided yet. I'm just talking about what I've seen in the Eastern Turlock sub basin. So we'll use the ET data. So you'll be able to look at this program and you'll be able to see your fields. Right. We'll likely manage it at like a field level. So instead of like all your separate parcels, here's your, you know, here's your orchard, like in these various parcels. And we'll be able to see based on ET data how much groundwater you've been extracting. And then there will be like tiered levels. So it'll be like Category 0 will be like native transitional.

records.finding: The GSA consultant said a district's developed-supply credit can be transferred only with GSA approval, and that surplus allocation (Oakdale's exceeds its historical use) would be redistributed. Banking and a trading programme are deferred to a later year.
records.quantitative_detail: Developed supply 122,000 AF total (about 90,000 MID and 31,000 OID as spoken, annual); Oakdale allocation about 23,900-24,000 AF above its estimated historical use (as stated 2025-11-18), to be redistributed by overlying area
records.meeting_body: Stanislaus and Tuolumne Rivers Groundwater Basin Association GSA Meeting
records.agenda_item: STRGBA GSA Workshop No. 5: Groundwater Use Management Program

And so that's in this example. That is the goal is to be able to again reallocate some of that water. ... we will look into things like overall looking at banking a potential trading program, but that's going to be a continuation throughout the next year

At the 2025-09-09 MID board workshop a presenter described the same reallocation of about 20,000 AF of Oakdale allocation beyond historical use, with the water owned by the management area; a speaker there objected that areas that protected supply would subsidise others.

records.finding: A landowner commenter argued that spreading Non-District East's 42,000 AF over about 71,000 acres (0.6 AF/acre), rather than the 27,000 irrigated acres (1.55 AF/acre), would leave allocation orphaned. The commenter noted there is no ready trading programme to move it to growers who would use it. The GSA's answer is not captured.
records.quantitative_detail: 42,000 AF over about 71,000 acres = 0.6 AF/acre; over 27,000 irrigated acres = 1.55 AF/acre (annual, commenter's calculation)
records.meeting_body: Stanislaus and Tuolumne Rivers Groundwater Basin Association GSA Meeting
records.agenda_item: STRGBA GSA Workshop No. 5: public comment
records.evidence_text: As I read this, we're allocating 42,000 acre feet across the entire 71,000 acres. And so if we do that, we end up with 0.6 acre foot per acre. I think my math is okay. If we allocate it to the 27,000 actually developed farmed and irrigated acres that actually drive the economy here in the, here in the county, we end up with 1.55 acre feet. In 2014, maybe it was 15. The county put through a well ordinance that restricted drilling of new wells outside the district boundaries. And so no one outside the irrigation district in north district east that isn't currently farming orchards and vineyards can even go put in a well and put in orchards or vineyards. So I'd strongly advise, please reconsider, allocate that 42,000 acre feed to the currently farmed acreage at least for the first year or two. And then if someone can show actual beneficial use of groundwater out There on the rangeland or wherever they're, whether they haven't been irrigating historically, spread that allocation out to whatever the newly irrigated acres are. Don't restrict anyone's ability to, by virtue of this process to put in orchards or vineyards. They're going to have other hindrances, banks, the county, the well ordinance. But if you don't do this, and that would still cut out of District North District east growers down to 1.55 acre feet per year, but it wouldn't cut us down to 0.6 acre feet per year and let all that other water go orphaned and unused, all that other allocation. ... So, and I don't see here any ready trading program that would allow the recipients of that, those water, groundwater users, to transact it to growers who actually want to want to use that water on their farms and pay them something for it.
records.notes: Commenter's own arithmetic (0.6 vs 1.55 AF/acre) is not confirmed by staff. Also bears on MLRP-2.3a (allocation tied to non-irrigated land). Figures are annual as stated.

records.finding: In the sub-basin model, extra demand reduction of about 2,000 AF/yr in Non-District East was equated to about 500 fewer acres in agriculture, which removed the remaining modelled undesirable results. This is a modelling scenario, not an adopted retirement programme.
records.quantitative_detail: 2,000 AF per year of demand reduction (annual, modelled scenario 2) in Non-District East; about 500 acres of agricultural acreage
records.meeting_body: Stanislaus and Tuolumne Rivers Groundwater Basin Association GSA Board
records.agenda_item: Sustainable yield and projects/management action modelling update

records.section: 2.5 Data Source and ET Product Choice
records.finding: A Modesto Subbasin consultant scope (Woodard & Curran) proposes a geospatial tool combining OpenET, PRISM precipitation and surface-supply records on parcel maps to estimate monthly net groundwater use, with validation against CIMIS and reference ET. The board said it still wanted to discuss whether to proceed.

records.meeting_body: Stanislaus and Tuolumne Rivers Groundwater Basin Association GSA Board
records.agenda_item: Woodard & Curran work release / scope and budget amendment (Task 5)
records.evidence_text: Under this subtask, Woodard & Curran will conduct an analysis of options to calculate consumptive GW use, including remote sensing and OpenET. Under this task, Woodard & Curran will develop a geospatial tool to estimate monthly net groundwater use in the Modesto Subbasin. The tool will integrate evapotranspiration data from OpenET, precipitation data from PRISM, and local surface water supply records, and intersect these with GSA boundaries, management areas, and parcel maps. By comparing water demand with available supplies, the tool will identify areas of likely groundwater extraction to support basin-wide metering. The tool will be developed in close coordination with GSAs and local agencies to ensure it meets management and reporting needs. A validation process will assess the accuracy of OpenET and PRISM using local weather data, CIMIS stations, and reference ET.
records.notes: Optional Subtask 5.2 of a scope amendment; the transcript shows the chair saying the group still wanted to discuss OpenET and remote metering, so whether it was funded is not confirmed. Applies to all pumping, not to repurposed land specifically.

records.finding: Mound's GSA concluded ISW criteria were not applicable because its wells pump deep aquifers separated from the surface by clay, but acknowledged that, on a strict reading of the regulations, unpumped shallow groundwater is connected to surface water and the GSA has to do something about it.

The issue here is that there is shallow groundwater in the very shallowest sediments that's not being pumped. ... So from a very strict reading of the regulations, we do have surface water interconnected with groundwater. It's just not groundwater that we're using or really managing because the wells are pumping from the aquifers that are hundreds of feet below.

records.finding: Napa sets two ISW criteria: groundwater levels at eight shallow wells against a 2005-2014 base-period threshold, and a modelled June to October streamflow depletion volume at two USGS gauges, defined as an interim minimum threshold. The depletion volume compares no-pumping and pumping model runs.
records.quantitative_detail: 8 shallow ISW monitoring wells (up from 5); depletion volume computed for June to October each year at Napa River at Oak Knoll and at Pope Street
records.meeting_body: Napa County Groundwater Technical Advisory Group
records.agenda_item: Water year 2025 annual report: groundwater conditions
records.evidence_text: We also look at a volume of depletion occurring during the period from June to October, which is a more sensitive period that was chosen during the development of the GSP because of the kinds of beneficial uses that can be impacted during that period. We're looking at a volume of streamflow depletion. And this is based on using the modeling. And we're looking at what is the condition of the stream system when there's no pumping, and what is the amount of depletion occurring when there is pumping. Now, this volume of stream flow depletion is defined as an interim minimum threshold.
records.notes: Speaker unlabelled; consultant inferred. Napa is one of few basins using a modelled depletion metric.

records.finding: Napa applied a California Environmental Flows Framework analysis to inform interconnected surface water criteria with a focus on steelhead, concluding tributaries disconnect by July on average and that stage-discharge relationships tied to minimum riffle depths for juvenile passage can set minimum thresholds. The consultant called the stage-discharge link a first guess to test with 2027 field data.
records.quantitative_detail: tributaries disconnect in July on average; juvenile out-migration needs flow through at least June; monitoring through 2028 at least
records.meeting_body: Napa County Groundwater Technical Advisory Group (special joint meeting with the GSA)
records.agenda_item: Periodic evaluation: refinement of sustainable management criteria for interconnected surface water
records.evidence_text: section A and B of the CEPH was applied to the sub basin to inform sustainable management criteria for interconnected surface water with a focus on steelhead. As at least what I've presented today. Stream temperature and dissolved oxygen are too stressful for juvenile steelhead rearing in the main stem and tributaries become disconnected in July on average. That means most of the fish that you're going to see coming through are coming through from tributaries into the main stem. So once those tributaries become disconnected, you're going to have fewer fish moving through the system. Sustaining populations of steelhead requires supporting juvenile steelhead out migration and intra basin movement through at least June. And stage discharge relationships associated with minimum depths for juvenile passage can be used to determine minimum thresholds.
records.notes: 'CEPH' in the transcript is likely the California Environmental Flows Framework (machine transcription); speaker is a consultant or RCD ecologist (unlabelled).

records.finding: Napa's annual-report modelled June–October streamflow depletion exceeded the minimum threshold at both USGS gauges (Oak Knoll, Pope Street) in water years 2024 and 2025 and at Oak Knoll in 2023. records.finding: A Napa modeller cautions that the model's pumping reduction from idling a parcel is not the same as net groundwater-use reduction, because higher water tables raise root uptake on neighbouring land. Net groundwater-use reduction has not yet been tallied.

records.agenda_item: Recharge feasibility study: replant scenario update
records.evidence_text: if you stop pumping in a, in one parcel, you know, the groundwater levels will increase in adjacent areas. records.quantitative_detail: Default stream depletion factor up to 25% of transfer volume; no result stated
records.agenda_item: Water bank update: stream depletion factor analysis plan
records.evidence_text: The stream depletion factor analysis plan. This is a plan that we recently put together to explain to the state and the Feds how we plan to advance the work there. It's getting on the same page with them so that we can get better terms as it relates to stream depletion factor. Right now that's up to 25%. Essentially what that is is if you do a groundwater substitution transfer or transfer out of the bank. Right now it's the default state and fed percent which is again 25. So that means your, your, the revenue from that transfer and the volume is, is 25% less.
records.notes: This is a transfer-accounting factor, not a GSP ISW metric; 2026-06-18 SCGA presenter said "we haven't done the analysis yet". Same point recurs 2025-10-09, 2026-08-13 and 2026-10-08.

records.finding: SGA's water accounting system credits recharge (in lieu and direct) net of losses (about 8% a year) and tracks recovery. It shows 222,000 AF banked in the North American and 248,000 AF in the South American Subbasin after losses, and a 25% default stream-depletion deduction applies to transfers.
records.quantitative_detail: 222,000 AF (North American) and 248,000 AF (South American) banked after losses (cumulative, 27 years); losses ~8% per year on average; default stream depletion factor 25% on transfers out
records.agenda_item: Water bank update
records.evidence_text: after losses, there's 222,000 acre feet banked in the North American sub basin and 248,000 acre feet in the South American sub basin. ... So losses being I think about 8% on average per year.
records.notes: The 8% figure is hedged ('I think'); stream depletion factor figure comes from the same presentation, not the quoted passage. Banking, not repurposing. Basin-wide rule; not specific to repurposed land.

records.finding: SGA's roll call includes a designated director seat for 'Agriculture and self supplied' users, absent at this meeting. The transcript shows no seat for domestic well owners or disadvantaged communities.

records.finding: [Distributive] SGA member agencies pay a connection-based base fee plus a groundwater fee on five-year average pumping, with a board target of 42% base and 58% groundwater. Staff said the split seems to achieve equity among members; the City of Sacramento warned that banking-driven drops in pumping distort the average.

It is, it seems to be achieve equity amongst the members.

records.section: 3.1.4 Domestic Well Protection as an Equity Outcome
records.finding: At the SGA workshop on sustainable management criteria, staff said the old thresholds were replaced by ones built around beneficial users: using well completion reports, they picked the shallowest well among at least 10 near each monitoring site, because many domestic wells sat far below the old thresholds. Final thresholds went to a public workshop.
records.quantitative_detail: At least 10 wells per monitoring site; 21 thresholds finalized; old thresholds allowed about 100 ft more drop than some domestic wells could tolerate (as stated)
records.agenda_item: Workshop: sustainable management criteria update
records.evidence_text: we saw that a lot of domestic walls were actually much lower than our previous minimum threshold. So we didn't want to allow a drop of, you know, 100ft or so from our previous threshold ... We used at least 10 of those wells. ... Let's look at the shallowest one out of all of those.
records.notes: Speaker is staff or consultant (unlabelled); 'walls' and 'smc' are transcription of 'wells'.

records.section: 3.1.4 Domestic Well Protection as an Equity Outcome
records.finding: In the draft 2026 update, SGA reset its domestic well protection criterion: in each square mile, a minimum threshold exceedance is set 10 ft above the screen of the shallowest domestic well. No breakdown of disadvantaged versus other areas is mentioned.

Then we had the screen interval set reset the criteria for what constitutes an under minimum threshold exceedance 10ft above that screen interval.
records.notes: Transcript is garbled around 'every square mile'; detail of the 2025-12-11 workshop shows the method.

records.finding: Staff reported the ISW criteria: 19 key shallow wells near waterways, minimum thresholds set at historic spring lows (1992 or 2016), and an undesirable result only if more than 25% of key wells fall below threshold. 18 of 19 were above threshold; the one below has been below for years, so staff suspect its threshold or construction.

The MTS are based on historical lows during spring in either 1992 or 2016 because those were low spring years. And our undesirable result requires more than 25% of the key wells to be below the MT before action needs to be taken. We have 18 of our 19 wells above the minimum threshold.
records.notes: Groundwater-level proxy for ISW; no depletion rate is quantified. Presenter (Maureen Reilly per transcript label) role inferred as district staff or consultant.

records.section: 2.5 Data Source and ET Product Choice
records.finding: San Benito County WD plans to estimate groundwater pumping for its fee from OpenET, corrected for other water supplies, because constituents in Zones 3 and 6 did not accept meters; landowners who dispute the OpenET figure may request a meter instead. Staff will recommend keeping the parcel-based fee as an interim step while the OpenET method is developed and evaluated.

records.finding: OBGMA's consultant presented the five-year water quality update for the GSP evaluation. Three entities monitor the basin, seven constituents are of concern, and 2021-2025 results were compared with the GSP's 2010-2020 baseline well by well.
