The monitoring includes collection of a wide array of of minerals, metals and organic and inorganic chemicals, of which there are seven constituents of potential concern in the basin, including total dissolved solids, or tds, sulfate, chloride, boron nitrate, iron and manganese. ... Of the 23 wells sampled, three wells have concentrations above the secondary maximum contaminant level or MCL of 1,000 milligrams per liter and those are denoted by the red circles. Now when comparing the maximum concentrations measured between 2010 and 2020 to the max concentration measured between 2021 and 2025, TDS concentrations increased in five wells and decreased in 16 wells. ... with one well having a concentration above the MCL of 10 milligrams per liter, the eastern portion of the basin
records.notes: Presentation by Dudek's Devin Peterson; domestic-well status of the sampled wells and any resident communication are not mentioned; sample count may vary by constituent.

records.finding: OBGMA's consultant reported progress on a data management system to store and visualise all hydrologic data collected in the basin; the framework was built in water year 2025 and is still being tested. Whether the public or domestic well owners can use it is not stated.
records.agenda_item: Water year 2025 annual report and GSP implementation summary
records.evidence_text: This is a system to store and visualize all the hydrologic data that's collected in the basin. So in water year 2025 developed the kind of the framework for that data management system and started transferring data into it to test its functionality and it's still in the works but some significant progress has been made and hopefully will soon be in use.
records.notes: Presenter is unlabeled (consultant by inference); on 2025-10-30 the general manager said the extraction database was moving to the cloud, which is not clearly the same system.

records.finding: A PVID director said Metropolitan's new programme manager reads the fallow agreement as requiring land that returns to production to be farmed for 12 consecutive months before it can re-enter fallow, and as dropping land not farmed 2 years in 5. Directors disputed this, since land extended into fallow through December returns to farming on 1 January.
records.quantitative_detail: 12 consecutive months of farming before re-fallowing; 2 of every 5 years farmed; fallow term limit of 5 years (as stated by speaker); a 50% reduction from 1 January 2027 was also mentioned
records.agenda_item: Water Rights - Usage / Colorado River discussion
records.evidence_text: What that means is that we're going to get a whole bunch of ground back right on January 1st and that ground may not re. Enter Fallow for 12 consecutive months of farming, which is new. ... your land has to be farmed for 2 out of every 5 years. Even though. And if it's not farmed for 2 out of every five years it is no longer eligible for the follow program.
records.notes: Transcript is unlabelled and the 50% figure is only 'the fallowing being reduced 50%' in a question; the same dispute is picked up on 2026-09-17; surface-water programme.

records.finding: PVID's water-rights committee backed commissioning an environmental impact statement so that fallow-program water could be sent to destinations other than Metropolitan, since approval takes up to a year and a half. A consultant said that using unused fallow-program capacity for another buyer had cost PVID a brokerage fee.
records.quantitative_detail: EIS approval lead time up to 1 to 1.5 years; committee vote 2 of 3 in favour
records.agenda_item: Water Rights - Usage: proposal for an environmental impact statement
records.evidence_text: it was the whole intent of having an EIS is when we have other destinations for water that are non metropolitan within the framework of the existing fallow program, we're going to need environmental approval for it. And so we we're looking to be ready rather than having as an approval like this takes up to a year, year and a half to completion. ... The only thing we lost was by utilizing the existing, you know, the unused portion of our fallow program, We had to pay a brokerage fee for the use of that.
records.notes: First speaker is the committee chair, second a consultant (introduced as Jeff Harvey) by context; Colorado River water, not groundwater.

records.finding: A PVID board speaker (director or manager) said Metropolitan now interprets some fallow-program rules differently from how PVID administered them. He argued that rotating fields into fallow, which takes 30 to 60 days of crop termination, gains Metropolitan water, and that PVID's CPI-limited per-acre-foot compensation is about a third of the IID-San Diego price.
records.quantitative_detail: 30 to 60 days to terminate a crop before a field can enter fallow; 'above $900 per acre foot' for the San Diego-IID transfer next year versus PVID about one third of that (speaker's estimate)
records.agenda_item: Water Rights - Usage / Forbearance and Fallowing Program
records.evidence_text: And I, I've always maintained that when you prep a field to fallow, obviously you have to get rid of the existing crop or if it's already gone good, you have to have weeds controlled. It takes at least 30 days, maybe 60 days to terminate one crop and then have that field ready to go into fallow. Well, all that time you're still following the original submitted field and you've got this other field that's being prepped for fallow that's not being farmed. And so they gain, every time we do a rotation, they actually gain water. ... For example next year, not exactly sure but the San Diego number back to IID is going to be above $900 per acre foot and ours is like a third of that.
records.notes: Speaker unlabelled (a PVID director or the manager); the dispute is over how rotation and eligibility rules credit fallowed acres, not over an ET method; Colorado River surface-water programme.

records.finding: Metropolitan's 2026 Colorado River supply estimate lists the PVID Fallowing Program (and the Bard and Quechan fallowing programmes) at zero AF. A footnote says it is not a Metropolitan supply in 2026 and that the water becomes system water in USBR's Lower Colorado Conservation Program.
records.quantitative_detail: 0 AF Metropolitan supply from PVID fallowing in 2026; IID/MWD conservation programme 105,000 AF in the same table
records.agenda_item: Water supply conditions report, 2026 supply estimate
records.evidence_text:
PVID Fallowing Program 1 0

Exchange w/ SDCWA (IID/Canal Lining) ... Not a supply for Metropolitan in 2026 . Water generated from

these programs becomes system water as part of USBR’s Lower Colorado Conservation Program to help protect Lake Mead.
records.notes: Shows how fallowing-generated Colorado River water is booked in a supply ledger; surface-water conservation, not groundwater; row placed with the Palo Verde subbasin because the land lies there.

records.finding: PVID staff reported that the Metropolitan fallowing and forbearance programme is in its 21st of 35 contract years, with up to 25,947 acres fallowed. District staff run routine field inspections and contact participants about fields with volunteer crops and weeds; no water-savings accounting method is described.
records.quantitative_detail: 25,947 acres maximum fallowed, about 29% of the valley, contract year beginning 2025-08-01 (year 21 of 35)
records.agenda_item: Status Report: Forbearance and Fallowing Program Agreement
records.evidence_text: The 21st contract year of the 35 year program program is following the maximum 25,947 acres or approximately 29% of the Valley for this contract year. Staff is continuing routine field inspections. Some fallow fields still need attention. Circulate fields which were in alfalfa before going into fallow. Volunteer alfalfa, cotton, salt cedars and arrowweeds continue to be a problem in some fields.
records.notes: 'Following' in the transcript is fallowing; Colorado River (surface-water) conservation, included for monitoring practice on fallowed land (also bears on MLRP-2.10a); PVID is not a GSA; the person reading the status report is not identified.

records.finding: PVID's land-utilization committee chair reported that Metropolitan's committee is considering an early alfalfa termination pilot for one year rather than two, with money still to be discussed. He said river uncertainty means nobody wants to do more than this one small pilot. No accounting or monitoring method was described.
records.quantitative_detail: One-year pilot proposed instead of two years; no acreage or payment stated
records.agenda_item: PUC - Land Utilization
records.evidence_text: We had discussions with the MWD PUC committee about pushing forward the early alfalfa termination program that we've discussed. They have since taken it back to their committee. Our committee is going to need to meet again to have that discussion. Again. The one thing that they they are talking about is only doing a one year program instead of a two year program and all it is is a pilot program. ... nobody's wanting to really jump out and really do much more at this point with us being at full silo and just wanting to do this one small pilot program to begin.
records.notes: Speaker is a PVID director chairing the committee by context; no accounting or monitoring method for the pilot is described.

records.finding: At the IID board, IID staff described an amended forbearance agreement among California Colorado River contractors that expands the Palo Verde Fallowing Program to the last five months of the year, not covered by the existing agreement, and increases the volume for the Bard Water District, so the conserved water stays in Lake Mead.
records.quantitative_detail: Extra 5 months of the year for the PVID fallowing programme; no acreage or AF stated
records.agenda_item: System conservation / forbearance agreement
records.evidence_text: What this forbearance agreement is intended to cover is some modifications to those programs. One is an expansion of the Palo Verde Fallowing Program for the last five months of the year, which wasn't covered under the existing agreement, as well as an increase in volume for the Barred Water District. Both of those come under the authorities of a metropolitan-ski agreement.
records.notes: Evidence is about land in Palo Verde Valley, reported at another district's board; Colorado River conservation, not groundwater; 'metropolitan-ski' is a transcription of 'Metropolitan-style'.

records.finding: United Water began sampling Santa Clara River water for a suite of landfill-leachate constituents after the Chiquita Canyon landfill reaction; a GSA speaker said DWR's review of the GSPs faulted them for saying the basins have no water quality problems beyond legacy salts. The sampling is of surface water, upstream of the Piru groundwater basin.
records.quantitative_detail: About $10,000 per sampling event for the full constituent suite (as spoken)
records.meeting_body: Fillmore and Piru Basins GSA Board of Directors
records.agenda_item: Executive Director's report
records.evidence_text: United has started a sampling program of the, of the Santa Clara river water based upon the, the list of constituents. That's about $10,000 a pop for the, you know, for that suite of chemicals. ... I think we got dinged on our gsps by saying our basins don't have any water quality problems except for some legacy salts.
records.notes: Speaker is unlabeled but is the executive reporting on meetings with the landfill operator; the sampling is surface water, not groundwater (confirmed by a director's follow-up question); 'dinged' refers to DWR GSP review, not specified.

records.finding: A director asked whether the landfill-related sample results are public and would be on United Water's website. The reply was that they probably would not be posted there, but some could be made available; SCV Water is compiling operator and monitoring data so the agencies share the same information.
records.meeting_body: Fillmore and Piru Basins GSA Board of Directors
records.agenda_item: Executive Director's report
records.evidence_text: Presumably, the results of those samples are public information. Yeah. Will that be on United's website? I don't think it will be on the website, but we can definitely. We can definitely make some of that available. And so SCB Water has asked. They. They're basically compiling all of the sampling that the landfill operator has done, as well as the monitoring. So the goal is to try to make sure we all have the same information. Surface water, groundwater. And then I think it will make sense for us to take a look at maybe some downstream key wells, that there might be some things we could monitor groundwater. But I think at this point, it's more, you know, get the coordination done, get our act together, get our sampling program going
records.notes: Director and respondent are unlabeled; no public notice or translated material is mentioned; this is a residents' information question raised by a board member, not by the public.

records.finding: Asked about measured data behind the back-calculated stream recharge to the basin, a GSA speaker agreed stream flow data are a data gap and said no stream-gauge installation is planned. This concerns water-budget inflow, not pumping depletion of streams.
records.quantitative_detail: About 14,000 AF, back-calculated stream recharge from the western hills (period not stated)
records.meeting_body: Pleasant Valley GSA Board of Directors
records.agenda_item: 5a. SGMA implementation/compliance activities, including the GSP
records.evidence_text: It seems like it's mostly stream, you know, recharge coming in from the. The hills to the west. We've only really back calculated those numbers and I think 14,000 acre feet has been been talked about. ... I'm not aware that there are plans to install them on the part of the gsa. I think it's been. I, you know, you're right as far as that. It's a data gap.
records.notes: Questioner (labelled james.farrow) and respondent (labelled PVWD) roles are inferred from labels; figure is as spoken and may be garbled; not about interconnected surface water depletion itself.

records.finding: The November 2025 allocation policy splits the 28,000 AF annual pool 90/10 between irrigated and non-irrigated land. The consultant says this implies about 1.15 AF/acre for irrigated parcels and 0.1 AF/acre for non-irrigated land. Land idled since 2015 thus keeps only a small entitlement.
records.quantitative_detail: 28,000 AF/yr total allocation (15,000 AF sustainable + 13,000 AF transitional); implied 1.15 AF/acre irrigated vs 0.1 AF/acre non-irrigated; ~23,000 irrigated acres
records.agenda_item: Allocation workshop: application of the 90/10 split
records.evidence_text: But groundwater users, this would have to have to be 1.15 acre feet per acre for groundwater users and point one for non groundwater users. If we're doing this 9010 split this way.
records.notes: The per-acre figures were framed as implied by the split, not formally adopted rates; the 9/30/2026 meeting shows the 90/10 approach still contested. The policy covers only Pleasant Valley GSA's ~72% of the subbasin.

records.finding: Landowners who left acreage unplanted or fallow, or conserved water, objected that an allocation tied to historical irrigated use gives them less than owners who planted aggressively. This shows how an irrigated-since-2015 rule can penalize earlier fallowing.
records.quantitative_detail: 90/10 split of the allocation between irrigated and non-irrigated land
records.agenda_item: Public comment on the 90/10 allocation
records.evidence_text: Why should a landowner who conserve water, left acreage unplanted and did not maximize historical pumping, received less water than those that planted unsustainably and increased demand on an already limited basin.
records.notes: Speaker is a landowner in public comment; other commenters and counsel for Gladstone Land raised similar objections. No allocation change was adopted on this date.

records.finding: Under the draft penalty policy an over-pumper has a year to cure by reducing next year's allocation, buying from or transferring from a willing party, or other options. A director urged that transfers be run through a GSA-managed market rather than private deals.
records.quantitative_detail: 12-month cure period; up to $500/AF penalty later adopted (2026-07-28)
records.agenda_item: Item: draft penalty policy for exceedance of allocation
records.evidence_text: You can take it away from your next year's application. You can buy it from a willing party or transfer it from a willing party
records.notes: The GSA-managed market idea was voiced by a director and not adopted; no geographic limits discussed. Basin-wide rule; not specific to repurposed land.

records.finding: The proposed allocation would cover only Pleasant Valley GSA's ~72% share of native yield (about 11,500 AF of 16,000 AF). The consultant said the city and county could sell unused entitlement or recharge credits if they join the policy, and that a leave-behind fraction from the pending recharge policy could be made available for common benefit.
records.quantitative_detail: Native yield ~16,000 AF/yr; PVGSA ~72% share; ~11,500 AF allocable before reserve pool of 0-2,000 AF
records.agenda_item: Workshop: proposed revised groundwater allocation policy
records.evidence_text: if they want to be part of the allocation, they could potentially sell those credits.
records.notes: No vote; numbers are discussion figures. Leave-behind percentages for the recharge policy were still being set. Basin-wide rule; not specific to repurposed land.

records.finding: The baseline for which land counts as irrigated is the maximum extent irrigated at least once since 2015, from DWR/Land IQ crop maps and a grower survey, not a recent-year or average figure.
records.quantitative_detail: ~23,000 acres irrigated at least once since 2015; annual irrigated acreage varies roughly 12,000 (dry) to 18,000 (wet) acres
records.agenda_item: Allocation workshop: irrigated vs non-irrigated classification
records.evidence_text: But the policy was set up in a way that's such that we're trying to identify what has been irrigated since 2015. So we're trying to find the maximum, greatest extent.
records.notes: This sets an allocation baseline, not a repurposing water-savings baseline. MLRP link: the irrigated/non-irrigated classification decides whether land idled or fallowed since 2015 falls in the 10% non-irrigated pool (landowners objected on these grounds on 2026-09-30).

records.section: 2.5 Data Source and ET Product Choice
records.finding: Pleasant Valley uses DWR's statewide Land IQ crop mapping to classify irrigated land, citing state acceptance and Land IQ's roughly 98% claimed accuracy, and then corrects it with a landowner survey. Land IQ ground-truths about 20% of fields.
records.quantitative_detail: ~98% claimed accuracy (Land IQ, weighted across crops); ~20% of ~85,000 fields ground-truthed each year; ~24,000 acres reduced to ~23,000 after the grower survey
records.agenda_item: Allocation workshop: crop data set and validation
records.evidence_text: DWR is contracted with, with LandIQ, they're a consultant that, that does annual crop surveys. ... It's about 98% accurate is what they claim.
records.notes: Speaker is the GM (Sarah Woolf) presenting consultant slides; only crop mapping, no ET product, is used. MLRP link: the irrigated/non-irrigated classification decides whether land idled or fallowed since 2015 falls in the 10% non-irrigated pool (landowners objected on these grounds on 2026-09-30).

records.section: 2.5 Data Source and ET Product Choice
records.finding: A landowner at the workshop said Land IQ's irrigated-acreage accuracy on his farm was about 60%, not the 98% cited; the consultant replied that young perennials such as one-year-old pistachios look like fallow ground from space and the 98% is a weighted average.
records.quantitative_detail: 60% (landowner's own farm) vs 98% (weighted average claimed); ~50% accuracy for young perennials per consultant
records.agenda_item: Allocation workshop: landowner comments
records.evidence_text: PWR had our farm paid pretty high for irrigated acres. And after submitting, our accuracy is about 60%, not 98% like you're reporting.
records.notes: 'PWR' is likely DWR (transcription); the landowner himself suggested a third layer of proof and a staff speaker agreed the 98% may not hold for individual farms. MLRP link: the irrigated/non-irrigated classification decides whether land idled or fallowed since 2015 falls in the 10% non-irrigated pool (landowners objected on these grounds on 2026-09-30).

records.section: 2.5 Data Source and ET Product Choice
records.finding: When a late allocation request came before the board, the engineer-verified irrigation record said irrigated while a director's check of the Land IQ comparison said not irrigated; the board denied the request. The disagreement between data products and engineer verification was decided by vote, not by a set rule.
records.agenda_item: Item 5B: late 2026 allocation request (Spice World/Valley Garlic APN)
records.evidence_text: What we did. I used what James had in the file. I didn't compare it to what Land IQ had. ... Land IQ says that this APN was not irrigated from total.
records.notes: Vote counts in the transcript are chaotic and the first speaker's name is a first name only; the transcript garbles 'Provost and Pritchard' as 'Provo and Picture'. Basin-wide rule; not specific to repurposed land.

records.finding: Pleasant Valley GSA's board adopted a domestic well mitigation policy on September 30, 2026. If an investigation finds GSA projects or management actions degraded domestic-well water quality, the GSA funds a $3,000 reverse osmosis system or agreed alternative, and refers owners to resources such as Self-Help Enterprises.
records.quantitative_detail: Up to $3,000 per well for reverse osmosis or agreed alternative
records.meeting_body: Pleasant Valley GSA Board of Directors (special meeting)
records.agenda_item: Item 5: Domestic Well Mitigation Policy
records.evidence_text: But the PMAs, or if the PMAs cause degradation of the water quality, there's basically an investigation into this mitigation application determines that it's water quality degradation. Then we'll fund a $3,000 of a reverse osmosis system or a mutually agreed upon alternative. And then there's also some services, resources available to domestic users, you know, some self help enterprises. ... I'll need a motion to adopt number five. I'll make a motion. I'll need a second. I'll second.
records.notes: Policy text is not in the corpus; the consultant's sentence is partly garbled by transcription. Adoption inferred from motion and "yes" votes in the transcript; the State Water Board requested the policy. A board member asked that de-designation of the aquifer be written into it; staff advised pursuing it separately.

records.finding: Pleasant Valley GSA set provisional water-quality minimum thresholds from existing data in a buffer around each monitoring well; staff said an exceedance counts only if caused by GSA activity. Constituents are not named in the passages read.
records.meeting_body: Pleasant Valley GSA Board of Directors
records.agenda_item: Monitoring network and water quality sampling update
records.evidence_text: for the water quality MCLs and MTs, we actually we used a method to look at existing data, created a buffer zone around that well, and then use statistics of all samples that were within that buffer zone to set the MTS as a provisional value in the gsp.
records.notes: Transcript is garbled; a nitrate comment refers to a monitoring well near city percolation ponds. Exceedance count ("five of six wells") is hard to read and is not asserted.

records.finding: Pleasant Valley GSA's adopted exceedance policy has a water-quality procedure: notify of the exceedance, confirm with a sample, notify well owners, investigate the area and report to the subbasin. Notification goes to parties within about two miles; the radius is set by the investigation.
records.quantitative_detail: Notification radius: parties within 2 miles (two-mile / two-square-mile area stated in transcript)
records.meeting_body: Pleasant Valley GSA Board of Directors (special meeting)
records.agenda_item: Item 6: Subbasin Exceedance Policy and Action Plans
records.evidence_text: Finally, for water quality, we're going to issue notification of the exceedance, confirm it with a sample to make sure that we can still see that it is an exceedance, notify the owners of water quality and then investigate the area around the exceedance, initiate project management actions and then report out to the sub basin. ... It all starts off with a validation of the exceedance followed by a notification of parties within a two mile radius
records.notes: Transcript renders "owners of water quality" (likely well owners) and "2 square mile" versus "two mile radius"; policy text not in corpus. Applies to groundwater-level, subsidence and water-quality thresholds.

records.section: 3.3.3 Domestic Wells and Community Water System Consolidation
records.finding: A Pleasant Valley board member questioned why a domestic well mitigation policy is needed, saying nobody uses wells for drinking, and that the Lost Hills community uses wells only for landscaping. Consultants answered that a small southern community is listed as domestic users and the State Board requires a formal commitment.
records.meeting_body: Pleasant Valley GSA Board of Directors
records.agenda_item: Update: response to State Water Board comments and draft implementation policies
records.evidence_text: There's actually a small community of people in the southern part of the basin that do use or listed as domestic well users. ... there has to be a commitment formally in a well mitigation plan to address any impacts to domestic wells.
records.notes: No domestic-well inventory or count is cited; the aquifer is designated municipal beneficial use per the consultant, who also said shallow irrigation-well impacts were deferred. Speakers: board member, EKI consultants.

records.finding: Consultants told the board USGS finished updating the San Antonio Creek Integrated Model through water year 2023, with climate scenarios on effects on Barka Slough and its species. The GSA also uses a satellite vegetation-index study of the slough.
records.quantitative_detail: USGS model extended through water year 2023 (speaker unsure)
records.agenda_item: GSP five-year periodic evaluation draft chapters
records.evidence_text: USGS completed their update of the San Antonio Creek integrated model where they extended the model through I think water year 23 off the top of my head. And that included projected climate scenarios and how that would impact the slough and then different species in the slew.
records.notes: Presenter role inferred (hired consultant); the 'water year 23' end date was stated with uncertainty. The model's depletion outputs were not reported at this meeting.

records.finding: The periodic evaluation reported that ISW is monitored at a single stream gauge and that the minimum threshold was never breached over the evaluation period. The annual report packet separately says ISW thresholds were not exceeded in water year 2025.
records.quantitative_detail: No ISW minimum-threshold exceedance, water years 2019-2025 evaluation period; the 2026-03-18 packet reports none for water year 2025
records.agenda_item: GSP five-year periodic evaluation draft chapters
records.evidence_text: So interconnected surface water. We use the Casimalia stream gauge as our monitoring network. And so in no instance during the valuation period were we below the minimum threshold.
records.notes: Gauge name is garbled in the transcript ('Casimalia'); the threshold value and the gauge's location were not stated.

records.finding: The GSA tracks Barka Slough groundwater-dependent vegetation with a satellite enhanced vegetation index, first done for the GSP and now updated through water year 2025, to see whether groundwater-level changes show up as vegetation health changes.
records.quantitative_detail: EVI analysis updated through water year 2025
records.agenda_item: GSP five-year periodic evaluation draft chapters
records.evidence_text: So our, we updated our enhanced vegetation index, which was a essentially a study based on satellite imagery of varka slough and health vegetation. And could we determine whether changes in groundwater elevations of the slough, can we see that in any changes in vegetative health? And so we did that for the GSP period and we've updated it through y year 25.
records.notes: Results of the vegetation analysis are not stated here. The 2026-03-18 packet and 2026-02-18 meeting also cite the EVI update.

records.finding: The GSP-implementation budget proposal says no new stream gauges are needed because the GSA uses USGS/Vandenberg gauges, and puts three shallow piezometers in Barka Slough in FY 2027-28 at about $20,000, not in the FY 2026-27 budget; a satellite/model approach may replace them.
records.quantitative_detail: $20,000 estimate for 3 shallow piezometers, FY 2027-28 (not in the FY 2026-27 budget)
records.agenda_item: Item 10: GSP implementation budget, address data gaps
records.evidence_text: ii. Install Stream Gages and Piezometers at Barka Slough: No stream gages needed at this time. SABGSA is utilizing gages that USGS/VSFB have provided. Estimate $20,000 in FY 27-28 for planning, equipment, and installation of 3 shallow piezometers in the Slough. ... (Not included in FY 26-27 Budget).
records.notes: Budget memo author not named; the same text appears in the 2026-06-17 packet.

records.finding: On DWR's corrective action to evaluate the rate, timing and volume of ISW depletions, consultants told the board no immediate action is needed: DWR's ISW guidance is still a draft and the GSA will review it once final.
records.agenda_item: GSP five-year periodic evaluation: DWR recommended corrective actions
records.evidence_text: DWR is issuing best management practices for implementing sustainable management criteria for the sustainability indicators. The interconnected surface water guidance is still draft. So when that becomes finalized, it'll be reviewed and then we can implement, you know, consider and review implementing those methodologies.
records.notes: The corrective-action wording comes from the 2026-06-17 packet (rate, timing and volume of depletions of interconnected surface water and support for specific SMCs), not from this passage.

records.section: 2.5 Data Source and ET Product Choice
records.finding: San Antonio Basin GSA (working with consultant GSI) estimates agricultural pumping for its annual report by pairing LandIQ crop maps with OpenET satellite evapotranspiration, using a different method for covered crops (greenhouses, hoop houses) that satellites cannot read well.
records.agenda_item: Annual report: land use and water use estimate
records.evidence_text: We get this data from a company called Land iq. ... we pair the Land IQ Lambda use data with another company called Open et. And so that is satellite measured evapotranspiration. ... It's hard to measure things through plastic. ... We use a slightly different method to calculate water use for those.
records.notes: Speaker is unlabeled and appears to be the GSA's manager (who mentions working with the consultant GSI). On 2026-09-16 the consultant added that the GSA moved from a water-duty-factor spreadsheet to this satellite method; this concerns basin-wide annual-report pumping, not repurposed land. Basin-wide rule; not specific to repurposed land.

records.finding: Distributive: Santa Barbara County runs a well meter assistance program reimbursing San Antonio basin landowners up to $500 each for meter installation, and GSA staff reminded landowners of the four documents needed. In September 2026 rebates were still available that fiscal year.
records.quantitative_detail: Reimbursement up to $500 per landowner (one flow meter)
records.agenda_item: Executive director report
records.evidence_text: So the county has their well meter assistance program identical to landowners that have installed meters within the San Antonio basin. So you can apply for up to a 500 reimbursement per landowner. Matt Scudado from the county reached out to me and said that they have received a couple applications from landowners within the bas. However they've been incomplete. So I just wanted to remind you the four documents that you need to submit to the county is a complete Y map application, the calibration documentation from the manufacturer, the receipts, either original or a copy that shows the meter serial number and the cost and then photos of the installed meter that also show the serial number, make and model. So Matt's had some where he's gotten, you know, the application in and maybe the calibration, but not the receipt or the photos or some combination thereof. So just a reminder everybody, there's four things to submit and we encourage you to submit before June 30
records.notes: Cost relief is for metering compliance, mostly agricultural users; no income test is mentioned.

records.finding: San Antonio Basin GSA emails landowners before each quarterly monitoring event, sends periodic mailings (a third was approved for December 2025) and posts FAQs on its metering ordinance. Staff reported one inquiry, from a de minimis owner confirming no meter is required.
records.quantitative_detail: Third landowner mailing due first week of December 2025; Q4 monitoring event Nov 25-26, 2025
records.agenda_item: Executive director/administrator report
records.evidence_text: Q4 groundwater level monitoring event is set to take place next week on the 25th and 26th. And the email notifications were sent out to landowners yesterday. And then since the last meeting, I've only had one inquiry regarding the metering ordinance and that was from a de minimis owner. ... So we have already approved the mailing number three that's going to go out the first week of December. We also approved at the last meeting our frequently asked questions and that's been posted to the website
records.notes: Speaker is GSA staff inferred from content; labels in this transcript are generic. Audience is landowners and well owners.

records.section: 3.3.3 Domestic Wells and Community Water System Consolidation
records.finding: San Antonio Basin GSA keeps a registry of wells under its Ordinance 25-001, with 286 registered and 219 (about 77%) in compliance, and tracks non-compliance in tiers. Registration is mandatory, and de minimis users are exempt from metering.

records.section: 3.3.3 Domestic Wells and Community Water System Consolidation
records.finding: SCV Water's SGMA-grant-funded domestic well survey infers private well locations from satellite imagery and well completion reports; a pilot request to Los Angeles County for 33 canyon wells took about two months and yielded limited information on 7, so staff are estimating canyon-area use from land-use features and demand factors.
records.quantitative_detail: 33 wells requested from LA County on 2025-06-20 (San Francisquito Canyon pilot); limited information on 7 of 33; about 2 months turnaround
records.agenda_item: Staff report: GSP implementation (domestic well survey)
records.evidence_text: Staff has been conducting a domestic well survey funded under the Sustainable Groundwater Management Act Implementation Grant. The survey objective has been to document the existence and location of private wells, determine well status and the potential annual production at the zone level. Staff used satellite imagery and well completion reports to infer the locations of wells. To further validate the locations and statuses, staff submitted a request to Los Angeles County on June 20, 2025, for any available information on 33 wells in the San Francisquito Canyon area. If this “pilot” request proved successful, staff planned to seek additional well information for other canyon areas. Approximately 2 months later Los Angeles County provided documents related to the request. Upon review, staff determined limited information was available for 7 of the 33 wells requested. Though information helped confirm some well locations, the two month turnaround time is significant, when considering this initial request was only a pilot test seeking limited information. Due to the difficulty in obtaining clear well record data from the State and County, staff is conducting an analysis to estimate groundwater use at the zone level within the canyon areas. Using satellite data, staff identified features such as lawns, horse ranches, houses, and pools.
records.notes: Collector is the GSA; participation is not voluntary or reported as such; the passage is from the written staff report in the packet; the 2025-11-04 packet repeats that staff are building demand factors for lawns, horse ranches, residences and pools.

records.section: 2.5 Data Source and ET Product Choice
records.finding: Santa Ynez's Prop 68 demonstration tested flow meters, pump power use, LandIQ ET stations and OpenET at nine sites across the three GSAs (Apr 2025-Mar 2026). Meters and power use matched closely; ET showed far more use than pumping on vineyards, and OpenET has added uncertainty from greenhouses, cloud cover and fallow land. The consultant said he would hesitate to rely on ET.

records.evidence_text: So last year was 7,813 acre feet. For agriculture, we estimated 379 acre feet domestic with a plus or minus 20%, you know, certainty on there. And then for the municipal wells that we actually get the big records for, there was 574 acre.
records.notes: Speaker labelled Gus Tolley (DBS&A); municipal figure is garbled in transcript ('574 acre'); the 913 total mentioned afterward combines domestic and municipal.

records.finding: The South American Subbasin annual report map classifies streams as interconnected, disconnected, or unknown, and the consultant calls the unknown stretch a data gap in the monitoring network.
records.quantitative_detail: Monitoring: twice a year (spring and fall); ISW wells identified separately from the level network; WY2025 annual report
records.agenda_item: Annual report: monitoring network
records.evidence_text: Blue lines are interconnected, the red lines are disconnected and then there's a yellow line where we're not really sure yet. That's considered a data gap in terms of our network.
records.notes: Speaker is Bryan Thoreson per transcript labels; stream names not given in the excerpt.

records.finding: A Regional Water Authority presenter told SCGA that CoSANA modeling shows banking has raised groundwater levels and added about 16,000 acre-feet per year of baseflow to the American River. This is a net benefit figure rather than a pumping-depletion estimate.
records.quantitative_detail: ~16,000 AFY average added contribution to the American River (previously banked water analysis; model analysis over 27 years of banking)
records.agenda_item: Water bank / previously banked water analysis
records.evidence_text: Here we use the Woodard, the Cosana model that of course you're relying upon as well in this basin for groundwater sustainability planning. ... And the analysis suggests that it's about the losses equates to about 16,000 acre feet on average that was contributing to the American River.
records.notes: Speaker unlabeled; probably RWA executive staff (also SGA). Covers North American, South American and Cosumnes (CoSANA domain). SGA staff gave ~15,000 AFY on 2025-12-11 and 2026-08-13.

records.finding: The Harvest Water project (Sacramento Regional County Sanitation District) has nine groundwater monitoring wells installed and 9-10 more planned, and has committed to monitor groundwater in five riparian forests.
records.quantitative_detail: 9 wells installed; 9-10 more planned next season; 5 riparian forests monitored; shallow zone to ~100 ft
records.agenda_item: Harvest Water program update (monitoring well coordination)
records.evidence_text: So we in fact have nine wells installed. ... So we're committed to them to monitor groundwater in five riparian forests.
records.notes: Speaker is the Harvest Water presenter (SRCSD), not SCGA staff; SCGA board members asked to adopt the wells in its network. Project area in South American Subbasin.

records.finding: OHWD has installed stream gauges on the Cosumnes River and a creek under a state grant; data go to CDEC as stage only until rating curves from field flow measurements are done, at which point streamflow will be published.
records.quantitative_detail: Grant about $250,000 total (2025-10-21; speaker figure unclear); "of the 145 ... received about half" (2026-03-17)
records.agenda_item: CalSIP stream gauge grant update
records.evidence_text: the connection to the state website cdec California Data Exchange center is there now, but it's just reporting the, the stream stage for the moment. And so eventually when the updated rating curves are in, it'll. It'll put streamflow up on their website as well. ... The only thing left really on the CALIP grant is a lot of the calibration which they're going to have to do.
records.notes: Speakers are a researcher (Andrew Calderwood) and OHWD manager; the grant name is garbled ("CalSIP/CALIP"); OHWD is indexed to Cosumnes but its recharge project is described as South American.

records.section: 1.5 Per-well Attribution and the Cumulative Pumping Problem
records.finding: SCGA's consultant said its ISW assessment looks beyond near-stream wells to groundwater levels across the whole subbasin and to total pumping compared with pre-SGMA, because distant pumping eventually affects streams.
records.quantitative_detail: Average annual pumping after SGMA lower than before SGMA (no figure stated)
records.agenda_item: Periodic Evaluation draft: ISW analysis
records.evidence_text: I think one of the main takeaways is that groundwater pumping distant from the streams also eventually impacts the streams, which is one of the reasons when we looked at isw, we not only looked at the groundwater levels near the streams, but we looked at the groundwater levels more broadly and also looked at the volume of pumping that has occurred in the sub basin compared to pre sigma.
records.notes: Speaker is Bryan Thoreson (SCGA consultant), labelled in the transcript.

records.finding: An SCGA board member noted a well used as an ISW/GDE well draws from the lower aquifer and shows consistently low levels, and asked whether the cause is local pumping or the river, indicating depth matters for reading ISW monitoring data.
records.agenda_item: Aerojet / Mather update (board discussion)
records.evidence_text: one of the wells right near you is considered an interconnected surface water well for groundwater dependent ecosystems. Yet it's a lower aquifer well and it's consistently showing low. So is that you, Is that our pumping elsewhere? Is that the river?
records.notes: Speaker labeled Barbara Evoy; she addressed the Aerojet presenter. Which well is not identified.

records.finding: The Harvest Water presenter said its monitoring wells are mostly shallow, to about 100 feet, and it would add one deep well to the Mehrten Formation.
records.quantitative_detail: Shallow wells: surface to ~100 ft; one deep well to the Mehrten Formation proposed
records.agenda_item: Harvest Water program update (monitoring well coordination)
records.evidence_text: most all of our monitoring wells that are in so far are really focused on the shallow zone. So we're looking at, you know, ground surface down to 100ft. We'd like to install one deep monitoring well down to the Merton Formation.
records.notes: "Merton Formation" in transcript is read as Mehrten; speaker is the SRCSD project presenter.

records.finding: An SCGA board member said the South American Subbasin is light on shallow wells and called groundwater-dependent ecosystems and interconnected surface water the weakest point in the GSP.
records.agenda_item: Harvest Water program update (monitoring well coordination)
records.evidence_text: I think we're particularly light on shallow wells. And the GD and interconnected surface water issue is the one that I've always asserted is our weakest point in our gsp.
records.notes: Speaker is labeled "Barbara" in the transcript (full name Barbara Evoy elsewhere); the quote is her statement, not the GSA's formal position.

records.finding: An SCGA board member warned that the proposed network changes would leave the northeast corner thinly monitored, including near interconnected surface water, and that the draft no longer maps the ISW areas considered in 2022.
records.quantitative_detail: Board member cites: ~20% of network wells affected, 8 wells dropped, 88% coverage proposed, 29 volunteer domestic wells to be added (her statements, garbled transcript)
records.agenda_item: Periodic Evaluation draft: monitoring network changes
records.evidence_text: it also makes recommendations to our representative monitoring network of about 20% of our wells. ... we now no longer seem to have a graphic that shows interconnected surface water areas that were considered in 2022. So showing the wells for interconnected surface water separate from the bodies of water that we are trying to monitor seems like a disconnect in the document.
records.notes: Speaker is Barbara (board member); numbers like "drop eight" come from a garbled transcript passage. DWR accepted the network per staff.

records.finding: SCGA's consultant and executive director said the South American Subbasin will wait for DWR's ISW guidance before drafting a plan, and a placeholder ISW line item is going into the next fiscal-year work plan. The May 2026 cost-share table shows $10,000 for "ISW: Scoping for Compliance".
records.quantitative_detail: $10,000 FY2027 (Larry Walker Associates, "ISW: Scoping for Compliance", from 2026-05-19 packet)
records.agenda_item: Annual report / periodic evaluation update
records.evidence_text: So our current thinking is that we're basically waiting until the guidance comes out and hopefully it's going to come out in time that we can develop a plan that will be in the periodic evaluation that then we will plan to execute over the next five years. ... So ISW is something that we are putting a placeholder in the next year's fiscal year's work plan of kind of developing that something that we may need to do.
records.notes: Speakers are Bryan Thoreson (consultant) and Piret Harmon (SCGA executive director) per transcript labels; the $10,000 comes from the 2026-05-19 OHWD packet, not this transcript.

records.finding: A DWR representative told SCGA that the ISW guidance is now expected in the third quarter and that DWR wants the three released ISW papers incorporated, while saying it will not pre-approve plans.
records.quantitative_detail: Guidance expected Q3 (2026); three draft ISW papers (introduction, techniques, examples) released
records.agenda_item: Periodic Evaluation draft: DWR comments
records.evidence_text: the latest guidance we've got is Q3, so we'll see. But what is out are those three papers already on ISW.
records.notes: Speaker is a DWR attendee; garbled name. Earlier (2026-02-11 ESJ, 2026-02-17 OHWD) the expectation was Q1 2026.

records.finding: OHWD's packet describes its Cosumnes River recharge project as a response to pumping-lowered groundwater levels that disconnected the river from the aquifer, aiming to raise levels enough to reconnect the river and extend flow periods.
records.quantitative_detail: 326 acre-feet recharged last year (reported 2026-02-17)
records.agenda_item: Groundwater Recharge Project MND addendum (board packet)
records.evidence_text: Historically, the Cosumnes River has had a physical connection to the groundwater basin, which helped improve the flow within the river for fish migration, among additional beneficial uses. However, years of groundwater pumping have lowered groundwater levels. The Project is intended to increase groundwater recharge adjacent to and under the Cosumnes River, allowing the groundwater level to be raised to historic levels that would reconnect with, and thereby allow, the Cosumnes River to run for longer periods during the spring and summer and begin flowing earlier in the fall.
records.notes: Environmental document language (MND addendum) included in the board packet; no depletion metric is given.

records.finding: The regional water bank team said a loss factor will be applied each year to recharged water and re-evaluated every five years. Asked what would stop districts selling surface water and fallowing ground, the presenter said the bank is not a fallowed-land transfer and cited DWR/USBR transfer requirements (data, benchmark, investments). About 53% of water banked on paper remains in the basin.
records.quantitative_detail: About 900,000 AF of conjunctive use on paper in both subbasins over 27 years vs ~450,000 AF remaining (53% retained, cumulative to 2024); ~16,000 AF/yr average added to American River flow
records.agenda_item: Regional water bank / water accounting system update
records.evidence_text: We now have a loss factor that we're going to apply every year on the amount of water that's recharged. ... So this is not a fallowed land transfer. That's a whole different type of potential transfer activity.
records.notes: Presenter unnamed in this extract (water bank program manager). Bank covers North and South American Subbasins; the fallowed-land remark is a short answer, not a rule. Banking, not repurposing. Basin-wide rule; not specific to repurposed land.

records.section: 2.5 Data Source and ET Product Choice
records.finding: The South American Subbasin annual report estimates agricultural pumping from estimated ET and estimated surface water in the basin water balance; the presentation names no ET product and describes no local validation.
records.quantitative_detail: Context: storage +7,000 AF in the reported year; 187,900 AF total extractions vs 235,000 AF sustainable yield (including remediation pumping; year as stated 'last year')
records.agenda_item: SASb annual report presentation
records.evidence_text: Agricultural pumping is estimated based on the estimated ET and estimated surface water.
records.notes: ET product (OpenET, LandIQ or other) not named; the 'Cassana' model is probably the Cosana model. Basin-wide rule; not specific to repurposed land.

records.finding: SacSewer's Harvest Water project, the main SGMA project for the South American Subbasin, will deliver up to 50,000 AF/yr of recycled water: 32,500 AF to farmers so they leave groundwater unpumped, the rest for habitat in the non-irrigation season. Named co-benefits include groundwater restoration, wetlands, water quality and Cosumnes River flow.
records.quantitative_detail: Up to 50,000 AF/yr recycled water (project total, from 2027); 32,500 AF for in-lieu agricultural irrigation; over 4,000 acres of wetland; deliveries expected 2027
records.speaker_role: GSA staff — SacSewer Harvest Water project manager
records.agenda_item: Harvest Water update presentation
records.evidence_text: We deliver up to 50,000 acre feet per year of recycled water. The 32,500 acre feet are for agricultural irrigation during the growing season and and that's the inland recharge portion. And then the balance is for habitat benefits through the non irrigation season. ... And I mentioned 32,500 acre feet of inland recharge that we're providing by delivering recycled water to farmers, allowing them to leave the groundwater in the ground.
records.notes: This is an in-lieu recycled-water supply with habitat water, not fallowing or retirement; 'inland recharge' is the speaker's phrase for in-lieu. Landowners in the north area under development pressure declined 10-20 year commitments.

records.finding: SCGA's consultant presented the Wilton Road floodplain reconnection on the Cosumnes River as a potential multi-benefit project for recharge and flood reduction with an initial project report done; at the 2026-02-11 SCGA meeting he said SCGA should consider it for grant funding. No benefit metrics were given.
records.agenda_item: SASb annual report presentation
records.evidence_text: There's also another project that's the Wilton Road floodplain reconnection along the Cosumnes river that there's initial report that's been done. It's a nice multi benefit project that would do recharge and also help with floods.
records.notes: Project sits along the Cosumnes River and is listed under the South American Subbasin; Sacramento County staff (Austin Miller) are working on it per the 2026-02-11 meeting. No ECOFIP reference was found in either transcript.

records.finding: A South American Subbasin advisory group of domestic well owners is being reconvened at SCGA staff's invitation, with July topics of water banking, floodMAR and well monitoring. Its role is discussion; no board decision tied to its input is shown, and a commenter later called the advisory committee inactive.
records.agenda_item: Informational items: interagency Drought Task Force update
records.evidence_text: I got a message from Lisa Butler that we're scheduling a South American Sub Basin Advisory Group meeting again. And so we have the dates to pick sometime in July. And the topics that are open for interest for discussion are water banking, flood mar. Well monitoring.
records.notes: Reporter is Suzanne Pecci; OHWD's 2026-07-21 report calls the July meeting a 'Domestic Advisory Group' meeting where domestic wells were described as stable.

records.finding: During SCGA's governance review, a director asked that the consultant interview the chair of the domestic well advisory group, calling the voluntary well group a critical part of the GSP. The chair said non-board members should not be interviewed and public input belongs in the public workshops. The advisory group's formal role is not defined.
records.quantitative_detail: 3 public workshops planned for the governance review
records.agenda_item: Governance review and strategic visioning consultant
records.evidence_text: we have our domestic, well, advisory group, you know, is the chair of that group who could perhaps facilitate those comments ... I think it's not appropriate to interview people who are not on the board. I think the appropriate place for public participation is in the public workshops.
records.notes: Speakers are directors (Hunley and the chair per transcript) and are mostly unlabelled; the advisory group chair is the public commenter Suzanne Pecci.

records.finding: No designated seat for domestic well owners appears on SCGA's board: a director said a domestic well advocate is represented through her city and agricultural directors ('dual representation'). This is a director's description, not a board rule.
records.agenda_item: Governance review and strategic visioning consultant
records.evidence_text: Ms. Pecci is one of the residents within the city of Elk Grove and I'm one of her representative in addition to Agra's representation here. So she gets dual representation and I tremendously respect her.
records.notes: Speaker is the director Shoab per context; 'Agra' is as transcribed. Absence is inferred from this remark and the roll calls, not from the JPA text.

records.finding: Presenting the regional water bank, a speaker listed benefits including supply reliability for domestic well users and agriculture beyond the participating urban agencies. These are stated qualitatively; none are measured or credited to domestic well users in the passage.
records.agenda_item: Regional water bank and Harvest Water update
records.evidence_text: Provides additional water supply reliability for entities beyond the urban and municipal entities that are participating in the bank right now. It helps with providing water supply for domestic well users, AG and others
records.notes: Speaker is the SCGA executive director or consultant presenting the water bank (unlabelled); this is about benefits to domestic well users, not a DAC definition.

records.finding: [Distributive] A director told the board that domestic well users cannot bank water and, with shallower wells, would likely go dry first in a drought, so the water bank and recharge decisions should be viewed region-wide, not only from the purveyors' side.
records.agenda_item: Water bank working group update (board discussion)
records.evidence_text: some of our groundwater users are domestic well users. They do not have the ability to bank water. Right. And usually most of them have shallower wells, which in a drought would most likely go dry first and they will be the most impacted.
records.notes: Director (Shoab) per the chair's call; no decision follows in the passage.

records.finding: [Procedural] SCGA's manager told the OHWD board that a plan amendment has a mandatory 90-day public comment period while a plan update does not, but she said SCGA may still circulate the update for comment so all groundwater users can review it.
records.quantitative_detail: 90-day comment period for an amendment (as stated); none required for an update
records.agenda_item: South American Subbasin update: periodic evaluation
records.evidence_text: amendment has a mandatory public comment period. It needs to be open for 90 days. ... if it's just an update, it does not have such requirement. But also thinking that we will have. We are kind of early in the process and we have the draft periodic evaluation done in June. Even if we're not required to have a public comment period with update, we may still want to do it
records.notes: Speaker Piret Harmon (SCGA manager per transcript labels); the 90-day figure is her statement and a consultant said 'I think so'.

records.finding: [Procedural] Before approving a fee study (up to $135,599), a director asked how affected landowners would be informed and engaged. The consultant's stated goals include improving equity and transparency among stakeholders; he said the scope includes outreach materials (presentations, FAQs, fact sheets) and direct community meetings, with room to add more.
records.quantitative_detail: Fee study contract not to exceed $135,599; target completion spring 2027
records.agenda_item: Action item: comprehensive fee study agreement
records.evidence_text: how will you plan outreach to impacted classes of customers, particularly individual landowners, who may be getting assessments through this process? How will we communicate and engage with them? Yeah, absolutely. So, you know, as a part of our scope, we have the development of outreach materials. So that may include presentations, FAQs, fact sheets, that sort of thing. And we also have some meetings, some direct community meetings involved. ... simplify the revenue structure, reduce administrative burden, improve equity and transparency among stakeholders
records.notes: Consultant is from the firm named in the motion (Confluence Engineering Solutions); the ad hoc committee membership is partly cut off in the transcript.

records.section: 3.1.4 Domestic Well Protection as an Equity Outcome
records.finding: The GSA's consultant told the board that domestic wells in the northeast corner will keep being monitored but will have no minimum thresholds because the area is managed under the Superfund cleanup. A director had asked whether domestic wells there could be added to the voluntary monitoring set.
records.quantitative_detail: 29 wells to be added to the volunteer monitoring program (as described by the director)
records.agenda_item: Five-year update and annual report: review of draft sustainable management criteria
records.evidence_text: As to the volunteer monitoring program, we talked about having 29 wells added ... Should there be domestic wells that we could access in the northeast corner. ... The plan is to continue to monitor those wells just as we have been. They just would not have MTs because of the management of the super fund area there.
records.notes: Director (Barbara) and consultant (Bryan Thoreson) speak in the same passage; the transcript does not say these wells are in a disadvantaged community.

records.finding: A DWR intro meeting on 2025-09-24 presented the Community Monitoring Program in the South American Subbasin with three options: monitoring by a group, by an individual owner, or by DWR with loaned equipment. Sign-ups followed and DWR staff began visiting domestic well sites to pick candidates.
records.quantitative_detail: 3 participation options; meeting 2025-09-24; 'a few' sign-ups
records.agenda_item: Informational items: interagency Drought Task Force update
records.evidence_text: talked about the three options of community monitoring by group, or. by individual and, uh, or DWR and loaning of the, uh, um. equipment to, you know, for monitoring. So. they had a few sign-ups, and they're in the process now, DWR staff are going to be visiting. The sites of the, uh, domestic wells to see which ones might be appropriate for monitoring.
records.notes: Report is by Suzanne Pecci to the OHWD board; activity is DWR's, in the South American Subbasin.

records.finding: The consultant outlined outreach for the five-year evaluation: three dedicated public meetings (a launch on December 18, then March and June) plus presentations at the executive committee. No attendance figures or interpretation are mentioned.
records.quantitative_detail: 3 dedicated public meetings (2025-12-18, March 2026, June 2026)
records.agenda_item: Five-year evaluation and annual report: project status
records.evidence_text: We've got outreach and public engagement. We have a launch meeting scheduled for December 18, a week from tomorrow. And we'll have another meeting in March and another meeting in June with the dates to be scheduled.

records.finding: By February 2026 DWR's domestic well community monitoring pilot in the South American Subbasin had eight wells monitored by DWR and about 11 owners monitoring their own wells and sending data to DWR. The reporter also described a drought task force public meeting scheduled for April 17.
records.quantitative_detail: 8 wells monitored by DWR; about 11 resident-monitored wells; as of 2026-02-17
records.agenda_item: Informational items: interagency Drought Task Force update
records.evidence_text: As far as I know at this time there are eight wells that are being monitored by DWR and the surveys have been completed of the wells and I think about 11 are in the resident monitoring program where they are collecting data and forwarding it to dwr.
records.notes: Reporter (Suzanne Pecci) hedges ('as far as I know', 'I think about 11').

records.finding: A domestic well advocate told the OHWD board she briefed the Elk Grove City Council on SB 552 drought planning, and that the city's Climate Action Committee wants to join the South American Subbasin domestic well group, which she called encouraging.
records.agenda_item: Informational items: interagency Drought Task Force update
records.evidence_text: I went before the City of Elk Grove City Council a couple months ago and gave an update on SB552. And the city of Elk Grove has indicated an interest Climate Action Committee has wanted to be part of or join our Sacramento South American Sub Basin domestic well group.
records.notes: Reported by Suzanne Pecci; her remark is about one land-use agency's willingness, not a count of agencies.

records.finding: [Procedural] A domestic well owner said the public cannot find how to comment on the five-year update documents, there is no submission portal, and the advisory committee has been inactive. She said real outreach to domestic well owners is needed and that she is often the only public attendee. No board answer is recorded.
records.quantitative_detail: Representative monitoring network of 27 wells over about 7 square miles; 3 DWR-monitored domestic wells included (commenter's description)
records.agenda_item: Public comment on the five-year update and annual report
records.evidence_text: there's such a vagueness as far as the public's ability to even access these documents or their awareness that there are such documents. ... I don't see any portal to submit the documents or it just is very, very vague. ... Whether it's through the advisory committee which has, I don't know, been non functioning for a long period or some other mechanism. We really need to draw people in domestic well owners in and make them part of SCGA and the SGMA process.
records.notes: Commenter is Suzanne Pecci; the claim that the advisory committee is non-functioning is her opinion ('I don't know'). OHWD reports on 2026-05-19 say an advisory group meeting is being scheduled.

records.finding: A director said public workshop and comment notices for the GSP update reach her agency, which reposts them on social media; the third GSP update workshop was in July. She said many Elk Grove residents do not know SCGA and asked to give the city council a presentation.
records.quantitative_detail: 3 GSP update workshops held by July 2026 (as stated)
records.agenda_item: Board member comments
records.evidence_text: we had the third workshop for the GSP update in July. ... A lot of residents in El Grove are not familiar with the CGA and to that effort, I would like to take you on your previous offer if you're still willing to maybe do a quick presentation to city council on ACGA and what we do
records.notes: Speaker (chair or director Persephonie Riley per transcript) refers to SCGA as 'ACGA/CGA' in the machine transcript.

records.finding: The consultant updating South American's five-year evaluation said DWR's dry well reporting shows one dry well in the subbasin in 2022 and none other in five years. He said the update will also use DWR's domestic well susceptibility tool and the SB 552 domestic well vulnerability tool.
records.quantitative_detail: 1 reported dry well, 2022 (the only one in the last 5 years, as stated)
records.agenda_item: Five-year evaluation and annual report: project status
records.evidence_text: in this South American basin, why there's been one dry well in 2022 that in the very dry year. That's the only one in the last five years. And they also have a, a domestic well susceptibility tool that we'll also be using. That's new information. And then there's the SB522 domestic well vulnerability too.
records.notes: Consultant (Brian, GEI per other SCGA transcripts) speaking; transcript garbles 'SB 552' as 'SB522' and 'why' for 'only'.

records.finding: A director said the draft five-year update's Table 5-2 shows wells that could go dry, including one case of 57 of 1,511, but does not make clear whether the figures add up or where the wells are. She noted the group on handling dry wells had been put off. The consultant took the comments for later.
records.quantitative_detail: 57 of 1,511 wells in one modelled case (per director); about 60 wells over 10 to 15 years (director's reading)
records.agenda_item: Five-year update and annual report: review of draft
records.evidence_text: Table 5, 2 is where it discusses which of the potential wells might go dry. And I need some help understanding that whether those are additive numbers or not. ... if we are looking at in one case it was 57 of 1511, it would certainly be good to know where those are and whether or not that's a near term or long term kind of program we should be talking about. We have put off some of the Voluntary or some of the work with the group to discuss how we would deal with dry wells.
records.notes: Draft table is not in the transcript; the director's reading of 57 of 1511 and '60 in 10 years or 15 years' could be garbled.

records.finding: DWR's recommended corrective actions require the South American Subbasin to either set a minimum threshold for arsenic or explain why not; the consultant said the water quality network uses GAMA wells and is checking which have arsenic. A director asked what a threshold would achieve for a natural constituent.
records.quantitative_detail: No arsenic SMC in current GSP; 4 recommended corrective actions in total
records.agenda_item: Five-year evaluation: recommended corrective actions
records.evidence_text: the first corrective action is related to arsenic as a water quality indicator. It was not. We did not set a SMC for arsenic in the gsp. DWR is asking that we either set an SMC for arsenic or provide additional information why we should not set an SMC for arsenic. We're looking into which wells have that as a water quality indicator right now for the water quality network. We're using the gamma wells that are available in this region.
records.notes: Transcript renders GAMA as 'gamma'; consultant is GEI per other SCGA transcripts.

records.finding: In the water year 2025 annual report, South American Subbasin water quality sentinels are tracked against thresholds for nitrate (10 mg/L) and specific conductance (1,600 micromhos/cm), with no exceedances. Arsenic, iron and manganese have no thresholds but are tracked: 2 of 20 wells exceeded the arsenic MCL.
records.quantitative_detail: WY2025: nitrate MT 10 mg/L, trigger 5 mg/L; specific conductance MT 1,600, trigger 900 micromhos/cm; 2 of 20 wells above arsenic MCL (10 ug/L), Jan 2005 to Sept 2025; 21 representative wells
records.agenda_item: Agenda packet: draft Water Year 2025 annual report
records.evidence_text: There were no exceedances of nitrate nor specific conductance MTs at any of the RMPs during WY 2025. ... Two of the 20 resulted in an exceedance of the arsenic MCL, seven of the 20 resulted in an exceedance of the iron SMCL, and 11 of the 20 resulted in an exceedance of the manganese SMCL.
records.notes: Draft annual report text in the board packet (consultant-authored for SCGA); the wells exceeding arsenic MCL are not located in this passage.

records.finding: A Regional Water Board official briefed SCGA on the Aerojet Superfund groundwater cleanup: perchlorate, NDMA and TCE plumes are tracked through about 1,400 monitoring wells and 60 local water supply and irrigation wells, with compliance and sentinel wells triggering agency notification. These are cleanup-program data, not SGMA water quality indicators.
records.quantitative_detail: About 115 extraction wells; about 1,400 monitoring wells and about 60 water supply and irrigation wells sampled; 8 treatment systems at about 15,000 to 20,000 gpm; estimated treatment time about 240 years (2001 decision)
records.agenda_item: Aerojet groundwater remediation update (Regional Water Board)
records.evidence_text: Aerojet does routine sampling of those wells, along with about 1400 monitoring wells and about 60 local water supply and irrigation wells. ... So if one of those three main CoCs is detected in a compliance or a sentinel well at a concentration exceeding the compliance level, that triggers a agency notification to myself, DTSC and EPA and then submittal of a compliance action plan.
records.notes: Presenter is the Regional Water Quality Control Board's Aerojet project staffer (first name Jeff in the transcript); sampling is by Aerojet, not SCGA.

records.finding: The Water Board presenter said the cleanup's reports are public on the GeoTracker website, Sacramento County reviews any well permit within 2,000 feet of a known plume, and Aerojet must have backup water within 24 hours if a supply becomes unusable. Notification is through these channels, not SCGA.
records.quantitative_detail: 2,000 ft county consultation zone; backup water supply within 24 hours; about 1 to 2 permit notifications per year
records.agenda_item: Aerojet groundwater remediation update (Regional Water Board)
records.evidence_text: This report along with the other documents I've shown today are available on the Geo Checker website. ... any application for a well permit within 2,000ft of a known grommet or contaminant plume is subject to a special review. ... within 24 hours if a water supply becomes unusable due to aerodrous contamination, that they have a backup water supply on hand.
records.notes: Transcript garbles 'GeoTracker' as 'Geo Checker' and 'known contaminant plume'; the 24-hour requirement is Aerojet's under a US EPA order.

records.finding: A commenter said rural homes classed on state maps as inside a public water district boundary cannot get free well testing, data tracking or bottled-water programs, and that districts do not test their water. records.finding: A director said the Aerojet cleanup pumping may be lowering water levels at SCGA monitoring wells and that coordination between the cleanup and SGMA minimum thresholds has not advanced in a year. records.section: 3.3.3 Domestic Wells and Community Water System Consolidation
records.finding: SCGA's consultant said domestic well data for the subbasin comes from DWR's voluntary monitoring pilot (levels aligning well with network wells), DWR's well completion database, and a dataset from the Community Water Center, used to update the likely number of domestic wells.

And I think those are also wells that we could consider for the assessing the monitoring network. ... we recognize that there is privacy issues with domestic well owners on many of these.
records.notes: Tools are named as inputs to a work in progress; use by the public is not described. 'Level C' is as transcribed.

records.finding: A domestic well owner on DWR's drought task force asked whether the watershed resilience pilot would coordinate with the domestic well monitoring pilot and whether its outreach had reached vulnerable domestic well owners. And do we have gaps?

I am asking for you, as a Board of members of SCGA and GSAS under SGMA to support the program in the South American subbasin and direct the Advisory Committee to support and help to facilitate the RCAC program ... critical mapping loophole that leaves an estimated 2,500 domestic wells in the South American subbasin unprotected by the SEAVI Salts Nitrate Control Program ... if you could please look into that for us and give us some feedback on that, I would appreciate it

records.meeting_body: Redwood Valley County Water District Board

records.section: 3.3.3 Domestic Wells and Community Water System Consolidation
records.finding: Redwood Valley County Water District directors said SAFER funding requires fewer water agencies and that about $75 million in potential funding is at risk if local districts do not agree to combine, with an August SAFER meeting expected to press the point.
records.quantitative_detail: about $75 million potential SAFER funding at risk (speaker's figure)
records.meeting_body: Redwood Valley County Water District Board
records.agenda_item: SAFER consolidation discussion

You're hearing it from the horse's mouth at that point. And that will make people make a decision. If you're not on board, it will make you get on board. Because we can't afford to go lose $75 million
