records.finding: Upper Valley ISW mapping for the amendment uses the updated model with a 10%-of-months connection cutoff, which staff said gives nearly the same extent as 50% or 90% cutoffs and shows ISW along the main river stem. Two new ISW monitoring wells were also added in the Upper Valley.
records.quantitative_detail: Connection cutoff 10% of months (previously 50%); 2 new Upper Valley ISW wells
records.speaker_role: mixed — GSA staff and M&A presenters (no speaker labels)
records.meeting_body: SVBGSA Forebay and Upper Valley Aquifer Subbasin Committees (joint special meeting)
records.agenda_item: 4.2 Periodic Evaluation - New Information Collected/Data Gaps Filled
records.evidence_text: So we use a 10% cutoff which should help make the state happier. And essentially it's no different than the 50% or the 90%. We have updated maps, they're very simple. So the blue is where the model connected over 10% of the time. The upper valley here, main along river stem and then for the four bay as well.
records.notes: Joint meeting with unlabeled speakers; the same cutoff applies to Forebay and 180/400 mapping.

records.finding: Superposition runs on the SVBGSA model show that turning off Upper Valley pumping increases Salinas River flow by about 40,000 AF/yr on average over 1980-2022; a Coalition consultant put the upstream pumping effect at about 15% of historical flow at the Chualar gauge. Staff said the runs will not be used directly in GSP work.
records.quantitative_detail: Upper Valley pumping off, average 1980-2022: Salinas River flow +~40,000 AF/yr; Forebay to 180/400 flow +~30,000 AF/yr; 40,000 AF/yr against ~240,000 AF/yr historical flow at the Chualar gauge, about 15%
records.speaker_role: mixed — Bob Abrams (consultant to Salinas Basin Water Alliance) and Dwight Smith (consultant to Salinas Valley Water Coalition), interpreting M&A model runs
records.agenda_item: 2.1 Interbasin Flow Modeling Results
records.evidence_text: And so what, what the graph shows is that when you turn off pumping in the upper valley, the flow in the river increases by about 40,000 acre feet per year and the flow from the four bay to the 180 increases by about 30,000 acre feet per year. ... the majority of the impact there, 40,000 acre feet contrasted to 240,000 acre feet that historically discharges through the Chular gauge already is 15%. You've reduced the flow in the Salinas river by 15%.
records.notes: Figures are stakeholder consultants' rounded readings of runs funded by two stakeholder groups, and Smith's 40,000 AF may refer to Upper Valley and Forebay pumping combined.

records.finding: UVRGA's model is a MODFLOW-based coupled groundwater and surface-water model built from scratch for the GSP; it simulates both groundwater and surface-water flow.
records.quantitative_detail: Original calibration 2005-2019; recalibration extended through water year 2022
records.agenda_item: Item 6A Numerical model update
records.evidence_text: we had no prior groundwater model for this basic, so this model was developed completely from scratch ... a Modflow-based model. We just call it the UVRJ model, or the Upper Ventura River model. ... what it does is it simulates not only groundwater flow, but also the surface water flow.
records.notes: Speaker inferred as the executive director who oversaw the consultant (INTERA).

records.finding: Verification showed the model over-predicted low streamflows after the original calibration, so the GSA recalibrated it to USGS in-basin measurements only, cutting the average low-flow error to about half.
records.quantitative_detail: Mean low-flow error at USGS Foster Park measurements 1.82 cfs to 0.85 cfs (about 60 calibration points); verification-period RMS error more than double and mean error about 3x calibration period
records.agenda_item: Item 6A Numerical model update
records.evidence_text: the streamflow's model was over-predicting low streamflows, which is… pretty critical for our GSB, because. Our depletion, um. Minimum threshold criteria for depletion. Or in the low flow range. ... stream flow estimation from 1.82 CFS, which is the earlier point. Down to 0.85 CFS
records.notes: Transcript is machine-garbled; the 60-point count and RMS/mean-error multiples come from nearby passages and are described approximately.

records.finding: ISW depletion modelling uses gauged streamflow both as inflow (county gauges at the top of the basin and tributaries) and as the one calibration point (Foster Park), and now metered private-well pumping.
records.agenda_item: Item 6A Numerical model update
records.evidence_text: We use Streamflow in two different ways. It's an input to the model, the top of the basin. And at any tributary point. San Antonio Creek being the main one. And then there's one outflow point where we use data and we calibrate. The model to that outcome. ... now people are metering the private wells, so we've incorporated updated information about which wells have been and how much.
records.notes: Gauge types are from adjacent passages; bedrock depth near Foster Park was also named as a data gap but is not quoted.

records.finding: Model output reported by well group: lag times from pumping curtailment to Foster Park flow, and the share of curtailed pumping that arrives as stream flow, in both cumulative and single-month scenarios.
records.quantitative_detail: Miners Oaks wells: lag 15-20 days (minimum) to 200-400 days (maximum); share of curtailed pumping arriving at Foster Park median about 50%, up to 60-80%; during exceedance periods median 3-7% (50-year projection)
records.speaker_role: GSA staff (executive director) and consultant (INTERA) on call
records.agenda_item: Item 11 Interconnected surface water depletion modeling update
records.evidence_text: The maximum lag time ranged from 200 to almost 400 days. The minimum 15 to 20. ... pumping containment is not particularly effective at increasing stream float. Foster part particularly during critical dry periods where we're seeing less than about 10% of curtailed pumping actually arriving stream flow.
records.notes: Results are draft and model-based; percentages for the exceedance period are read from the group-1 slide and transcribed loosely ('3 to 7%').

records.finding: After three years of monitoring, UVRGA's consultant said flow-only minimum thresholds may not be the best way to prevent undesirable results and asked whether groundwater levels could update the Foster Park threshold or set one for the Confluence.
records.agenda_item: Item 11C Aquatic GDE three-year summary
records.evidence_text: minimum thresholds based on flow or flow alone might not actually be the best way to assess and prevent undesired results. ... can grounder levels be used to update for Foster PARC or establish for Confluence those management thresholds?
records.notes: Presented as questions for next steps, not a proposed amendment.

records.finding: A director asked when the 2 cfs Foster Park minimum threshold would be reevaluated; the ED said the GSP planned that for now, but the wet years left no low-flow biological data.
records.quantitative_detail: Minimum threshold 2 cfs at Foster Park
records.speaker_role: mixed — board member and GSA staff
records.agenda_item: GSP periodic evaluation briefing
records.evidence_text: We have a 2 CFS minimum threshold now at Foster Park. Is there a schedule for reevaluating that at some point, and if so, what would that be as part of this, or is this further down the road? ... So the idea when we wrote the GSP is that we would reevaluate that at this time, but because it's been wet, our biological monitoring program hasn't collected much, if any, data at the conditions that we need to see in order to wait.
records.notes: Last sentence of the answer is incomplete in the transcript.

records.finding: The GSP set no ISW criteria for the Confluence area because staff could not tell whether pumping causes significant effects there; monitoring is under way to decide.
records.agenda_item: GSP periodic evaluation briefing
records.evidence_text: We did not set criteria for depletion of surface water in the confluence area because we weren't sure if pumping was causing significant effects in that area. So we're doing monitoring to determine if that's happening.

records.finding: In its draft periodic evaluation UVRGA said the Foster Park threshold is a moving flow target (no pumping-caused flow below about 2 cfs) and that the basin met its interim milestone, despite one brief minimum-threshold exceedance in 2023 (transcribed also as 'late 2020').
records.quantitative_detail: Minimum threshold about 2 cfs at Foster Park; one brief exceedance (year garbled, 2023 per another passage)
records.agenda_item: GSP periodic evaluation workshop (public draft)
records.evidence_text: That means the minimum threshold is constantly a changing number because the stream flow is constantly changed. So the amount of depletion that would cause it to go to flow to pump it's always good. That's what this orange line is at any point in time. The orange line tells you how much depletion you could have without how to go below 2. ... we're in compliance because our inner milestone is this black, black, see solid.
records.notes: Garbled; the 2023 exceedance year comes from 'we briefly went below the minimum threshold 20, 23' elsewhere in the same talk.

records.finding: The GSP estimates pumping-attributable depletion as the difference between model runs with and without pumping; the presenter showed a GSP example with a 2 to 7 cfs gap.
records.quantitative_detail: Example gap 'two to seven CFS' (as transcribed, time period unclear)
records.agenda_item: Item 6A Numerical model update
records.evidence_text: we ran the model once with all the pumping, and then we ran them all without the pumping. And we get two curves, and the difference between those curves is the impact. On the surface water ... Here, in this period of this year, two to seven CFS depletion.
records.notes: Example figure is illustrative and the period is garbled in the transcript.

records.finding: The GSP depletion estimate is the gap between model runs with and without pumping; the 50-year GSP simulation (prior model version) showed eight exceedances of the Foster Park minimum threshold.
records.quantitative_detail: 8 minimum-threshold exceedance events in a 50-year simulation (prior model version, GSP)
records.agenda_item: Item 11D Indirect depletion modeling
records.evidence_text: And so the difference between those two is an estimate of depletion of stream flow caused by groundwater open. ... There was eight of them over the 50 years that we predicted would cause an exceedance of the GSP minimum threshold.
records.notes: 'groundwater open' is a garble of 'pumping'; the simulation is projected future hydrology, not observed.

records.finding: With the recalibrated model, a 50-year GSP-style projection now shows two periods where the Foster Park minimum threshold is exceeded, against eight reported in the GSP-era run.
records.quantitative_detail: 2 minimum-threshold exceedance periods (updated model, 50-year projection) vs 8 (GSP, 50-year simulation)
records.agenda_item: Item 11 Interconnected surface water depletion modeling update
records.evidence_text: in that updated projection we found two periods where our GSP minimum thresholds were exceeded.
records.notes: The 8 figure comes from the 2026-02-12 meeting; the two runs differ in model version and city protocols, and the speakers did not say whether the projections are otherwise identical.

records.finding: UVRGA splits depletion into direct (City of Ventura's Foster Park facilities, governed by operating protocols) and indirect (the cumulative effect of all other upstream pumping); the GSP's pending management action targets indirect depletion.
records.agenda_item: Item 11D Indirect depletion modeling
records.evidence_text: The blue line is the portion of the depletion that's associated with the pumping facilities right in that area. We call that direct depletion. ... The difference between the black and the blue is the effect of all the pumping upstream of Foster part cumulatively on. On the stream flow depletion.
records.notes: No well count given; later work (May 2026) groups non-city wells.

records.finding: ISW monitoring combines GPS mapping of where flow starts and stops, a continuous rating-curve gauge at Camino Cielo, and satellite NDVI/NDMI imagery for riparian GDEs.
records.quantitative_detail: 17 groundwater-level monitoring locations; 3 years of aquatic GDE monitoring (WY2023-2025)
records.agenda_item: Item 11C Monitoring programs update (water year 2024-25)
records.evidence_text: the data that we're collecting here are GPS locations. They mark the locations of intermittent flow. ... includes remotely sensed data from satellites. So the ndvi, ndmi, ... developing a rating curve where we're able to develop continuous flow measurements.
records.notes: Program details also covered in the 2025-10-09 ED report (monthly walk of the dry reach, snorkel surveys).

records.finding: The board was asked to replace fixed-flow triggers for aquatic GDE monitoring with condition-based triggers so surveys are done when low-flow conditions best test the Foster Park criteria and the need for Confluence criteria.
records.quantitative_detail: Third round of workplan amendments since 2022; Rincon letter dated July 31, 2026
records.agenda_item: Item 11(a) Aquatic GDE monitoring plan amendments
records.evidence_text: The proposed amendments would refine the low flow prioritization approach by replacing fixed flow-based triggers with condition-based triggers that allow field biologists to mobilize monitoring when conditions are most relevant for evaluating the Foster Park Aquatic Habitat Area SMC and the potential need for SMC in the Confluence Aquatic Habitat Area.
records.notes: Agenda-packet staff report; outcome of the vote not captured in the excerpt.

records.finding: Monthly field flow measurements at five points along the Ventura River were reported to the board, with the Camino Cielo inflow and Foster Park values.
records.quantitative_detail: End of September 2026 snapshot: Camino Cielo 8.7 cfs, upper confluence 11.1 cfs, lower confluence 14.1 cfs, upper Foster Park 10.6 cfs, USGS gauge about 8 cfs
records.agenda_item: Executive director report (monitoring networks)
records.evidence_text: going north to south cielo. There was 8.7 cfs entering the basin at lower. I'm sorry upper confluence. That was 11.1 cfs lower confluence. So below San Antonio Creek confluence 14.1 cfs. Upper Foster Park 10.6. And then at the USGS gauge eight.
records.notes: Transcription garbled; a director noted the upper Foster Park value exceeds the USGS gauge and the difference was not reconciled.

records.section: 1.5 Per-well Attribution and the Cumulative Pumping Problem
records.finding: The ED proposed attributing indirect depletion to groups of wells by turning each group's pumping off month by month, working backwards from a modelled threshold-exceedance event, to relate pumping location and timing to Foster Park flow.
records.quantitative_detail: Three or four well groups proposed (later six); monthly curtailment steps
records.agenda_item: Item 11D Indirect depletion modeling
records.evidence_text: we're going to take the model and we're going to identify four groups of wells. We're going to identify Ventura river water districts wells, Miners Oaks wells, and then we're going to also consider a condition where those two wells, sets of wells together. ... we'll start removing, turning off the pumping for that well group for a month. Then we'll turn it off two months and we're going to keep going backwards, adding one month at a time and rerunning the model until we see no effect on the stream flow
records.notes: Proposal stage; the May 2026 meeting reported results using six groups.

records.section: 1.5 Per-well Attribution and the Cumulative Pumping Problem
records.finding: Attribution was run by well group, starting with Miners Oaks and Ventura River Water District wells; the City of Ventura's wells were held at the interim-order protocols and so not treated as a factor.
records.quantitative_detail: Six well groups
records.agenda_item: Item 11 Interconnected surface water depletion modeling update
records.evidence_text: group number one is Miners Oaks wells. ... Group two is Ventura River Water District's wells that are near the river. ... The city of Ventura's facilities are operated in the base model according to the interim order protocols. So they're not really a factor in this.
records.notes: Attribution is to groups of wells, not individual wells; Meiners Oaks northern wells excluded because projections covered only southern wells.

records.section: 1.5 Per-well Attribution and the Cumulative Pumping Problem
records.finding: ISW effects are handled spatially by well group and position: wells nearer Foster Park show shorter lag times, and river-alluvium wells (group four) are a separate group from wells outside the alluvium.
records.agenda_item: Item 11 Interconnected surface water depletion modeling update
records.evidence_text: Group four is all other wells that are in the river alluvium, so along the river channel. ... The further away we are from Foster park, the longer the lag times and vice versa.
records.notes: Quote 1 is the group definition; quote 2 is a results statement later in the talk.

records.section: 1.5 Per-well Attribution and the Cumulative Pumping Problem
records.finding: The analysis runs cumulative scenarios (curtailment extended month by month back from an exceedance) and single-increment scenarios, plus an all-wells group, to see how combined pumping affects Foster Park flow.
records.quantitative_detail: 1- or 3-month increments; groups 3 (two districts) and 6 (all wells)
records.agenda_item: Item 11 Interconnected surface water depletion modeling update
records.evidence_text: We did it cumulatively. So we started turning off pumping at the end of the depletion event and just kept taking off pumping one or three months at a time, all the way back until we saw no effect. We also did that non cumulatively. ... Group 6, which is not illustrated on here, is everything together.
records.notes: 'Cumulative' here means sequential curtailment over time; the aggregate-wells question is covered by the group 3 and group 6 runs.

records.finding: The ED found USGS flow measurements near the Foster Park staff gauge were taken over a ~1,400 ft reach where modelled flow varies by up to 5 cfs, versus a 2 cfs minimum threshold, which he called a huge problem.
records.quantitative_detail: Up to 5 cfs variation over about 1,400 ft (600 ft upstream to 800 ft downstream of gauge); minimum threshold 2 cfs
records.agenda_item: Item 6A Numerical model update
records.evidence_text: Varies along the river, up and downstream of the staff gauge, by as much as 5 CFS. Well, our minimum threshold is 2. ... So that's a huge, huge problem.
records.notes: Figure is a model-derived range; directors questioned it in the Q&A.

records.finding: A director said the key unknown, which the GSA has sought for years, is how much and when stream flow at Foster Park would respond to cutting back pumping.
records.agenda_item: Item 11 GSP implementation (indirect depletion plan)
records.evidence_text: we don't know what the effect of a cutback in our pumping would be quantity wise or timing wise. ... We've been trying to get that for several years now. We still don't have it.
records.notes: Speaker not named; statement made as part of a discussion of slowing the indirect-depletion work.

records.finding: Staff and directors noted that two of three monitoring years were very wet, so pumping effects have not been tested, and a director warned that non-groundwater dynamics (fire, scour) may swamp the groundwater signal.
records.quantitative_detail: Aquatic GDE monitoring WY2023-2025; two of three years very wet
records.speaker_role: mixed — GSA staff and board members
records.agenda_item: Item 11C Riparian GDE monitoring and aquatic GDE summary
records.evidence_text: two of the three years we've been monitoring have been very wet. So we haven't seen the types of conditions where pumping effects could be significant. ... the non groundwater dynamics may be larger than the groundwater effect.
records.notes: Second excerpt is a director's view (unnamed).

records.finding: The board authorized Work Order 13 to update depletion estimates with the recalibrated model, including estimating their uncertainty and running simulations.
records.quantitative_detail: $65,000 plus 10% contingency, authorization $71,452; earlier $150,000 allocation for model update and depletion estimates already spent
records.agenda_item: Item 6B Work Order 13 (modeling support, indirect depletion)
records.evidence_text: Our obsidian is, yes, $65,000, and we typically include 10% contingency. The total authorization would be just over $71,000. ... which would involve… estimating the uncertainty in those estimates. ... do we authorize the Executive Director to issue workload number 13 to the tariff? For a co-authorization amount of $71,452.
records.notes: Roll call recorded affirmative votes in the transcript (one director absent); 'tariff' is a garble of the consultant's name.

records.finding: Staff said USGS would keep its current visit frequency at the Foster Park gauge with the City, plus Casitas and county funding, supplementing visits to twice that frequency.
records.quantitative_detail: Frequency of USGS visits to be doubled (cost not given)

records.finding: After a small agricultural operator pushed back on mandatory five-year flow meter accuracy testing, the executive director analysed pumping by user group and proposed exempting wells up to 10 or 25 AF/year; the board redrew testing intervals in Ordinance No. 5. Testing costs about $300 per well.
records.quantitative_detail: About 94% of pumping is by public suppliers; the 11 private wells pumping 2 to 10 AF/year total about 1% of pumping; accuracy test cost about $300 per well; 81 wells under 2 AF/year have no meter (2026-01-08)
records.agenda_item: Well registration, metering and extraction reporting ordinance amendments
records.evidence_text: First test case was well before agent one, one of our small agricultural operators, they pushed back on this, sent some documentation. Basically they're saying they have a whole forever. I looked at that. I look at the warranty on the meters only for two years. So you know, I'm not convinced that if we want the meter to be tested that that's a really good reason to exempt them. But stepping back, this made me think about our ordinance and it made me go back through and look at kind of the distribution of pumping we have that subject to meter requirements. So I put together a table and maybe if you could go to page 64 folks, they can see this online, Zoom in on that. Okay, so I just want to break this down so there's perspective. So almost 94% of our pumping is by our agencies, the public water suppliers. They pump anywhere from just over 100 acre feature year to almost as 2500. And then if we break down the rest of the other 6% of pumping, which is all private, it, it breaks down with one pumper who pumps more than 53 that are between 25 and 50 acre feet per year, one who's between 10 and 25. And then we've got this group of five, sorry, number five of 11. More than the two acre foot threshold for being considered the minimums and less than 10. So between 2 and 10, the reason 2 is important is because if you're less than 2, you don't have to have a pump. That's that last group in the table. So those 81 wells that pump less than 2 do not have meters. Part of a meter you don't have to worry about proving attack or serious. So the well owner raised this issue about, you know, not thinking they need to test their accuracy. Is one of the 11 equal between 2 and 10. And so if we look at that group, you Know they pump as a group 1% of the annual pumping. And I started to think about well, how important is it to know if their meter is 95 to 105%. I did a quick, just theoretical calculation. If their meters were say 85% accuracy, 75%, the fiscal impact is $1,000 per year. We probably would spend that much or just tracking whether they're in compliance. And compelling compliance takes a lot of follow up as you can see somebody who's challenging it. So I think we actually from a purely fiscal standpoint come out behind by requiring them to test accuracy every five years. So that's one consideration. The other consideration is what does this mean in terms of managing basin. So again if they were say 85% accurate instead of 95% accurate, that's 6 acre feet per year in that group of 11 wells. That's point 1% the pumping in the basin. So my, my thinking on this is that you know, this isn't probably making sense from a fiscal standpoint and it doesn't move the needle in terms of a ability to manage the basin. So I'm recommending that the consider pursuing an ordinance amendment so that we can exempt this group number five and maybe even group number four.
records.notes: Public input is from a pumper (an agricultural business), not a DAC or resident; the 2026-02-12 transcript describes the revised intervals (details as spoken are garbled) and the 2026-03-12 transcript shows the board approving the ordinance after a public hearing with no comments; the adoption is read from the roll call, not a stated ordinance number.

records.finding: UVRGA's consultant explained that the GSP's only water quality undesirable result is pumping spreading the nitrate-affected area (transcribed as Miramonte) into places with domestic wells that lack an alternative water source; other constituents like boron are screened out because pumping does not affect them.

Pumping doesn't affect boron. So we kind of screen that one out.

records.section: 3.3.3 Domestic Wells and Community Water System Consolidation
records.finding: UVRGA's well registration found only about half of the domestic wells assumed active in the GSP are still in use, so projected domestic pumping fell by roughly half. The registration process also served as the GSP's domestic well survey.
records.quantitative_detail: Private domestic well extraction projection 172 AF/year (GSP) versus 89 AF/year (periodic evaluation), -48%, average annual over the future projection period (agenda table, 2026-10-08); about 70 wells found not in use (2026-01-08)

The reason for that is there were there's a large number of domestic wells historically drilled in the basin. And did the GSP assume they were all still active? The registration process we determined about half of them, maybe a little bit more are actually still active. Wells have been filled in, not used. A lot of people didn't even know there was well in the property, that kind of thing. So. So a lot less domestic use than we assumed in gsp. ... identify the need to do the domestic well survey, which was part of the registration process.
records.notes: Presenter is unlabeled; the transcript fragment 'a lot less domestic use' begins mid-sentence; collection is mandatory under the registration ordinance, and the 2026-10-08 agenda table gives the 172 and 89 AF/year figures.

records.finding: Vina's SGMA-funded data-gap project sampled Big Chico Creek and Butte Creek for radon during the 2025 dry season to detect groundwater inflow. No sampled location showed inflow, which staff read as indicating disconnected streams.

So if there's no radon in the water, then there's no water, Groundwater kind of continuously coming in at that location. So based on those samples, all of them from top to bottom in big chico creek and top to bottom in Butte Creek across 2025 dry season. So, like April to October, none of those locations showed input. records.finding: Vina's staff described the North Sacramento corridor group's 15-page draft ISW work plan: shared field data along the Sacramento and Feather Rivers and Butte Creek, a refined regional model built with DWR, and a regional guidance document of options for local sustainability standards. Early talks with DWR on funding are under way.
records.quantitative_detail: draft work plan about 15 pages; no cost stated here
records.agenda_item: Interbasin coordination update
records.evidence_text: So regional data collection. So field teams, they would go collect data along the river, Sacramento River, Feather River, Butte Creek and other shared streams so that we could improve the understanding of how water moves between rivers and the underground aquifer. records.agenda_item: 2026 amended GSP and periodic evaluation
records.evidence_text: we have done the modeling that has shown that it's not interconnected surface water consistent with the guidance that has been released to date. When we met with DWR review team, they verbally indicated that the GSP, the 2022 GSP had conflicting information and highly recommended that the GSA makes the determination of no interconnected surface water consistent in the document. ... we're going to want to make sure our GSP is bolstered with our expanded description of our modeling work that we've conducted consistent with the DWR best management practices.
records.notes: Model name not stated; the GSA's groundwater flow model (updated with LandIQ ET, no subsidence package per 2025-08-05) is the likely candidate but that is not confirmed here.

records.finding: White Wolf's GDE consultant report (reported to the board) rated GDE health as intermediate, found a long-term decline in evapotranspiration at many GDE areas since 2020, and recommended removing about 15 of 870 acres as non-GDE. NDVI showed GDEs below the Springs fault respond to rainfall while those above follow persistent groundwater trends.
records.quantitative_detail: About 870 acres of mapped GDE; about 15 acres recommended for removal; canopy dieback under 25% over 2020-2025; ET trend back to 2020 via OpenET.
records.agenda_item: GDE survey and SMC update
records.evidence_text: overall GDE health is quantified as intermediate. There are some indications that there have been ecological stresses, but most of the ecological processes remain intact. The canopy dieback was typically low to moderate, so less than 25% of dieback was observed over the 2020-2025 period. ... you can see in many of the areas of the GDEs there's been a long evapotranspiration decline which does indicate long term drying of these GDE areas. And then as part of the field survey and the remote sensing analysis they are actually recommending removing about 15 acres. It's a small amount of the total 870 acres of the GDE areas based on the vegetation type, they are not actually GDEs.
records.notes: Outputs are GDE health indicators rather than a depletion volume; the board was told the report was still in review.

records.finding: In the WY2025 annual report summary, White Wolf's consultant said all three ISW wells remained above the preliminary minimum thresholds, which are 30 feet below ground surface.
records.quantitative_detail: Preliminary ISW minimum threshold 30 ft below ground surface; WY2025 annual report.
records.agenda_item: WY2025 annual report preview
records.evidence_text: And for interconnected surface water, all wells remain above those preliminary MTs which is 30ft below ground surface.
records.notes: Whether '30 ft' applies to every well is not stated; the transcript is machine-generated.

records.finding: After an April 20, 2026 meeting, DWR told White Wolf that having both a no-ISW finding and preliminary ISW criteria was confusing. The GSA proposed eliminating the preliminary criteria and keeping the three shallow wells as supplemental groundwater-level monitoring wells, which DWR viewed favorably.
records.quantitative_detail: Three shallow upland wells (about 50 ft deep) would become supplemental monitoring wells; DWR meeting 2026-04-20.
records.agenda_item: Periodic evaluation / SMC revisions
records.evidence_text: although we did not get a recommended corrective action for interconnected surface waters, there was a recommendation in there to reassess and update the GSP since we had identified it as a data gap. ... So following that direction from DWR, we are proposing to eliminate the preliminary SMCs that have been established for interconnected surface waters and instead move these three wells that do exist in this upland port of the basin to become supplemental monitoring wells for groundwater levels. So the GSA will still commit to monitoring these areas. However, there's not going to be any management actions triggered with the, with the changing conditions in these uplands portions of the basin and DWR was favorable of this
records.notes: Arvin Edison (06-09) and Wheeler Ridge-Maricopa (06-10, 08-12) board meetings repeat the removal; a July 2026 board update reportedly says ISW was removed as an indicator; Fish and Wildlife later objected (2026-10-06 row).

records.finding: The California Department of Fish and Wildlife commented on White Wolf's draft amended GSP, objecting to the finding of no interconnected surface water and no GDEs because it fears future groundwater development in the shallow aquifer above the Springs fault. The GSA plans to expand the GSP text rather than change the finding.
records.quantitative_detail: One comment letter received 2026-09-11, six days after the 60-day comment period closed on 2026-09-05.
records.speaker_role: consultant (EKI, relaying a state agency letter)
records.agenda_item: 2026 amended GSP and periodic evaluation
records.evidence_text: They it was mostly in regards to the finding of no interconnected surface water and no groundwater dependent ecosystems because the shallow alluvial aquifer is separated from the principle principal aquifer. ... they there may be future groundwater development in that shallow aquifer upgradient of the springs fault. And so you know, we took this to mean that we really need to bolster the GSP on the sections pertaining to the that shallow alluvial aquifer area.
records.notes: Letter was not read verbatim; the response is the GSA's proposal, not an adopted change; dates are from the consultant's remarks.

records.finding: White Wolf's ISW network is three shallow representative monitoring wells upgradient of the Springs fault plus an El Paso Creek stream flow meter. For the five-year update the GSA also commissioned a late-October 2025 field biological survey and a satellite remote-sensing (Nature Conservancy metrics) analysis of GDE health.
records.quantitative_detail: Wells about 50 ft deep; El Paso Creek October base flow about 0.5 cfs; all wells above measurable objective (measured 2025).
records.agenda_item: GSP implementation update
records.evidence_text: the interconnected surface water network, these are the shallow representative monitoring wells to the south of the springs fall. They're only 50ft deep, but we are using them to gather more information on the potential groundwater dependent ecosystems which are shown in green. ... And currently the October base flow is around 0.5 cfs. So we do continue to have flow in that creek. And in general, if you look at the, these charts are showing depth to water here, but all wells are above where we had set the measurable objective ... There was a field biological survey conducted in late October of this year where we had a biologist go out and visually inspect and document the various vegetation species, very similar to what was conducted in 2020. So they visited the same locations, use the same metrics to document surface water presence, soil moisture and vegetation. And then on top of that field study, they're conducting a desktop remote sensing analysis on GDE Health. There's some different satellite metrics that are produced by the Nature Conservancy that are used to support that.
records.notes: Speaker identified as Christina Lucero of EKI from the transcript labels.

records.section: 1.5 Per-well Attribution and the Cumulative Pumping Problem
records.finding: White Wolf's response to Fish and Wildlife points to the Tejon Ranch Conservation Area, which covers the shallow alluvial aquifer above the Springs fault, where a land use agreement bars any expansion of groundwater extraction. This is a spatial protection set outside the GSA's own SMCs.
records.agenda_item: 2026 amended GSP and periodic evaluation
records.evidence_text: It is fully contained within the Tejon Ranch Conservation Area which it is protected under the land use agreement which specifically states there cannot be an expansion of groundwater extraction practices in that area.
records.notes: The land use agreement is described by the consultant, who has not cited its text; it is not a GSA rule.

records.finding: White Wolf's consultant told the board that perched groundwater conditions south of the Springs fault are separate from the GDEs in the principal aquifer where the main irrigation pumping occurs. She noted the GSP defines only one principal aquifer, so the treatment of this shallow zone needs checking for consistency.
records.agenda_item: GDE survey and SMC update
records.evidence_text: And so we are seeing this difference in the GDEs where the springs fall. And these perched grommeter conditions are really separate from the GDEs in the principal portion of the aquifer where the main irrigation pumping occurs. ... I will say that the way our GSP is defined is that there is only one principal aquifer. So we don't have these separate, you know, we don't have this perched groundwater aquifer as its own. So I think we need to look at how the principal aquifer is defined and how GDEs and interconnected surface waters are defined to make sure that we are being internally consistent with how we are establishing SMCs and protecting, you know, all beneficial users.
records.notes: Related to ISW-1.6b below.

records.finding: Asked how to treat the shallow upland GDEs, the consultant offered options: define the shallow system as separate from the principal aquifer, or make it a management area that is effectively unmanaged, and either formalize the preliminary criteria or justify not needing them. A technical committee call with DWR was proposed.
records.agenda_item: GDE survey and SMC update
records.evidence_text: I think the question comes in is, you know, how we want to maybe define the principal aquifer. Do we want to call this area separate? Do we want to completely separate it from the principal aquifer itself as a shallow system? The other option is we could set up management areas with this being its own management area that is effectively unmanaged. ... whether we formalize those preliminary SMC or we justify that we don't need SMCs to protect the GDEs because they are not being influenced by managed conditions.
records.notes: Options under discussion, not a decision; the 2026-06-02 meeting records DWR feedback and the proposed outcome (supplemental monitoring wells).

records.finding: White Wolf's consultant said the GSP's interconnected surface water criteria were set as preliminary because the data were too thin. Earlier meetings repeat that the three shallow wells had only just been installed, so the thresholds had to be reassessed after four to five years of data.
records.quantitative_detail: Preliminary ISW criteria adopted in the 2021/2022 GSP; reassessment after roughly 4 to 5 years of data.
records.agenda_item: GSP implementation update
records.evidence_text: The interconnected surface water sustainable management criteria were set as preliminary since we did not have enough data to support and so this data will be used to formalize those.
records.notes: The transcript says the GSP was 'adopted back in 2021'; other meetings say 2022 GSP; the same passage supports ISW-1.8a (preliminary label).

records.finding: To close the ISW data gap, White Wolf is documenting the 2025 GDE field survey and remote-sensing results in an appendix to the five-year GSP update and using them to formalize the preliminary ISW criteria. No separate funding line for this work is given.
records.quantitative_detail: Field survey late October 2025; results to go in an appendix to the five-year GSP update; no cost stated.
records.agenda_item: GSP implementation update
records.evidence_text: These results will be documented in an appendix to the five year update to the GSP and will also be used to support the interconnected surface water sustainability indicator as part of the GSP that was adopted back in 2021. The interconnected surface water sustainable management criteria were set as preliminary since we did not have enough data to support and so this data will be used to formalize those.
records.notes: Funding for the GDE survey not stated in this passage.

records.finding: At the 2026 amended-GSP stage, White Wolf's consultant reminded the board that DWR's final ISW guidance had still not been released, so the no-ISW determination rests on guidance published to date. DWR reviewers verbally urged the GSA to make that determination consistently in the document.
records.quantitative_detail: DWR final ISW guidance not released as of 2026-10-06; GSP amendment out for 60-day public comment (closed September 2026).
records.agenda_item: 2026 amended GSP and periodic evaluation
records.evidence_text: DWR's final guidance on interconnected surface waters has not yet been released. And so you know, based on our current understanding, we have done the modeling that has shown that it's not interconnected surface water consistent with the guidance that has been released to date. When we met with DWR review team, they verbally indicated that the GSP, the 2022 GSP had conflicting information and highly recommended that the GSA makes the determination of no interconnected surface water consistent in the document.
records.notes: DWR's view is relayed by the consultant, not stated by DWR.

records.finding: White Wolf's consultant stated that no management actions will be triggered by changing conditions in the upland area once ISW criteria are dropped, though the GSA will keep monitoring. A district director said the data will remain useful for future five-year reviews.
records.agenda_item: Periodic evaluation / SMC revisions
records.evidence_text: So the GSA will still commit to monitoring these areas. However, there's not going to be any management actions triggered with the, with the changing conditions in these uplands portions of the basin and DWR was favorable of this
records.notes: An explicit statement that no action follows ISW conditions, resulting from the no-ISW determination rather than an omission.

records.finding: White Wolf's amended GSP moves management actions on metering, pumping limits, allocations and water markets from the individual districts to the subbasin GSA, because water districts lack authority to lead them. They are to be initiated 'if and when the time comes'; no change to their content.
records.agenda_item: Public review draft: periodic evaluation and amended GSP
records.evidence_text: it consolidates a lot of the management actions that were related to metering, pumping limitations, allocations, water markets. All of those, those were currently identified by each district. However, those are technically not within the authority of a water storage district or a water district to lead. And so we've consolidated those into just sub basin GSA led management actions that would be initiated if and when the time comes.
records.notes: Presenter is the GSA consultant (EKI) summarising GSP redlines; a director adds that PMAs became district projects while management actions sit with the GSA. No water market design is described. Basin-wide rule; not specific to repurposed land.

records.finding: White Wolf's annual report tabulates each project and management action with its status and any observed quantified benefit. The list includes land retirement and conversion of fallowed land to solar, the groundwater service charge and Land IQ, but the presentation gives no quantified benefit for the land actions.
records.agenda_item: WY2025 annual report overview: projects and management actions
records.evidence_text: getting into some of the management actions which includes, you know, land retirement and conversion of crops being fallowed or changing to other land uses like solar draft allocation policy, the groundwater service charge, you know, using LandIQ etc.
records.notes: Annual report for water year 2025; earlier slide wording is 'if there was an observed quantified benefit from that'. Whether the land-retirement action has a figure is not stated.

records.section: 2.5 Data Source and ET Product Choice
records.finding: White Wolf GSA estimates basin pumping with a soil moisture budget model that combines land use (including fallow land and solar), Land IQ ET and district surface water deliveries, with pumping as the residual. Only a few wells have meters; the rest of the 30,600 AF is modelled.
records.quantitative_detail: About 30,600 AF estimated basin pumping, water year 2025, split between a few metered wells and the SMB model; 1 AF municipal and industrial
records.agenda_item: WY2025 annual report overview
records.evidence_text: we use a soil moisture budget accounting model or what we call the SMB. And what that does is it takes into account land use, evapotranspiration from land IQ and surface water deliveries to calculate what's the remaining demand on based on the crop type to estimate groundwater pumping as the residual.
records.notes: Presenter is Christina Lucero of EKI, the GSA's consultant. Land use map shows 'quite a few fallow lands' and 'pockets of solar' but no savings from either are quantified.

records.section: 2.5 Data Source and ET Product Choice
records.finding: At White Wolf's board, a member-agency manager raised replacing Land IQ ET with well meters, with a free ET product (OpenET) as a backstop for unreported pumping. He said OpenET had raised accuracy concerns in the Kern Subbasin, with no error size known, and noted pumping is now inferred as ET minus deliveries.
records.speaker_role: GSA staff — Wheeler Ridge-Maricopa WSD (member agency)
records.agenda_item: FY 2026-2027 budget; Land IQ and well metering discussion
records.evidence_text: Right now we determine groundwater pumping by taking et our deliveries. ... One of the free online is open ET and within the Kern sub basin there was some discussion there. It was generally, and I haven't done this review myself, there was some concern that the information that they provided was not, not accurate.
records.notes: Speaker is labelled Wheeler Ridge-Maricopa in the transcript and refers to his own district's board, so he is member-agency staff, not EKI; he says he has not done the OpenET review himself.

records.section: 2.5 Data Source and ET Product Choice
records.finding: White Wolf's technical committee recommended renewing Land IQ ET for three years because open-source ET products lacking ground truthing give larger ET and could overstate pumping, with vineyard timing off. A 6 percent first-year escalator drew objection; meters were called a long-term transition.
records.quantitative_detail: Proposed 3-year contract; 6% escalation year 1 then 3% in years 2 and 3; terms through 2029; priced by cropped vs non-cropped acreage
records.agenda_item: Land IQ contract
records.evidence_text: There are other ET products out there that are open source and less expensive. However, in our review of them they because they do not have ground truthing, they do typically have larger ET signatures which could result in additional pumping that we don't being calculated that we don't really think is occurring. And some of the timing, especially for vineyards we've noticed is off in those open source products compared to the ground truth ET data.
records.notes: Speaker is Christina Lucero (EKI). The AI recap says a motion carried but its terms were not stated, so the renewal decision is unconfirmed. Basin-wide rule; not specific to repurposed land.

records.finding: White Wolf's consultant said a public-noticed stakeholder workshop, remote and in person, was planned for April 30, 2026, as a forum for public input on methods to address DWR's corrective actions in the periodic evaluation; the grant commits the GSA to hold it.
records.quantitative_detail: 1 workshop, 1-2 hours (est.), planned 2026-04-30
records.agenda_item: Water Year 2025 Annual Report and periodic evaluation update
records.evidence_text: the technical committee is recommending the subbasin holds a stakeholder workshop on April 30th. And so I wanted to make sure that the board was aware that we are planning for that. There'll be public noticing for this workshop and it will be an informational meeting to and a forum for the public to provide input to the GSA on the methods that we're recommending to address those recommended corrective actions. ... it both ways, Wheeler Ridge-Maricopa Water Storage District: remote and in person.
records.notes: Speaker is Christina Lucero (EKI). Arvin-Edison, a White Wolf GSA member, announced the same April 30 workshop on 2026-03-10 as a two-hour event for community members. Attendance not reported.

records.finding: White Wolf monitors three constituents (arsenic, nitrate, selenium) at four representative wells, two of them former Tut Brothers wells, and reported all results below MCLs and minimum thresholds for WY2025.
records.quantitative_detail: 4 representative WQ wells; 3 constituents; all below MCL and MT, water year 2025
records.agenda_item: Water Year 2025 Annual Report review
records.evidence_text: There are four representative monitoring wells for water quality across the basin. These are the two of the TCWD backup wells and two of the TUT brother wells. As we've talked about in many of the prior meetings, all concentrations sampled in these wells for the three constituents, arsenic, nitrate and selenium were below both the MCL and the minimum threshold. So no undesirable results are occurring per the definition in the the gsp.
records.notes: Speaker is Christina Lucero (EKI).

records.finding: White Wolf's two designated domestic-well water-quality sites (former Tut Brothers wells, registered as domestic wells) are non-operational, so sampling would require the GSA to pay for a generator and pump. A director questioned paying to test a well no one uses; staff said few domestic wells are available for testing.
records.agenda_item: Item 8b: Tut Brothers wells
records.evidence_text: So we did meet with Ted Brothers. They have the domestic wells that we need to provide our report to DWR on domestic water quality. Currently, the wells are not in use and they were proposing that if we need to use these wells and take our sample, they don't want to spend the money to kick them on. They're actually not even repaired after the vandalism. So they're saying if we are willing, the GSA willing to pay costs for a generator and turn them on and grab the sample, they are okay with that. So it's now for bringing it to the board. We don't know what the cost is. Honestly, I don't. I haven't looked into it. We can, if you direct us to go and see how much it would cost to get this done, we can bring it back to the board and have you look at it. Please remind the board what the purpose of having these wells tested is for and to what benefit will it help our gsa? It's part of our compliance with DWR in our reporting. They have been part of our list of wells monitoring wells. So it's, it's something that we need to do. So why are we wanting to spend money or needing to spend money on a well that is not producing water to be tested for constituents that are supposed to. We're supposed to test water for the benefit of people and community or who they're supporting. But if it's not being used, why would we invest towards that? ... We don't have many options in the basin for domestic well water quality testing
records.notes: 'Ted Brothers' is the transcription of Tut Brothers; speakers are unlabelled.

records.finding: White Wolf priced a $4,700 pump rental to sample the idle former Tut Brothers wells, and instead proposed two public-supply wells that, with two others, would sit within three miles of about 80% of main-basin domestic wells.
records.quantitative_detail: ~$4,700 rental of gearhead and motor (excludes power); 4 proposed network wells cover about 80% of domestic wells in main portion of basin within 3 miles
records.agenda_item: Representative monitoring wells for water quality
records.evidence_text: There's two that require annual groundwater sampling for the GSP compliance and because of the owner change, the wells are currently non operational. The new well owner did include with the GSA if the GSA would cover cost to have a generator brought out and a temporary pump to enable sampling of those wells. So the GSA was able to get a quote from Bakersfield well and pump. That cost estimate for the rental of the gearhead and the motor is about $4,700. ... We did this general 3 mile radius around the wells to see how many domestic wells this may capture, to see what the water quality would be like in those shallower wells. And we can see that it covers about 80% of the domestic wells in the main portion of the basin.
records.notes: Speaker unlabelled; consultant role inferred (presentation). On 2026-10-06 staff recommended 'supplemental well 4' because its screen interval resembles domestic wells.

records.finding: White Wolf's consultant cross-checks its groundwater level results against the DWR online dry well reporting portal each year and reported no dry wells, using the state tool as a validation step.
records.quantitative_detail: 0 reported dry wells, water year 2025
records.agenda_item: Water Year 2025 Annual Report review
records.evidence_text: we say that undesirable results are not occurring. And we validate that by also checking the DWR online portal for dry well reporting. And there were no reported dry wells.
records.notes: Also answers COM-3.3.1b; the tool is DWR's dry well reporting portal as described by the speaker (Christina Lucero, EKI).

records.finding: Wyandotte Creek GSA staff told the board that its water year 2025 annual report shows no sign of interconnected surface water depletion and that the subbasin is on track for 2027 interim milestones. No ISW-specific threshold or method is described.
records.quantitative_detail: water year 2025; interim milestones for 2027
records.agenda_item: Water year 2025 annual report brochure
records.evidence_text: Interconnected surface waters or the depletion of surface water systems, we are currently not seeing any. Anything that we need to worry about.
records.notes: Brief remark; the basis for 'not seeing any' is not stated.

records.finding: Wyandotte Creek GSA has installed stream gauges and shallow monitoring wells along Wyman Ravine, Wyandotte Creek and North Honcut Creek to support recharge projects and improve understanding of interconnected surface water and groundwater-dependent ecosystems. The data will feed annual reports and the 2032 periodic evaluation.
records.quantitative_detail: data feeds annual reports and 2032 periodic evaluation
records.agenda_item: GSP amendment: sustainable management criteria
records.evidence_text: monitoring wells along Wyman Ravine, Wyandotte Creek and then North Honcut Creek. And that's to support project implementation. There's a few recharge projects that we've identified in the Palermo area. So these stream gauges will help that process. In addition, it will improve our understanding of interconnected surface waters and GDEs.
records.notes: Presenter is Ryan Fulton of Larry Walker Associates per transcript; grant source not stated in this passage.

records.finding: Before proposing a new regulatory fee, Wyandotte Creek GSA staff took the question to its Wyandotte Advisory Committee (WAC) and interviewed water and sewer districts and landowners, as the board had directed. Committee members from Cal Water, agriculture, environment and business attended.
records.agenda_item: Fee structure: stakeholder feedback
records.evidence_text: So since the end of August, we did did some research and we attended the WAC meeting. That's the advisory committee meeting on November 6. At that meeting, these representatives were at the meeting, sorry, Cal Water. We had two agriculture representatives, the environmental representative and the business association representative. So we had pretty good attendance from the WAC at that meeting
records.notes: Speaker is the fee-study consultant or program manager (unlabelled); whether the WAC's feedback changed the proposal is shown later in the item.

records.finding: Wyandotte Creek GSA's 10-seat advisory committee had a vacant tribal stakeholder seat, and the board noted it has no tribal representation; staff promised an update on tribal outreach.
records.quantitative_detail: advisory committee has 10 positions; 2 vacancies (agricultural user, filled this meeting; tribal, unfilled)
records.agenda_item: Consideration of appointments to the Wyandotte Creek GSA Advisory Committee
records.evidence_text: We have no tribal representation. No, we don't have any more tribal. But I can give you a little bit of an update on our tribal outreach connection or outreach at the program manager's report.
records.notes: Speakers unlabelled (board member and staff); vacancy count comes from staff just before the excerpt.

records.finding: Staff reported that Wyandotte Creek's advisory committee (WAC) preferred a 5% domestic-well risk level for the minimum threshold because it lowers mitigation costs, as the board weighed 5%, 10% and 15% options. The July 2026 meeting later describes the adopted threshold as based on protecting 5% of domestic wells.
records.quantitative_detail: 5%, 10% and 15% domestic-well risk options considered; WAC preferred 5%
records.agenda_item: Groundwater level minimum thresholds: domestic well risk
records.evidence_text: I did just want to note one thing and I think Becky had mentioned that at the wac, their work, just so you understand what their recommendation was, is they saw those numbers because it was kind of related to the mitigation program is they thought the 5. I think their preference was the 5% because then you could account for less in the mitigation plan. Just so you're aware, that was what the WAC had agreed upon is.
records.notes: Speaker unlabelled; outcome of the vote is inferred from the later meeting (2026-07-16) not this one.

records.finding: Wyandotte Creek's new regulatory fee charges agriculture and managed wetlands per cropped or managed acre, plus a domestic parcel charge. Unused acres within a parcel are not charged, which staff present as aligning cost with groundwater use.
records.quantitative_detail: example: 100-acre orchard with 90 cropped acres is charged for 90 acres; flat parcel fee $20.50, ag $15.58 per cropped or managed wetland acre (AI recap)
records.agenda_item: Public hearing: SGMA regulatory fee
records.evidence_text: So part two fees reflect groundwater use patterns. So there's the agriculture who pay for a fee per cropped acre. Then there is the managed wetlands. Again, that is also an acreage free fee. And then the domestic parcels. And I do want to, if you someone does have an orchard, they have 100 acres. If only 90 of those acres are cropped, that's what they're charged for. They're not going to get charged that fee for the 10 that are not being used.
records.notes: Dollar rates are from the AI recap, not this excerpt; public commenters at the hearing objected to ag costs.

records.section: 3.1.4 Domestic Well Protection as an Equity Outcome
records.finding: Wyandotte Creek's groundwater-level minimum threshold was set to protect domestic wells, using a 5% well-impact level or a 20 ft buffer below historical lows. The explanation was given in answer to a board question and is not disaggregated by community.
records.quantitative_detail: MT based on protecting 5% of domestic wells (per speaker) or 20 ft buffer below historical low
records.agenda_item: GSP amendment: sustainable management criteria
records.evidence_text: Wyandotte Creek selected the MT based on protecting 5% of the domestic wells or a 20 foot buffer below the historical load to provide some operational flexibility.
records.notes: Transcript phrase 'protecting 5% of the domestic wells' is ambiguous: it may mean 5% of wells impacted or 95% protected.

records.finding: Wyandotte Creek's consultant told the board that a mitigation programme for domestic wells that go dry is effectively required by DWR, and that the share of domestic wells at risk under the minimum threshold sets the programme's cost, which accrues over time to 2042 rather than all in year one.
records.quantitative_detail: consultant's example: 20% of domestic wells at risk accruing over the period to 2042; about $1 million mentioned as illustrative
records.agenda_item: Groundwater level minimum thresholds: domestic well risk
records.evidence_text: the reason why we look at the dollar amount for mitigation is because a mitigation program in case domestic wells go dry is kind of required by Department of Water Resources right now. Because the GSA can decide and say, I don't care, I'm fine with even 20% of the well, the domestic well, sorry, at risk of going dry. But no worries, we have a plan and we have the money. And again, it's not 20% on year one. This is something to keep in mind. It's 20% over up to 2042.
records.notes: Speaker unlabelled; consultant (LWA) inferred. DWR 'requirement' is the speaker's characterisation. The $1 million figure is illustrative.

records.section: 3.3.3 Domestic Wells and Community Water System Consolidation
records.finding: At Wyandotte Creek's board, Butte County drought-planning staff said only one domestic-well volunteer is in the community monitoring system and that the county is committed to improving its domestic well inventory using the Wyandotte and Vina inventories, with clusters of domestic wells identified in Palermo.
records.agenda_item: County Drought Resilience Plan update
records.evidence_text: Having a well, we have one volunteer in the community monitoring system with the GSAs. But observing the shallow groundwater monitoring network and seeing what's happening at the shallower levels where domestic wells tend to be talking about well destruction. It's really important obviously in educating people that when they replace a well that they need to abandon, properly abandon and destroy their existing well for water quality issues. And then just again, the county has committed to improving its domestic well inventory.
records.notes: Speaker is county water and resource conservation staff, unlabelled; Palermo clusters are mentioned slightly earlier.

records.finding: Minutes recorded in the July 2025 packet say DWR's GSP assessment included a corrective action asking Yucaipa to describe how it will evaluate the rate, timing and volume of ISW depletion and to support specific sustainable management criteria for it. No method or criterion is given; responses are due to DWR by January 2027.
records.quantitative_detail: Response due January 2027
records.meeting_body: Yucaipa Sustainable Groundwater Management Agency Board (packet contains minutes of an earlier meeting)
records.agenda_item: Packet: minutes of a prior meeting, DWR corrective actions overview
records.evidence_text:
Corrective Action No. 9 – Address the approaches to evaluate the rate, timing

and volume of depletions of interconnected surface water and support for

establishing specific sustainable management criteria for depletions of

interconnected surface water.

Responses need to be submitted to DWR by January 2027.
records.notes: The excerpt is minutes of an earlier, undated-in-excerpt meeting reproduced in the 2025-07-23 packet; corrective action 7 in the same minutes also lists interconnected surface water for the San Timoteo management area.

records.finding: In the San Timoteo management area (two agricultural wells, no municipal users) the Yucaipa GSP uses depth to water at well points near groundwater-dependent ecosystems in the San Timoteo Creek corridor as its criterion: a 20-foot level triggers investigation of GDE stress and 30 feet is the minimum threshold. This is a groundwater-level proxy, not a depletion rate.
records.quantitative_detail: 20 ft depth to water = investigation level; 30 ft depth to water = minimum threshold; levels reported as hovering near it 'about three times' since 2010 (wording unclear)
records.meeting_body: Yucaipa Sustainable Groundwater Management Agency Board
records.agenda_item: GSP implementation update: groundwater conditions, water year 2025
records.evidence_text: what we established here in terms of sustainability criteria is we're taking a look at. The water table, elevation, or depth of water at some well points where we have identified some groundwater ecosystems. These wells are located, you know, in the Santa Mateo Creek corridor. We're looking at is. So what? This is depth to water, so these two well points are kind of been averaging. You're seeing some influences from from rainfall, but they've been above this 20 foot threshold that we've established as if water levels would fall to some point. We start investigation looking at whether or not these GDS will start to, you know, expressing some stress because of this water, low water levels and then our 30 foot. Depth here represents our minimum threshold. Results at that point, most of your riparian habitat will start exhibiting stress and conditions like that
records.notes: Transcript has no speaker labels; role inferred as the GSP implementation consultant (minutes name Steve Stuart) presenting results; 'Santa Mateo' in the text is San Timoteo Creek by context.

records.finding: Yucaipa's consultant reported that stream-gauge funding for the basin came through flood control and the City of Beaumont (not the GSA) and that the new gauges must give real-time 15-minute data. Staff noted the flood-control gauges were built for peak flows, and that no gauge covers Yucaipa Creek outflow into San Timoteo Creek.
records.quantitative_detail: 15-minute real-time data requirement; gauges to be operable by October 2026 (stated as 'by 2026'); operating funding for about five years then 100% local agencies
records.meeting_body: Yucaipa Sustainable Groundwater Management Agency Board
records.agenda_item: Update on stream gauging stations
records.evidence_text: The requirements for that program are, you know, to provide real time data at a 15 minute frequency. This is all available through. The telemetry and then to have these gauging stations operable by October 1st. ... Those stations were designed for peak flows. So you know, per personal communication with them, you know they said I wouldn't rely on any of the data we get from particularly for normal flows or even dry flows. ... there's funding for them to operate. I think for five years after that, then after that, then 100% of the funding comes from these agencies.
records.notes: The funding programme is transcribed as 'county seat program' (probably DWR's stream gauge programme); speakers unlabelled and the gap near the basin outlet is raised by the consultant.

records.section: 3.3.3 Domestic Wells and Community Water System Consolidation

He plans to contact well owners the GSA has details for over the next year to collect information on their wells and how they operate them, and a domestic well advisory group has been discussed but not formed.

records.meeting_body: Yucaipa Sustainable Groundwater Management Agency Board
records.agenda_item: Private well owner outreach

It talks about in the PE, the periodic evaluation coming up to develop a private well inventory. ... So over the next year as we start working on this document, I'll start reaching out to the folks that we have contact information for. Just start putting you know a list to. Or contact information who they are and specifically asking for information about their wells, how they operate them, you know, get them engaged, be a part of it.
records.notes: Unlabelled speaker taken as the GSP consultant; wording 'we did talk about forming a domestic well advisory group' does not say it was formed.

records.section: 3.3.3 Domestic Wells and Community Water System Consolidation
records.finding: At a Yucaipa GSA workshop a speaker said that in a year and a half the GSA has talked repeatedly about tracking private well use without doing it, and that well-owner friends say nobody has asked them; another speaker said outreach had been tried. Total private use was put at around 600 AF or less.
records.quantitative_detail: About 600 acre feet total private use, period and basis not stated; 25 AF per year participation threshold discussed

Well they don't want to participate. We can't make. Well I, I know several of them. Several of them are my friends. I talk to them all the time. Hey, have you been contacted? Are you interested in this? Has anybody asked? No, I don't know anything about it. Well, just interested in how much water you use. Nobody ever asked me.

records.finding: DWR's planned SGMA portal upgrades will collect sustainable management criteria for more indicators, but staff said ISW (and water quality) criteria likely will not be included at first, so ISW thresholds would stay outside the state's structured data.
records.agenda_item: DWR portal updates: GSP reporting system and annual reports
records.evidence_text: But we expect to develop the ability to start to collect the other sustainable management criteria, likely for land subsidence, change in storage and seawater intrusion, potentially the other two, water quality and interconnected surface waters, but those likely aren't expected.
records.notes: Statewide item; plans were described as early and not finalized; release possibly Q3/Q4 2026 or later.

records.section: 1.5 Per-well Attribution and the Cumulative Pumping Problem
records.finding: Metropolitan staff described a proposed amendment to the Yuba Accord transfer agreement under which the Yuba seller would be responsible for streamflow depletion losses from the groundwater-substitution supplies; the existing agreement ignored them. No method or volume was given.

records.agenda_item: Yuba Accord / DWR transfer agreement amendment (information)

records.finding: DWR said Prop 4 technical assistance is expected to support identifying groundwater-dependent ecosystems, and called GDEs and ISW connected but distinct. The program is about $386 million, with draft guidelines expected in fall 2026.
records.quantitative_detail: About $386.25 million Prop 4 groundwater funding; draft guidelines expected fall 2026 (AI summary)
records.agenda_item: Prop 4 sustainable groundwater management funding: Q&A

And then, obviously there is some connection there between ISW or interjective surface water and so but, but they are distinctively different things.
records.notes: Statewide item; only GDE identification is promised as support, not ISW monitoring itself; the $386.25M figure and fall-2026 timing come from the AI summary, not the quoted passage.

records.finding: DWR told the Fall 2025 GSA Forum its ISW depletion guidance would be a guidance document, would aim to turn the earlier scientific papers into practical expectations, and was targeted for the end of 2025 or Q1 2026, with outreach to local agencies afterwards. DWR called the measurement methodology not well established and complicated.
records.quantitative_detail: Target: end of 2025, possibly Q1 2026 (not met as of 2026-04-30)
records.agenda_item: DWR program updates: depletion of ISW guidance document
records.evidence_text: Another important indicator, depletion of interconnected surface water. And this is going to be a guidance document. ... But the methodology on measuring it, managing it, was not really well established. It was taking some time to get this together. It's fairly complicated. So we are looking to get this done again by the end of the year. ... So again, probably by the end of the year, maybe the first quarter 2026
records.notes: Statewide item. In the same talk DWR said best management practice documents sit above guidance documents and can lead to regulation, said while describing the subsidence BMP. Same expectation voiced at the 2025-10-17 DRIP meeting by a participant. Later meetings show the release slipped (see the 2026-04-30 row).

records.finding: At a DWR Prop 4 workshop, staff said they have no specific release date for the ISW guidance, are targeting later in 2026, and have it in executive review. It will be released for public comment first. The earlier end-of-2025 target had slipped.
records.quantitative_detail: Release target: later in 2026, with public comment period
records.agenda_item: Prop 4 sustainable groundwater management funding: Q&A
records.evidence_text: when do we anticipate releasing our interjective source water guidance document? We don't have a specific date. We're targeting a little bit later this year. We know this is of high importance, but and so we're trying to get this right. It's going through some executive reviews right now, and want to make sure that you know it's at a place where it needs to be before release it to the public. But what we do, it'll be out for public comment, so you'll be able to provide input at that point
records.notes: Statewide item; transcript renders 'interconnected surface water' as 'interjective source water'. The answer was given in response to an attendee question.

records.finding: A DWR staff update to the California Water Commission said DWR is prioritizing subsidence and, 'soon', interconnected surface water in its GSA outreach, and that for subsidence some GSAs may need to reassess minimum thresholds and sustainable yields; the same effect is plausible for ISW.
records.agenda_item: DWR groundwater update (SGMA work plan / groundwater trading)

records.notes: Statewide item; the reassessment remark is about subsidence, the extension to ISW is mine, not the speaker's.

records.finding: State Water Board staff described the statutory interim plan for probationary basins: it must set actions for long-term overdraft or for groundwater extraction that significantly depletes interconnected surface waters, with a schedule, monitoring and possible pumping limits.
records.meeting_body: California State Water Resources Control Board (SGMA hearing)
records.agenda_item: Probationary basins: interim plan development
records.evidence_text: the interim plan must identify the actions necessary to correct conditions of long term overdraft or conditions where groundwater extraction significantly deplete interconnected surface waters. The interim plan must include a time schedule for actions, which may include reporting requirements and potential pumping limits. They must describe monitoring to be undertaken to determine the effectiveness of the plan, and must be consistent with water rights priorities.
records.notes: Statewide description of the process, made in a hearing for probationary basins (Tule speakers present); no ISW-based action is cited for any specific subbasin.

records.finding: A Mission Springs Water District board packet (Sacramento legislative update) reports that the 2025-26 State Budget appropriated $32 million from Proposition 4 (Climate Bond) Chapter 2 for DWR's Multi-benefit Land Repurposing Program. $32 million available for the Multi-benefit Land Repurposing Program for

records.finding: At a Blueprint meeting a grower representative asked for a dollar amount for land retirement and repurposing in the plan, noting little funding trickles to white-area growers. And this is just the cost of infrastructure does not include the cost of land repurposing and the remaining gap is still not zero.

records.finding: DWR described the Prop 4 groundwater section as $386.25M, split between SGMA implementation projects and conjunctive use and recharge, with 40% to benefit disadvantaged communities. records.finding: The Blueprint's consultant described fallowing, land conversion and pumping restrictions as demand-management actions costing a couple of hundred dollars per AF. The consultant said how they combine to produce water is left to GSAs. No method for counting water savings from repurposing is given.

records.meeting_body: Water Blueprint for San Joaquin Valley Board
records.agenda_item: Unified Water Plan Chapter 5: water supply actions and demand management
records.evidence_text: I think there's a land fallowing is identified specifically in some of the GSPs, not all of them. And then land conversions, pumping, restriction and related tools and conservation. And there's some basic cost numbers on this. Again, each one of these items that we're identifying are coming in with costs that are in the couple $100 per acre foot range. What's not totally clear is how these need to combine to actually produce the water supply, or if some of them would be alternative ways of providing the same water supply, and that's hard to sort out, right? That gets sorted out at the GSA level. That's not something that can be sorted out at the unified water plan level, because that would require basically a even a deeper dive analysis and integrating all the projects within the GSPs, which is really beyond the intent of this document.
