records.finding: A dairy-industry advocate illustrated the repurposing math as an acreage x water-duty calculation. With about 1 AF/acre of native groundwater against 3-4 AF/acre crop consumption, only about 30 of 100 acres could be farmed in the southern Valley. It is an illustration, not an adopted method.
records.quantitative_detail: About 1 AF/acre native groundwater; 3-4 AF/acre crop consumption (annual); about 30 of 100 acres farmable
records.speaker_role: NGO/advocate — Milk Producers Council (Geoff Vanden Heuvel)
records.agenda_item: DWR Vision for the San Joaquin Valley: commissioner questions
records.evidence_text: So in the Southern, you know, really say Merced south, you know, a couple hundred miles, the southern 200 miles of San Joaquin Valley, the native amount of water available if your groundwater only is probably at most an acre foot per acre. So if you're farming almonds or any kind of a crop is going to take around 3 acre feet to 4 acre feet of consumption. And if you've got 100 acres, you need then say 350 acre feet of water to grow that crop. But you're going to get one acre foot per acre for your hundred acres. You're going to get 100 acre feet of water. So what does that mean? That means that you can only farm about, of your hundred acres, you can farm about 30 of it.
records.notes: Speaker introduced by the commission as Director of Regulatory and Economic Affairs at the Milk Producers Council (also active in the Water Blueprint); the 350 AF in the quote is the speaker's rounding of 3-4 AF x 100 acres. Rule of thumb for the southern Valley, not any one GSA.

records.finding: A Blueprint participant proposed planning for ecosystem uses of land that will be retired anyway, estimating at least one million acres will come out of production. The consultant agreed and said Department of Conservation funding of retirement had gone well. Habitat and water supply benefits are discussed, not measured.
records.quantitative_detail: 'At least a million acres' expected to come out of production (speaker's figure, no date)
records.meeting_body: Water Blueprint for San Joaquin Valley Board
records.agenda_item: Unified Water Plan Chapters 4 and 5 review
records.evidence_text: the opportunity for ecosystem enhancements, the way I imagine they need to come forward, is taking a look at what would naturally happen in terms of land retirement, absent any sort of specific environmental initiative, and then try and understand what, what kind of funding would be needed to change the lands that are retired for ecosystem benefits. Or, as far as I understand, we're, we're looking at at least a million acres of land that is probably going to have to come out of production. ... some of the funding for this, we've seen the Department of Conservation provide some funding. And I think you know where that has happened. It's been those decisions for for retiring land have been very good to date.
records.notes: First speaker introduced himself as Jeff Payne (role in Blueprint not stated); second excerpt is the plan consultant, name not captured. 'At least a million acres' is the speaker's figure and differs from other estimates quoted at the Blueprint and Commission.

records.finding: A consultant on the Blueprint's Unified Water Plan said random, scattered retirement of parcels harbours pests and creates dust, so the plan prioritizes which lands come out of production to limit harm to remaining farmers.
records.meeting_body: Water Blueprint for San Joaquin Valley Board
records.agenda_item: Unified Water Plan Chapters 4 and 5 review
records.evidence_text: We, we don't want a lot of land just individual squares coming out in a sort of a random pattern throughout the valley, right? It's not good for the existing land owners because it harbors pest and it creates dust and all sorts of problems. So the idea here was to put together a plan where we've got, you know, where we prioritize the lands that are going to come out of production. So this land does have to come out of production, it achieves sort of as many of the benefits as possible, so that, you know, we're minimizing the impact on people that are still farming. We're maximizing the environmental benefits.
records.notes: Speaker not named in the transcript (answering questions as the plan consultant). Raised as a planning rationale; no dust measurement or control standard mentioned. San Joaquin Valley-wide.

records.finding: In a report in Friant's board packet, the Water Blueprint said it supports DWR near-term strategies to raise groundwater recharge, naming MLRP, especially where subsidence is a problem. MLRP is treated here as a recharge and subsidence tool, not as a water-savings programme.

records.finding: DWR's draft Subsidence BMP lists demand reduction and land repurposing among pumping-reduction management actions for GSAs. It notes the community and industry impacts of fallowing. In the section quoted, no method for counting savings or co-benefits is given.

records.finding: A DWR deputy director told the Water Commission that the 2028 California Water Plan will cover demand management, including land repurposing and fallowing as SGMA takes effect in 2040. How it fits with SGMA work was still to be sorted out with the SGMA team. Statewide.

And we know with Sigma implementation coming in 2040, we're going to be seeing some of that in certain portions of the state. And so making sure that we are working with my colleague Paul Goslin and the SIGMO team to how this fits together, I think is another important conversation.
records.notes: Speaker not named in the passage (DWR planning lead presenting the Water Plan update). Same remarks on 2026-02-18 and 2026-06-17.

records.finding: DWR told local agencies that LandFlex was funded from the general fund, so not every LandFlex project can qualify for Prop 4 bond grants. Legal review is under way on which components can be added as eligible project types under a proposed 'ag land adaptation' priority. This is a statewide item.
records.quantitative_detail: No dollar figure given for LandFlex-type projects; Prop 4 groundwater section total is $386.25 million (see separate row)
records.meeting_body: California Department of Water Resources (DWR) Meeting
records.agenda_item: Prop 4 Sustainable Groundwater Management grant: proposed funding priorities
records.evidence_text: some of you are probably familiar with the land flex grant program the department conducted during the last drought and I funded a number of demand management activities, but that program was funded with general funds, and those have much greater flexibility in terms of what, what you know, activities can be funded that bond funds do. And so what this means is that we're not going to be able to make all of the projects that were funded by land flex eligible for the Sustainable Groundwater implementation grant program. But what we're doing right now is working with our legal to identify what components of land flex that we can fund with bond dollars, so we can add them as eligible project types to this grant program.
records.notes: Statewide funding design item (webinar for Prop 4 groundwater and watershed grants). Earlier in the webinar DWR also said local agencies had asked for LandFlex-type support.

records.finding: A speaker for DWR told the Water Commission that land repurposing is the likely result of SGMA because supply will not cover current agriculture, that locals will decide how it happens, and that state funding is far below the need. DWR is talking with the Department of Conservation about a strategy.
records.speaker_role: state agency — DWR (Joel Metzger, deputy director)
records.agenda_item: DWR Vision for the San Joaquin Valley: commissioner questions
records.evidence_text: When we talk about land repurposing as one of the things that may be a result of sgma, in fact, we said it likely would be, it's that we just don't see enough water when we look out into the future to SGMA implementation to support the agriculture that's currently in production across the San Joaquin Valley. And so exactly how that happens, I think the locals are going to be driving that. But we do want to provide technical assistance to them. We want to provide funding where possible, although we know that the funding needed is likely much more than what we have been able to provide. But we do want to try to create a glide path for communities that are facing a really, really difficult situation. And we know it's not just the farmer themselves, it's all of those associated folks who that farmer is relying on. And communities are definitely going to be really at risk due to what's coming. So that's the high level answer on that. I do, I will let you know that we are talking with Department of Conservation and others, other state agencies about how we can think about this in a strategic way and best support this transition as we move toward SGMA implementation.
records.notes: Answering speaker is DWR's Joel Metzger (the next speaker thanks 'Joel'; he introduced himself earlier as DWR deputy director); a commissioner asked the question. Statewide / San Joaquin Valley item.

records.finding: The facilitator of the San Joaquin Valley Water Collaborative Action Program cited LandFlex and MLRP as past programmes and said the Valley should start securing resources now to transition at least 500,000 acres (PPIC's lower estimate) to habitat, parks and solar. And I think it's, it's prudent to be prepared to do that so that we don't have empty fields that we can instead have habitats, parks and solar projects that are providing economic benefit for the valley.

records.finding: Friant's end-of-session legislative report listed AB 929, which would have barred a GSA from charging fees to a small community water system serving a disadvantaged community, as a bill that died in committee, under 'The Good'. It was a repeat of a bill the Governor vetoed.
